The solution must provide a service map showing inter-service call relationships and latency percentiles without requiring application code rewrites. Which observability approach meets these needs?
tags: Designing event-driven, microservice, and/or multi-tier architectures based on requirements

answers.A: Enable detailed CloudWatch Container Insights for the ECS cluster to collect per-task CPU, memory, and network metrics, then correlate high-latency tasks manually.
answers.B: Instrument each microservice with custom CloudWatch embedded metric format logs that include trace IDs and build a CloudWatch dashboard with latency widgets per service.
answers.C: Deploy a self-managed Jaeger cluster on ECS to collect distributed traces and build a custom service map UI for developers.
answers.D: Enable AWS X-Ray integration with the ECS task definitions using the X-Ray sidecar container and the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry to automatically capture traces and generate a service map with latency analysis.

explanation: D is correct because AWS X-Ray with a sidecar container and OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation captures distributed traces across ECS services, generating a service map with latency percentiles without rewriting application code. A provides infrastructure metrics but not distributed traces or service maps. B requires code changes to emit custom metrics and does not produce a service map. C requires deploying and managing a separate tracing infrastructure.

stem: A healthcare company runs a patient-data processing platform on Amazon EKS. Their compliance team mandates that no two patients' workloads share the same underlying compute instance. The cluster currently uses managed node groups with pod anti-affinity rules, but is consistently overprovisioned by 45% to guarantee per-patient node separation. Which EKS compute strategy provides hardware-level pod isolation while eliminating the overprovisioning waste?
tags: AWS compute services with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS Batch, Amazon EMR, AWS Fargate)

answers.A: Migrate all workloads to AWS Fargate profiles scoped to individual patient namespaces, where each pod runs in its own isolated microVM, eliminating shared-node scheduling entirely.
answers.B: Switch to self-managed node groups with EC2 Dedicated Instances and keep the existing pod anti-affinity rules to ensure each patient's pods land on exclusively owned hardware.
answers.C: Enable EKS managed node groups with per-patient node taints and corresponding tolerations in pod specs, combined with OPA Gatekeeper policies to block cross-patient scheduling.
answers.D: Deploy a dedicated EKS cluster per patient group, routing requests through a shared API Gateway, while maintaining separate managed node groups in each cluster.

explanation: A is correct because AWS Fargate for EKS runs each pod in its own isolated microVM by design, providing hardware-level isolation without the need to overprovision nodes. B introduces Dedicated Instances but still relies on pod anti-affinity to prevent co-scheduling; if anti-affinity is misconfigured, two patient pods can land on the same dedicated node, and overprovisioning persists. C uses taints and OPA Gatekeeper, which are scheduling controls, not hardware isolation — two pods can still run on the same physical node if scheduling rules are met, and overprovisioning is unchanged. D introduces separate clusters per patient group, which significantly increases operational complexity and control-plane costs without addressing the overprovisioning problem.

stem: An e-commerce company runs a product recommendation API on Amazon EKS with three replicas. Traffic spikes up to 40× normal volume within 4 minutes during flash sales. New EC2 nodes in the managed node group take 4-5 minutes to become schedulable, but the company needs new recommendation pods to be available within 90 seconds of a traffic spike without changing the node instance type. Which approach meets this requirement?
tags: Identifying metrics and conditions to perform scaling actions
Determining scaling strategies for components used in an architecture design

answers.A: Deploy Karpenter with a NodePool targeting the same instance type and set the consolidation policy to WhenUnderutilized, relying on Karpenter to provision nodes when HPA creates pending pods.
answers.B: Pre-deploy a low-priority overprovisioning Deployment of pause pods that consume available node capacity, allowing HPA-triggered recommendation pods to immediately preempt pause pods and schedule within seconds.
answers.C: Configure the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler with a stabilization window of 0 seconds and use an EventBridge Scheduler to increase minimum replicas to peak count 10 minutes before each flash sale.
answers.D: Migrate the recommendation service to AWS Lambda using a container image with provisioned concurrency, connecting it behind API Gateway to bypass Kubernetes node provisioning entirely.

explanation: B is correct because pause pods (low-priority placeholder pods) pre-warm node capacity. When HPA scales up recommendation pods, they preempt the pause pods and schedule immediately on already-running nodes — well within 90 seconds and without changing the node type. A (Karpenter) is faster than Cluster Autoscaler at provisioning nodes but still requires 1.5-3 minutes for EC2 initialization, exceeding the 90-second constraint. C requires knowing the flash sale schedule in advance and pre-scaling manually; the question describes unexpected traffic spikes that must be handled dynamically. D migrates to Lambda, which changes the deployment architecture and violates the 'without changing node type' constraint.

stem: A retail company is containerizing a legacy .NET order-management application and deploying it on Amazon EKS. The application currently stores HTTP session data in process memory, connects to a self-managed PostgreSQL database, and must support zero-downtime deployments with the ability to roll back traffic within one minute if errors spike. Which deployment architecture satisfies all three requirements?
tags: How to migrate applications into containers
Designing event-driven, microservice, and/or multi-tier architectures based on requirements

answers.A: Containerize the application retaining in-process session state, deploy on EKS as a Deployment with a rolling update strategy and minSurge=25%, and migrate PostgreSQL to Amazon RDS.
answers.B: Decompose the application into separate microservices before containerizing, deploy each on EKS with independent rolling updates, and migrate the database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL.
answers.C: Containerize the application, externalize session state to Amazon ElastiCache for Redis, deploy on EKS with weighted traffic shifting across blue and green ALB target groups, and migrate to Amazon RDS PostgreSQL.
answers.D: Deploy the containerized application as a StatefulSet on EKS with EBS volumes per replica for session persistence, use a rolling update strategy, and keep PostgreSQL on self-managed EC2.

explanation: C is correct because externalizing session state to ElastiCache Redis makes pods stateless, enabling zero-downtime deployments without session loss. Weighted ALB routing between blue and green target groups allows instant rollback by shifting 100% of traffic back to the stable version in under a minute. A retains in-process session state; during a rolling update, requests may hit different pods that do not share session data, causing session loss. B adds the risk of a microservices decomposition on top of the containerization migration, increasing complexity and delivery time without being required by the stated constraints. D uses EBS volumes per replica for session state; EBS is block storage scoped to a single pod and does not solve the session-sharing problem across replicas, and the self-managed PostgreSQL on EC2 adds operational burden.

stem: A fintech company processes regulatory compliance reports by reading input files from Amazon S3, enriching the data with a 2 GB reference dataset loaded from Amazon RDS into memory, and writing structured output back to S3. Each job takes 5-25 minutes depending on input size, and the reference dataset must remain resident in memory between consecutive jobs to avoid repeated 3-4 minute database cold-load delays. Jobs are triggered by S3 file uploads averaging 400 per day at irregular intervals. Which architecture minimizes management overhead while keeping the reference dataset in memory across consecutive jobs?
tags: Determining when to use serverless technologies and patterns
Serverless technologies and patterns (for example, AWS Fargate, AWS Lambda)

answers.A: Configure S3 event notifications to invoke Lambda functions with 10 GB memory, load the reference dataset into the Lambda execution environment during initialization, and rely on warm invocations to retain it between calls.
answers.B: Route S3 event notifications to an Amazon SQS queue and run a persistent ECS Fargate task that loads the reference dataset at container startup and processes each queued job using the dataset held in memory.
answers.C: Trigger an AWS Glue ETL job for each S3 event via EventBridge, store the reference dataset in a Glue job bookmark so it is not reloaded on subsequent runs, and write output to Amazon S3.
answers.D: Use EventBridge to submit an AWS Batch job with Fargate launch type for each S3 event, with the container loading the reference dataset from Amazon ElastiCache at the start of each job run.

explanation: B is correct because a persistent ECS Fargate task loads the 2 GB reference dataset once at container startup and retains it in memory for all subsequent jobs processed from the SQS queue, eliminating repeated cold-load delays and requiring no EC2 management. A is incorrect because Lambda functions have a maximum duration of 15 minutes, which is less than the 25-minute maximum job runtime; warm invocation state retention is also unreliable under concurrent scaling. C is incorrect because Glue job bookmarks track which data has already been processed, not persist an in-memory reference dataset across job runs; every Glue job re-reads the reference data from its source. D is incorrect because AWS Batch creates a new container instance per job, so the reference dataset must be reloaded from ElastiCache on each job start, which still introduces a network round-trip and does not maintain the dataset in persistent memory.

stem: A healthcare platform ingests patient data via a FHIR REST API. Each request triggers a five-step processing pipeline: validate the payload, extract key fields, call a third-party anonymization service, transform to Parquet, and write to Amazon S3. The full pipeline completes in 2-8 seconds per request. Traffic averages 60 requests per minute with burst spikes to 600 per minute during hospital batch exports. The team wants a fully serverless architecture that minimizes per-invocation cost. Which design achieves this?
tags: Determining when to use serverless technologies and patterns
Serverless technologies and patterns (for example, AWS Fargate, AWS Lambda)
Designing event-driven, microservice, and/or multi-tier architectures based on requirements

answers.A: Accept requests via Amazon API Gateway, invoke a single Lambda function that executes all five pipeline steps sequentially, and write completed Parquet files to Amazon S3.
answers.B: Accept requests via API Gateway, orchestrate five separate Lambda functions using an AWS Step Functions Express Workflow with one state per pipeline step, and write output to Amazon S3.
answers.C: Accept requests via API Gateway, write payloads to an SQS queue, and process them with an ECS Fargate service that executes all five pipeline steps and auto-scales on queue depth.
answers.D: Accept requests via API Gateway, stream payloads into Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, process records with a Lambda consumer using bisect-on-error retry logic, and write Parquet to Amazon S3.

explanation: A is correct because a single Lambda function handling all five steps incurs only one invocation cost, handles the 2-8 second runtime comfortably within Lambda's 15-minute limit, and scales automatically with API Gateway without additional infrastructure. B orchestrates five Lambda functions via Step Functions Express Workflows, which charges per state transition; at 600 requests per minute with 5 states each, the state-transition cost is meaningfully higher than a single-function approach. C uses ECS Fargate, which adds container startup latency and requires managing auto-scaling policies for a workload that Lambda handles natively at lower cost for sub-10-second stateless operations. D introduces Kinesis Data Streams for a non-streaming request-response workload, adding per-shard-hour costs and latency without a performance benefit.

stem: A ride-sharing company needs to detect when a driver deviates from their assigned route by more than 500 meters. Drivers send GPS updates every 2 seconds; the platform currently tracks 30,000 active drivers simultaneously. Route assignments change every 15-30 minutes and must be retrievable with single-digit millisecond latency during detection. The team wants a fully managed, serverless solution that scales with driver growth without managing servers or clusters. Which architecture meets these requirements?
tags: Determining when to use serverless technologies and patterns
Designing event-driven, microservice, and/or multi-tier architectures based on requirements

answers.A: Ingest GPS updates via Amazon MSK topics, process records with an AWS Lambda consumer using MSK triggers, store route assignments in Amazon ElastiCache Redis, and publish deviation alerts to Amazon SNS.
answers.B: Write GPS updates to Amazon SQS FIFO queues with driver ID as the message group ID, trigger Lambda per message, read route assignments from Amazon S3, and send deviation alerts to Amazon SNS.
answers.C: Ingest GPS updates via Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, process records with a Lambda consumer, store route assignments in Amazon RDS with read replicas, and publish deviation alerts to Amazon SNS.
answers.D: Ingest GPS updates via Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, process records with a Lambda consumer that looks up route assignments from Amazon DynamoDB, and publish deviation alerts to Amazon SNS.

explanation: D is correct because Kinesis Data Streams is purpose-built for high-throughput real-time data ingestion at scale, Lambda consumers are serverless and scale automatically, and DynamoDB provides single-digit millisecond lookups for route assignments per driver ID — meeting all stated requirements with no servers to manage. A uses Amazon MSK, which requires provisioning and managing broker instances; MSK is not a fully serverless service and incurs minimum cluster costs regardless of traffic. B uses SQS FIFO queues, which have a throughput limit of 3,000 messages per second per queue even in high-throughput mode — insufficient for 30,000 drivers sending updates every 2 seconds (15,000 messages per second). C stores route assignments in Amazon RDS with read replicas; RDS read replica replication lag and connection overhead make sub-millisecond route lookups unreliable under high concurrency.

stem: A company is building a mobile application that lets users sign in with Google or Facebook credentials. After authentication, the app must allow users to upload files directly to their own private prefix in an Amazon S3 bucket and read items from an Amazon DynamoDB table scoped to their user ID. The company wants to use a fully managed AWS identity solution that avoids long-term credentials in the mobile app. Which solution meets all requirements?
tags: Security services with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS Cognito, AWS GuardDuty, AWS Macie)

answers.A: Create a Cognito user pool with Google and Facebook as identity providers, generate an ID token on sign-in, pass the token to a Lambda authorizer that issues scoped IAM credentials to the mobile app.
answers.B: Create a Cognito user pool for authentication with Google and Facebook as federated identity providers, connect an identity pool to the user pool, and assign an IAM role to authenticated users with resource-based conditions scoped to their Cognito sub.
answers.C: Use AWS IAM Identity Center to federate Google and Facebook logins, assign permission sets that allow S3 and DynamoDB access, and distribute IAM Identity Center access portal URLs to mobile users.
answers.D: Register each mobile user as an IAM user with a programmatic access key, store keys securely in AWS Secrets Manager, and retrieve them at runtime using the app's own service account.

explanation: B is correct because Cognito user pools handle social federation (Google, Facebook) and issue tokens; the identity pool exchanges those tokens for temporary IAM credentials scoped to the authenticated user's Cognito identity, enabling fine-grained S3 and DynamoDB access using policy conditions on cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub — all without long-term credentials in the app. A uses a Lambda authorizer as an intermediary; this is a custom implementation that duplicates what identity pools do natively and adds operational complexity. C uses IAM Identity Center, which is designed for workforce (employee) SSO, not consumer mobile apps with social logins; it does not support Google or Facebook as identity providers. D creates one IAM user per mobile user, which violates AWS best practices, does not scale, and requires distributing long-term credentials — the opposite of the requirement.

stem: A SaaS company operates a multi-tenant analytics platform. Each tenant's users must only access data stored in the tenant's own Amazon S3 prefix and DynamoDB partition. The application already uses Amazon Cognito user pools for authentication, and tenants are defined as custom user groups. Access must be enforced at the AWS API level, not solely in application code. Which configuration achieves per-tenant isolation with the least operational overhead?
tags: Security services with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS Cognito, AWS GuardDuty, AWS Macie)
Designing a flexible authorization model that includes IAM users, groups, roles, and policies

answers.A: Add a custom claim containing the tenant ID to each user's ID token in a Cognito pre-token generation Lambda trigger, and validate that claim in the application's middleware before serving S3 and DynamoDB requests.
answers.B: Create a separate Cognito user pool per tenant, configure a dedicated identity pool for each user pool, assign unique IAM roles per tenant, and update client applications to use the correct pool endpoint per tenant.
answers.C: Configure a Cognito identity pool with role-based access control mapping each Cognito group to a separate IAM role, where each role's policy uses condition keys on the Cognito group claim to restrict S3 prefixes and DynamoDB partition keys.
answers.D: Deploy a Lambda authorizer on the API Gateway layer that decodes the Cognito JWT, extracts the group claim, and injects tenant-scoped S3 and DynamoDB policies into the IAM session using AWS STS AssumeRole before forwarding the request.

explanation: C is correct because identity pool role-based access control maps Cognito groups to IAM roles at the AWS level; the resulting temporary credentials carry an IAM policy with conditions on the tenant's group claim, enforcing isolation in S3 and DynamoDB without application-code checks and without creating separate pools per tenant. A adds the tenant claim to the ID token and validates it in application middleware, but this enforcement is in application code — not at the AWS API level as required. B creates a separate user pool and identity pool per tenant, which multiplies operational overhead as the number of tenants grows and requires client-side logic to route to the correct pool. D uses a Lambda authorizer to call AWS STS AssumeRole at request time, adding latency on every API call and requiring custom code to maintain what identity pools provide natively.

stem: A financial services company is integrating its customer-facing web application with its enterprise identity provider (IdP), which supports SAML 2.0. End users must authenticate using their corporate credentials, and the application must receive a Cognito-issued access token to call downstream AWS services via API Gateway. The solution must not require maintaining user records in Cognito for enterprise employees. Which configuration satisfies these requirements?
tags: Security services with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS Cognito, AWS GuardDuty, AWS Macie)
AWS federated access and identity services (for example, IAM, AWS IAM Identity Center)

answers.A: Add the corporate SAML 2.0 IdP as an identity provider in the Cognito user pool, enable just-in-time user provisioning so user records are created automatically on first sign-in, and configure the app client to use the hosted UI with the SAML provider.
answers.B: Configure an AWS IAM SAML provider for the corporate IdP, use AWS STS AssumeRoleWithSAML to generate temporary IAM credentials after the enterprise login, and exchange those credentials for a Cognito identity pool token.
answers.C: Create Cognito user pool accounts for all enterprise employees by importing them from the IdP's user directory, configure the app client password authentication, and redirect users to the Cognito hosted UI.
answers.D: Deploy a custom OpenID Connect (OIDC) proxy service that translates SAML assertions to OIDC tokens, add the proxy as an OIDC identity provider in the Cognito user pool, and disable direct SAML integration.

explanation: A is correct because Cognito user pools support SAML 2.0 identity providers natively; just-in-time provisioning creates a shadow user record only on first sign-in, so pre-existing user records in Cognito are not required. Users authenticate against their corporate IdP, receive a SAML assertion, and Cognito issues its own JWT access tokens for API Gateway. B uses STS AssumeRoleWithSAML to generate IAM credentials, which are not Cognito-issued tokens; API Gateway Cognito authorizers require Cognito tokens, not raw IAM credentials. C pre-creates Cognito user pool accounts for all employees, directly violating the requirement to not maintain user records in Cognito, and replaces corporate password management with Cognito passwords. D builds a custom OIDC proxy to translate SAML assertions, adding engineering complexity that Cognito's native SAML provider support eliminates.

stem: A data engineering team runs Apache Spark jobs on Amazon EMR to process clickstream logs. They have two categories of jobs: nightly batch jobs that process 500 GB of data and run for 45-60 minutes on a predictable schedule, and ad-hoc analyst queries that run for 2-10 minutes on datasets ranging from 1 GB to 50 GB at unpredictable times throughout the day. The team wants to minimize total infrastructure cost while avoiding idle cluster charges. Which EMR deployment model best fits each job category?
tags: Selecting appropriate compute options for data processing (for example, Amazon EMR)

answers.A: Use EMR Serverless for both job categories, relying on automatic resource provisioning for nightly batches and pre-initialized workers to reduce cold-start latency for ad-hoc queries.
answers.B: Use a persistent EMR cluster with reserved EC2 core nodes for nightly batches; for ad-hoc queries, submit jobs to the same cluster to share already-running capacity.
answers.C: Use a scheduled, transient EMR cluster with Spot task nodes for the nightly batch, terminating the cluster after each run; use EMR Serverless for ad-hoc analyst queries to avoid provisioning delays.
answers.D: Use EMR Serverless for nightly batch jobs to avoid managing clusters; for ad-hoc queries, provision a long-running EMR cluster with auto-scaling enabled to handle variable analyst demand.

explanation: C is correct because a transient EMR cluster (started at schedule time, terminated after completion) with Spot task nodes minimizes cost for the predictable nightly batch by charging only for the 45-60 minute runtime. EMR Serverless handles ad-hoc queries without idle charges — resources are provisioned per job and released immediately after. A uses EMR Serverless for the nightly batch, which is valid but pre-initialized workers for ad-hoc queries incur a baseline cost even when no queries are running, increasing idle charges. B keeps a persistent cluster running 24/7 for both categories, paying for idle core nodes outside the nightly window and during gaps between analyst queries. D reverses the optimal assignment: EMR Serverless for the large predictable nightly batch adds provisioning overhead, while a persistent auto-scaling cluster for ad-hoc queries incurs continuous idle charges.

stem: A media analytics company processes video engagement data using Apache Spark jobs that depend on custom native C++ libraries compiled into the Spark executor environment. Jobs run on 10-50 TB datasets stored in Amazon S3, take 30-90 minutes to complete, and require fine-grained control over Spark configuration parameters such as spark.sql.shuffle.partitions and executor memory ratios. The team wants a managed AWS service to run these jobs without maintaining EC2 clusters. Which service best meets these requirements?
tags: Selecting appropriate compute options for data processing (for example, Amazon EMR)
Transforming data between formats (for example, .csv to .parquet)

answers.A: Use AWS Glue with a custom connector, package the native C++ libraries in a Glue job Python shell, and override Spark configuration using Glue job parameters for each run.
answers.B: Use Amazon Athena Spark notebooks to run PySpark code interactively on the S3 datasets, upload the C++ libraries as Athena session resources, and adjust Spark settings via notebook configuration cells.
answers.C: Use AWS Glue ETL jobs with the Glue Spark runtime, attach the C++ libraries as Glue job extra files, and tune Spark parameters through the Glue job configuration in the AWS Console.
answers.D: Use Amazon EMR Serverless with a custom Docker image that includes the native C++ libraries, submit Spark jobs via the EMR Serverless API with Spark configuration overrides in the job run request.

explanation: D is correct because EMR Serverless supports custom Docker images for the job runtime environment, allowing native C++ libraries to be pre-compiled into the image. It also supports arbitrary Spark configuration overrides in each job run request, providing the fine-grained control required, while AWS manages the underlying infrastructure. A and C both use AWS Glue, which uses a managed Spark runtime with a fixed set of supported libraries; Glue does not support arbitrary native shared libraries (.so files) or custom runtime Docker images, and Spark configuration tuning is limited to Glue-exposed parameters. B uses Amazon Athena Spark, which is an interactive notebook environment not designed for 30-90 minute production batch jobs on 10-50 TB datasets, and does not support custom native library injection in the executor environment.

stem: A machine learning team runs daily feature engineering pipelines using PySpark on 2 TB of raw event data. Each pipeline run takes 3-4 hours and requires high memory instances to avoid excessive disk spilling. The output is stored in Amazon S3 as Parquet files for downstream model training. The team has observed that Spot Instance interruptions on task nodes have caused several pipeline failures. Which EMR configuration minimizes cost while ensuring pipeline reliability?
tags: Selecting appropriate compute options for data processing (for example, Amazon EMR)
AWS purchasing options (for example, Spot Instances, Reserved Instances, Savings Plans)
Instance types, families, and sizes (for example, memory optimized, compute optimized, virtualization)

answers.A: Use On-Demand r6g memory-optimized instances for the EMR core node group to ensure task stability, and add a Spot-backed task node group for additional capacity; enable EMR graceful decommission for Spot task nodes.
answers.B: Run the entire EMR cluster on Spot Instances using r6g memory-optimized instances for all node types, and configure automatic retry of failed pipeline steps with a maximum of three retries.
answers.C: Use On-Demand c6i compute-optimized instances for all core nodes to maximize CPU throughput, and eliminate task nodes to avoid Spot interruptions entirely during the pipeline run.
answers.D: Switch to AWS Glue ETL jobs with the G.4X worker type for high-memory processing, eliminating the need to manage EMR clusters and Spot interruption handling.

explanation: A is correct because using On-Demand r6g (memory-optimized) instances for core nodes ensures that the HDFS data and active task state are protected from Spot interruptions, while Spot-backed task nodes provide cost savings for additional parallel processing capacity. EMR graceful decommission migrates in-flight tasks off task nodes before they are terminated, preventing job failures. B runs all nodes including core nodes on Spot Instances; Spot interruption of a core node causes HDFS data loss and pipeline failure, which retries cannot reliably recover. C uses compute-optimized instances for a memory-intensive workload, which worsens the disk spilling problem the team is already experiencing with their 2 TB dataset. D migrates to Glue with G.4X workers, which is a significant rewrite of the PySpark pipeline and Glue G.4X workers have fixed memory ratios that may not match the team's current Spark tuning.

stem: An e-commerce platform stores its product catalog in Amazon RDS MySQL. Product detail pages generate 8,000 read requests per second at peak, but product data changes only a few hundred times per hour via an internal management console. A solutions architect needs to add a caching layer to reduce RDS load. Cache entries must reflect updates within 30 seconds of a product record change. Which caching strategy meets these requirements?
tags: Caching strategies and services (for example, Amazon ElastiCache)
Integrating caching to meet business requirements

answers.A: Configure Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached as a lazy-loading cache in front of RDS; set a TTL of 30 seconds on all cached product entries so stale data expires automatically.
answers.B: Configure Amazon ElastiCache for Redis as a write-through cache; update the application to write product changes to both RDS and the Redis cache atomically, ensuring the cache always reflects the latest data.
answers.C: Enable Amazon RDS read replicas to distribute the 8,000 read requests per second across multiple replica endpoints, and configure the management console writes to target only the primary instance.
answers.D: Deploy Amazon CloudFront in front of the product detail API with a cache TTL of 30 seconds, using Cache-Control headers from the API to control stale content expiration.

explanation: B is correct because a write-through strategy with ElastiCache Redis updates the cache synchronously on every product write, so the cache always contains the latest data without waiting for TTL expiration. This immediately reduces the 8,000 read requests per second reaching RDS while guaranteeing freshness. A uses a lazy-loading cache with a 30-second TTL; although this technically meets the 30-second staleness budget, any cache miss still hits RDS, and with low TTLs the cache hit rate drops, reducing effectiveness. C uses RDS read replicas, which reduces per-replica load but still processes all 8,000 requests against the database tier; read replicas do not provide the order-of-magnitude latency improvement or RDS load reduction that an in-memory cache offers. D uses CloudFront, which caches HTTP responses at edge locations; this can reduce origin load but does not cache at the data tier level and introduces 30-second potential staleness for all users globally.

stem: A gaming application stores player leaderboard data in Amazon DynamoDB with player ID as the partition key. During tournament events, a small number of top-ranked players receive 50,000 read requests per second against their items, causing ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors despite the table being sized for average traffic. Writes to leaderboard items occur every 5-10 seconds per player. The application is latency-sensitive and needs sub-millisecond read responses. Which caching solution resolves the hot key read problem with the lowest application-code changes?
tags: Caching strategies and services (for example, Amazon ElastiCache)
Integrating caching to meet business requirements
Data access patterns (for example, read-intensive compared with write-intensive)

answers.A: Deploy Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) as an in-memory cache in front of DynamoDB; update application endpoints to use the DAX cluster endpoint, which is API-compatible with DynamoDB.
answers.B: Enable DynamoDB adaptive capacity to automatically redistribute read throughput toward hot partition keys, increasing the effective read capacity on frequently accessed items.
answers.C: Add Amazon ElastiCache for Redis in front of DynamoDB, implement a cache-aside pattern in the application layer, and set a TTL of 5 seconds to align with leaderboard write frequency.
answers.D: Switch the leaderboard table to DynamoDB on-demand capacity mode so that read throughput scales automatically to absorb the 50,000 requests per second without throttling.

explanation: A is correct because DAX is a fully managed, DynamoDB-compatible in-memory cache that intercepts GetItem and Query calls. Switching the application to the DAX endpoint requires minimal code changes (no cache logic needed), absorbs the hot key reads in microseconds, and returns sub-millisecond responses. B enables adaptive capacity, which shifts provisioned throughput toward hot partitions but does not add caching; it helps balance capacity but does not reduce the raw read load hitting DynamoDB, and throughput limits are still applied at the partition level. C uses ElastiCache Redis with a cache-aside pattern, which requires custom application code to check the cache, handle misses, populate the cache, and manage TTLs — significantly more code changes than switching to the DAX endpoint. D switches to on-demand capacity, which automatically scales but still processes every read request against DynamoDB at cost; on-demand mode does not provide caching or sub-millisecond responses.

stem: A retail company's order management API runs as a stateless service on Amazon EC2 behind an Application Load Balancer. User sessions contain authentication tokens and shopping cart state that currently require a database lookup on every request, adding 15-20 ms of latency. Sessions are created on login and expire after 60 minutes of inactivity. Traffic peaks at 20,000 concurrent sessions. The team wants to store session data in a distributed cache to eliminate per-request database reads. Which configuration is most appropriate?
tags: Caching strategies and services (for example, Amazon ElastiCache)
Integrating caching to meet business requirements

answers.A: Configure Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached with a multi-node cluster; store serialized session objects with a 3600-second TTL, using the session ID as the cache key across all API EC2 instances.
answers.B: Enable sticky sessions (session affinity) on the Application Load Balancer target group so that each user's requests always route to the same EC2 instance, keeping session state local to each server.
answers.C: Configure Amazon ElastiCache for Redis in cluster mode with Multi-AZ replication; store session data with a sliding TTL reset on each access, and use the session ID as the key across all API instances.
answers.D: Store session data in Amazon DynamoDB with a TTL attribute set to 60 minutes after last access; use DynamoDB's single-digit millisecond read latency to eliminate the existing database lookup overhead.

explanation: C is correct because ElastiCache for Redis in cluster mode provides a distributed, highly available session store accessible by all EC2 API instances with sub-millisecond latency. Redis supports sliding TTL by updating the key expiry on each access, correctly implementing inactivity-based expiration. Multi-AZ replication ensures session data survives a node failure. A uses ElastiCache for Memcached, which lacks native replication; a node failure causes session data loss for the affected node's keyspace, forcing re-authentication for active users. B uses ALB sticky sessions, which route requests to the same EC2 instance; if that instance is replaced during a scaling event or deployment, all sessions pinned to it are lost, and this approach scales poorly as each instance stores a different subset of sessions. D uses DynamoDB, which adds 5-10 ms read latency per request compared to sub-millisecond ElastiCache; it improves on the existing 15-20 ms but does not eliminate the database-tier read as efficiently as an in-memory cache.

stem: A SaaS company's core application uses a single Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster. Recent performance analysis shows that 90% of database calls are SELECT queries, while the remaining 10% are INSERT and UPDATE operations from a batch processing job that runs hourly. Peak concurrent read connections reach 800, causing connection wait timeouts on the Aurora writer instance. The application currently hard-codes the cluster writer endpoint. Which architecture change resolves the connection contention with the least application redesign?
tags: Data access patterns (for example, read-intensive compared with write-intensive)
Configuring read replicas to meet business requirements

answers.A: Add Aurora read replicas and update the application to explicitly route SELECT queries to a read replica endpoint and write operations to the writer endpoint, using application-level logic to distinguish query types.
answers.B: Enable Aurora Auto Scaling to add read replicas automatically when CPU utilization exceeds 70%, and configure the application to use the reader endpoint for all database connections.
answers.C: Migrate the application to use Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the Aurora writer, enabling connection pooling to reduce the impact of 800 concurrent connections on the writer instance.
answers.D: Deploy Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the Aurora cluster and configure the application to connect to the proxy endpoint; configure the proxy to pin SELECT-only connections to the Aurora reader endpoint.

explanation: D is correct because RDS Proxy multiplexes application connections into a smaller pool of database connections, resolving the connection wait timeouts with minimal application change (only the endpoint string changes). When configured with the Aurora reader endpoint for read-only connections, RDS Proxy routes SELECT traffic to reader instances while write traffic goes to the writer, distributing the load without requiring the application to implement routing logic. A adds read replicas and routes explicitly in the application, which requires code changes to classify and route every query — more redesign than switching a single connection string. B enables auto-scaling of replicas but still requires the application to connect to the reader endpoint; the hard-coded writer endpoint means all 800 connections still hit the writer until the application is updated. C deploys RDS Proxy in front of the writer only, which reduces writer connection overhead via pooling but does not offload the 90% read traffic to read replicas.

stem: An IoT platform ingests sensor readings from 500,000 devices that each write one record per minute, totaling approximately 8,300 writes per second. An analytics dashboard queries aggregated sensor data for specific device groups every hour, with read traffic peaking at 200 queries per second during business hours. The payload per record is 256 bytes. A solutions architect must select a DynamoDB capacity mode that minimizes cost while sustaining both workloads. Which configuration is most cost-effective?
tags: Data access patterns (for example, read-intensive compared with write-intensive)
Database capacity planning (for example, capacity units, instance types, Provisioned IOPS)

answers.A: Use DynamoDB provisioned capacity with 8,500 write capacity units and 800 read capacity units, enable auto-scaling with a 70% target utilization, and configure DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) for the analytics read layer.
answers.B: Use DynamoDB on-demand capacity mode to handle the variable write and read workloads without managing capacity, accepting the higher per-request pricing in exchange for eliminating capacity planning.
answers.C: Use DynamoDB provisioned capacity with 8,500 write capacity units and 800 read capacity units without auto-scaling, and configure a DynamoDB global table to distribute both write and read traffic across two Regions.
answers.D: Use DynamoDB on-demand capacity mode for writes to handle the 8,300 per-second ingestion without throttling, and create a separate DynamoDB table in provisioned mode for analytics query results populated by a Lambda function.

explanation: A is correct because the write workload is consistent at ~8,300 writes/second (steady IoT stream), making provisioned capacity significantly cheaper than on-demand mode for predictable, high-volume writes. Auto-scaling handles minor variance, and DAX absorbs the analytics read bursts at lower cost than additional RCUs. B uses on-demand mode; at 8,300 writes/second continuously, on-demand write pricing is approximately 2-3× more expensive than equivalent provisioned WCUs, making it cost-inefficient for a steady workload. C provisions the correct capacity but disables auto-scaling; without auto-scaling, any write spike above the provisioned limit will cause throttling, and global tables double write costs by replicating all 8,300 writes/second to a second Region unnecessarily. D splits the table into separate modes, adding a Lambda fan-out layer that introduces replication lag, additional Lambda costs, and operational complexity without a cost benefit over option A.

stem: A financial application uses Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL for transaction processing. The OLTP workload runs at 3,000 transactions per second during business hours. At the end of each trading day, the risk team runs complex analytical queries that perform full-table scans on 6 months of transaction history. These queries take 20-40 minutes and consume 90% of Aurora writer CPU, degrading OLTP transaction latency by 3×. The risk team requires query results within 45 minutes of market close. Which architecture isolates the analytical workload without duplicating the full dataset?
tags: Data access patterns (for example, read-intensive compared with write-intensive)
Configuring read replicas to meet business requirements

answers.A: Enable Aurora parallel query on the existing Aurora PostgreSQL cluster to offload analytical query processing to the storage layer, reducing CPU load on the writer and improving OLTP latency during analytics runs.
answers.B: Add a dedicated Aurora read replica for analytical queries; configure the risk team's query tool to connect to the replica endpoint and schedule end-of-day analytical queries exclusively against the replica.
answers.C: Export transaction history to Amazon S3 using AWS DMS at market close, run analytical queries using Amazon Athena against the S3 export, and load query results back to Aurora for the risk team's dashboard.
answers.D: Provision an Amazon Redshift cluster, use AWS Glue to replicate 6 months of transaction history from Aurora nightly, and redirect all analytical queries from the risk team to Redshift.

explanation: B is correct because a dedicated Aurora read replica receives a continuous stream of changes from the writer via Aurora's storage replication (typically lag under 10 ms), so the replica contains current data without a full dataset duplication in a separate service. Scheduling analytical queries against the replica completely isolates its CPU consumption from the OLTP writer, restoring normal transaction latency and meeting the 45-minute result window. A enables Aurora parallel query, which offloads scan processing to the distributed storage layer but does not eliminate CPU contention on the writer instance for query coordination and sorting; writer CPU degradation would persist. C exports to S3 at market close, but the export via DMS and subsequent Athena query on large datasets may not complete within the 45-minute window, and the export adds 10-20 minutes of preparation time. D uses Redshift with nightly Glue replication, which introduces 24-hour data lag (nightly sync means end-of-day analytics run on yesterday's data) and adds significant infrastructure cost.

stem: A data analytics team in Account B needs to read Amazon S3 objects that are encrypted using an AWS KMS customer-managed key stored in Account A. The objects are owned by Account A, and Account B must be able to decrypt them from an AWS Glue ETL job running in Account B. A solutions architect must grant the minimum necessary access. Which set of changes achieves cross-account decryption with the least privilege?
tags: Implementing access policies for encryption keys
Designing a role-based access control strategy (for example, AWS STS, role switching, cross-account access)

answers.A: In Account A, create a KMS key policy statement that allows kms:Decrypt to the root ARN of Account B; create an IAM policy in Account B that grants the Glue job role kms:Decrypt on the key ARN.
answers.B: In Account A, add Account B's Glue job IAM role ARN directly to the KMS key policy with kms:Decrypt permission; no IAM policy change is needed in Account B because the key policy grants access.
answers.C: In Account A, update the KMS key policy to allow kms:Decrypt to the specific Glue job IAM role ARN in Account B; in Account B, attach an IAM policy to the Glue role granting kms:Decrypt on the Account A key ARN.
answers.D: In Account A, create a KMS grant for the Account B Glue role with kms:Decrypt permission; in Account B, attach a broad kms:* IAM policy to the Glue role so that the grant can be utilized.

explanation: C is correct because cross-account KMS access requires two independent controls to both be satisfied: the KMS key policy in Account A must explicitly allow the specific consuming role in Account B (not just the account root), and the IAM policy in Account B must grant the specific key ARN — both conditions are needed for least privilege. A grants access to the entire Account B root ARN, which allows any IAM principal in Account B with the IAM policy to use the key — not the minimum necessary access scoped to the Glue role specifically. B adds the Glue role to the key policy; when the key policy explicitly names an external role, an IAM policy in Account B is still required for the principal to use the key cross-account — the key policy alone is insufficient without a corresponding IAM allow. D creates a KMS grant (valid for delegation) but then attaches a broad kms:* IAM policy, which violates least privilege by granting the Glue role unrestricted KMS permissions beyond the single key.

stem: A company uses a single AWS KMS customer-managed key to encrypt data written by three Lambda functions: an order-processing function, a payment-processing function, and an audit-logging function. The security team requires that each Lambda function can only perform the KMS operations necessary for its role: the order function needs Encrypt and Decrypt, the payment function needs GenerateDataKey and Decrypt, and the audit function needs only Decrypt. All three functions currently use the same IAM execution role with broad kms:* permissions. Which change enforces least privilege with the fewest KMS key policy statements?
tags: Implementing access policies for encryption keys
AWS security best practices (for example, the principle of least privilege)

answers.A: Create three separate KMS keys — one per Lambda function — each with a key policy granting only the operations that function requires, and update each Lambda's IAM role to reference its dedicated key ARN.
answers.B: Keep the single KMS key and single IAM role; add an SCP at the organization level that explicitly denies kms:Encrypt for the audit function and kms:GenerateDataKey for the order function.
answers.C: Keep the single KMS key; create three separate IAM execution roles each allowing only the required KMS actions for that function; update each Lambda function to use its dedicated role.
answers.D: Keep the single KMS key; create three separate IAM execution roles each allowing only the required KMS actions on the key ARN; update each Lambda function to use its dedicated role and remove kms:* from all roles.

explanation: D is correct because creating three IAM roles — each scoped to only the specific KMS actions required — enforces least privilege at the IAM layer without modifying the KMS key policy or creating additional keys. The single key policy remains unchanged (or grants broad access to the account), and IAM policies restrict each function to its required operations, satisfying the requirement with the fewest key policy modifications. A creates three separate KMS keys, which adds key management overhead and cost without being necessary; IAM role separation achieves the same isolation on a single key. B uses an SCP to deny operations, which applies at the account level rather than per-function; SCPs cannot distinguish between Lambda functions that share an execution role, and denying operations for one function would also deny them for all other principals in the account with that permission. C is functionally equivalent to D; both describe creating three IAM roles with scoped permissions. The difference is D explicitly removes the existing kms:* from all roles, which is required to enforce the restriction — without removing the broad permission, the three roles still carry kms:* and the new scoped permissions are redundant.

stem: A CloudOps engineer is tasked with enforcing a company policy that all EC2 instances in every AWS account within the organization must have detailed monitoring enabled. The solution must automatically detect non-compliant instances and trigger remediation without manual intervention, and must scale across 40 AWS accounts. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
tags: AWS Config rules and conformance packs
AWS Config rules and conformance packs for compliance
Using AWS Config remediation actions to correct non-compliant resources

answers.A: Create an AWS Config rule in each account using the ec2-instance-detailed-monitoring-enabled managed rule. Write a Lambda function that polls Config for non-compliant resources hourly and enables detailed monitoring using the AWS SDK. Deploy the Lambda function to all 40 accounts using CloudFormation StackSets.
answers.B: Deploy an AWS Config conformance pack across the organization using AWS Organizations integration, including the ec2-instance-detailed-monitoring-enabled managed rule with an automatic remediation action using the AWS-EnableEC2InstanceDetailedMonitoring SSM Automation document.
answers.C: Use AWS Security Hub with a custom security standard that checks for detailed monitoring. Configure an EventBridge rule to detect Security Hub findings and invoke a Lambda function that enables detailed monitoring. Deploy via CloudFormation StackSets to all accounts.
answers.D: Create a CloudWatch Events rule in each account that fires on EC2 RunInstances API calls. Trigger a Lambda function that checks whether detailed monitoring is enabled and enables it if not. Manage rule deployment using AWS Systems Manager Distributor.

explanation: Option B is correct because AWS Config conformance packs can be deployed organization-wide through AWS Organizations integration from the management account, covering all member accounts automatically. The conformance pack includes the managed Config rule and a Systems Manager Automation remediation action that triggers automatically on non-compliant resources—no custom Lambda or polling logic is needed. Option A requires per-account deployment and polling Lambda functions, increasing operational overhead. Option C uses Security Hub which adds an unnecessary layer and still requires Lambda automation per account. Option D triggers only on new instance launches and misses already-running non-compliant instances, plus requires per-account deployment.

stem: A company deployed a conformance pack using AWS Config across its AWS Organization that includes a rule requiring all S3 buckets to block public access. An audit reveals that a newly created S3 bucket in a member account is non-compliant, but no remediation has occurred. The engineer confirms the AWS Config recorder is active and the conformance pack is deployed. What is the MOST likely reason remediation has not triggered?
tags: AWS Config rules and conformance packs
Enabling AWS Config rules to detect and alert on non-compliant resources

answers.A: The AWS Config recorder in the member account is set to record only global resource types and is not capturing S3 bucket configuration changes.
answers.B: The conformance pack was deployed from the management account but the remediation action IAM role was created in the management account rather than in the member account.
answers.C: The remediation action associated with the Config rule is configured as manual remediation rather than automatic remediation, requiring an operator to invoke it explicitly.
answers.D: Conformance packs deployed via AWS Organizations do not support automatic remediation actions; remediation must be configured independently in each member account.

explanation: Option C is correct. AWS Config remediation actions must be explicitly configured as automatic (rather than manual) to trigger without operator intervention. If the remediation action is set to manual, AWS Config will mark the resource as non-compliant but will not invoke the remediation document automatically. Option A is plausible but AWS Config records S3 buckets regardless of the global resources setting since S3 buckets are regional resources. Option B is incorrect because the remediation role is assumed in the member account context; if the role were missing from the member account, remediation would fail with an error rather than silently not triggering. Option D is incorrect; conformance packs deployed via Organizations do support automatic remediation actions when correctly configured.

stem: A company manages a fleet of 500 EC2 instances running a mix of Amazon Linux 2 and Windows Server 2019. The security team requires that critical patches be applied within 24 hours of release and that all patching activity be auditable. Patch application must not disrupt production workloads running continuously. Which Systems Manager configuration meets these requirements?
tags: AWS Systems Manager capabilities (Run Command, Session Manager, Patch Manager, Maintenance Windows, Automation)
Configuring Systems Manager Patch Manager and patch baselines
Scheduling maintenance tasks using Systems Manager Maintenance Windows

answers.A: Create separate patch baselines for Amazon Linux 2 and Windows Server 2019 with critical severity patches set to auto-approve with a 0-day delay. Configure a Maintenance Window that runs every 6 hours using a staggered patch group strategy where only 10% of instances patch concurrently. Associate the patch baselines with patch groups and enable Systems Manager Compliance for audit logging.
answers.B: Create a single patch baseline covering both OS types with critical patches set to auto-approve after a 3-day delay. Schedule a daily Maintenance Window at 2 AM UTC that patches all instances simultaneously. Enable CloudTrail to audit the patch API calls made during the window.
answers.C: Use Systems Manager Run Command with the AWS-RunPatchBaseline document, triggered by an EventBridge scheduled rule every 24 hours. Set the concurrency to 100% and error threshold to 5%. Review Run Command history for audit purposes.
answers.D: Configure Patch Manager with a patch baseline that targets all instances using a single patch group. Use a Maintenance Window set to run once per week during off-peak hours. Enable S3 logging for the Maintenance Window task to capture patch compliance data.

explanation: Option A is correct. Separate patch baselines per OS type ensure correct patch selection. A 0-day auto-approve delay on critical patches ensures patches are available for application immediately upon release, satisfying the 24-hour requirement. Running the Maintenance Window every 6 hours with staggered concurrency (10% at a time) means critical patches can be applied within the window while limiting blast radius to avoid broad production disruption. Systems Manager Compliance provides built-in audit logging. Option B uses a 3-day delay which violates the 24-hour requirement, and patching all instances simultaneously risks production disruption. Option C uses 100% concurrency which could disrupt all instances simultaneously, and Run Command alone lacks the scheduling granularity and compliance reporting of Patch Manager. Option D uses a weekly window which cannot meet the 24-hour patching requirement.

stem: A company has strict security requirements prohibiting inbound SSH or RDP ports on EC2 security groups. Administrators need interactive shell access to instances in private subnets for troubleshooting. Instances have no public IP addresses and sit behind a NAT gateway. The solution must log all session activity to a centralized location for audit purposes. Which combination of AWS services and configurations achieves this?
tags: AWS Systems Manager capabilities (Run Command, Session Manager, Patch Manager, Maintenance Windows, Automation)
Using Systems Manager Session Manager for secure shell access without SSH

answers.A: Deploy a bastion host in a public subnet with SSH enabled. Restrict bastion access using a security group that allows inbound SSH from corporate IP ranges only. Configure VPC Flow Logs on the bastion's ENI and route logs to CloudWatch Logs for audit purposes.
answers.B: Attach an IAM role with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy to the EC2 instances. Configure an interface VPC endpoint for the EC2 service. Enable Session Manager and configure session logging to an S3 bucket.
answers.C: Configure AWS Systems Manager Session Manager with interface VPC endpoints for ssm, ssmmessages, and ec2messages. Grant users IAM permissions for ssm:StartSession. Store session logs in CloudWatch Logs by configuring the Session Manager preferences in the Systems Manager console.
answers.D: Attach an IAM role with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy to each EC2 instance. Create interface VPC endpoints for com.amazonaws.region.ssm, com.amazonaws.region.ssmmessages, and com.amazonaws.region.ec2messages in the private subnet's VPC. Configure Session Manager preferences to stream session logs to CloudWatch Logs and enable KMS encryption for sessions.

explanation: Option D is correct. For EC2 instances in private subnets with no public IP and no internet-facing security group rules, Session Manager requires three interface VPC endpoints: ssm, ssmmessages, and ec2messages. The instances need the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore IAM role to register with Systems Manager. Session Manager preferences must be configured to log session data to CloudWatch Logs for centralized auditing. Option A uses a bastion host which introduces an inbound SSH port, violating the security requirement. Option B creates only the EC2 endpoint, which is insufficient—the ssm and ssmmessages endpoints are also required for Session Manager. Option C is almost correct but omits the critical step of attaching the IAM role to the instances; without it, instances cannot register with Systems Manager and sessions cannot be established.

stem: A CloudFormation stack update is replacing an Amazon RDS instance with a new configuration. A stack policy currently allows updates to all resources. The team wants to ensure the RDS instance is never accidentally replaced or deleted during future stack updates while still allowing modifications to other resources like EC2 instances and Lambda functions. What is the correct approach?
tags: CloudFormation rollback triggers and stack policies
Diagnosing and resolving CloudFormation stack deployment failures

answers.A: Add a DeletionPolicy: Retain attribute to the RDS resource in the CloudFormation template. This prevents both deletion and replacement of the RDS instance during stack updates without requiring a stack policy change.
answers.B: Enable CloudFormation termination protection on the stack. This prevents the RDS instance from being replaced or deleted during stack updates while allowing other resources to be modified.
answers.C: Update the stack policy to deny Update:Replace and Update:Delete actions for the RDS resource using its logical resource ID, while explicitly allowing all update actions for all other resources.
answers.D: Set the UpdateReplacePolicy to Retain on the RDS resource in the CloudFormation template. Then configure a stack policy that denies the Update:Delete action for AWS::RDS::DBInstance resource type.

explanation: Option C is correct. CloudFormation stack policies control which update actions are permitted on stack resources. By setting the stack policy to deny Update:Replace and Update:Delete for the specific RDS resource (identified by logical resource ID), and allowing all actions for other resources, the RDS instance is protected from accidental replacement or deletion while the rest of the stack can be updated normally. Option A is incorrect because DeletionPolicy: Retain controls what happens when a resource is removed from the template or the stack is deleted, but it does not prevent CloudFormation from replacing the resource during an update triggered by a property change. Option B is incorrect because termination protection prevents the entire stack from being deleted, not individual resource updates. Option D partially addresses the requirement: UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain prevents the old instance from being deleted on replacement, but the replacement itself still occurs; combining it with a stack policy deny on Update:Delete alone is insufficient to prevent replacement.

stem: A team performs a CloudFormation stack update that changes an Auto Scaling group launch template. Three minutes after the update completes, a CloudWatch alarm monitoring application error rates fires. The team wants this alarm to automatically trigger a stack rollback if it fires within 5 minutes of a future stack update. The alarm already exists. Which CloudFormation feature and configuration achieves this?
tags: CloudFormation rollback triggers and stack policies
AWS services for automating remediation (for example, Systems Manager Automation, AWS Lambda, EventBridge)
Amazon CloudWatch alarms and alarm actions

answers.A: Configure a rollback trigger on the CloudFormation stack by specifying the CloudWatch alarm ARN and setting the monitoring time to 5 minutes. On future stack updates, CloudFormation will monitor the alarm and automatically roll back the stack if the alarm enters the ALARM state during the monitoring period.
answers.B: Create an EventBridge rule that matches CloudWatch alarm state change events for the alarm. Configure the rule to invoke a Lambda function that calls cloudformation:ContinueUpdateRollback on the stack. Set the EventBridge rule to be active only during stack update windows.
answers.C: Add a CloudWatch alarm action that publishes to an SNS topic when the alarm fires. Subscribe a Lambda function to the SNS topic that calls the CloudFormation API to cancel the update and initiate rollback. Update the stack with this new alarm action configuration.
answers.D: Enable CloudFormation drift detection on the stack and configure it to run every 5 minutes. When drift is detected after a stack update, a CloudWatch alarm action triggers an SSM Automation document that rolls back the launch template version to the previous one.

explanation: Option A is correct. CloudFormation natively supports rollback triggers, which allow you to specify one or more CloudWatch alarms and a monitoring period (in minutes). During a stack update, CloudFormation monitors the specified alarms; if any alarm enters the ALARM state within the monitoring period after the update completes, CloudFormation automatically initiates a rollback. This is the built-in, direct mechanism for this requirement. Option B describes a workaround using EventBridge and Lambda; cloudformation:ContinueUpdateRollback is used to resume a rollback that was manually rolled back, not to initiate one, making this approach incorrect. Option C also describes a Lambda-based workaround that lacks the timing precision of rollback triggers and requires additional configuration and maintenance. Option D conflates drift detection (which compares actual resource config to the template) with rollback triggering; drift detection does not initiate stack rollbacks.

stem: A company runs a multi-Region active-active application with endpoints in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Traffic must be distributed based on the geographic location of the requesting user, with us-east-1 serving North American users and eu-west-1 serving European users. If one Region becomes unavailable, all traffic must automatically route to the healthy Region. Which Route 53 configuration achieves this with automatic failover?
tags: Route 53 routing policies and health checks
Route 53 health checks and DNS failover
Configuring Route 53 routing policies (simple, weighted, latency, failover, geolocation, geoproximity)

answers.A: Create two A records using failover routing policy — one primary pointing to us-east-1 and one secondary pointing to eu-west-1. Attach Route 53 health checks to both records. Configure a separate latency-based routing policy for the primary record to direct North American users to us-east-1.
answers.B: Create geolocation routing records: one for North America pointing to us-east-1 and one for Europe pointing to eu-west-1, each with associated Route 53 health checks. Create a default geolocation record pointing to us-east-1. Ensure each geolocation record has a health check so that Route 53 fails over to the next-best geolocation match if the primary becomes unhealthy.
answers.C: Use Route 53 latency-based routing with two records — one for us-east-1 and one for eu-west-1. Attach health checks to each latency record. Latency routing will naturally direct North American users to us-east-1 and European users to eu-west-1 based on latency.
answers.D: Create geolocation records for North America and Europe pointing to the respective Regions. Configure Route 53 Resolver to perform health checks and automatically update the geolocation record weights if a Region becomes unavailable.

explanation: Option B is correct. Geolocation routing with associated health checks is the right combination. When a geolocation record has a health check and the associated endpoint is unhealthy, Route 53 falls back to less-specific geolocation records (for example, from continent to default). By configuring health checks on each geolocation record and having a default record, Route 53 automatically routes all traffic to the healthy Region when one becomes unavailable. Option A incorrectly combines failover and latency routing in a way that cannot enforce geolocation-based routing; failover routing does not distribute traffic geographically. Option C uses latency routing, which can naturally route North American users to us-east-1 and European users to eu-west-1 due to network proximity, but the question explicitly requires geographic-based routing; latency routing is not guaranteed to respect geographic boundaries and cannot enforce that North American users always go to us-east-1. Option D invents a non-existent Route 53 Resolver health-check capability for geolocation records.

stem: A company uses Route 53 weighted routing to split traffic 80/20 between a stable version (weight 80) and a canary version (weight 20) of an application. During a deployment, the canary version begins returning HTTP 500 errors. The operations team needs the Route 53 weighted record for the canary to stop receiving traffic automatically when the canary health check fails, without manual changes. The health check already monitors the canary endpoint. How should the weighted record be configured?
tags: Route 53 routing policies and health checks
Setting up Route 53 health checks and configuring failover routing
Configuring CloudWatch alarm actions to trigger notifications or Auto Scaling actions

answers.A: Set the canary weighted record's weight to 0. Route 53 will interpret a weight of 0 as directing no traffic to the endpoint, effectively removing it from rotation when errors occur. Monitoring the health check is then optional.
answers.B: Associate the existing health check with the canary weighted record. When Route 53 detects the health check is unhealthy, it removes the canary record from the weighted set entirely and redistributes traffic proportionally across remaining records.
answers.C: Associate the existing health check with the canary weighted record. Route 53 will omit the canary record from DNS responses when the health check is unhealthy, causing all traffic to be served by the stable record with weight 80.
answers.D: Create a CloudWatch alarm that monitors the HTTP 500 metric for the canary endpoint. Configure an alarm action that invokes a Lambda function to update the canary Route 53 record weight to 0 via the Route 53 API when the alarm fires.

explanation: Option C is correct. When a Route 53 health check is associated with a weighted record and the health check reports unhealthy, Route 53 automatically omits that record from DNS responses. All traffic is then directed to the remaining healthy weighted records (in this case, the stable version with weight 80). This happens without any manual intervention. Option A is incorrect; setting a weight to 0 with Route 53 does not instruct Route 53 to exclude the record based on health — a weight of 0 means Route 53 will not route to that record, but this requires a manual change, not automatic behavior. Option B is incorrect in its description: Route 53 does not remove the record from the weighted set; it simply excludes it from DNS responses while the health check is unhealthy and restores it when it recovers. Option D introduces unnecessary Lambda automation when Route 53 health check integration with weighted records is a built-in feature.

stem: A company runs a data analytics workload that requires 200 vCPUs of compute capacity consistently for 3 years. The workload can tolerate interruptions and resume from checkpoints. Additionally, the company has unpredictable burst workloads that require up to 50 additional vCPUs for a few hours several times per month. The company wants to minimize compute costs while ensuring baseline capacity is always available. Which purchasing strategy meets these requirements?
tags: EC2 purchasing options (On-Demand, Reserved Instances, Savings Plans, Spot Instances)
Identifying and purchasing appropriate Reserved Instances or Savings Plans
Identifying underutilized resources and taking action to reduce costs

answers.A: Purchase Compute Savings Plans covering 200 vCPUs worth of compute spend for a 3-year term with all-upfront payment. Configure an EC2 Auto Scaling group with a baseline of On-Demand instances sized to 200 vCPUs and add Spot Instances for the burst capacity up to 50 additional vCPUs.
answers.B: Purchase 200 vCPUs worth of Standard Reserved Instances in a specific Region and instance family for a 3-year term. Provision additional On-Demand instances for burst capacity as needed, using instance type flexibility from Convertible RIs for the burst portion.
answers.C: Use Spot Instances for the full 200 vCPUs baseline using a diversified Spot fleet across multiple instance types and Availability Zones. Purchase On-Demand capacity for the 50 vCPU burst to guarantee availability during peak periods.
answers.D: Purchase EC2 Instance Savings Plans for 200 vCPUs with a 3-year term. Configure the Auto Scaling group to use On-Demand for baseline capacity and Spot Instances for bursts. Supplement with On-Demand instances if Spot capacity is unavailable during bursts.

explanation: Option A is correct. Compute Savings Plans provide the highest flexibility across instance families, sizes, and even services (EC2 and Fargate), making them well-suited for a sustained 3-year baseline. Using On-Demand instances as the baseline ensures the 200 vCPU baseline is always available (Savings Plans lower the cost of these On-Demand instances). Spot Instances are ideal for the burst workload since the analytics job can tolerate interruptions and resume from checkpoints. Option B uses Standard Reserved Instances which provide good savings but are tied to a specific instance family and size, reducing flexibility. Using Convertible RIs for burst is a mischaracterization — Convertible RIs are long-term commitments, not suitable for short burst periods. Option C is incorrect because using Spot for the entire 200 vCPU baseline means the baseline is not guaranteed; Spot Instances can be interrupted, and the question requires baseline capacity to always be available. Option D is partially correct but EC2 Instance Savings Plans are less flexible than Compute Savings Plans (restricted to a specific instance family in a Region), and supplementing bursts with On-Demand removes the cost optimization for that capacity.

stem: A company is evaluating Reserved Instance (RI) coverage for its EC2 fleet. AWS Cost Explorer shows that over the last 3 months, the fleet consistently runs 100 On-Demand t3.large instances in us-east-1 for a Linux workload. The finance team wants to reduce costs but is concerned about flexibility if the team migrates to t3.xlarge instances in 6 months. Which purchasing option provides the best cost savings with the most flexibility for potential instance type changes?
tags: EC2 purchasing options (On-Demand, Reserved Instances, Savings Plans, Spot Instances)
AWS Cost Explorer and cost allocation tags
Using AWS Cost Explorer to analyze spending trends and identify cost drivers

answers.A: Purchase 100 Standard Reserved Instances for t3.large in us-east-1 with a 1-year term and partial upfront payment. Standard RIs offer the highest discount for t3.large and can be exchanged for t3.xlarge instances through the RI Marketplace.
answers.B: Purchase 100 Convertible Reserved Instances for t3.large in us-east-1 with a 1-year term and partial upfront payment. Convertible RIs can be exchanged for t3.xlarge instances of equal or greater value at any time, allowing migration without losing the commitment.
answers.C: Purchase a 1-year Compute Savings Plan with a commitment covering the equivalent spend of 100 t3.large instances. Compute Savings Plans automatically apply to any EC2 instance family, size, OS, or Region, providing flexibility for migration to t3.xlarge while reducing costs compared to On-Demand.
answers.D: Purchase a 1-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the t3 instance family in us-east-1. EC2 Instance Savings Plans apply to any size within the t3 family, automatically covering both t3.large and t3.xlarge instances in the same Region.

explanation: Option C is correct. Compute Savings Plans offer the highest flexibility — they apply to any EC2 instance family, size, tenancy, OS, and Region, as well as Fargate and Lambda. This means if the team migrates from t3.large to t3.xlarge, the Savings Plan automatically applies to the new instances without any action required. The discount is slightly lower than Standard RIs but higher than On-Demand, and the flexibility far exceeds other RI or Savings Plan types. Option A is incorrect; Standard Reserved Instances cannot be directly exchanged for a different instance size through the RI Marketplace in the same straightforward way — exchange is a feature of Convertible RIs, not Standard RIs. The RI Marketplace allows selling Standard RIs, which is not the same as exchanging them. Option B is partially correct — Convertible RIs do allow exchanges, but the exchange process requires contacting AWS and involves value matching rules; Compute Savings Plans are simpler and more flexible without requiring an exchange action. Option D is partially correct — EC2 Instance Savings Plans apply to any size within a specific instance family in a specific Region, so they would cover t3.xlarge automatically. However, they are less flexible than Compute Savings Plans because they are locked to a Region and instance family.

stem: A company uses AWS Organizations with multiple OUs. The security team needs to prevent all member accounts from disabling AWS CloudTrail logging across the entire organization. The policy must be enforced even if a member account administrator has AdministratorAccess permissions. The management account itself must retain the ability to perform these actions for break-glass scenarios. Which approach correctly implements this requirement?
tags: Configuring SCPs to restrict actions across AWS accounts in an organization
AWS CloudTrail log content and routing

answers.A: Enable CloudTrail as an organization trail from the management account. Attach an SCP to the Root of the organization that denies cloudtrail:DeleteTrail, cloudtrail:StopLogging, and cloudtrail:UpdateTrail for all principals. Apply the SCP to all accounts including the management account.
answers.B: Attach an SCP to the Root of the organization that denies cloudtrail:DeleteTrail and cloudtrail:StopLogging. Add a condition to the SCP: StringNotEquals aws:PrincipalAccount: management-account-id to exempt the management account from the denial.
answers.C: Attach an SCP to each member account OU that denies cloudtrail:DeleteTrail, cloudtrail:StopLogging, and cloudtrail:UpdateTrail. Do not attach any SCP to the Root or to the management account OU to preserve management account access.
answers.D: Attach an SCP to the Root of the organization that denies cloudtrail:DeleteTrail, cloudtrail:StopLogging, and cloudtrail:UpdateTrail. SCPs do not apply to the management account regardless of where they are attached, so the management account retains full permissions by default.

explanation: Option D is correct. A key property of SCPs is that they never affect the management account, regardless of where the SCP is applied — even if attached to the Root. Attaching the deny SCP at the Root ensures it applies to all member accounts in the organization, preventing member account administrators from disabling CloudTrail even with AdministratorAccess (because SCPs function as permission guardrails that override IAM policies in member accounts). The management account is inherently exempt. Option A would also enforce the SCP at the Root correctly; however, the premise that the SCP 'applies to the management account' is incorrect — SCPs never apply to the management account, and stating so reflects a misunderstanding. Option B adds an unnecessary condition; since SCPs never apply to the management account, the StringNotEquals condition is redundant overhead.
