Option C attaches SCPs only to specific OUs rather than Root, which is less scalable and misses any future OUs that may be created.

stem: An AWS Organization has an SCP attached to the "Production" OU that denies the ec2:TerminateInstances action. A member account in the Production OU has an IAM role with an explicit Allow for ec2:TerminateInstances. An engineer using that role attempts to terminate an EC2 instance and receives an AccessDenied error. A second engineer suggests attaching the SCP to the root of the organization instead of the Production OU and removing it from the OU. What is the effect of this change if the management account is in a different OU?
tags: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies, roles, and permission boundaries
Configuring SCPs to restrict actions across AWS accounts in an organization

answers.A: The SCP will now apply to all accounts in the organization including the management account, which will also lose the ability to terminate EC2 instances. Member accounts in the Production OU will no longer be affected since the SCP was removed from the OU.
answers.B: The SCP will apply to all member accounts across all OUs in the organization, including the Production OU account, so the engineer in the Production OU account will still receive an AccessDenied error. The management account will not be affected by the SCP.
answers.C: Moving the SCP to Root means it now applies at a higher precedence level and overrides any OU-level SCPs. Since the Production OU no longer has the SCP, the IAM role's explicit Allow will take effect for accounts in that OU, and the engineer can now terminate instances.
answers.D: The SCP at Root will only affect accounts directly under Root and not accounts inside OUs, so the Production OU member account is no longer restricted. The engineer can now terminate EC2 instances using the IAM role.

explanation: Option B is correct. SCPs attached to the Root apply to all member accounts in the organization — all accounts in all OUs, because OUs are nested under Root. When an SCP is attached to Root, it is inherited by all child OUs and their member accounts. Therefore, the Production OU account still inherits the SCP and the engineer still receives AccessDenied. Critically, SCPs never apply to the management account regardless of attachment point — the management account is always exempt. Option A is incorrect because SCPs do not apply to the management account even when attached to Root. Option C is incorrect because SCP precedence works through inheritance, not override layers; moving the SCP to Root while removing it from the OU means the account inherits it through Root, so the deny still applies. Option D is incorrect because SCPs attached to Root are inherited by all OUs and their member accounts — they are not limited to accounts directly under Root.

stem: A company runs a business-critical application backed by a single-AZ Amazon RDS MySQL 8.0 instance in us-east-1. The team wants to achieve an RPO of less than 5 minutes and an RTO of less than 2 minutes for database failures without application code changes. Storage I/O should not be impacted during the backup window. Which RDS configuration change achieves these objectives?
tags: Amazon RDS read replicas and Multi-AZ deployments
Configuring RDS Multi-AZ for high availability
Recovery point objective (RPO) and recovery time objective (RTO)

answers.A: Convert the RDS instance to a Multi-AZ deployment. RDS Multi-AZ uses synchronous replication to a standby in a different AZ, providing an RPO of near zero and an RTO typically under 2 minutes during automatic failover. Automated backups on Multi-AZ instances use the standby for I/O, eliminating backup I/O impact on the primary.
answers.B: Create an RDS read replica in the same Region in a different AZ. Promote the read replica manually if the primary fails. Enable automated backups with a 1-day retention period to meet the RPO requirement.
answers.C: Enable RDS automated backups with a 5-minute transaction log backup interval and configure a backup window during off-peak hours. Restore from the latest snapshot plus transaction logs to achieve an RPO under 5 minutes in case of failure.
answers.D: Create an RDS read replica in a different AWS Region. Configure Route 53 health checks to detect primary failure and update the application's database endpoint to the replica's endpoint using Route 53 DNS failover routing.

explanation: Option A is correct. RDS Multi-AZ uses synchronous replication, meaning every write to the primary is synchronously replicated to the standby before the write is acknowledged. This gives an RPO of near zero (typically seconds). Failover to the standby is automatic and typically completes in 1-2 minutes, meeting the RTO under 2 minutes requirement. Automated backups in Multi-AZ configurations use the standby replica for I/O, so backup operations do not impact primary instance performance. No application code changes are required — the CNAME endpoint automatically points to the new primary after failover. Option B uses a read replica with asynchronous replication, which cannot guarantee RPO under 5 minutes and requires manual promotion — failing the RTO under 2 minutes without manual intervention requirement. Option C describes the restore-from-backup process, which has an RTO of many minutes to hours (provisioning time plus restore time), far exceeding the 2-minute RTO requirement. Option D uses a cross-Region read replica, which has higher network latency for replication and much longer failover time; DNS-based failover alone cannot achieve an RTO under 2 minutes.

stem: A company has an Amazon RDS MySQL Multi-AZ instance serving a read-heavy workload. The application server connects using a single endpoint. Read queries account for 85% of database traffic and are causing high CPU utilization on the primary instance during peak hours. The engineering team wants to offload read traffic with minimal application changes. Which approach is MOST operationally efficient?
tags: Amazon RDS read replicas and Multi-AZ deployments
Setting up read replicas for RDS to offload read traffic
Amazon ElastiCache and its caching strategies

answers.A: Promote the Multi-AZ standby to a standalone read replica. Update the application to send read queries to the promoted instance endpoint and write queries to the primary. This requires one endpoint change in the application configuration.
answers.B: Create an RDS read replica in the same Region. Update the application to use two separate database connection strings: one for writes pointing to the primary endpoint and one for reads pointing to the read replica endpoint.
answers.C: Create one or more RDS read replicas. Use Amazon RDS Proxy with a read-only endpoint that load-balances across read replicas. Update the application to send read queries to the RDS Proxy read-only endpoint and writes to the primary cluster endpoint.
answers.D: Scale up the RDS primary instance to a larger instance type with more vCPUs to handle the increased read load. Enable RDS Performance Insights to identify and optimize slow read queries causing the CPU spike.

explanation: Option C is correct. RDS read replicas offload read traffic from the primary instance. Using RDS Proxy with a read-only endpoint abstracts the connection management and load balances read queries across multiple replicas automatically. This minimizes application changes — only the read endpoint URL changes. RDS Proxy also improves connection pooling efficiency. Option A is incorrect because the Multi-AZ standby cannot be promoted to a read replica; the standby is not accessible and is used exclusively for failover. Promoting a standby would remove Multi-AZ protection and convert the instance to standalone, which reduces availability. Option B creates read replicas but requires the application to maintain two separate connection strings and implement read/write splitting logic — more application-side changes than Option C. Option D scales up the primary instance, which is a vertical scaling approach that does not fundamentally address the read-heavy pattern and becomes increasingly expensive; it also does not offload reads.

stem: A security team suspects that an EC2 instance in a private subnet is communicating with a known malicious IP address. VPC Flow Logs are enabled and sent to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. The team wants to identify all outbound connections from that specific instance to external IP addresses in the last 72 hours that were accepted, without downloading raw log files. Which combination of tools should the engineer use?
tags: VPC Flow Logs and their use cases
CloudWatch metrics, CloudWatch Logs, and CloudWatch Logs Insights
Configuring VPC Flow Logs and routing them to CloudWatch Logs or Amazon S3

answers.A: Navigate to the VPC Flow Logs console, filter by the instance's ENI ID, and download the log file for the last 72 hours. Use a spreadsheet to filter rows where the action field is ACCEPT and the destination IP is external.
answers.B: Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query the VPC Flow Logs log group. Write a query filtering by the instance's source IP address, action field equal to ACCEPT, and timestamps within the last 72 hours, then visualize or export results directly from the console.
answers.C: Enable Amazon Detective and connect it to the VPC Flow Logs. Use the Detective console to pivot on the EC2 instance and review all accepted outbound connections for the selected time range.
answers.D: Export the VPC Flow Logs CloudWatch Logs group to Amazon S3 using the CloudWatch console. Create an Amazon Athena table over the S3 bucket and run a SQL query filtering by source IP, ACCEPT action, and the 72-hour time window.

explanation: Option B is correct. CloudWatch Logs Insights provides an interactive query interface directly in the console that can query VPC Flow Logs stored in CloudWatch Logs without downloading any files. The engineer can filter by the instance's source IP (or ENI ID if the flow log format includes it), filter on action = ACCEPT, and restrict to the last 72 hours — all without leaving the AWS console. Results can be viewed or exported directly. Option A requires downloading raw log files, which the question explicitly prohibits. Option C requires enabling Amazon Detective (a separate service that requires prior GuardDuty enablement and a setup period) — it does not provide immediate query capability and is not necessary for this task. Option D exports to S3 and uses Athena, which is a valid approach for large-scale analysis but involves more steps and is not the most direct way to analyze logs already in CloudWatch Logs without downloading files.

stem: A company enables VPC Flow Logs for a VPC and routes them to an S3 bucket. After one week, the security team notices that traffic between two EC2 instances within the same subnet is not appearing in the flow logs. The flow logs are configured at the VPC level with the default log format. What is the MOST likely explanation?
tags: VPC Flow Logs and their use cases
Configuring VPC Flow Logs and routing them to CloudWatch Logs or Amazon S3
Common causes of VPC connectivity failures

answers.A: VPC Flow Logs capture traffic at the ENI level. Traffic between instances in the same subnet that stays within the hypervisor and does not traverse a virtual network interface may not be captured, or the traffic is using instance-level communication that bypasses ENI logging in certain configurations.
answers.B: VPC Flow Logs configured at the VPC level only capture traffic that crosses subnet boundaries. Traffic that remains within a single subnet between instances is not logged by design.
answers.C: The S3 bucket policy does not grant the VPC Flow Logs delivery service the necessary permissions to write log files. The absence of intra-subnet traffic records indicates a partial delivery failure for specific traffic patterns.
answers.D: VPC Flow Logs do not capture traffic generated by instances with enhanced networking (SR-IOV) enabled when the instances communicate within the same subnet, because SR-IOV bypasses the hypervisor network stack where flow log capture occurs.

explanation: Option A is correct. VPC Flow Logs capture traffic at the elastic network interface (ENI) level. Traffic between instances in the same subnet does traverse ENIs and is captured by VPC Flow Logs at the VPC level — however, there are specific exclusions: VPC Flow Logs do not capture traffic to the Amazon DNS server (169.254.169.253), instance metadata service (169.254.169.254), Amazon Time Sync (169.254.169.123), DHCP traffic, and Windows license activation traffic. If the missing traffic is one of these excluded types, it will not appear. More importantly, traffic between instances in the same subnet is generally captured by VPC Flow Logs; if it is not appearing, it may be one of the documented exclusion categories. Option B is factually incorrect — VPC Flow Logs do capture intra-subnet traffic between instances; they operate at the ENI level and do not have a subnet-boundary restriction. Option C would result in all flow logs being missing, not just intra-subnet traffic, so it does not match the described symptom. Option D is incorrect; SR-IOV (enhanced networking) does not exempt traffic from VPC Flow Log capture — AWS's virtualization layer still captures ENI traffic regardless of the networking driver.

stem: A company runs a web application on an EC2 Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. The application experiences a predictable traffic spike every weekday between 9 AM and 11 AM UTC that target tracking scaling cannot respond to quickly enough, causing latency issues during the first 20 minutes of the spike. The team wants to proactively add capacity before the spike. Which Auto Scaling configuration BEST addresses this?
tags: EC2 Auto Scaling types (dynamic scaling, predictive scaling, scheduled scaling)
Implementing scheduled scaling actions to handle predictable load changes
Configuring target tracking and step scaling policies

answers.A: Replace the target tracking policy with a step scaling policy. Configure step scaling to add 5 instances when CPU utilization exceeds 60% and add 10 more instances when it exceeds 80%. This provides faster capacity additions during the ramp-up period.
answers.B: Add a scheduled scaling action that increases the minimum and desired capacity of the Auto Scaling group to the anticipated peak capacity at 8:45 AM UTC on weekdays. Keep the target tracking policy for handling unexpected load variations. Add a second scheduled action to return capacity to the baseline at 11:15 AM UTC.
answers.C: Enable predictive scaling in forecast-only mode for one week to gather baseline data. After validation, switch predictive scaling to forecast-and-scale mode to automatically provision capacity ahead of the predicted spike without needing scheduled actions.
answers.D: Configure a warm pool for the Auto Scaling group with pre-initialized instances in the Stopped state. Ensure the warm pool size matches the expected peak capacity. Target tracking will pull instances from the warm pool faster than launching cold instances.

explanation: Option B is correct. Scheduled scaling actions allow you to proactively set the desired and minimum capacity at a specific time, before the predictable traffic spike begins. By increasing capacity at 8:45 AM — 15 minutes before the 9 AM spike — instances are launched and warmed up before traffic arrives, eliminating the 20-minute latency window. The existing target tracking policy continues to handle any unexpected load beyond the scheduled capacity. A second scheduled action at 11:15 AM restores baseline capacity. Option A replaces target tracking with step scaling, which still reacts to load after it spikes rather than proactively provisioning ahead of it — this does not solve the 20-minute warm-up problem. Option C describes predictive scaling, which is a valid long-term solution, but predictive scaling requires historical data and a learning period, and in forecast-and-scale mode it provisions capacity based on ML predictions, not a hard guaranteed schedule. For a known predictable spike occurring right now, scheduled scaling is more immediately reliable. Option D describes warm pools correctly — warm pools do reduce instance launch time by keeping pre-initialized instances ready — but the question states target tracking cannot respond quickly enough, suggesting the issue is the reaction time of the policy itself, not just the instance launch time; proactive scheduling is the direct fix.

stem: A company uses an EC2 Auto Scaling group to run a distributed cache. When a new instance launches, it must download a 2 GB data set from S3 and warm the cache before receiving traffic. Currently, instances are added to the load balancer target group immediately upon launch, causing cache misses during warm-up. The company wants instances to complete warm-up before receiving production traffic. Which approach resolves this?
tags: Implementing Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks to perform custom actions during instance launch or termination
EC2 Auto Scaling types (dynamic scaling, predictive scaling, scheduled scaling)

answers.A: Increase the health check grace period in the Auto Scaling group to 30 minutes. This prevents the Auto Scaling group from registering instances with the load balancer until the grace period expires, giving instances time to complete warm-up.
answers.B: Configure a custom AMI that pre-populates the 2 GB cache data during the AMI bake process using EC2 Image Builder. Launch new instances from this AMI so that cache data is available at startup without requiring a download.
answers.C: Configure the Auto Scaling group to use a slow-start configuration on the target group. Set the slow-start duration to 10 minutes so that new instances receive an increasing proportion of traffic over the warm-up period rather than full traffic immediately.
answers.D: Configure an EC2 Auto Scaling lifecycle hook on the EC2_INSTANCE_LAUNCHING transition. When the lifecycle hook fires, a Lambda function or SSM Automation document downloads the data set and warms the cache. When warm-up completes, the process sends a CompleteLifecycleAction signal to allow the instance to proceed to InService state and register with the load balancer.

explanation: Option D is correct. EC2 Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks allow you to pause the launch process at the EC2_INSTANCE_LAUNCHING transition, keeping the instance in a Pending:Wait state and out of the load balancer's target group until the custom action completes. Once the warm-up script finishes and sends CompleteLifecycleAction with the CONTINUE result, the instance moves to InService and registers with the load balancer. This precisely prevents instances from receiving traffic until cache warm-up is complete. Option A is incorrect because the health check grace period does not prevent the instance from registering with the load balancer — it prevents Auto Scaling from acting on health check failures during that period. Instances can still receive traffic immediately after launch. Option B pre-populates the cache in the AMI, which could work for static data, but the scenario implies the data set may change (requiring a fresh download per launch), and rebaking AMIs for every data update is operationally expensive. Option C configures slow-start at the ALB target group level, which gradually ramps up the traffic percentage to a new instance — but instances still receive some traffic immediately, causing cache misses during the ramp period. Lifecycle hooks are the correct mechanism to hold instances out of traffic entirely during warm-up.

stem: A company uses AWS Backup to protect RDS instances, EBS volumes, and DynamoDB tables across three AWS accounts in an AWS Organization. The compliance team requires that backup copies be immutable for 7 years and stored in a separate AWS account that the application teams cannot modify or delete. Which AWS Backup feature combination meets this requirement?
tags: AWS Backup service and backup plans
Configuring cross-account and cross-Region backup copies using AWS Backup
Recovery point objective (RPO) and recovery time objective (RTO)

answers.A: Configure AWS Backup backup plans in each source account with cross-account copy rules targeting a dedicated compliance AWS account. In the compliance account, create a backup vault with an S3 Object Lock-like retention policy of 7 years to enforce immutability.
answers.B: Create an AWS Backup organization backup policy from the management account that copies backups to a centralized vault in a dedicated compliance account. Enable MFA delete on the backup vault in the compliance account to prevent deletion by application teams.
answers.C: Create an AWS Backup organization backup policy from the management account that copies backups to a centralized vault in a dedicated compliance account. Enable AWS Backup Vault Lock on the compliance vault with a minimum retention period of 7 years in compliance mode. Restrict application team IAM permissions so they cannot access the compliance account's vault.
answers.D: Configure AWS Backup backup plans in each source account with lifecycle rules to transition backups to cold storage after 90 days and retain them for 7 years. Enable S3 Versioning on the backup vault's underlying storage to prevent deletion of backup data.

explanation: Option C is correct. AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode enforces immutability on backups stored in the vault — once enabled in compliance mode, even the root user and AWS cannot delete backups before the minimum retention period expires. Setting the minimum retention to 7 years ensures backups cannot be deleted for that period. Organization backup policies allow the management account to centrally deploy backup plans across all member accounts, including cross-account copy rules to the compliance vault. Restricting application team IAM permissions prevents them from accessing the compliance account. Option A is incorrect because S3 Object Lock is an S3 feature, not an AWS Backup feature; AWS Backup vaults do not use S3 Object Lock. Backup Vault Lock is the correct mechanism. Option B uses MFA delete, which is an S3 bucket versioning feature and does not apply to AWS Backup vaults; also, MFA delete only applies to specific delete API calls on S3 object versions, not backup recovery points. Option D describes lifecycle rules for cold storage transition, which is a valid cost optimization but does not provide immutability; S3 Versioning does not apply to AWS Backup vault storage.

stem: A company has a backup plan in AWS Backup that runs daily EBS snapshot jobs. After a review, the operations team discovers that backup jobs for several EBS volumes are failing with the error "ResourceNotFoundException." The volumes exist and are in the "available" state. The AWS Backup vault is in the same Region. What is the MOST likely cause of the failure?
tags: AWS Backup service and backup plans
Creating and managing AWS Backup plans and vaults
Creating EBS snapshots and AMIs and restoring from them

answers.A: The EBS volumes are encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key, and the AWS Backup service role does not have kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt permissions for that KMS key. The ResourceNotFoundException is returned when KMS access is denied during snapshot initiation.
answers.B: The backup plan's resource assignment uses specific resource ARNs or tags to target the EBS volumes, and the volumes that are failing either no longer match the tag-based selection criteria or their ARNs were removed from the resource assignment, causing AWS Backup to report a ResourceNotFoundException for those volumes.
answers.C: The AWS Backup vault has a vault access policy that explicitly denies the backup:CreateBackupVault action for the service role, preventing the backup job from writing the recovery point to the vault and reporting it as a ResourceNotFoundException.
answers.D: The EBS volumes are in a different Availability Zone than where the backup vault is configured. AWS Backup requires the vault and the source EBS volume to be in the same AZ to create snapshots, and the mismatch causes the ResourceNotFoundException error.

explanation: Option B is correct. A ResourceNotFoundException from AWS Backup for EBS snapshot jobs most commonly occurs when the resource targeted by the backup plan cannot be found by the AWS Backup service at job execution time. If the backup plan uses tag-based resource selection and the tags were removed from the volumes, or if the plan uses explicit ARNs that were updated or removed from the selection, AWS Backup cannot locate the resource and reports ResourceNotFoundException. The volumes existing in 'available' state in the same account does not mean they are still matched by the backup plan's selection criteria. Option A describes a KMS permissions issue, which would produce an error related to encryption or authorization (AccessDeniedException or similar), not a ResourceNotFoundException. Option C incorrectly describes a vault access policy error — this would produce an AccessDeniedException when the service role attempts to write to the vault, not a ResourceNotFoundException for the EBS volume. Option D is incorrect; AWS Backup is a regional service, not AZ-specific; EBS snapshots are regional resources, and the vault and EBS volumes only need to be in the same Region, which the question confirms.

stem: A financial services company runs a customer-facing REST API built on AWS Lambda and Amazon API Gateway. The API must respond within 500 ms at the 99th percentile during business hours (9 AM to 5 PM). Outside business hours, traffic drops to near zero. A recent load test revealed that cold-start latency for the Java Lambda function averages 3 seconds. The team wants to eliminate cold-start impact during business hours with minimal cost outside business hours. Which approach meets these requirements?
tags: Lambda cold starts and ways to mitigate them (for example, provisioned concurrency)
Lambda function configuration settings (for example, memory, concurrency, timeout, runtime, handler, layers, extensions, triggers, destinations)
Tuning Lambda functions for optimal performance

answers.A: Enable reserved concurrency set to 100 on the Lambda function. Reserved concurrency guarantees execution capacity and prevents cold starts by keeping containers warm continuously.
answers.B: Configure provisioned concurrency on the Lambda function alias and use an Amazon EventBridge Scheduler rule to scale provisioned concurrency to the required level at 8:45 AM and back to zero at 5:05 PM each weekday.
answers.C: Increase the Lambda function memory to 10,240 MB. Higher memory allocates more CPU and reduces Java JVM initialization time, effectively eliminating cold starts at any traffic level.
answers.D: Deploy the Lambda function inside a VPC and attach an Elastic Network Interface. VPC-attached functions reuse network interfaces across invocations, which prevents cold starts for Java runtimes.

explanation: Provisioned concurrency pre-initializes a configurable number of execution environments so they are ready to respond immediately with no cold start. Using EventBridge Scheduler to adjust provisioned concurrency before and after business hours ensures warm environments exist only when needed, minimizing cost. Reserved concurrency (A) limits concurrency but does NOT keep environments warm or prevent cold starts. Increasing memory (C) can speed up initialization slightly but cannot eliminate 3-second JVM cold starts for Java. VPC attachment (D) no longer causes additional cold starts since AWS resolved that issue in 2019, and it never prevented JVM initialization latency.

stem: A developer is building an asynchronous order-processing pipeline using AWS Lambda. When the Lambda function fails after all retries, the team needs to capture the full event payload, the failure reason, and the function version that executed so they can replay or audit orders. The team also needs to route successful completions to a downstream SNS topic. They want to implement this with minimal additional code. Which Lambda feature should the developer configure?
tags: Lambda function invocation types (synchronous, asynchronous, poll-based event sources)
Creating, interpreting, and testing Lambda function error handling

answers.A: Configure a Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) on the Lambda function pointing to an SQS queue for failures. For successes, add code inside the handler to publish to the SNS topic after processing each order.
answers.B: Wrap the handler body in a try-except block. On exception, call the SQS SendMessage API with the event data and error. On success, call SNS Publish. Deploy this updated code to handle both routing cases.
answers.C: Configure Lambda Destinations on the function: set the On Failure destination to an SQS queue and the On Success destination to the SNS topic. Lambda will automatically route invocation records containing the event, response or error, and function version to the respective destination.
answers.D: Enable Lambda event source mapping error handling by setting a bisect-on-error flag and pointing the destination to SQS. Configure an SNS subscription to the Lambda function ARN for success notifications.

explanation: Lambda Destinations for asynchronous invocations automatically send an invocation record to the configured destination after each invocation completes. The record includes the full event payload, the response or error reason, and function version metadata — exactly what the team needs without additional code in the handler. On Failure routes to SQS and On Success routes to SNS as specified. A DLQ (A) only captures the event payload on failure and does not provide success routing or include function version. Manual try-except publishing (B) adds application code and cannot capture certain failure modes like timeouts or out-of-memory errors. Bisect-on-error (D) is specific to event source mappings (poll-based), not asynchronous invocation.

stem: A developer configures an Amazon SQS queue as an event source for an AWS Lambda function. The function processes records in batches of 10. During a load spike, some records within a batch fail validation while others succeed. The team requires that only the failed messages be retried and that successfully processed messages not be reprocessed. What must the developer do to implement this behavior?
tags: Lambda function invocation types (synchronous, asynchronous, poll-based event sources)
Creating event source mappings for Lambda functions

answers.A: Enable ReportBatchItemFailures on the SQS event source mapping. In the Lambda handler, catch per-record errors and return a response body with a batchItemFailures list containing the messageId of each failed record. Lambda will delete successful messages and return only the failed ones to the queue.
answers.B: Set the batch size to 1 on the event source mapping. Processing one message at a time means a failure only affects that single message, so only that message is retried while the others have already been deleted.
answers.C: Manually delete successful messages from the SQS queue using the DeleteMessage API inside the Lambda handler after processing each record. Lambda will only retry messages that were not explicitly deleted.
answers.D: Configure a Lambda DLQ pointing to a separate SQS queue. When any record in a batch fails, Lambda automatically moves only the failed message to the DLQ and deletes the successful messages from the source queue.

explanation: ReportBatchItemFailures is the correct mechanism for partial batch success with SQS event source mappings. The function must return a specific JSON structure listing only the failed messageIds; Lambda will then delete the successful messages from the queue and return the failed ones for retry. Setting batch size to 1 (B) avoids the problem but does not scale efficiently and does not fulfill the requirement of batch processing. Manually deleting messages (C) is not supported in the SQS event source mapping model — Lambda manages deletion automatically, and calling DeleteMessage inside a Lambda triggered by an SQS event source mapping can cause double-delete errors. A DLQ (D) on Lambda is for when the entire invocation fails after all retries and applies to asynchronous invocations, not SQS event source mappings.

stem: A social media company stores user activity events in Amazon DynamoDB. The table uses user_id as the partition key and timestamp as the sort key. At peak hours, writes throttle heavily on 1% of user IDs that are extremely active, while 99% of partitions sit idle. The company needs to resolve the hot-partition problem without redesigning the application data model significantly. Which solution best addresses the throttling?
tags: High-cardinality partition keys for balanced partition access in DynamoDB
DynamoDB capacity modes (on-demand, provisioned) and auto scaling
Designing DynamoDB tables for efficient queries (for example, choosing partition keys, sort keys, and indexes)

answers.A: Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode. On-demand mode automatically scales to any traffic level and eliminates throttling on any partition regardless of access patterns.
answers.B: Enable DynamoDB auto scaling with a target utilization of 70% on the provisioned table. Auto scaling will increase capacity in response to the hot partitions within seconds.
answers.C: Create a Global Secondary Index (GSI) on user_id with a different sort key. Writes to the GSI will be distributed more evenly across partitions than the base table.
answers.D: Apply a write-sharding strategy by appending a random suffix (for example, a number between 1 and 10) to the user_id partition key for writes. Use scatter-gather reads across all suffix variants when querying a specific user.

explanation: Write sharding distributes writes for a hot user_id across multiple logical partitions by appending a random suffix. This is the standard DynamoDB technique for resolving hot-partition write throttling without changing the table schema. On-demand capacity (A) does eliminate per-partition throttle limits to a degree but still has a per-partition throughput ceiling (1,000 WCU/second per partition); extremely hot individual partitions can still throttle under on-demand. Auto scaling (B) responds in minutes, not seconds, and cannot react fast enough to instantaneous spikes; it also cannot help a single hot partition exceed its physical limit. A GSI (C) does not change how writes are distributed on the base table partition key — writes to a hot user_id still hit the same physical partition.

stem: A developer is building a reporting feature on a DynamoDB table that stores order records. The table partition key is order_id. The reporting feature must find all orders for a given customer_id sorted by order_date within the last 30 days with high read efficiency. The operations team prohibits scan operations because the table contains 500 million items. Which solution meets the requirements without using Scan?
tags: Amazon DynamoDB keys and indexing (for example, partition key, sort key, global secondary index, local secondary index)
Differences between query and scan operations in DynamoDB
Designing DynamoDB tables for efficient queries (for example, choosing partition keys, sort keys, and indexes)

answers.A: Add a Local Secondary Index (LSI) on the base table with customer_id as the sort key. Query the LSI using a KeyConditionExpression that filters by order_id and customer_id.
answers.B: Create a Global Secondary Index (GSI) with customer_id as the partition key and order_date as the sort key. Query the GSI using a KeyConditionExpression that specifies customer_id and a sort key condition for the last 30 days.
answers.C: Enable DynamoDB Streams on the table and process the stream with a Lambda function that writes customer_id-to-order_id mappings into a separate lookup table. Query the lookup table first, then batch-get items from the base table.
answers.D: Use DynamoDB PartiQL to run a SELECT statement filtered by customer_id and order_date. PartiQL uses an optimized index-aware query planner that avoids full table scans automatically.

explanation: A GSI with customer_id as partition key and order_date as sort key allows an efficient Query operation that retrieves all orders for a customer with a date range condition, which is exactly what the reporting feature needs. No table Scan is involved. An LSI (A) requires the same partition key as the base table (order_id), so it cannot be queried by customer_id alone — the query would still need to know the order_id, which defeats the purpose. A Lambda streams-based lookup table (C) adds significant complexity and introduces eventual consistency lag. DynamoDB PartiQL SELECT without specifying the partition key (D) performs a full table Scan under the hood unless the query can resolve to a primary key or index lookup; filtering by customer_id on the base table would still scan all 500 million items.

stem: A healthcare company must encrypt patient records before writing them to Amazon S3. Each record can be up to 100 MB. The security team mandates that data encryption keys (DEKs) never be stored in plaintext on disk and that the master key never leave AWS KMS. Application latency for encryption must be minimized. Which implementation satisfies all requirements?
tags: AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) API (for example, Encrypt, Decrypt, GenerateDataKey, GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext)
Implementing envelope encryption using AWS KMS and the AWS Encryption SDK

answers.A: Call KMS GenerateDataKey to obtain a plaintext DEK and an encrypted DEK. Use the plaintext DEK to encrypt the record locally with AES-256. Store the encrypted record and the encrypted DEK together in S3. Discard the plaintext DEK from memory after use.
answers.B: Call KMS Encrypt on the full patient record to encrypt it directly using the KMS master key. Store the ciphertext in S3. Use KMS Decrypt to retrieve the plaintext when needed.
answers.C: Call KMS GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext to receive only an encrypted DEK. Use the encrypted DEK directly as the encryption key for the record. Store the record and encrypted DEK in S3.
answers.D: Generate a random AES-256 key locally in the application. Encrypt the patient record with this key. Store the plaintext key in an S3 object with server-side encryption enabled using SSE-KMS, co-located with the encrypted record.

explanation: This is the standard envelope encryption pattern. GenerateDataKey returns both a plaintext DEK (used in memory to encrypt the large record locally) and an encrypted DEK (stored alongside the ciphertext). The plaintext DEK is discarded immediately after use, so it never persists. The master key never leaves KMS. Local symmetric encryption is fast, minimizing latency for large records. Direct KMS Encrypt (B) is limited to data under 4 KB and would be extremely slow for 100 MB records due to round-trip API calls for every record. GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext (C) returns an encrypted DEK that cannot be used directly for encryption without first decrypting it via KMS — it is meant for generating DEKs on one system for use on another. Storing the plaintext key in S3 (D) violates the requirement that plaintext DEKs never be stored on disk, regardless of SSE-KMS on the key object.

stem: A developer in Account A needs to encrypt data using a customer-managed KMS key owned by Account B and store the ciphertext in an S3 bucket in Account A. The developer IAM role is in Account A. What combination of steps is required to allow this cross-account KMS encryption?
tags: AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) API (for example, Encrypt, Decrypt, GenerateDataKey, GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext)
AWS KMS key types (for example, customer-managed keys, AWS managed keys, data keys, key policies)

answers.A: In Account B, add the Account A IAM role ARN to the KMS key resource-based policy granting kms:Encrypt. No changes are needed in Account A because the key policy alone grants cross-account access.
answers.B: In Account A, create an IAM policy on the developer role granting kms:Encrypt on the Account B key ARN. Attach this policy to the role. No changes are needed in Account B because IAM policies in the calling account are sufficient.
answers.C: In Account B, update the KMS key policy to allow the Account A IAM role (or Account A root) access to kms:Encrypt. In Account A, attach an IAM policy to the developer role granting kms:Encrypt on the specific Account B key ARN. Both the key policy and the IAM policy must allow the action.
answers.D: In Account B, create a cross-account IAM role with kms:Encrypt permission on the key. In Account A, configure the developer role to assume this Account B role using sts:AssumeRole before calling KMS. The developer role itself does not need direct KMS permissions.

explanation: AWS KMS cross-account access requires both the key policy in the key-owning account (Account B) to explicitly allow access and an IAM policy in the calling account (Account A) to permit the action. Neither alone is sufficient for cross-account KMS access — the key policy acts as a permission boundary. Option A is incorrect because a key policy alone grants access only if it explicitly allows the Account A root, not individual roles, and even then an IAM policy in Account A is still needed unless the key policy grants access to the Account A root with full delegation. Option B is incorrect because an IAM policy in Account A cannot override or bypass the KMS key policy in Account B. Option D describes a valid alternative pattern but is not what is asked; the developer role would need permission to assume the Account B role, and this adds an extra hop not required for direct cross-account key usage.

stem: A mobile application must authenticate users with their corporate SAML 2.0 identity provider (IdP), then allow the authenticated users to call Amazon S3 and DynamoDB APIs directly from the mobile app using temporary AWS credentials. The solution must not require a backend proxy for AWS API calls. Which Amazon Cognito configuration achieves this?
tags: The comparison of user pools and identity pools in Amazon Cognito
Identity federation (for example, Security Assertion Markup Language [SAML], OpenID Connect [OIDC], Amazon Cognito)
Implementing Amazon Cognito user pools and identity pools

answers.A: Create a Cognito user pool. Configure a SAML IdP in the user pool as a federated identity provider. The user pool will issue temporary AWS credentials that the app uses to call S3 and DynamoDB directly.
answers.B: Create a Cognito identity pool only. Configure SAML 2.0 as a direct authentication provider in the identity pool. The identity pool will exchange the SAML assertion for a JWT token the app uses for AWS API calls.
answers.C: Create a Cognito user pool with a SAML IdP federation. Issue a Cognito user pool JWT to the mobile app. The app passes this JWT directly to S3 and DynamoDB as a bearer token for authorization.
answers.D: Create a Cognito user pool with the SAML IdP configured as a federated identity provider. Create a Cognito identity pool and configure it to accept tokens from the user pool. The mobile app exchanges the user pool token for temporary AWS credentials via the identity pool and uses those credentials to call S3 and DynamoDB directly.

explanation: Cognito user pools handle authentication (including SAML federation) and issue JWTs. Cognito identity pools exchange those JWTs for temporary AWS credentials (via AWS STS) that grant direct access to AWS services like S3 and DynamoDB. The combination of user pool (for auth) plus identity pool (for AWS credential vending) is the correct architecture for direct AWS API access from a mobile app. Option A is wrong because user pools issue JWTs, not temporary IAM credentials — they cannot directly authorize calls to S3 or DynamoDB. Option B is wrong because identity pools do not directly accept SAML assertions from arbitrary enterprise IdPs without a user pool or OIDC token exchange in between. Option C is wrong because S3 and DynamoDB do not accept Cognito user pool JWTs as bearer tokens for authorization.

stem: A single-page application (SPA) built with JavaScript uses Amazon Cognito for authentication. The security team mandates the authorization code flow with PKCE instead of the implicit flow because the SPA cannot securely store a client secret. After authentication, the SPA needs to call a protected REST API hosted on Amazon API Gateway. What is the correct sequence for this flow?
tags: Implementing OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow with PKCE
Bearer tokens (for example, JSON Web Token [JWT], OAuth, AWS Security Token Service [AWS STS])
Using Amazon Cognito Hosted UI for authentication

answers.A: The SPA generates a code_verifier and code_challenge. It redirects to the Cognito Hosted UI with the code_challenge. After login, Cognito redirects back with an authorization code. The SPA exchanges the code and code_verifier for tokens. The SPA uses the access token as a bearer token in the Authorization header when calling the API Gateway endpoint.
answers.B: The SPA generates a code_verifier and code_challenge. It redirects to the Cognito Hosted UI with the code_challenge. After login, Cognito redirects back with an access token in the URL fragment. The SPA extracts the token from the fragment and presents it to API Gateway. The code_verifier is not used in token exchange.
answers.C: The SPA calls the Cognito USER_PASSWORD_AUTH flow directly with the user credentials and receives tokens. It uses the ID token as a bearer token in the Authorization header when calling the API Gateway Cognito authorizer.
answers.D: The SPA generates a code_verifier and code_challenge. It redirects to the Cognito Hosted UI with the code_challenge. After login, Cognito redirects back with an authorization code. The SPA sends the authorization code along with the client secret to exchange for tokens. The access token is then used in API Gateway calls.

explanation: In the authorization code flow with PKCE, the client generates a code_verifier (a random secret) and derives a code_challenge from it. The challenge is sent in the authorization request to the Cognito Hosted UI. After authentication, Cognito returns an authorization code (not tokens) in the redirect. The SPA then exchanges the authorization code plus the original code_verifier (no client secret needed) for tokens at the token endpoint. The access token is then used as a bearer token for API Gateway. Option B describes the implicit flow (tokens in URL fragment), which is the flow the security team explicitly rejected. Option C describes the resource owner password credentials grant, which bypasses the authorization redirect entirely and is not PKCE. Option D incorrectly requires a client secret, which contradicts PKCE usage for public clients like SPAs.

stem: A team deploys a new version of an AWS Lambda function using AWS CodeDeploy with the Canary10Percent5Minutes deployment configuration. After deployment begins, Amazon CloudWatch detects an elevated error rate on the new version within the first 2 minutes. What will CodeDeploy do, and what must the developer have configured in advance for automatic rollback to occur?
tags: AWS CodeDeploy appspec.yml structure and deployment hooks
Lambda deployment strategies (for example, canary, linear, all-at-once) via CodeDeploy
Creating and configuring deployment strategies for Lambda using CodeDeploy

answers.A: CodeDeploy will automatically detect the CloudWatch alarm and roll back immediately without any pre-configuration because canary deployments monitor Lambda error metrics by default. No alarm configuration is needed in the appspec.yml.
answers.B: CodeDeploy will wait the full 5 minutes before evaluating alarms. If the alarm is still triggered at the 5-minute mark, CodeDeploy shifts 0% of additional traffic and marks the deployment failed. The developer must specify the alarm in the Hooks section of appspec.yml.
answers.C: CodeDeploy will automatically roll back the deployment if a CloudWatch alarm enters the ALARM state, provided the developer has configured the alarm in the Alarms section of the deployment group and enabled automatic rollback on alarm in the CodeDeploy deployment group settings.
answers.D: CodeDeploy shifts 10% of traffic to the new version and monitors Lambda function errors internally. If Lambda itself returns errors during the canary period, CodeDeploy rolls back. CloudWatch alarms are only used for EC2 and ECS deployments, not Lambda.

explanation: For Lambda CodeDeploy deployments, automatic rollback on CloudWatch alarm requires the developer to explicitly configure the CloudWatch alarm in the CodeDeploy deployment group (Alarms section) and enable the automatic rollback option when an alarm activates. CodeDeploy then monitors that alarm throughout the deployment and triggers a rollback if it enters ALARM state, even during the canary window. Option A is wrong because CodeDeploy does not auto-discover CloudWatch alarms; they must be explicitly associated with the deployment group. Option B is wrong because CodeDeploy does not wait the full canary interval before evaluating alarms — it monitors continuously. Option D is wrong because CloudWatch alarm-based rollback works for Lambda, ECS, and EC2 CodeDeploy deployments.

stem: A company runs a containerized microservice on Amazon ECS using the Fargate launch type. They want to deploy a new version with zero downtime using AWS CodeDeploy blue/green deployment. Traffic should shift 10% immediately, then the remaining 90% after 5 minutes if no alarms trigger. Which deployment configuration and listener setup achieve this?
tags: Defining CodeDeploy deployment configurations (for example, in-place, blue/green)

answers.A: Use the CodeDeployDefault.ECSCanary10Percent5Minutes deployment configuration. Configure an Application Load Balancer with a production listener on port 443 and a test listener on port 8080. Define both listeners in the CodeDeploy deployment group. CodeDeploy routes 10% of production traffic to the green task set immediately and the remaining 90% after 5 minutes.
answers.B: Use the CodeDeployDefault.ECSLinear10PercentEvery1Minutes deployment configuration. Configure a single ALB listener on port 443. CodeDeploy shifts 10% every minute until 100% is on the new version, totaling 10 intervals.
answers.C: Use the CodeDeployDefault.ECSAllAtOnce deployment configuration. Configure the ALB with a weighted target group rule at 90/10 in the listener rules. CodeDeploy respects the existing listener weights and shifts only the remaining traffic.
answers.D: Use the CodeDeployDefault.ECSCanary10Percent5Minutes deployment configuration. Configure the ECS service with a deployment circuit breaker. The circuit breaker automatically adjusts the canary percentage based on task health checks without requiring a separate ALB test listener.

explanation: ECSCanary10Percent5Minutes shifts 10% of traffic to the green (new) task set immediately, waits 5 minutes, then shifts the remaining 90% if no configured alarms fire. This requires an ALB with a production listener and an optional test listener defined in the CodeDeploy deployment group; CodeDeploy manages the listener rule weights. Option B describes Linear10PercentEvery1Minutes which shifts traffic in equal increments every minute rather than the canary pattern requested. Option C is wrong because ECSAllAtOnce shifts all traffic at once and does not honor pre-existing weighted listener rules for partial shifts. Option D is wrong because the deployment circuit breaker operates on task health (ECS-level) and does not replace the ALB listener configuration required for traffic shifting; additionally, the circuit breaker does not control canary percentages.

stem: A developer is troubleshooting latency spikes in a distributed application. The application uses AWS Lambda to call Amazon DynamoDB and an external REST API. The developer wants to measure the latency of DynamoDB calls and external API calls individually within a single Lambda invocation trace, and wants to filter all traces by a custom attribute called customer_tier. Which X-Ray instrumentation steps are required?
tags: Instrumenting code with AWS X-Ray SDK
Adding annotations and metadata for AWS X-Ray traces

answers.A: Enable X-Ray active tracing on the Lambda function. X-Ray automatically creates subsegments for all outbound DynamoDB and HTTP calls and records their latency. Add custom annotations by calling xray.put_annotation inside the Lambda handler after the DynamoDB and HTTP calls complete.
answers.B: Enable X-Ray active tracing on the Lambda function. Instrument the AWS SDK client calls and external HTTP client calls by wrapping them with the X-Ray SDK captureAWSClient and captureHTTPs methods respectively. Create manual subsegments around each call group if needed. Add customer_tier as an annotation using xray.put_annotation so the attribute is indexed and searchable in the X-Ray console.
answers.C: Enable X-Ray active tracing on the Lambda function. Add customer_tier as X-Ray metadata (not annotation) using xray.put_metadata. Metadata is indexed by X-Ray and searchable via filter expressions in the console, while annotations are only visible in the trace timeline.
answers.D: Deploy the AWS X-Ray daemon as a Lambda layer. The daemon intercepts all outbound SDK calls and HTTP traffic, automatically creating subsegments and indexing all key-value pairs in the request context as annotations without any code changes.

explanation: To capture per-call latency for DynamoDB and external HTTP calls as individual subsegments, the developer must wrap the AWS SDK client with captureAWSClient (or use the patched version) and wrap the HTTP client with captureHTTPs. These create subsegments automatically. To filter by customer_tier in X-Ray filter expressions, the attribute must be added as an annotation (not metadata) because only annotations are indexed and searchable. Option A is partially correct — active tracing does enable Lambda-level tracing — but X-Ray does not automatically create subsegments for all outbound calls without SDK instrumentation. Option C has the annotation vs. metadata distinction reversed: metadata is NOT indexed and is not searchable via filter expressions; annotations are indexed. Option D is wrong because the X-Ray daemon is a trace aggregator/forwarder, not a code interceptor; it does not automatically instrument SDK calls or create subsegments.

stem: An engineering team instruments a high-throughput microservice using AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT). The service receives 50,000 requests per minute. The team wants to trace 5% of requests by default but trace 100% of requests that result in HTTP 5xx errors, without modifying application code after initial instrumentation. Which X-Ray configuration supports this?

answers.A: Set the X-Ray SDK sampling rate to 5% in the application configuration file. Add a try-catch block in the application code that forces a trace flush for requests that throw HTTP 5xx exceptions, effectively capturing 100% of error requests.
answers.B: Configure an X-Ray sampling rule with a fixed rate of 5% and no conditions. Create a second sampling rule with a reservoir of 50,000 per minute and a fixed rate of 100% with a URL path condition matching /error. Errors will match the second rule.
answers.C: Configure the ADOT Collector with a probabilistic sampler at 5%. For 5xx error tracing, deploy a separate Lambda function subscribed to CloudWatch Logs that re-instruments failed request IDs. X-Ray correlates these separate traces automatically.
answers.D: Create an X-Ray sampling rule with a lower priority number, a fixed rate of 5%, and no attribute conditions for default sampling. Create a second X-Ray sampling rule with a higher priority number and a fixed rate of 100% with an http.status attribute condition matching 5xx responses. ADOT respects X-Ray sampling rules via the remote sampler configuration.

explanation: AWS X-Ray custom sampling rules allow attribute-based conditions including HTTP response codes. By configuring a high-priority rule (lower numeric priority value in X-Ray means evaluated first) that matches 5xx responses with 100% rate, and a lower-priority catch-all rule at 5%, all error requests are captured while normal traffic is sampled at 5%. ADOT supports X-Ray remote sampling when the collector is configured with the X-Ray remote sampler, so no code changes are needed after initial instrumentation. Option A requires code changes for each new condition, violating the no-code-change requirement. Option B has the priority logic reversed: the 5xx rule must have a higher priority (lower numeric value) than the default rule to be evaluated first; additionally, matching 5xx errors by URL path is imprecise. Option C introduces significant complexity and does not produce a single trace per request — it creates separate, unrelated traces.

stem: A developer manages a REST API in Amazon API Gateway and needs to deploy a breaking change to a new Lambda integration version. They want to send 10% of live production traffic to the new Lambda version for validation before fully promoting it, without creating a separate API stage. Which API Gateway feature allows this?
tags: Amazon API Gateway deployment strategies (for example, canary deployments)
Configuring canary and blue/green deployments in API Gateway

answers.A: Create a new API Gateway stage named canary pointing to the new Lambda version. Configure an Application Load Balancer with weighted target groups that route 10% of requests to the canary stage and 90% to the production stage.
answers.B: Deploy a new API Gateway version (v2) pointing to the new Lambda version. Use Amazon Route 53 weighted routing policies to split 10% of DNS traffic to the v2 endpoint and 90% to the v1 endpoint.
answers.C: Enable a canary release deployment on the existing production stage. Set the canary traffic percentage to 10% and deploy the updated integration (pointing to the new Lambda version) as the canary. API Gateway routes 10% of production stage requests to the canary deployment and 90% to the base deployment.
answers.D: Create a Lambda function alias that weights 10% to the new version and 90% to the old version. Update the API Gateway stage integration to point to the Lambda alias ARN. API Gateway will automatically split traffic according to the Lambda alias weights.

explanation: API Gateway canary release deployments allow a percentage of traffic on an existing stage to be routed to a new deployment without creating a separate stage. The canary is configured on the stage itself, and the developer sets the percentage. This meets the requirement of no new stage. Using an ALB (A) requires infrastructure outside API Gateway and creates routing complexity not needed here. Route 53 weighted routing (B) does require separate endpoints and does not operate at the stage/deployment level within API Gateway. Lambda alias weighting (D) does provide traffic splitting at the Lambda level, but it splits at the Lambda invocation layer, not the API Gateway deployment layer — it also does not test configuration changes in API Gateway itself (such as mapping templates, models, or authorizers in the new deployment).

stem: An API hosted on Amazon API Gateway is receiving traffic bursts that exceed its throttle limits. Some clients report HTTP 429 errors while others report HTTP 502 errors from the same endpoint during the same burst. The developer needs to understand what each error type indicates. Which statements correctly describe the causes of each error code in the API Gateway context?
tags: API Gateway error types (for example, 4xx client errors, 5xx server errors)
Amazon API Gateway throttling and usage plans

answers.A: HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) is returned by API Gateway when a request exceeds configured throttle limits (either account-level, stage-level, or usage plan limits). HTTP 502 (Bad Gateway) is returned by API Gateway when the backend integration (such as Lambda) returns an invalid response, times out, or is unreachable.
answers.B: HTTP 429 is returned by API Gateway when the client sends a malformed request payload that fails schema validation. HTTP 502 is returned when API Gateway throttle limits are exceeded at the regional level.
answers.C: HTTP 429 is returned by API Gateway when the AWS Lambda function returns a handled error object. HTTP 502 is returned by API Gateway when the Lambda function is throttled by Lambda reserved concurrency limits.
answers.D: HTTP 429 is returned by both API Gateway throttling and Lambda throttling, and these cannot be distinguished from the client side. HTTP 502 is returned when the API Gateway WAF blocks a request for a security rule violation.

explanation: HTTP 429 in API Gateway means the request was rejected at the gateway level due to throttling (rate limiting). This can come from account-level throttling, stage-level settings, or usage plan quotas. HTTP 502 Bad Gateway means API Gateway received an invalid or unexpected response from the backend integration — most commonly a Lambda function that returned a malformed response, an unhandled exception causing an invalid payload, or a backend timeout. Option B incorrectly reverses the two codes. Option C is wrong: Lambda returning a handled error (a well-formed error object) results in HTTP 200 from API Gateway with an error payload; Lambda throttling results in HTTP 429 from Lambda which API Gateway surfaces as HTTP 429 or 502 depending on the integration type. Option D is partially inaccurate because WAF blocks return HTTP 403 (Forbidden), not 502.

stem: A developer stores RDS PostgreSQL database credentials in AWS Secrets Manager. The DBA team requires automatic rotation every 30 days. During rotation, in-flight application connections must not fail. The developer writes a rotation Lambda function using the standard rotation template. Which actions must the rotation Lambda perform during the createNewSecret and setSecret rotation steps to ensure zero-downtime rotation?
tags: Secrets management (for example, AWS Secrets Manager, AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store)
Rotating credentials using AWS Secrets Manager

answers.A: In createNewSecret: generate a new password and immediately overwrite the current secret version with the new password. In setSecret: call the RDS API to update the database master password to match. Applications will receive the new credentials on the next GetSecretValue call.
answers.B: In createNewSecret: generate a new password and store it as a new secret version with the AWSPENDING staging label, keeping the AWSCURRENT version unchanged. In setSecret: use the AWSPENDING credentials to create or update the database user with the new password. Applications continue reading AWSCURRENT and are unaffected until finishSecret promotes AWSPENDING to AWSCURRENT.
answers.C: In createNewSecret: generate a new password and store it with the AWSCURRENT label to make it immediately available. In setSecret: update the database password to match AWSCURRENT. Applications will automatically pick up the new password with no downtime because Secrets Manager caches the current version.
answers.D: In createNewSecret: call the RDS ModifyDBInstance API to set a new master password, then store the new credentials as AWSPENDING. In setSecret: verify connectivity using the new credentials. The database update is already complete from createNewSecret so no further action is needed.

explanation: Secrets Manager uses a four-step rotation process: createNewSecret, setSecret, testSecret, and finishSecret. To achieve zero downtime, createNewSecret must create a new secret version labeled AWSPENDING without changing AWSCURRENT — so existing applications continue reading the old credentials uninterrupted. setSecret then applies the AWSPENDING credentials to the actual database (creating or updating the database user). Only when finishSecret runs does Secrets Manager atomically relabel AWSPENDING as AWSCURRENT. Option A overwrites the current secret immediately, causing applications that call GetSecretValue to receive the new password before the database has been updated, breaking connections. Option C sets the new password as AWSCURRENT before the database is updated, causing the same race condition. Option D calls RDS to change the master password in createNewSecret before the secret is stored, violating the rotation order and potentially leaving the secret out of sync if setSecret fails.

stem: A Lambda function reads a database password stored in AWS Secrets Manager on every invocation by calling GetSecretValue inside the handler function. A code review identifies this as a performance and cost concern. What is the recommended approach to reduce Secrets Manager API calls while keeping the cached secret reasonably fresh?
tags: Secrets management (for example, AWS Secrets Manager, AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store)
Referencing AWS Secrets Manager secrets in Lambda environment variables and application code

answers.A: Store the database password in a Lambda environment variable at deployment time. Environment variables are encrypted at rest by KMS and eliminate the need for Secrets Manager API calls entirely. Update the environment variable whenever the password is rotated.
answers.B: Call GetSecretValue at the start of each handler invocation but implement a client-side TTL cache in the handler scope. If the cached value is less than 60 seconds old, skip the API call. Reset the cache between Lambda cold starts.
answers.C: Move the GetSecretValue call outside the handler function to the Lambda initialization code (module-level or static block). Cache the secret value in a module-level variable. The secret is fetched once per execution environment initialization (cold start) and reused for the lifetime of the warm container, reducing API calls significantly.
answers.D: Replace AWS Secrets Manager with AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store SecureString. Parameter Store GetParameter calls are free for standard parameters and do not require caching because they have no per-call cost.

explanation: The recommended pattern is to initialize the Secrets Manager client and fetch the secret outside the handler in the Lambda initialization code. This runs once per execution environment (cold start) and the secret is reused across all warm invocations of that environment, dramatically reducing API call frequency and latency. Option A is a security anti-pattern: storing credentials as Lambda environment variables persists them as plaintext in the function configuration and requires manual updates when rotated, negating Secrets Manager's rotation benefit. Option B implements caching inside the handler, which means the cache resets between invocations if the execution environment is recycled — this still calls GetSecretValue on every cold start and on the first warm invocation after expiry for each request; it is less efficient than initialization code caching. Option D is partially valid as an alternative service but does not address the architectural question of where to cache, and advanced Parameter Store GetParameter calls are not free for high-throughput use.

stem: A developer creates an AWS CodePipeline pipeline that pulls source from CodeCommit, runs unit tests in CodeBuild, and deploys to production only after a manual approval. The team wants the CodeBuild stage to fail automatically if test coverage drops below 80%, preventing promotion to the approval stage. Which buildspec.yml configuration correctly implements this gate?
tags: Automated software testing (for example, unit testing, mock testing, integration testing)
Branches and actions in AWS CodePipeline

answers.A: In the build phase of buildspec.yml, run the test suite and capture the coverage percentage. Add a shell command that reads the coverage output and exits with a non-zero exit code if coverage is below 80% (for example, awk or python -c). CodeBuild marks the build failed when any phase command exits non-zero, which fails the pipeline stage and blocks the approval action.
answers.B: In the post_build phase of buildspec.yml, add a shell command that checks coverage and calls aws codepipeline put-job-failure-result if coverage is below 80%. This triggers CodePipeline to mark the stage as failed and stop execution.
answers.C: In the reports section of buildspec.yml, define a test coverage report with a coverage threshold of 80. CodeBuild automatically fails the build if the measured coverage falls below the configured threshold without any shell commands.
answers.D: Add a condition in the CodePipeline stage configuration using a VariableNamespace. Reference the CodeBuild output variable COVERAGE_PCT in the approval stage condition. Pipeline will skip the approval action and halt if the variable is below 80.

explanation: The most reliable way to gate a CodeBuild stage on coverage is to emit a non-zero exit code from a build phase command when coverage is below the threshold. CodeBuild treats any non-zero exit code from a phase command as a build failure, which causes CodePipeline to mark that stage as failed and stop further execution. Option B using aws codepipeline put-job-failure-result is only applicable for custom action types with Lambda or Jenkins worker integrations, not standard CodeBuild actions. Option C is partially correct: CodeBuild does support coverage thresholds in the reports section, but this feature sets the build's overall status to failed based on the threshold — this is valid, but option A is more explicit and universally supported. Option D is incorrect because CodePipeline approval actions do not support variable-based conditional execution in standard pipeline configurations; stopping a pipeline requires the prior stage to fail or a custom lambda action.

stem: A developer uses AWS SAM to build a serverless application with a Lambda function triggered by an SQS event source mapping. During local development, the developer needs to test the Lambda function locally without deploying to AWS, passing a sample SQS event payload. The SAM template must configure the SQS event source mapping with a batch size of 5 and a maximum concurrency of 2. Which combination of SAM CLI command and template property achieves local testing of the function?
tags: AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM) specification
AWS SAM local (for local testing of Lambda functions)
Running AWS SAM local for local testing

answers.A: Use sam local start-lambda to start a local Lambda endpoint. Send an SQS-formatted event payload by calling the local endpoint with the AWS CLI invoke-local command. In the SAM template, add BatchSize: 5 and MaximumConcurrency: 2 under the SQS event Properties.
answers.B: Use sam local invoke with a --event flag pointing to a JSON file containing a sample SQS event payload. In the SAM template, configure the SQS event source under Events with BatchSize: 5 and FunctionResponseTypes: [ReportBatchItemFailures] to achieve batch control. MaximumConcurrency is not a valid SAM property.
answers.C: Use sam local start-api to expose the Lambda function as a REST endpoint. POST a JSON body representing the SQS event to the local endpoint. In the SAM template, set BatchSize: 5 and MaximumConcurrency: 2 under the SQS event Properties.
answers.D: Use sam local invoke with a --event flag pointing to a JSON file containing a sample SQS event payload. In the SAM template, configure the SQS event source under Events with Type: SQS and Properties including BatchSize: 5 and ScalingConfig with MaximumConcurrency: 2. SAM translates ScalingConfig into the Lambda event source mapping configuration.

explanation: sam local invoke is the correct command to invoke a Lambda function locally with a specific event payload without deploying to AWS. The --event flag specifies a JSON file with the event. In AWS SAM templates, the SQS event source BatchSize is set directly under Properties, and the maximum concurrency for an SQS event source mapping is configured via ScalingConfig: MaximumConcurrency in the SAM template Properties, which SAM translates to the Lambda event source mapping configuration. Option A describes sam local start-lambda which starts a persistent local endpoint for repeated invocations but requires calling it programmatically; invoke-local is not a valid AWS CLI command. Option B incorrectly states that MaximumConcurrency is not a valid SAM property — it is, via ScalingConfig. Option C describes sam local start-api, which only works for API Gateway-triggered functions, not SQS events.

stem: A developer needs to emit custom business metrics from a high-throughput AWS Lambda function invoked 10,000 times per minute without the latency and cost of individual CloudWatch PutMetricData API calls. The metrics must be queryable as standard CloudWatch Metrics for alarms and also searchable as structured log data using CloudWatch Logs Insights. Which approach meets all requirements?
tags: Application metrics (for example, custom metrics, embedded metric format)
Amazon CloudWatch Logs, metrics, and alarms
Implementing code that emits custom metrics

answers.A: Use the boto3 CloudWatch client to call PutMetricData in a background thread within the Lambda handler. Running it asynchronously in a thread prevents added latency to the main handler response while still publishing each metric.
answers.B: Use the CloudWatch Embedded Metric Format (EMF) by writing structured JSON log lines that include the _aws EMF metadata block to stdout. CloudWatch Logs automatically extracts the metric values and publishes them as CloudWatch Metrics. The same log lines are also queryable via CloudWatch Logs Insights.
answers.C: Write metrics as JSON objects to an SQS queue at the end of each Lambda invocation. A separate consumer Lambda function aggregates the queue messages and calls PutMetricData in batches of 20, reducing API call volume. CloudWatch Logs Insights queries the consumer Lambda logs for metric values.
answers.D: Enable Lambda enhanced monitoring via AWS Lambda Powertools Metrics with batch mode. Powertools aggregates all metric values within a single invocation and flushes them as a single PutMetricData call at the end of the handler, reducing API calls to one per invocation.

explanation: CloudWatch Embedded Metric Format (EMF) is specifically designed for this scenario. By writing structured JSON with the _aws metadata block to stdout, Lambda automatically forwards the logs to CloudWatch Logs. CloudWatch asynchronously extracts the embedded metric values and publishes them as standard CloudWatch Metrics — with zero additional API calls and zero added invocation latency. The same log data is queryable via CloudWatch Logs Insights. Option A still makes PutMetricData API calls (one per invocation in a thread), incurring cost and potential Lambda execution time extension. Option C adds significant architectural complexity (SQS queue, consumer Lambda) and the Logs Insights query model does not provide real-time CloudWatch Metrics. Option D using AWS Lambda Powertools Metrics does batch metrics within an invocation and flush via PutMetricData, but at 10,000 invocations per minute this still makes 10,000 PutMetricData calls per minute — the same throughput problem — whereas EMF avoids all direct PutMetricData calls.

stem: A company runs a microservices application on Amazon EC2 instances managed by AWS CodeDeploy. During a deployment, the team needs to run a health-check script after the new application version is installed but before the load balancer starts routing traffic to the instance. The script must verify database connectivity and confirm that critical background processes are running. If the script exits with a non-zero code, the deployment must automatically roll back. Which AppSpec file hook and CodeDeploy configuration should the team use to implement this requirement?
tags: AWS CodeDeploy AppSpec file structure for EC2/on-premises and Lambda deployments
AWS CodeDeploy deployment lifecycle hooks (BeforeInstall, AfterInstall, ApplicationStart, ValidateService, etc.)

answers.A: Place the health-check script in the BeforeInstall hook. Set the deployment group's automatic rollback configuration to roll back on deployment failure.
answers.B: Place the health-check script in the ValidateService hook. Set the deployment group's automatic rollback configuration to roll back on deployment failure.
answers.C: Place the health-check script in the AfterInstall hook. Set the deployment group's automatic rollback configuration to roll back on deployment failure.
answers.D: Place the health-check script in the ApplicationStart hook. Set the deployment group's automatic rollback configuration to roll back on deployment failure.

explanation: ValidateService is the final lifecycle hook in a CodeDeploy EC2 deployment and runs after the application has started, making it the correct place to verify that the new version is healthy before CodeDeploy completes the deployment. Enabling automatic rollback on deployment failure means CodeDeploy will roll back if the ValidateService script exits non-zero. BeforeInstall runs before files are copied and cannot verify the new version. AfterInstall runs after files are copied but before the application starts, so the new processes are not yet running. ApplicationStart runs as the application is being started, but the service may not have fully initialized and database connectivity cannot yet be confirmed reliably.

stem: A financial services company deploys a customer-facing AWS Lambda function that processes payment transactions. The team wants to shift 10% of production traffic to the new function version for five minutes before routing all traffic, and automatically roll back if a CloudWatch alarm fires during that window. Which CodeDeploy deployment configuration and rollback mechanism should the team configure?
tags: Lambda deployment configurations and traffic shifting
Deployment strategies: blue/green, canary, rolling, in-place, linear
Implementing automated rollbacks based on CloudWatch alarms

answers.A: Use the CodeLinear10PercentEvery1Minute deployment configuration. Configure a CodeDeploy deployment group alarm that references the CloudWatch alarm to trigger rollback.
answers.B: Use the LambdaAllAtOnce deployment configuration. Configure a CloudWatch alarm action that invokes a Lambda function to call the CodeDeploy StopDeployment API.
answers.C: Use the CodeDeployDefault.LambdaCanary10Percent5Minutes deployment configuration. Configure a CodeDeploy deployment group alarm that references the CloudWatch alarm to trigger rollback.
answers.D: Use the CodeDeployDefault.LambdaLinear10PercentEvery3Minutes deployment configuration. Configure a CodeDeploy deployment group alarm that references the CloudWatch alarm to trigger rollback.

explanation: CodeDeployDefault.LambdaCanary10Percent5Minutes shifts exactly 10% of traffic to the new version, waits 5 minutes, then shifts the remaining 90%—matching the requirement. Configuring a deployment group alarm that references the CloudWatch alarm causes CodeDeploy to automatically roll back if the alarm enters ALARM state during the bake period.
