stem: A legal tech company uses an LLM-as-judge approach with a GPT-based evaluator to score its Amazon Bedrock-powered contract analysis system. The evaluation pipeline rates 90% of outputs as high quality. When the same outputs are reviewed by human lawyers, only 60% meet the quality bar. Which limitation of LLM-as-judge evaluation best explains this gap, and what is the recommended mitigation?
tags: LLM-as-judge evaluation approaches and their limitations
Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation capabilities (for example, automated evaluation, human evaluation, custom evaluation tasks)
Human evaluation frameworks (for example, preference ranking, Likert scale scoring)
Setting up LLM-as-judge evaluation pipelines to automate quality assessment at scale

answers.A: The LLM-as-judge uses the same foundation model as the chatbot, creating a self-consistency bias where the judge model systematically rates outputs from its own distribution as high quality. The mitigation is to use a different independent model as the judge and calibrate it against periodic human expert labels.
answers.B: The evaluation sample size is too small for the automated pipeline to be representative. The team should scale automated evaluation to at least 10,000 examples and use an ensemble of multiple judge models.
answers.C: Human lawyers apply stricter formatting and citation requirements not captured in the evaluation rubric. The mitigation is to add formatting and citation accuracy checks to the automated pipeline dimensions.
answers.D: The LLM judge evaluates too many dimensions simultaneously, causing score dilution across the three categories. The team should create a separate single-dimension judge for each evaluation criterion.

explanation: Option A is correct. When the LLM judge shares a model family or is identical to the system under evaluation, it exhibits self-consistency bias — it tends to score outputs from its own distribution highly because they match its internal priors about what constitutes a good response, independent of actual accuracy on the legal domain. Using an independent, different model as judge and anchoring scores against periodic human expert labels is the standard mitigation. Option B sample size does not explain a systematic 30-point gap between automated and human scores; increasing examples would not change the bias direction. Option C is a plausible partial explanation but formatting checks alone would not close a 30-point quality gap driven by substantive legal accuracy issues. Option D dimension separation improves interpretability but does not address the fundamental bias in how the judge model scores outputs.

tags: Data ingestion and preprocessing for generative AI (for example, chunking strategies, document parsing, metadata extraction)
Data types and formats used in generative AI pipelines (for example, unstructured text, PDFs, images, audio, structured tabular data)
AWS data services relevant to generative AI pipelines (for example, Amazon S3, AWS Glue, Amazon Kinesis, Amazon OpenSearch Service)
Designing data preprocessing pipelines for generative AI applications using AWS services

answers.A: Use Amazon Comprehend to extract named entities from raw OCR text, then store entities in Amazon DynamoDB alongside original text chunks to support hybrid retrieval at query time.
answers.B: Use Amazon Textract with the tables and forms extraction feature to parse scanned PDFs, preserving table structure as structured key-value data. Store the structured output in Amazon S3, then ingest into Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases for embedding and retrieval.
answers.C: Use AWS Glue DataBrew to clean and normalize OCR text output by applying column-split transforms to reconstruct table rows before passing the text to the embedding pipeline.
answers.D: Re-scan all PDFs at higher DPI to improve OCR source quality, then rerun the existing text extraction pipeline with the same chunking strategy on the higher-resolution scans.

explanation: Option B is correct. Amazon Textract is purpose-built to extract structured data from scanned documents including tables, forms, and key-value pairs. Its tables API reconstructs row-column structure from scanned PDFs that plain OCR flattens into unstructured text. Storing this structured output in Amazon S3 and ingesting into Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases preserves the relational context needed for faithful retrieval. Option A Amazon Comprehend extracts entities but does not reconstruct table structure from OCR-flattened text, so critical tabular relationships remain lost. Option C AWS Glue DataBrew column-split transforms require structured delimiters; scanned OCR text does not provide reliable column delimiters, making reconstruction unreliable. Option D higher DPI improves image resolution but does not change the fact that the existing pipeline discards table structure during text extraction.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: A retail company ingests point-of-sale transaction data into an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base for a store-operations assistant. The data contains customer names, email addresses, and partial payment card numbers. The data engineering team must ensure PII is removed before embedding and storage, and the pipeline must scale to millions of records per day. Which architecture best meets the PII removal and scale requirements using AWS-managed services?
tags: Data privacy and security considerations for AI training and inference data
Data ingestion and preprocessing for generative AI (for example, chunking strategies, document parsing, metadata extraction)
AWS data services relevant to generative AI pipelines (for example, Amazon S3, AWS Glue, Amazon Kinesis, Amazon OpenSearch Service)
Applying appropriate data anonymization or redaction techniques before using data for AI training

answers.A: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to stream transactions to Amazon S3. Configure a Lambda data transformation within Firehose to call Amazon Macie for PII detection and redact fields before data lands in S3, then sync to Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.
answers.B: Ingest transactions into Amazon S3. Use an AWS Glue ETL job to call Amazon Comprehend DetectPiiEntities on each record, redact identified PII fields, and write cleaned data to a separate S3 prefix. Configure Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to ingest from the cleaned prefix.
answers.C: Ingest transactions directly into Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with an Amazon Bedrock Guardrails sensitive information redaction policy applied at query time to prevent PII from appearing in model responses.
answers.D: Stream transactions through Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to an Amazon ECS container running a custom PII scrubber, then write cleaned records to S3 for ingestion into Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.

explanation: Option B is correct. AWS Glue ETL jobs scale horizontally to handle millions of records per day with minimal operational overhead. Amazon Comprehend DetectPiiEntities is the purpose-built managed service for PII detection in text, and writing cleaned records to a separate S3 prefix before Knowledge Base ingestion ensures PII never enters the vector store. Option A Amazon Macie is designed for PII discovery and data lake security scanning, not for real-time record-level redaction within a Firehose transformation; it also adds latency and cost per record. Option C Bedrock Guardrails redaction at query time leaves raw PII in the embedded knowledge base, which violates the requirement to remove PII before storage. Option D a custom ECS scrubber requires building and maintaining the PII detection logic rather than using a managed service.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: A multinational corporation runs Amazon Bedrock workloads across development, staging, and production AWS accounts within an AWS Organizations structure. The security team requires that only approved foundation models can be invoked in the production account, that all model invocations are auditable, and that developers in the development account cannot invoke production Bedrock endpoints. Which combination of controls enforces all three requirements?
tags: Identity and access management for generative AI services (for example, IAM roles, resource-based policies, service control policies)
AWS CloudTrail and Amazon Bedrock Model Invocation Logging for audit trails
Designing multi-account architectures for separating generative AI development, staging, and production environments
Designing least-privilege IAM policies for Amazon Bedrock and Amazon SageMaker AI access

answers.A: Apply an AWS Organizations Service Control Policy to the production account that denies bedrock:InvokeModel for all model ARNs except the approved list. Enable AWS CloudTrail data events for Amazon Bedrock in the production account. Use IAM permission boundaries in the development account to prevent developers from assuming roles in production.
answers.B: Use IAM resource-based policies on Amazon Bedrock in the production account to restrict model invocations to approved ARNs. Enable Amazon CloudWatch alarms to alert on unauthorized invocations. Use AWS IAM Identity Center to separate developer access between accounts.
answers.C: Deploy AWS Config rules in the production account to detect and auto-remediate invocations of unapproved models. Use AWS CloudTrail for auditability. Apply IAM permission boundaries to production roles to block developer access from the development account.
answers.D: Use VPC endpoint policies on the Amazon Bedrock VPC endpoint in the production account to restrict which model ARNs can be invoked. Enable CloudTrail for audit logging. Use separate IAM identity providers for each account to prevent cross-account role assumption.

explanation: Option A is correct. An AWS Organizations SCP applied to the production account is a preventive control that denies bedrock:InvokeModel calls for non-approved model ARNs regardless of any IAM policy in the account — it cannot be overridden by account-level admins. AWS CloudTrail data events for Amazon Bedrock provide a tamper-evident, account-level audit trail of all invocations. IAM permission boundaries in the development account constrain what roles developers can assume, preventing them from creating roles with cross-account production access. Option B IAM resource-based policies do not currently apply to Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel in the same way as S3 bucket policies; CloudWatch alarms are detective, not preventive. Option C AWS Config rules are detective and remediation is asynchronous — unapproved invocations can occur before remediation. Option D VPC endpoint policies restrict traffic to Bedrock through that endpoint but do not prevent direct invocations through other network paths.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: A company's Amazon Bedrock application calls an external third-party API using credentials stored as environment variables in an AWS Lambda function. A security review identifies this as a credentials exposure risk. The team must migrate to a secrets management solution that rotates credentials automatically and prevents plaintext credentials from appearing in application code or environment variables. Which solution meets these requirements with the least operational overhead?
tags: AWS Secrets Manager and AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store for API key and credential management
Data security controls for generative AI (for example, encryption at rest and in transit, AWS KMS, VPC endpoints)
Identity and access management for generative AI services (for example, IAM roles, resource-based policies, service control policies)
Implementing data loss prevention controls to prevent sensitive data from being sent to foundation models

answers.A: Store the credentials in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store as a SecureString parameter. Update the Lambda function to retrieve the parameter at runtime using the SSM API. Configure automatic rotation using a custom Lambda rotator function attached to the parameter.
answers.B: Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager. Update the Lambda function to retrieve the secret at runtime using the Secrets Manager API. Enable automatic rotation using the Secrets Manager built-in rotation mechanism for the third-party API credentials.
answers.C: Encrypt the credentials using AWS KMS and store the ciphertext as a Lambda environment variable. Decrypt the ciphertext at runtime in the Lambda function code using the KMS Decrypt API call.
answers.D: Store the credentials in an Amazon S3 object protected by a bucket policy restricting access. Grant the Lambda execution role read access to the S3 object and load the credentials at Lambda cold start.

explanation: Option B is correct. AWS Secrets Manager natively supports automatic credential rotation for many third-party services and provides a managed API for runtime retrieval without plaintext exposure. It removes the need to build or maintain a custom rotation mechanism. Option A AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store SecureString does not support automatic rotation natively — the question specifies automatic rotation — and a custom rotator Lambda adds operational overhead. Option C storing ciphertext in environment variables still exposes the ciphertext to anyone with Lambda configuration access and requires bespoke key management; it does not provide rotation. Option D S3 storage for credentials is non-standard, lacks native rotation, and introduces S3 access latency at cold start.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: A travel company builds a multi-turn booking assistant using Amazon Bedrock Agents. Users report that when a conversation exceeds 20 exchanges, the agent forgets destination preferences stated at the beginning of the session. The agent currently uses the default session memory configuration. The company wants to preserve user preferences across long sessions and between sessions without building a custom memory store. Which Amazon Bedrock Agents capability should the team enable and configure?
tags: Amazon Bedrock Agents configuration (for example, action groups, knowledge bases, orchestration strategy, memory)
Agentic AI design patterns (for example, ReAct, plan-and-execute, multi-agent orchestration)
Designing and implementing Amazon Bedrock Agents with action groups backed by AWS Lambda functions

answers.A: Enable Amazon Bedrock Agents session memory with a memory window spanning the full conversation, and configure memory summarization so the agent stores a condensed summary of user preferences that persists across subsequent sessions.
answers.B: Switch to a foundation model with a 200,000-token context window so the entire conversation history fits within a single inference call, preventing the agent from losing information stated early in the session.
answers.C: Implement a custom memory store in Amazon DynamoDB where the orchestrating application reads and injects conversation summaries as additional context into each new Bedrock Agent invocation.
answers.D: Configure the agent knowledge base to store conversation history as documents, and rely on knowledge base retrieval to surface relevant prior user preferences at each conversational turn.

explanation: Option A is correct. Amazon Bedrock Agents supports a native memory feature that maintains a summarized memory of conversation history across turns and across session boundaries. Enabling memory and configuring its summarization capability allows user preferences from earlier in a long session — or from previous sessions — to be preserved without any custom infrastructure. Option B using a larger context window prevents truncation within a single inference call but does not persist preferences between sessions and incurs much higher token costs for long histories. Option C a custom DynamoDB store meets the functional requirement but contradicts the constraint of not building a custom memory store. Option D the knowledge base is designed for document-based factual retrieval, not for dynamic per-user session memory; storing conversation history as documents creates indexing latency and retrieval noise.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: A software company serves an internal code-review assistant powered by Amazon Bedrock. Usage analytics show a consistent 500 requests per hour between 9 AM and 6 PM on business days, with virtually no usage outside those hours. Each request processes approximately 2,000 input tokens and 500 output tokens. The company wants to minimize monthly cost without affecting response quality. Which Amazon Bedrock pricing strategy should the company adopt?
tags: Provisioned throughput in Amazon Bedrock and when to use it vs. on-demand
Cost models for generative AI services on AWS (for example, on-demand token pricing, provisioned throughput, model customization costs)
Selecting provisioned throughput vs. on-demand mode based on traffic patterns and cost requirements
Latency vs. throughput trade-offs for different application patterns

answers.A: Use on-demand inference for all traffic because the usage pattern is predictable but the commitment period for provisioned throughput exceeds the expected project lifetime.
answers.B: Purchase provisioned throughput sized for the 500 requests-per-hour peak volume on a 1-month term, covering the business-hours window. Route all business-hours traffic through the provisioned endpoint to benefit from lower effective per-token cost at sustained volume.
answers.C: Purchase provisioned throughput for the peak volume on a 6-month term to maximize the per-unit discount, and configure an Amazon EventBridge schedule to switch to on-demand mode outside business hours to avoid charges during idle periods.
answers.D: Implement semantic caching with Amazon ElastiCache so repeated code-review queries are served from cache, reducing effective on-demand inference volume and cost without any throughput commitment.

explanation: Option B is correct. The usage pattern is predictable and sustained at 500 requests per hour during 9-hour business-day windows. Provisioned throughput in Amazon Bedrock offers lower effective per-token cost than on-demand at sustained moderate-to-high volumes, and a 1-month term minimizes commitment risk. Sizing to the consistent peak covers all traffic without over-provisioning. Option A on-demand inference is more cost-effective only for unpredictable or very-low-volume workloads; a consistent 500 RPH is well within the range where provisioned throughput breaks even. Option C a 6-month term maximizes discount but — critically — provisioned throughput in Amazon Bedrock is billed continuously regardless of usage, so charges accrue during nights and weekends when there is no traffic; this increases total cost, not reduces it. Option D code-review queries are highly unique per code submission, so semantic cache hit rates would be very low, providing minimal cost savings.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: A knowledge management platform ingests user manuals that follow a strict hierarchical structure: product, chapter, section, and subsection. Users ask questions that span multiple sections within a chapter. Fixed-size chunking at 256 tokens breaks sections across chunk boundaries, reducing retrieval coherence. The platform uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Which chunking strategy best preserves the document hierarchy for this use case?
tags: Chunking strategies and their impact on retrieval quality (for example, fixed-size, semantic, hierarchical chunking)
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases configuration and capabilities
RAG pipeline components (for example, document ingestion, chunking, embedding, vector storage, retrieval, augmentation, generation)
Selecting appropriate chunking strategies and embedding models based on document types and retrieval requirements

answers.A: Use fixed-size chunking with a chunk size matching the average subsection length, and add a 10% overlap between adjacent chunks to reduce boundary fragmentation.
answers.B: Use semantic chunking with a sentence-boundary embedding model to detect natural topic shifts, allowing chunk boundaries to align with semantic transitions in the manual.
answers.C: Use hierarchical chunking configured to split on document structure markers such as product, chapter, section, and subsection headings, creating parent chunks at the chapter level and child chunks at the section level for fine-grained retrieval with broad context.
answers.D: Preprocess each manual into a flat list of question-answer pairs generated by an LLM, then embed the Q-and-A pairs as individual chunks for direct retrieval alignment with user queries.

explanation: Option C is correct. Hierarchical chunking explicitly maps to the document's own structural hierarchy (product, chapter, section, subsection). By creating chapter-level parent chunks and section-level child chunks, the system retrieves precise child chunks by vector similarity while returning the enclosing chapter context to the LLM. This directly addresses questions spanning multiple sections within a chapter. Option A fixed-size chunking aligned to subsection length does not respect heading boundaries and overlaps only partially reduce semantic fragmentation; it does not solve cross-section questions. Option B semantic chunking is useful for unstructured prose without explicit headings; for documents with strict hierarchy, explicit structure-aware splitting is more reliable. Option D converting manuals to Q&A pairs before embedding loses the original narrative context and works only if the preprocessing LLM generates questions matching real user intent, which is not guaranteed.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: A company uses Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation to assess the quality of its customer support chatbot. The evaluation uses an automated LLM-as-judge pipeline with a 1-5 Likert scale for helpfulness, accuracy, and tone. The evaluation model is the same foundation model powering the chatbot. Post-deployment user satisfaction surveys show scores significantly below the automated evaluation scores. Which design flaw most likely explains the gap?
tags: LLM-as-judge evaluation approaches and their limitations
Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation capabilities (for example, automated evaluation, human evaluation, custom evaluation tasks)
Human evaluation frameworks (for example, preference ranking, Likert scale scoring)
Building regression test suites to detect quality degradation after model or prompt updates

answers.A: The evaluation dataset is too small to produce statistically representative scores. The team should expand the evaluation set to match production traffic volume before comparing automated and satisfaction scores.
answers.B: The LLM judge and the chatbot share the same foundation model, introducing self-serving bias where the model rates its own outputs favorably. The team should use a different model as the judge and calibrate automated scores against a held-out human evaluation set.
answers.C: The Likert scale dimensions do not capture the full scope of user satisfaction, which may depend on resolution speed and escalation rate. The team should add task-completion rate as an additional automated metric.
answers.D: The automated evaluation uses simulated test conversations that do not reflect the distribution of real user queries. The team should replace simulated prompts with a random sample of production conversations.

explanation: Option B is correct. Using the same foundation model as both the chatbot and the LLM judge introduces self-serving (positional or model-identity) bias: the evaluator model has the same priors and stylistic tendencies as the system under evaluation, so it systematically rates its own output patterns as high quality. This inflates automated scores relative to user satisfaction, which is assessed against real-world resolution of problems. Using a different, independent model as the judge and calibrating against human ground truth is the direct mitigation. Option A dataset size could explain variance but not a systematic directional gap between automated and satisfaction scores. Option C missing dimensions in the rubric is a partial explanation but does not account for the systematic over-inflation of all three existing dimensions. Option D using production conversations is a good practice but the core issue is judge model identity bias, not prompt distribution mismatch.

stem: A retail company uses AWS DMS to replicate changes from an on-premises Oracle database to Amazon S3 for analytics. The analytics team reports that the S3 data lake is missing some DELETE operations and late-arriving UPDATE events. The DMS task is configured in full-load-and-CDC mode. Which combination of actions will ensure all change events, including DELETEs, are captured reliably in S3?
tags: Batch data ingestion (for example, scheduled ingestion, event-driven ingestion)

answers.A: Switch the DMS task to full-load-only mode and reload the entire table nightly to capture all changes including deletes.
answers.B: Enable supplemental logging on the source Oracle database to ensure the redo logs contain before-image column values for UPDATE and DELETE events.
answers.C: Configure the DMS task to write to an intermediate Aurora PostgreSQL target to buffer CDC events before forwarding to S3.
answers.D: Set the DMS task setting includeOpTypes to include INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE, and configure the S3 target endpoint to write each operation type to a separate S3 prefix.
answers.E: Increase the DMS replication instance size to r5.4xlarge to reduce event processing latency and prevent redo log purging on the source.

explanation: B is correct because Oracle CDC relies on redo log supplemental logging; without it, before-image columns needed for DELETE and UPDATE are not written to the redo logs, causing DMS to miss those events. D is correct because configuring includeOpTypes and per-operation S3 prefixes ensures DELETE records are written instead of silently dropped. A uses full-load-only which does not capture ongoing changes. C introduces an unnecessary intermediate database. E addresses latency but not the root cause, which is a logging configuration issue on the source.

stem: A financial services company ingests trade events from an on-premises Kafka cluster into Amazon MSK. A downstream AWS Glue Streaming ETL job consumes from MSK and writes results to Amazon S3 in Parquet. During a 45-minute network partition, the Glue job fails and restarts. The team requires that no events are lost and events are never processed more than once. Which design achieves exactly-once semantics end-to-end?
tags: Reading data from streaming sources (for example, Amazon Kinesis, Amazon MSK, Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink)

answers.A: Configure Glue job checkpoints to Amazon DynamoDB and use at-least-once delivery with idempotent S3 writes keyed on a deterministic hash of the event ID.
answers.B: Enable MSK auto-rebalancing and set the Glue job retry count to 0 so that partial writes are never committed to S3.
answers.C: Deploy Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink with a Kafka source connector using exactly-once checkpointing and a two-phase commit S3 sink that atomically commits Kafka offsets and S3 file writes together.
answers.D: Extend the MSK consumer group offset retention to 7 days and reset the consumer group offset to the earliest position on every Glue job restart.

explanation: C is correct because Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink supports end-to-end exactly-once semantics via Flink checkpoint mechanism and two-phase commit S3 sink, which atomically commits Kafka offsets and S3 file writes. A achieves at-least-once, not exactly-once, even with idempotent keys. B setting retries to 0 causes event loss on failure rather than preventing duplicates. D resetting to earliest on every restart causes full reprocessing of all historical events, violating the no-duplicate requirement.

stem: A data engineering team runs a nightly AWS Glue ETL job that reads 5 TB of raw JSON from Amazon S3, joins with two 50 MB reference tables, and writes output as Parquet. The job consistently runs for 6 hours. The team wants to reduce runtime to under 2 hours without proportionally increasing cost. Which combination of optimizations will have the greatest impact?
tags: Optimizing data formats (for example, converting CSV to Parquet, using columnar formats for analytics)
Implementing partitioning strategies to improve query performance and reduce cost
Using AWS Glue to transform data (for example, AWS Glue DataBrew, AWS Glue Studio)

answers.A: Enable Glue job bookmarks and perform a one-time migration to convert raw JSON to partitioned Parquet. Configure the nightly job to read only new partitions using predicate pushdown.
answers.B: Increase Glue job maximum DPUs from 10 to 100 to parallelize JSON parsing across more workers without changing the data format.
answers.C: Broadcast the 50 MB reference tables as Spark broadcast variables to eliminate shuffle joins, and enable dynamic partition pruning on the main dataset.
answers.D: Move the Glue job to an Amazon EMR cluster using EC2 Spot Instances to reduce cost while keeping the same execution plan and data format.
answers.E: Enable Glue auto-scaling and switch the worker type to G.2X to allow each worker to handle larger data partitions without other changes.

explanation: A is correct because converting JSON to Parquet reduces scan volume dramatically through columnar reads and predicate pushdown, and bookmarks with partition-based reads eliminate reprocessing of already-processed data. C is correct because broadcast joins eliminate the expensive shuffle for small reference tables, often the dominant bottleneck in star-schema ETL joins. B adds compute cost without addressing JSON read inefficiency. D moves to Spot EMR without changing the execution plan, so runtime stays similar. E provides marginal improvement without addressing the fundamental I/O and join strategy inefficiencies.

stem: A media company orchestrates a 12-step sequential data pipeline plus 3 parallel EMR steps using AWS Step Functions. Occasionally, transient S3 throttling errors cause step 9 to fail, forcing the entire 4-hour pipeline to restart from step 1. Which Step Functions design pattern resolves this with the minimum code changes?
tags: Building workflows using AWS Step Functions (for example, state machines, parallel states, error handling)
Implementing retry logic and compensating transactions

answers.A: Replace Step Functions with Amazon MWAA so that individual task retries are natively supported at the DAG task level without restarting the full workflow.
answers.B: Add a Retry configuration on the step 9 Lambda state with exponential backoff targeting S3 throttling errors, and add a Catch block to route terminal failures to an SNS topic for alerting.
answers.C: Wrap the 12-step workflow in a Step Functions Map state so each invocation is independent and failures in one iteration do not affect others.
answers.D: Write intermediate results to DynamoDB after each step. On failure, read the DynamoDB checkpoint and skip completed steps using a Choice state in a new execution.

explanation: B is correct because Step Functions natively supports per-state Retry with exponential backoff and jitter. Adding Retry on step 9 for the specific S3 throttling error automatically retries only that state without restarting the pipeline, requiring only a state machine definition change. A replaces the entire orchestration system, which is a major architectural overhaul. C uses Map for parallelism, not sequential retry; it does not help a sequential step failure. D requires significant custom code for checkpoint-and-skip logic, far exceeding minimal changes.

stem: A genomics company needs to store 500 TB of DNA sequence data. Data is written once during experiments, queried infrequently for 90 days, then archived for 7 years for regulatory compliance. Active-period queries require sub-second range scans on sample ID and experiment timestamp. After 90 days, data must be retrievable within 12 hours. Which architecture minimizes total cost while meeting all requirements?
tags: Hot, warm, and cold data storage tiers
Selecting Amazon S3 storage classes (for example, S3 Intelligent-Tiering, S3 Glacier) based on data lifecycle requirements

answers.A: Store all data in Amazon DynamoDB with TTL set to 90 days. Use DynamoDB Streams to export expired items to S3 Glacier Deep Archive for the 7-year retention period.
answers.B: Store all 500 TB in Amazon S3 Standard. Configure a lifecycle rule to transition objects to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after 90 days for cost savings.
answers.C: Load sequence data into Amazon Redshift with a 90-day retention window. Use Redshift UNLOAD to export older data to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.
answers.D: Partition sequence data by sample ID and experiment date in Amazon S3 Standard. Configure a lifecycle rule to transition to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval at 90 days. Query active partitions using Amazon Athena with partition pruning.

explanation: D is correct because S3 Standard provides active storage with Athena enabling partition-pruned range scans on sample ID and experiment date. S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval standard retrieval (3-5 hours) or bulk retrieval (up to 12 hours) satisfies the 12-hour SLA at much lower cost than Instant Retrieval. Lifecycle rules automate the transition. A is wrong because DynamoDB is not cost-effective for 500 TB of write-once analytical data. B uses Glacier Instant Retrieval which is more expensive than Flexible Retrieval for a 12-hour SLA. C uses Redshift which is expensive for 500 TB of rarely queried data.

stem: A data platform team uses AWS Glue crawlers to discover schema for JSON files landing in an S3 data lake. When upstream producers add new optional fields, downstream Athena queries using SELECT * return incorrect results because new columns appear in new partitions but old partitions retain the original schema. The team needs backward-compatible schema evolution without breaking existing queries. Which approach best resolves this?
tags: Crawlers and classifiers in AWS Glue
Managing schema versions and handling schema evolution
Schema evolution strategies (for example, adding columns, backward and forward compatibility)

answers.A: Configure the Glue crawler with UpdateBehavior set to UPDATE_IN_DATABASE. Use a Glue ETL job to convert JSON to Parquet with the mergeSchema option enabled. Athena queries the merged schema, returning NULL for columns absent in older partitions.
answers.B: Create a separate Glue crawler per S3 partition date prefix so each crawler independently discovers and maintains schema for its partition without conflicting with other partitions.
answers.C: Disable the Glue crawler and manually update the Glue Data Catalog table schema using the AWS CLI each time upstream producers announce a schema change.
answers.D: Switch to Amazon Redshift Spectrum and use REFRESH EXTERNAL TABLE to detect new columns from S3. Let Spectrum handle schema inference at query time.

explanation: A is correct because UPDATE_IN_DATABASE allows the crawler to add new columns to the Glue Data Catalog without removing existing columns. Converting to Parquet with mergeSchema creates a unified schema where old partitions return NULL for new columns, enabling backward-compatible SELECT * queries. B creates schema fragmentation across crawlers, preventing cross-partition queries. C is operationally burdensome and error-prone at scale. D switches the query engine unnecessarily and Spectrum JSON inference has limitations with schema drift across partitions.

stem: A healthcare company stores patient records in Amazon S3. Regulatory requirements mandate that records must be retained unmodified for exactly 7 years after creation and then automatically deleted. The compliance team requires tamper-proof proof that no record was modified or deleted before the 7-year period expires. Which S3 configuration satisfies all requirements?
tags: Versioning and object locking (for example, Amazon S3 Object Lock, WORM)
Enabling and configuring Amazon S3 Object Lock for compliance and data protection
Creating and managing S3 lifecycle policies to transition or expire objects

answers.A: Enable S3 Versioning and configure a lifecycle rule to delete all versions after 7 years. Use S3 server access logs as audit evidence that records were not modified.
answers.B: Enable S3 Object Lock in Governance mode with a 7-year retention period. Configure a lifecycle rule to expire objects after 7 years. Export audit events from AWS CloudTrail.
answers.C: Enable S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode with a 7-year retention period and an S3 lifecycle expiration rule for current versions. Enable CloudTrail S3 data events and ship logs to a separate immutable S3 bucket as tamper-proof audit evidence.
answers.D: Store records in Amazon S3 Glacier with a Vault Lock policy set to deny deletions for 7 years. Use Glacier audit logs to demonstrate that records remained immutable.

explanation: C is correct because Compliance mode Object Lock prevents any user, including root, from deleting or overriding the retention period. The lifecycle expiration automates deletion once the lock expires. CloudTrail data events stored in a separate immutable bucket provide tamper-proof audit evidence. B uses Governance mode which allows privileged IAM users to delete or override retention, failing strict compliance. A uses versioning without Object Lock so objects can be deleted before 7 years. D uses Glacier Vault Lock which works for immutability but does not support automatic expiration and lacks granular object-level lifecycle policies.

stem: A data warehouse team is migrating a 200-million-row customer dimension to Amazon Redshift. The business requires tracking all historical changes to customer address and loyalty tier with the ability to query the state of any customer at any past date. The table receives approximately 50,000 updates per day. Which slowly changing dimension strategy and Redshift design minimizes storage while enabling point-in-time queries?
tags: Implementing slowly changing dimension strategies (for example, SCD Type 1, Type 2) in data pipelines
Designing relational schemas for analytical workloads in Amazon Redshift (for example, distribution keys, sort keys)

answers.A: Implement SCD Type 1 by overwriting address and loyalty tier in place. Add a last_updated_timestamp column. Use nightly Redshift materialized views to reconstruct historical snapshots from audit logs.
answers.B: Implement SCD Type 2 with effective_start_date, effective_end_date, and is_current columns. Use customer_id as the Redshift distribution key and effective_start_date as the sort key. Expire old rows on update and insert a new current row.
answers.C: Implement SCD Type 6 with prior_address, prior_tier, effective_start_date, and effective_end_date columns. Use DISTSTYLE ALL to replicate the entire dimension across all Redshift nodes.
answers.D: Implement SCD Type 2 in Amazon DynamoDB using a composite key of customer_id and effective_date. Join the DynamoDB dimension with Redshift fact tables using Redshift federated queries.

explanation: B is correct because SCD Type 2 with effective dates is the standard approach for full historical tracking with point-in-time queries. Using customer_id as the distribution key collocates dimension and fact rows for efficient joins. Sorting by effective_start_date optimizes range scans for point-in-time lookups. A uses SCD Type 1 which destroys history; materialized views cannot reconstruct overwritten history. C stores only one prior value (the Type 3 component), not full history, and DISTSTYLE ALL on a 200M-row table wastes storage. D stores the dimension in DynamoDB requiring cross-service federated queries that add latency and cost.

stem: A streaming analytics platform ingests IoT sensor readings into Amazon S3 in JSON format. Data scientists query this data with Amazon Athena and frequently filter on device_id, sensor_type, and event_date. Queries currently scan the entire 8 TB dataset regardless of filter predicates, causing high costs and slow response times. Which schema and storage design change most reduces query cost?
tags: Implementing partitioning strategies to improve query performance and reduce cost
Optimizing data formats (for example, converting CSV to Parquet, using columnar formats for analytics)
Ad hoc queries using AWS services (for example, Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift Spectrum)

answers.A: Migrate S3 data to Amazon DynamoDB with a GSI on device_id and sensor_type to enable indexed lookups and reduce analytical query latency.
answers.B: Convert JSON to Parquet and store all data in a single S3 prefix without partitioning to maximize file consolidation and reduce S3 API calls per Athena query.
answers.C: Convert JSON to Snappy-compressed Parquet. Partition by event_date, then sensor_type, then device_id. Register the table in the Glue Data Catalog with Athena partition projection enabled for metadata-free partition resolution.
answers.D: Compress existing JSON with GZIP and consolidate S3 objects to 128 MB each. Update the Glue Data Catalog to point to the consolidated compressed JSON files.

explanation: C is correct because converting to Parquet enables columnar reads and predicate pushdown within files, while partitioning by event_date, sensor_type, and device_id allows Athena to skip entire S3 prefixes. Partition projection eliminates Glue Data Catalog overhead. Together these can reduce data scanned by over 95% for typical filtered queries. A moves data to DynamoDB which is not designed for analytical range scans and is extremely expensive at 8 TB. B converts to Parquet but lacks partition pruning so all 8 TB is still scanned. D compresses JSON which is a row format; Athena must still deserialize every row to apply filters.

stem: A data engineering team deploys AWS Glue ETL jobs using AWS CloudFormation. A recent code change introduced a bug that corrupts output Parquet files and was deployed to production before detection. The team needs to safely roll back the Glue job and prevent similar incidents. Which combination of practices achieves this?
tags: Implementing CI/CD pipelines for data engineering workflows
Continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) for data pipelines
Deploying data pipeline infrastructure using AWS CloudFormation or AWS CDK

answers.A: Store Glue job scripts in AWS CodeCommit with branch protection on main. Manually test each script in a sandbox before pushing to main.
answers.B: Store Glue scripts in versioned S3 prefixes such as s3://bucket/scripts/v1.2.3/job.py. Reference the specific version in the CloudFormation template. Roll back by redeploying the previous CloudFormation stack version.
answers.C: Enable AWS Glue job bookmarks so the job can re-read previously processed partitions if a corruption is detected after the fact.
answers.D: Add an automated data quality validation stage to the CI/CD pipeline using AWS Glue Data Quality that runs on sample output after each deployment and gates production promotion on passing validation results.
answers.E: Configure AWS Config to detect drift in Glue job properties and automatically revert unauthorized changes to the job definition.

explanation: B is correct because versioning Glue scripts in S3 and pinning the CloudFormation template to a specific version enables deterministic rollback by redeploying the previous stack, restoring the exact prior script and configuration. D is correct because automated output quality validation in CI/CD catches corrupted output before production promotion, preventing the original incident. A uses manual testing which is insufficient for all regressions. C bookmarks prevent reprocessing but do not fix already-corrupted output or roll back the job code. E Config does not monitor Glue script content changes and cannot automatically revert code-level bugs.

stem: A Kinesis Data Streams consumer is falling behind with a steadily increasing GetRecords.IteratorAgeMilliseconds metric over 2 hours. The stream has 10 shards and a downstream AWS Lambda function processes batches of 100 records. Which actions will reduce the iterator age most effectively?
tags: Troubleshooting streaming pipeline issues (for example, Kinesis shard splitting, consumer lag)
Configuring CloudWatch alarms for data pipeline metrics (for example, Glue job failures, Kinesis iterator age)
Amazon CloudWatch metrics, logs, and alarms for AWS data services

answers.A: Split the 10 shards to increase the total shard count, proportionally increasing the number of concurrent Lambda executions processing the stream.
answers.B: Increase the Lambda function memory to 10240 MB to reduce individual record processing time on each invocation.
answers.C: Increase the Lambda event source mapping batch size from 100 to 1000 and enable parallelization factor up to 10 to process multiple batches per shard concurrently.
answers.D: Switch the Kinesis stream to enhanced fan-out with a dedicated consumer to eliminate the polling delay inherent in standard GetRecords calls.
answers.E: Enable automatic shard scaling on the Kinesis stream so shards are dynamically added when IteratorAgeMilliseconds exceeds a configured threshold.

explanation: A is correct because splitting shards increases parallelism by adding more shard-to-Lambda concurrency mappings, directly increasing aggregate throughput. C is correct because increasing batch size to 1000 reduces Lambda invocation overhead per unit time, and a parallelization factor up to 10 allows concurrent batches per shard, multiplying effective throughput. B increasing memory may slightly speed Lambda execution but does not address a fundamental throughput gap. D enhanced fan-out removes polling delay but the increasing iterator age indicates a processing throughput problem, not a polling delay problem. E Kinesis does not natively support automatic shard scaling.

stem: An AWS Glue job reads from Amazon S3 and writes transformed records to Amazon Redshift via the JDBC connector. The job intermittently fails with OutOfMemoryError in Spark executors when processing large partitions. Inspection shows certain date partitions contain 10x more records than others. Which change resolves the memory issue without over-provisioning all workers?
tags: Diagnosing and resolving AWS Glue job failures (for example, memory issues, schema mismatches)
Right-sizing compute resources for Amazon EMR, AWS Glue, and Amazon Redshift workloads
Common data pipeline failure modes (for example, schema changes, network failures, resource exhaustion)
Applying filtering, aggregation, and joins during data transformation

answers.A: Upgrade the Glue job worker type from G.1X to G.2X across all workers to double per-executor memory and prevent OOM errors on large partitions.
answers.B: Add a repartition() call in the Glue PySpark script after reading S3 data to redistribute records evenly across all executors before writing to Redshift. Tune the partition count based on expected data volume.
answers.C: Enable Glue job auto-scaling so additional DPUs are provisioned dynamically when memory pressure is detected on individual executors.
answers.D: Switch the Glue job to use the AWS Glue DynamicFrame API instead of Spark DataFrames because DynamicFrames automatically rebalance skewed partitions using native Glue optimizations.

explanation: B is correct because the root cause is data skew: certain partitions contain 10x more records, causing some executors to receive far more data than others and run out of memory. Calling repartition() after reading redistributes records evenly across all executors, eliminating skew-induced OOM without needing more worker memory globally. A doubles memory for all workers to handle the worst-case partition, which is wasteful over-provisioning. C auto-scaling adds DPUs but does not fix the skew; the large partition still maps to a single executor. D DynamicFrames do not automatically resolve data skew; they provide schema flexibility but not automatic partition rebalancing.

stem: A data pipeline processes customer orders via Amazon SQS. A Lambda function processes each order and writes to Amazon RDS. Malformed messages occasionally cause Lambda exceptions and after the maximum receive count is reached, messages move to a dead-letter queue (DLQ). After the Lambda function is fixed, the team needs to reprocess DLQ messages with the least operational overhead. Which approach achieves this?
tags: Dead-letter queues (DLQ) and error handling strategies
Implementing dead-letter queues with Amazon SQS for failed message handling
Implementing error notification using Amazon SNS, Amazon SQS, or Amazon CloudWatch

answers.A: Manually download DLQ messages, correct the message data locally, and re-upload corrected messages to the main SQS queue using the AWS CLI.
answers.B: Create a second Lambda function triggered by the DLQ that reads messages and publishes them back to the main SQS queue after applying a transformation.
answers.C: Configure the DLQ with a visibility timeout of 0 seconds so that after the Lambda fix is deployed, messages become immediately visible to consumers.
answers.D: Use the SQS dead-letter queue redrive feature in the AWS Console or API to move messages from the DLQ back to the source queue in managed batches after the Lambda fix is deployed.

explanation: D is correct because SQS natively supports dead-letter queue redrive (Start DLQ Redrive), which moves messages from the DLQ back to the source queue in managed batches without any custom code, providing the lowest operational overhead. A requires manual intervention and risks data corruption. B introduces a second Lambda with additional operational complexity and potential message routing issues. C setting visibility timeout to 0 makes messages visible in the DLQ but they remain in the DLQ; they do not automatically transfer to the source queue.

stem: A data engineering team runs daily ETL jobs loading data from multiple source systems into Amazon Redshift. Business analysts report that some fact table rows have NULL foreign keys that should always reference a valid dimension row. The team needs systematic data quality checks that prevent bad data from reaching analysts. Which solution detects NULL foreign keys and referential integrity violations with the least engineering effort?
tags: Data quality dimensions (for example, completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness)
Implementing data validation rules using AWS Glue Data Quality
AWS Glue Data Quality and DataBrew for data quality checks

answers.A: Add SQL ASSERT statements in the Redshift ETL stored procedure that raise exceptions when NULL foreign key counts exceed a threshold, and forward exception details via Amazon SNS.
answers.B: Schedule a daily Amazon Athena query that JOINs the S3 staging data against Redshift dimension tables via Redshift Spectrum and writes violations to a dedicated alert table.
answers.C: Define AWS Glue Data Quality rules using DQDL IsComplete and ReferentialIntegrity checks on the staging Glue Data Catalog tables. Run these rules within the Glue ETL job and fail the job on threshold violations with an SNS notification.
answers.D: Use Amazon QuickSight anomaly detection on Redshift data to automatically identify statistical anomalies in NULL foreign key distributions and send email alerts to data engineers.

explanation: C is correct because AWS Glue Data Quality with DQDL supports IsComplete rules (detecting NULLs) and ReferentialIntegrity rules (checking foreign key validity) natively. Running checks as part of the ETL job blocks bad data from reaching Redshift and triggers SNS alerts on failure, with minimal custom code. A requires custom SQL assertions in stored procedures, which is higher engineering effort. B uses a cross-service JOIN with Athena and Spectrum, adding latency and cost. D uses QuickSight anomaly detection after data is already in Redshift, not as a prevention gate before loading.

stem: A financial data pipeline ingests transaction records from multiple upstream systems into Amazon S3. Each system uses different date formats, currency codes, and status values. Analysts report duplicate transaction IDs in the final dataset. Which pipeline design addresses both standardization and deduplication requirements with minimum custom code?
tags: Data quality dimensions (for example, completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness)
Implementing deduplication logic in data pipelines
Using AWS Glue DataBrew to profile datasets and identify quality issues

answers.A: Use AWS Glue DataBrew to profile each source dataset and create standardization recipes for date formats, currency codes, and status values. In the Glue ETL job, apply dropDuplicates() on transaction_id after merging all sources, and log deduplication counts to Amazon CloudWatch.
answers.B: Load all raw records into Amazon Redshift and use SQL MERGE with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY transaction_id) to deduplicate and standardize values directly in the data warehouse.
answers.C: Configure Amazon AppFlow to ingest from each source system with built-in field mapping and deduplication, writing results directly to S3 without additional Glue processing.
answers.D: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose with a Lambda transformation to standardize fields, and write records to Amazon DynamoDB using transaction_id as the partition key to overwrite duplicates.

explanation: A is correct because DataBrew provides a visual profiling and recipe approach for standardization across heterogeneous sources with minimal code, and dropDuplicates() in the Glue ETL job explicitly handles deduplication at the transformation layer before data reaches the final dataset. Logging counts to CloudWatch enables ongoing monitoring. B pushes raw inconsistent data into Redshift first, violating clean-before-load principles. C uses AppFlow which is designed for SaaS source integration and has limited deduplication capabilities for multi-source financial transaction pipelines. D uses Firehose and DynamoDB for streaming deduplication, but the scenario involves batch ingestion and DynamoDB is not appropriate as the analytical store.

stem: A large enterprise runs a multi-team data lake on Amazon S3 managed by AWS Lake Formation. The security team requires that the data science team can query all customer table columns except ssn and credit_card_number and can only see rows where country equals US. The analytics team needs unrestricted access to the full customer table. Which Lake Formation configuration achieves this with the least administrative overhead?
tags: AWS Lake Formation permission model (for example, database, table, column, row-level security)
Configuring AWS Lake Formation permissions at the database, table, and column level
Granting and revoking access using AWS Lake Formation for data lake resources

answers.A: Create two separate S3 prefixes: one with full data for the analytics team and one with pre-filtered and pre-masked data for the data science team. Grant each team access via S3 bucket policies.
answers.B: Grant the data science team table-level SELECT with column exclusion for ssn and credit_card_number using Lake Formation column-level security. Apply a row filter expression for country equals US via a Lake Formation data filter. Grant the analytics team full table SELECT with no filters.
answers.C: Create IAM policies for each team that explicitly deny GetObject on S3 keys containing sensitive columns. Use S3 object metadata tags to identify rows by country for row-level filtering.
answers.D: Implement an Athena view that excludes ssn and credit_card_number and filters to country equals US. Grant the data science team SELECT on the view. Grant the analytics team SELECT on the base Glue Data Catalog table.

explanation: B is correct because Lake Formation natively supports column-level security (excluding specific columns) and row-level security (data filters with row filter expressions) centrally. This applies to all query engines including Athena, EMR, and Redshift Spectrum without duplicating data or maintaining views. A duplicates the dataset, creating management overhead and synchronization risk. C uses IAM and S3 metadata for row-level filtering, which does not work because S3 does not filter at the column or row level based on object metadata. D uses Athena views which only apply to Athena; EMR or Redshift Spectrum queries bypass the view and access the raw table directly.

stem: A healthcare data platform stores PHI in Amazon S3 and Amazon Redshift. The security team requires all data at rest to use a customer-managed KMS key (CMK) so access can be revoked immediately if needed. The ETL pipeline uses AWS Glue. Which configuration ensures end-to-end CMK-based encryption covering both storage and all Glue job metadata?
tags: AWS Key Management Service (KMS) key types and usage
Configuring server-side encryption for Amazon S3 using AWS KMS
Configuring AWS Glue encryption settings for job metadata, CloudWatch logs, and S3 data
Enabling encryption at rest for Amazon Redshift, Amazon RDS, and Amazon DynamoDB
Managing encryption keys using AWS KMS customer managed keys (CMKs)

answers.A: Enable SSE-S3 on the S3 bucket and Redshift encryption with the default AWS-managed key. No additional Glue encryption is needed because Glue job metadata does not contain PHI.
answers.B: Enable SSE-KMS on the S3 bucket using the CMK and Redshift encryption with the CMK. Configure a Glue security configuration to encrypt only the job bookmark using the same CMK.
answers.C: Create a KMS CMK and apply it across S3 default encryption via SSE-KMS, Redshift cluster encryption, and an AWS Glue security configuration covering S3 data target encryption, CloudWatch log encryption, and job bookmark encryption, all referencing the same CMK.
answers.D: Use AWS Certificate Manager to issue a customer-managed certificate for data-at-rest encryption across S3, Redshift, and Glue, and enable TLS on all data service endpoints.

explanation: C is correct because a Glue security configuration specifies the CMK for three categories: S3 data target encryption (data written by Glue jobs), CloudWatch Logs encryption (Glue logs may contain PHI field names or values), and job bookmark encryption (bookmark state may contain sensitive metadata). All three must reference the CMK for complete end-to-end coverage. Using the same CMK across S3, Redshift, and Glue enables centralized revocation. A uses SSE-S3 which is AWS-managed and cannot be revoked by the customer. B encrypts only the job bookmark, leaving CloudWatch Logs and S3 data written by Glue without CMK protection. D uses ACM for TLS certificates which protects data in transit, not data at rest.

stem: A compliance officer requires that all API calls to Amazon Redshift, AWS Glue, and Amazon S3 by data engineers are logged and retained for 5 years in tamper-proof storage and are queryable for ad-hoc investigations. Any S3 DeleteBucket or DeleteObject API call must trigger an immediate alert. Which architecture satisfies all requirements?
tags: AWS CloudTrail for API activity logging
Enabling and configuring AWS CloudTrail for data service API activity
Implementing alerting on security-relevant CloudTrail events using Amazon EventBridge and Amazon SNS
Centralizing logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs or Amazon S3 for auditing
Using Amazon Athena to query audit logs stored in Amazon S3

answers.A: Enable S3 server access logging for each data bucket. Write access logs to a separate S3 bucket with a 5-year lifecycle rule. Use Athena to query access logs. Configure S3 event notifications to SNS for DeleteObject events.
answers.B: Enable AWS CloudTrail for all regions writing to a single S3 bucket with log file validation enabled. Create an Athena table over the CloudTrail prefix. Configure an S3 lifecycle rule for 5-year retention.
answers.C: Enable CloudTrail data events for S3 and management events for Redshift and Glue. Stream events to CloudWatch Logs. Use Logs Insights for ad-hoc queries. Create a CloudWatch metric filter alarm on the DeleteObject event pattern.
answers.D: Enable a multi-region AWS CloudTrail trail with log file integrity validation writing to a dedicated S3 bucket with Object Lock in Compliance mode for 5-year retention and SSE-KMS. Create an Athena table on the CloudTrail prefix for ad-hoc queries. Configure an EventBridge rule matching CloudTrail DeleteBucket and DeleteObject events to trigger an SNS alert.

explanation: D is correct because a multi-region trail captures API activity across all regions; log file integrity validation proves logs are tamper-free; S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode prevents log deletion for 5 years even by administrators; Athena over CloudTrail JSON enables ad-hoc queryability; EventBridge rules on CloudTrail events provide real-time alerting on specific API calls. A uses S3 server access logs which capture only S3 HTTP requests, not Glue or Redshift API calls. B lacks Object Lock for tamper-proof storage and lacks a real-time alert mechanism. C uses CloudWatch Logs Insights which has a default 15-month retention limit and metric filter alarms are less reliable than EventBridge for specific API call detection.

stem: A global e-commerce company processes customer data subject to GDPR. A data subject submits a right-to-erasure request requiring deletion of all personal data within 30 days. The data platform uses Amazon S3 (data lake in Parquet), Amazon Redshift (data warehouse), and Amazon DynamoDB (operational store). Which approach satisfies the erasure requirement with minimal pipeline disruption?
tags: Data privacy regulations and compliance frameworks relevant to data engineering (for example, GDPR, HIPAA, CCPA)
Implementing data retention and deletion policies to meet regulatory requirements
Designing pipelines to handle PII data in compliance with privacy regulations

answers.A: Rewrite all S3 Parquet files to remove the customer's records, run targeted DELETE statements in Redshift, and use DynamoDB DeleteItem. Log all deletions to Amazon CloudWatch Logs for audit purposes.
answers.B: Pseudonymize customer PII at ingestion using a token mapped to customer_id in AWS Secrets Manager. For erasure: delete the Secrets Manager secret to break the mapping, delete the DynamoDB item, run a Redshift DELETE, and use Apache Iceberg row-level delete on S3 to avoid rewriting entire Parquet files.
answers.C: Use Amazon Macie to locate all occurrences of the customer's PII across S3 and Redshift. Export the Macie findings report to compliance officers as documented proof of erasure.
answers.D: Enable S3 Object Lock on the data lake to prevent any data modifications. Archive GDPR deletion requests in S3 Glacier and fulfill them in bulk during annual compliance reviews.

explanation: B is correct because pseudonymization with token-based indirection means deleting the Secrets Manager secret effectively anonymizes all pseudonymized records in S3 without rewriting files (GDPR considers effectively anonymized data outside its scope). For records with direct PII in Redshift and DynamoDB, targeted deletes are efficient. Apache Iceberg row-level deletes enable surgical removal from S3 Parquet without rewriting entire files, minimizing pipeline disruption. A requires rewriting all Parquet files to remove one customer, which is operationally expensive at scale. C Macie discovers PII but does not delete it; a findings report does not constitute erasure. D Object Lock prevents deletion, directly conflicting with the GDPR right-to-erasure requirement.

stem: A data platform team is building a data lakehouse on Amazon S3. They need to support concurrent reads and writes from multiple AWS Glue ETL jobs with ACID transaction guarantees, time-travel queries to past states, and schema evolution without breaking existing consumers. Which open table format and configuration best satisfies all three requirements on AWS?
tags: Open table formats (Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi, Delta Lake)
Building and maintaining idempotent data pipelines
Managing schema evolution in AWS Glue Data Catalog and with file formats like Avro and Parquet

answers.A: Use Apache Hudi with Copy-on-Write table type on Amazon S3. Register the Hudi table in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Use the Glue Hudi connector for concurrent ETL job writes.
answers.B: Use Delta Lake on Amazon S3 with the AWS Glue Delta Lake connector. Enable transaction log compaction to manage concurrent Glue job writes and support time-travel using TIMESTAMP AS OF queries.
answers.C: Use Apache Iceberg on Amazon S3 with the Glue Iceberg connector and optimistic concurrency control. Register the table in the Glue Data Catalog using Iceberg catalog integration. Leverage Iceberg schema evolution for adding and renaming columns and time-travel via snapshot IDs.
answers.D: Use Apache ORC files on S3 with a distributed lock in Amazon DynamoDB to coordinate concurrent Glue writes. Maintain a version table in DynamoDB to support time-travel queries.

explanation: C is correct because Apache Iceberg provides ACID transactions with optimistic concurrency control for concurrent writes, full time-travel via immutable snapshot IDs, and first-class schema evolution (add, drop, rename, reorder columns, widen types) natively. AWS Glue has a native Iceberg connector and the Glue Data Catalog supports the Iceberg REST catalog API. A Apache Hudi Copy-on-Write supports ACID and time-travel but has more limited schema evolution compared to Iceberg, particularly for column renaming and type widening. B Delta Lake works on AWS but its Glue connector has more limited support compared to Iceberg's first-class AWS integration. D custom DynamoDB locking is an anti-pattern requiring significant engineering and not providing true ACID semantics.

stem: A CloudOps team manages 40 CloudFormation stacks across three AWS accounts. After a manual change was made to an Auto Scaling group launch template outside of CloudFormation, the operations team wants to detect all stacks with configuration drift and automatically revert drifted resources to their expected state. Which combination of actions meets these requirements with the least operational overhead?

answers.A: Run aws cloudformation detect-stack-drift for each stack via a cron job on an EC2 instance. Parse JSON output and raise a support ticket for each drifted resource.
answers.B: Create an AWS Config rule that triggers drift detection via Systems Manager Automation. Use a CloudFormation stack policy with a remediation runbook that calls aws cloudformation update-stack --use-previous-template to restore expected configurations.
answers.C: Enable AWS Config continuous recording for CloudFormation resources. Use a Config remediation action linked to a Lambda function that calls detect-stack-drift on each stack, then re-deploys drifted stacks using the existing template and current parameter values.
answers.D: Schedule a CloudWatch Events rule to invoke a Lambda function hourly. The function calls detect-stack-drift on all stacks, then calls cancel-update-stack to halt any in-progress updates on drifted stacks.

explanation: Option C is correct: AWS Config continuously monitors CloudFormation resources and a remediation action linked to Lambda can automate drift detection and re-deployment, minimizing manual steps. Option A requires manual EC2 management and manual ticketing, increasing overhead significantly. Option B is plausible but a stack policy controls which resources can be updated, not drift; update-stack with use-previous-template alone does not revert drifted resource properties. Option D incorrectly cancels in-progress updates rather than reverting drift.

stem: A company runs a monolithic Java application on EC2 instances managed by AWS CodeDeploy with an in-place deployment strategy. A recent deployment caused a 12-minute outage because the application failed health checks after the new version was installed. The team requires zero-downtime deployments and must be able to roll back within 3 minutes if error rates exceed 5% during the deployment window. Which CodeDeploy configuration change meets these requirements?

answers.A: Switch to a rolling in-place deployment with minimum healthy hosts set to 50%. Configure a CloudWatch alarm on 5xx errors and link it to a CodeDeploy rollback trigger.
answers.B: Enable AllAtOnce in-place deployment and add a lifecycle hook in AfterInstall that runs smoke tests. If tests fail, the hook script calls the CodeDeploy API to stop and roll back the deployment.
answers.C: Switch to a blue/green deployment with an Application Load Balancer. Set traffic rerouting to immediate and configure automatic rollback when a CloudWatch alarm detecting HTTP 5xx errors above 5% triggers within the deployment window.
answers.D: Use a rolling in-place deployment with minimum healthy hosts at 75%. Add a BeforeInstall lifecycle hook that snapshots each EC2 instance using AWS Backup before replacing application files.

explanation: Blue/green deployment (Option C) keeps the original fleet running while deploying to a new fleet, enabling zero-downtime cutover and near-instant rollback by shifting ALB traffic back. The CloudWatch alarm threshold triggers automatic rollback within seconds. Option A uses rolling in-place, which still requires re-deploying the prior version to roll back — taking well over 3 minutes for a large fleet. Option B uses AllAtOnce which causes the same all-instances-down outage pattern. Option D snapshot-based rollback restoring instances takes far longer than 3 minutes for large fleets.

stem: A company uses AWS CodePipeline to deploy a Node.js API to AWS Lambda. The pipeline has Source, Build (CodeBuild), and Deploy (CloudFormation) stages. After adding a new dependency, the Build stage succeeds but the Deploy stage fails with: 'The runtime parameter of nodejs14.x is no longer supported.' The team needs to fix the pipeline failure and prevent similar runtime deprecation failures in future releases without adding manual steps. Which solution achieves both goals?

answers.A: Update the CloudFormation template to set the Lambda runtime to nodejs20.x. Add a CodeBuild step that runs cfn-lint against the CloudFormation template before the Deploy stage to catch unsupported runtimes and misconfigurations automatically.
answers.B: Add a manual approval stage between Build and Deploy. Require the release manager to verify runtime compatibility in the AWS console before approving each deployment to the Lambda function.
answers.C: Update the Lambda function runtime to nodejs20.x directly in the AWS Management Console. Rerun the failed pipeline execution from the Deploy stage without modifying the CloudFormation template.
answers.D: Configure a CloudWatch Events rule to detect CodePipeline Deploy stage failures and invoke a Lambda function that automatically updates the runtime property via the AWS SDK and re-triggers the failed pipeline stage.

explanation: Option A corrects the root cause by updating the template runtime and adds a static analysis gate (cfn-lint) to catch future deprecated runtimes before they reach the Deploy stage, all without manual steps. Option B adds human approval overhead and does not prevent future failures automatically. Option C fixes the console setting but leaves the CloudFormation template broken, so the next pipeline run will fail again with the same error. Option D is reactive and does not fix the template, so the same failure recurs on the next deployment.

stem: A company runs a fleet of 300 on-demand EC2 instances across M5 and R5 families for a memory-intensive analytics workload. AWS Compute Optimizer reports that 180 instances are over-provisioned with average CPU utilization of 12% and memory utilization of 28%, while 30 instances are under-provisioned. The team must reduce cost while maintaining performance SLAs and minimizing risk of disruption. Which approach should the team take first?

answers.A: Immediately stop all 180 over-provisioned instances and restart them with Compute Optimizer recommended instance types to reduce cost as quickly as possible.
answers.B: Export Compute Optimizer findings to S3. Remediate the 30 under-provisioned instances first to eliminate performance risk, then use Auto Scaling group instance refresh with a rolling update to migrate over-provisioned instances to recommended types in batches.
answers.C: Purchase Savings Plans matching the current M5 and R5 usage levels to reduce cost immediately. Defer instance right-sizing until the next planned maintenance window six months from now.
answers.D: Resize all over-provisioned instances to t3.medium simultaneously using AWS Systems Manager Run Command to minimize the overall change window duration.

explanation: Option B is correct: addressing under-provisioned instances first eliminates the immediate performance risk, and using rolling instance refresh maintains availability during right-sizing of the over-provisioned set. Option A risks a mass-outage by stopping 180 instances simultaneously without staged rollout. Option C purchases Savings Plans at the inflated over-provisioned baseline, locking in unnecessarily high cost for the commitment period. Option D downgrades all instances to t3.medium regardless of workload needs, risks severe performance degradation, and simultaneous changes increase blast radius.

stem: A FinTech company configured an AWS Budgets alert at 80% actual monthly spend against a $50,000 budget. At the end of month 2, spend exceeded $50,000 without triggering an alert. Investigation reveals the budget evaluated at 79.8% on day 28, then costs spiked sharply on day 29. The company wants alerting that fires before a budget overrun occurs. Which solution provides the earliest warning of an impending overrun?

answers.A: Add a second AWS Budgets alert at 100% actual spend so the finance team is notified immediately when the budget is breached.
answers.B: Switch to AWS Cost Explorer anomaly detection. Configure an anomaly monitor for the entire account with a per-day alert threshold of $1,000 to catch sudden cost spikes.
answers.C: Add an AWS Budgets alert at 80% of forecasted spend. Forecasted spend projects end-of-month totals from current run-rate, firing before actual spend reaches the threshold and providing advance warning.
answers.D: Enable a daily Cost Explorer report delivered to S3. Create a CloudWatch metric filter on the exported report to trigger an SNS alarm when cumulative monthly spend exceeds $40,000.

explanation: Option C is correct: a forecasted-spend alert projects end-of-month cost trajectory from current run-rate and fires before the actual threshold is crossed, giving the team time to act. In the described scenario, forecasted spend would have exceeded 80% earlier than day 29. Option A only notifies after the breach has occurred. Option B helps detect sudden anomalies but does not provide advance trajectory-based budget warning. Option D requires a custom metric pipeline with latency and does not leverage native Budgets forecasting.

stem: A company uses AWS Cost Explorer to analyze EC2 spending. Reserved Instance (RI) utilization for the M5 family has dropped from 94% to 61% after a major workload was decommissioned. The remaining RI commitment runs 14 more months. Standard One-Year RIs were purchased. The company wants to maximize recovery of the unused RI value immediately. Which action is most effective?

answers.A: List the unused M5 Standard RIs on the AWS Reserved Instance Marketplace to sell them to other AWS customers, recovering most of the remaining value at current market rates.
answers.B: Modify the unused M5 RIs to a smaller instance size within the same M5 family to match remaining workloads and reduce the effective per-instance commitment waste.
answers.C: Convert the Standard RIs to Convertible RIs so they can be exchanged for a different instance family that better matches current workload requirements.
answers.D: Enable Savings Plans coverage analysis in Cost Explorer and purchase a Compute Savings Plan to offset the unused RI commitment with a lower-cost alternative.

explanation: Option A is correct: Standard RIs can be listed on the RI Marketplace, enabling immediate recovery of most remaining value by selling to other AWS customers. Option B (modifying to smaller size) may reduce some waste but does not recover value from fully unused capacity. Option C is incorrect because Standard RIs cannot be converted to Convertible RIs; Convertible RIs must be purchased separately. Option D (purchasing an additional Savings Plan) adds new cost rather than recovering unused RI value and creates overlapping commitments.

stem: A company hosts a public-facing REST API behind an Application Load Balancer. The security team mandates that TLS certificates must be rotated automatically 30 days before expiration, private keys must never be extractable outside of AWS-managed infrastructure, and audit evidence of every certificate issuance must be stored immutably. Which solution satisfies all three requirements?
tags: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) for TLS certificate management

answers.A: Use ACM to provision a public certificate for the ALB. Enable automatic renewal in ACM. Export the certificate and private key to an S3 bucket with S3 Object Lock (WORM) enabled to satisfy the immutable audit requirement.
answers.B: Use ACM to provision a public certificate and associate it with the ALB HTTPS listener. ACM manages automatic renewal and private keys remain inside ACM and are never exportable. Enable AWS CloudTrail and store logs in an S3 bucket with S3 Object Lock for immutable audit evidence.
answers.C: Use AWS Private Certificate Authority to issue a certificate for the ALB. Schedule a CloudWatch Events rule to invoke a Lambda function 30 days before expiration to renew and re-associate the certificate automatically.
answers.D: Import a third-party CA-signed certificate into ACM. Configure a CloudWatch alarm on the ACM days-to-expiry metric to alert the team 30 days before expiration so they can manually renew and re-import.

explanation: Option B is correct: ACM public certificates auto-renew without any action needed, private keys are managed within ACM and cannot be exported, and CloudTrail records all ACM API calls with S3 Object Lock providing immutable audit evidence. Option A incorrectly assumes ACM public certificate private keys can be exported to S3; they cannot. Option C uses Private CA (suitable for internal PKI) and requires custom Lambda renewal logic rather than auto-renewal. Option D uses imported certificates which do not auto-renew and require manual intervention.

stem: A company uses AWS Elastic Beanstalk to run a Python Flask application across 200 application servers. A new deployment must achieve zero downtime, support rollback within 5 minutes if errors are detected, and ensure serving capacity never drops below 75% during the deployment. Which Elastic Beanstalk deployment policy satisfies all three constraints?
tags: AWS Elastic Beanstalk and its deployment options
