answers.A: Use the All at once deployment policy. Monitor error rates after deployment and re-deploy the previous application version if issues are found within the rollback window.
answers.B: Use the Rolling deployment policy with a batch size of 30%. If errors occur, redeploy the previous version. During deployment, at most 30% of instances serve the new version at any one time.
answers.C: Use the Rolling with additional batch deployment policy with a batch size of 25%. New instances are launched before old ones are replaced, maintaining 100% original capacity. Rollback is achieved by deploying the prior version in batches.
answers.D: Use the Immutable deployment policy. A new Auto Scaling group running the new version is launched alongside the existing fleet. Swap traffic when healthy. Rollback terminates the new Auto Scaling group immediately.

explanation: Option C is correct: Rolling with additional batch launches new-version instances before terminating old ones, so total capacity stays at 100% or above and the 25% batch size ensures no more than 25% of the fleet serves new code at a time. Rolling back by deploying the prior version in 25% batches completes within 5 minutes. Option A (All at once) causes 100% downtime. Option B (Rolling) removes old instances before adding new ones, temporarily reducing capacity by up to 30%. Option D (Immutable) provides zero-downtime but rolling back by terminating a 200-instance ASG can exceed the 5-minute rollback window.

stem: A company runs a stateless REST API on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. Historical traffic analysis shows predictable spikes every weekday at 09:00 UTC (3x baseline) and 18:00 UTC (2x baseline), with unpredictable bursts throughout the day. The team wants capacity available before predictable spikes and unpredictable bursts handled automatically, all at the lowest possible cost. Which Auto Scaling configuration achieves these goals?
tags: EC2 Auto Scaling types (dynamic scaling, predictive scaling, scheduled scaling)

answers.A: Configure scheduled scaling actions at 08:45 UTC (minimum to 3x baseline) and 17:45 UTC (minimum to 2x baseline). Layer a target tracking policy on CPU utilization at 60% to handle random bursts between scheduled windows.
answers.B: Enable predictive scaling in forecast-and-scale mode. Use the generated forecasts to pre-position capacity before recurring peaks. Add no additional scaling policies for random bursts.
answers.C: Use only target tracking scaling on CPU utilization at 50%. The policy adds instances reactively as CPU rises during both scheduled peaks and random bursts throughout the day.
answers.D: Provision Reserved Instances at 3x baseline capacity permanently. Add target tracking on CPU at 70% for additional on-demand capacity during extreme bursts above 3x baseline.

explanation: Option A is correct: scheduled scaling pre-positions capacity 15 minutes before known spikes (eliminating the reactive lag), and target tracking handles unpredictable bursts dynamically. Capacity scales back in after the scheduled window, keeping cost low. Option B (predictive scaling only) requires 14 days of historical data and does not react to random bursts outside of forecasted patterns. Option C (target tracking only) adds instances after CPU rises, so the peak is partially served at reduced capacity during scale-out lag. Option D permanently maintains 3x baseline as Reserved Instances, incurring significant cost during off-peak hours.

stem: A company operates a latency-sensitive gaming application with users in North America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific. The application runs on EC2 instances in us-east-1, eu-west-1, and ap-southeast-1. Route 53 latency-based routing is in use. Players in Asia-Pacific report 320ms average latency. The target is to reduce Asia-Pacific latency below 100ms with minimal architectural changes. Which solution is most effective?
tags: AWS Global Accelerator endpoints and health checks

answers.A: Replace Route 53 latency-based routing with Route 53 geolocation routing to always direct Asian traffic to ap-southeast-1 regardless of real-time latency conditions.
answers.B: Add an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the EC2 instances with the ALB in ap-southeast-1 as origin. Enable CloudFront caching at Asian edge locations to reduce origin traffic.
answers.C: Enable EC2 Enhanced Networking (ENA) on all instances in ap-southeast-1 and increase instance types to maximize network throughput for the gaming protocol.
answers.D: Deploy AWS Global Accelerator and add the ALBs in all three regions as endpoint groups with health checks. Global Accelerator routes players through the nearest AWS edge location over the AWS global backbone, reducing Asia-Pacific latency by bypassing most public internet hops.

explanation: Option D is correct: AWS Global Accelerator uses anycast IPs and routes traffic from the nearest AWS edge PoP over the low-latency AWS global backbone. For players in Asia-Pacific, this typically brings latency from 300+ ms to under 100 ms by eliminating multiple public internet hops. Option A (geolocation routing) routes Asian players to ap-southeast-1 already, and switching from latency-based routing does not optimize the network path. Option B (CloudFront) optimizes HTTP/HTTPS cacheable content, not stateful TCP gaming protocols. Option C (Enhanced Networking) improves intra-AWS instance throughput but has no effect on public internet routing latency.

stem: A company runs a critical Oracle database on an EC2 r5.8xlarge instance in us-east-1. The RPO requirement is 1 hour and the RTO requirement is 30 minutes. The company has no existing infrastructure in any other AWS Region. The team must implement a disaster recovery solution meeting both objectives at the lowest cost. Which solution meets all requirements?
tags: Recovery point objective (RPO) and recovery time objective (RTO)

answers.A: Configure hourly cross-Region EBS snapshot copies to us-west-2. During a disaster, create a volume from the latest snapshot and attach it to a new r5.8xlarge EC2 instance in us-west-2.
answers.B: Migrate the Oracle database to Amazon RDS Oracle Multi-AZ in us-east-1. RDS Multi-AZ provides near-zero RPO and RTO under 2 minutes for AZ-level failures.
answers.C: Deploy AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS) to continuously replicate the EC2 instance to us-west-2. DRS provides sub-second RPO through continuous block-level replication and RTO of minutes by launching a recovery instance on demand.
answers.D: Schedule hourly AWS Backup jobs for the EC2 instance that copy snapshots to us-west-2. During a disaster, restore the latest backup to a new r5.8xlarge instance in us-west-2.

explanation: Option C is correct: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery performs continuous block-level replication, giving sub-second RPO (well within 1 hour) and recovery times of minutes (within 30 minutes). Option A (hourly EBS snapshot copy) meets the 1-hour RPO but restoring an EBS volume and starting a new r5.8xlarge instance typically exceeds 30 minutes due to snapshot hydration time. Option B requires a database migration to RDS (a significant architectural change) and RDS Multi-AZ only protects against AZ failures, not region-wide outages. Option D has the same snapshot restoration latency problem as Option A.

stem: A company uses AWS Control Tower to manage 60 accounts across 5 organizational units (OUs). A new regulatory requirement mandates that all S3 buckets enforce server-side encryption with AWS KMS (SSE-KMS) across every account within 48 hours. The security team cannot touch each account manually. Which approach deploys the enforcement control most efficiently?

answers.A: Attach an SCP to the root OU that denies s3:PutObject requests lacking the x-amz-server-side-encryption header. Deploy through the AWS Organizations console to all accounts immediately.
answers.B: Use Customizations for AWS Control Tower (CfCT) to deploy a CloudFormation StackSet that creates an AWS Config conformance pack enforcing the S3 SSE-KMS rule across all accounts and OUs within the 48-hour window.
answers.C: Run an AWS Systems Manager Automation document across all 60 accounts using a cross-account IAM role. The document calls aws s3api put-bucket-encryption on every bucket in each account.
answers.D: Create an S3 bucket policy template in CloudFormation that denies PutObject without SSE-KMS. Deploy as a StackSet targeting each OU individually from the management account.

explanation: Option B is correct: Customizations for AWS Control Tower (CfCT) is specifically designed to deploy governance controls (including conformance packs via CloudFormation StackSets) across all enrolled accounts without per-account manual steps and also propagates to new accounts as they are enrolled. Option A (SCP) prevents new unencrypted uploads but does not retroactively enforce encryption on existing buckets or auto-remediate. Option C requires enumerating all buckets across 60 accounts and does not apply to new buckets created after the run. Option D requires targeting each OU separately and does not scale to all existing and future buckets automatically.

stem: A company uses CodeDeploy blue/green deployments for a microservices application on an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. The green fleet passes all ALB health checks but generates a spike in HTTP 502 errors within 90 seconds of traffic shift. The deployment rolls back automatically. Post-incident analysis shows the application needs a 45-second initialization period after startup before it can handle requests correctly. Which CodeDeploy configuration prevents this issue in future deployments?

answers.A: Add an AfterAllowTraffic lifecycle hook that pauses the deployment for 60 seconds after traffic is rerouted. If errors persist during the wait, the hook fails and triggers an automatic rollback.
answers.B: Set the deployment configuration to CodeDeployDefault.OneAtATime to slow the traffic shift. Each instance receives traffic one at a time, giving the application time to initialize sequentially.
answers.C: Add a BeforeAllowTraffic lifecycle hook that invokes a Lambda function. The function polls the application health endpoint until it returns HTTP 200 with a 60-second timeout. The hook only succeeds when the endpoint responds, then traffic is shifted.
answers.D: Increase the ALB target group health check grace period to 120 seconds and set the healthy threshold to 5 consecutive successful checks before the instance is considered healthy for traffic.

explanation: Option C is correct: the BeforeAllowTraffic hook runs before any traffic is shifted to the green fleet. A Lambda poller that waits for a successful health response ensures every instance has completed initialization before receiving real user traffic. Option A uses AfterAllowTraffic, which runs after traffic is already flowing to the green fleet, so 502 errors still occur during the warm-up period. Option B (OneAtATime) slows the rollout but does not add a pre-traffic readiness gate; the first instance still receives traffic before the 45-second initialization completes. Option D adjusts ALB health check parameters but does not prevent CodeDeploy from shifting traffic to instances that have not yet completed app initialization.

stem: A company connects its on-premises data center to AWS using a 1 Gbps AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection. The operations team reports intermittent packet loss during peak business hours. The team needs to identify the root cause and add redundancy to prevent future connectivity outages. Which TWO actions should the team take?
tags: AWS Site-to-Site VPN and AWS Direct Connect redundancy

answers.A: Enable VPC Flow Logs on all subnets attached to the Direct Connect gateway. Filter for REJECT entries and correlate timestamps with peak hours to locate the source of packet loss.
answers.B: Review CloudWatch metrics for the Direct Connect virtual interface, including ConnectionBpsEgress, ConnectionBpsIngress, and ConnectionErrorCount, to identify link saturation or physical-layer errors during peak hours.
answers.C: Create a second VPC in a different AWS Region and establish VPC peering between the two VPCs to provide a failover network path for on-premises traffic.
answers.D: Provision a second Direct Connect connection through a different Direct Connect location or configure an AWS Site-to-Site VPN as a backup path. Use BGP to prefer the primary Direct Connect and automatically failover to the backup link.

explanation: Option B is correct: Direct Connect CloudWatch metrics (ConnectionErrorCount, BpsEgress/Ingress) directly instrument the virtual interface and reveal saturation or physical errors, which is the correct tool for root-cause analysis. Option D is correct: adding a redundant Direct Connect from a different location, or a VPN backup with BGP failover, provides the required connectivity redundancy. Option A (VPC Flow Logs) captures IP-level traffic within the VPC but does not expose Direct Connect VIF-level metrics. Option C (VPC peering) is a VPC-to-VPC construct and does not provide a network path between on-premises and AWS.

stem: A company migrates its website to AWS, using Amazon CloudFront with an S3 static website origin and Route 53 for DNS. After migration, European users report that HTTPS connections to https://www.example.com show a certificate warning indicating the certificate is for '*.cloudfront.net' rather than 'www.example.com'. HTTP requests work correctly. What is the most likely root cause?
tags: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) for TLS certificate management

answers.A: The Route 53 alias record for www.example.com points to the S3 bucket endpoint instead of the CloudFront distribution domain name, causing DNS resolution to bypass CloudFront.
answers.B: The S3 bucket policy blocks HTTPS requests from CloudFront, forcing CloudFront to fall back to its default certificate instead of the custom ACM certificate.
answers.C: The ACM certificate for www.example.com was provisioned in an AWS Region other than us-east-1. CloudFront requires ACM certificates to be in us-east-1; the distribution falls back to the default CloudFront certificate.
answers.D: The CloudFront viewer protocol policy is set to HTTP Only, blocking HTTPS connections and causing the browser to display an untrusted certificate warning for the default CloudFront domain.

explanation: Option C is correct: CloudFront requires SSL/TLS certificates to be provisioned in us-east-1 (N. Virginia). When an ACM certificate is created in any other region, CloudFront falls back to the default *.cloudfront.net certificate, producing exactly the described certificate mismatch warning. Option A would cause DNS resolution failures for all traffic, not only HTTPS. Option B would result in HTTP 403 origin errors, not a TLS certificate name mismatch. Option D (HTTP Only viewer policy) would result in HTTPS connections being redirected or refused before TLS negotiation, not a certificate name mismatch.

stem: EC2 instances in a private subnet cannot reach an Amazon S3 bucket. The instances route internet traffic through a NAT Gateway in a public subnet. VPC Flow Logs show REJECT entries for outbound traffic from the private subnet instances on port 443 destined for S3 IP ranges. The S3 bucket policy explicitly allows the NAT Gateway Elastic IP address. What is the most likely root cause?
tags: VPC Flow Logs and their use cases

answers.A: The private subnet route table is missing a 0.0.0.0/0 route pointing to the NAT Gateway, so traffic cannot leave the subnet.
answers.B: The S3 bucket is in a different AWS Region from the VPC, and the bucket policy does not include a condition allowing cross-Region access from the Elastic IP.
answers.C: The NAT Gateway Elastic IP was recently changed, so the S3 bucket policy still references the old IP address and is rejecting the requests at the S3 service level.
answers.D: A network ACL or security group attached to the private subnet instances is blocking outbound traffic on port 443, causing the REJECT entries seen in VPC Flow Logs.

explanation: Option D is correct: REJECT entries in VPC Flow Logs indicate a security group or NACL is blocking traffic. NAT Gateway routing failures do not produce REJECT log entries; they produce no flow log entry at all. A missing route (Option A) would similarly result in no flow log entry. Option B (cross-Region S3 access) is allowed by default and would produce an S3 authorization error, not a VPC-level REJECT. Option C is plausible but the question states the bucket policy 'explicitly allows the NAT Gateway Elastic IP', implying the IP is current and correctly referenced.

stem: A company uses AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store to manage database credentials for dev, staging, and production environments using path-based hierarchy (/dev/, /staging/, /prod/). A developer accidentally overwrote the production database password with a staging value, causing an outage. The operations team must prevent unauthorized parameter modifications to /prod/ paths and enable rollback of production parameters within 15 minutes. Which solution meets both requirements?
tags: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store and Secrets Manager

answers.A: Enable Parameter Store Advanced tier for production parameters to retain version history. Attach an IAM policy to developer roles that explicitly denies ssm:PutParameter for /prod/* ARNs. Enable CloudTrail and create a CloudWatch metric filter on ssm:PutParameter events for /prod/ paths with an SNS alert.
answers.B: Migrate all production credentials from Parameter Store to AWS Secrets Manager. Enable Secrets Manager automatic rotation for the production database password and restrict access with a Secrets Manager resource-based policy.
answers.C: Tag all production parameters with Environment=production. Create a tag-based IAM condition restricting PutParameter for production-tagged resources to a dedicated ops role only.
answers.D: Create a Lambda function triggered by CloudTrail events for ssm:PutParameter on /prod/ paths. The function retrieves the previous parameter version and calls PutParameter to restore it within the 15-minute SLA.

explanation: Option A is correct: the IAM deny policy on /prod/* ARNs prevents unauthorized writes at the API level (immediate enforcement), Advanced tier retains parameter version history enabling rollback, and CloudTrail with CloudWatch metric filter provides audit visibility and alerts within 15 minutes. Option B (Secrets Manager) addresses credential rotation but does not prevent accidental overwrites by developers with access to the secret. Option C tag-based conditions require correctly applied and maintained tags; a missing tag bypasses the control. Option D automates rollback but does not prevent the overwrite from occurring; prevention via IAM deny is the correct first control.

stem: A company uses AWS Config to enforce tagging compliance across EC2 instances. A required-tags Config rule identifies 47 instances as NON_COMPLIANT because they lack the required 'CostCenter' tag. The security team wants non-compliant instances automatically stopped within 30 minutes of detection and needs an audit trail of every automated action. Which implementation meets both requirements with the least custom code?
tags: AWS Systems Manager OpsCenter and OpsItems

answers.A: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that triggers on AWS Config compliance change events. Route the event to a Lambda function that calls ec2:StopInstances for non-compliant instance IDs. Write execution results to CloudWatch Logs.
answers.B: Configure an AWS Config remediation action linked to an AWS Systems Manager Automation document that stops non-compliant EC2 instances. Enable automatic remediation. Systems Manager records each execution in its history, providing a built-in audit trail.
answers.C: Enable AWS Security Hub and create a custom action that routes NON_COMPLIANT Config findings to an SQS queue. A Lambda function polls the queue, stops non-compliant instances, and writes results to S3 for audit.
answers.D: Create a CloudWatch alarm on a custom Config compliance metric. Configure the alarm to publish to SNS. Subscribe a Lambda function to SNS that reads Config evaluation results and stops non-compliant instances.

explanation: Option B is correct: AWS Config remediation actions natively integrate with Systems Manager Automation, providing auto-remediation without custom Lambda code. SSM Automation records every execution (start time, parameters, output, status) in its execution history, fulfilling the audit trail requirement out of the box. Option A works but requires writing and maintaining custom Lambda code. Option C adds Security Hub overhead which is unnecessary for this targeted compliance use case. Option D's CloudWatch alarm approach is metric-based and less reliable for per-resource compliance remediation than native Config remediation.

stem: A company runs a containerized application on Amazon ECS on EC2 launch type. The operations team must collect custom application metrics (request latency in milliseconds, queue depth) from containers and display them on a CloudWatch dashboard shared with three other teams. The application does not expose a Prometheus endpoint. Which solution meets these requirements with the least operational overhead?
tags: CloudWatch metrics, CloudWatch Logs, and CloudWatch Logs Insights

answers.A: Install the CloudWatch agent on each EC2 host in the ECS cluster configured to collect StatsD metrics emitted by containers. Create a CloudWatch dashboard and share the dashboard URL with the three teams.
answers.B: Configure ECS task definitions to emit custom metrics to an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose stream. Use a Firehose transformation Lambda to convert records into CloudWatch PutMetricData API calls.
answers.C: Add an AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) sidecar container to each ECS task definition. Configure ADOT to emit metrics using CloudWatch EMF directly to CloudWatch. Create a shared CloudWatch dashboard using native cross-account dashboard sharing.
answers.D: Write application metrics from each container to Amazon DynamoDB. Schedule an AWS Glue job to read DynamoDB records every 5 minutes and publish aggregated metrics to CloudWatch using PutMetricData.

explanation: Option C is correct: AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry with CloudWatch EMF is the AWS-recommended pattern for custom container metrics without Prometheus. EMF embeds structured metric data in log events that CloudWatch automatically extracts as metrics. The ADOT sidecar requires no application-layer changes beyond log formatting, and CloudWatch dashboard cross-account sharing is a native feature. Option A (StatsD) requires the application to emit StatsD protocol data, which is an application code change. Option B (Kinesis Firehose + Lambda) introduces unnecessary infrastructure complexity. Option D (DynamoDB + Glue) adds a 5-minute delay and multiple additional services to maintain.

stem: A company's application uses Amazon SQS for decoupling services. Consumer EC2 instances run in an Auto Scaling group. When queue depth exceeds 10,000 messages, the group takes 8 minutes to provision new instances, causing processing delays that breach SLA. The team must ensure consumer instances are ready within 3 minutes of queue depth exceeding the threshold. Which solution reduces scale-out time most effectively?
tags: Auto Scaling policies and their triggers
Amazon CloudWatch alarms and alarm actions

answers.A: Reduce the CloudWatch alarm evaluation period for the SQS ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible metric from 5 minutes to 1 minute to trigger the scale-out alarm sooner.
answers.B: Switch from target tracking scaling on CPU to a step scaling policy on SQS ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible with two steps: add 5 instances above 5,000 and add 10 instances above 10,000.
answers.C: Enable predictive scaling on the Auto Scaling group to forecast queue depth increases and pre-provision instances before the threshold is crossed for recurring load patterns.
answers.D: Configure an Auto Scaling warm pool to maintain pre-initialized stopped instances. Combine with a step scaling policy on SQS ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible so warm pool instances are promoted to the active fleet in under 1 minute when queue depth exceeds 10,000.

explanation: Option D is correct: a warm pool maintains instances that have already completed AMI boot and application initialization, so they can be promoted from stopped state to active in under a minute rather than the 8-minute cold-start time. Step scaling on the SQS metric triggers the promotion immediately when depth exceeds the threshold. Option A reduces alarm evaluation latency by a few minutes but does not address the 8-minute instance launch time. Option B improves scaling aggression but still requires cold-start instance launch time of approximately 8 minutes. Option C (predictive scaling) is beneficial for recurring loads but new or irregular spikes still incur the full cold-start time without a warm pool.

stem: A data engineering team runs an AWS Glue ETL job that reads raw CSV files from Amazon S3, applies transformations using PySpark, and writes Parquet output to a target S3 prefix. During peak hours, the job takes 4 hours to complete, but the business SLA requires completion within 90 minutes. The team has already set the maximum DPU to 50. The Glue job metrics show that the executor CPU utilization averages only 18% and the shuffle write volume is 400 GB. Which action will most likely reduce the job runtime to meet the SLA?
tags: Implementing partitioning strategies to improve query performance and reduce cost
Applying filtering, aggregation, and joins during data transformation

answers.A: Increase the maximum DPU to 200 and enable Glue auto-scaling so that the job can provision additional executors on demand.
answers.B: Repartition the input DataFrame to align partition count with the number of available Glue worker cores, and broadcast the smaller lookup datasets to eliminate shuffle operations.
answers.C: Switch the Glue job type from Spark to Python Shell to reduce startup overhead and allow the job to run on a single high-memory node.
answers.D: Enable Glue job bookmarks so that subsequent runs skip previously processed files, reducing the data volume processed per execution.

explanation: The metrics reveal that CPU utilization is only 18% despite 50 DPUs, and shuffle write is 400 GB. This indicates a data skew or insufficient partitioning problem: most work is concentrated on few tasks (low parallelism) and excessive shuffling inflates runtime. Repartitioning the DataFrame to match the available cores distributes work evenly, and broadcasting small lookup tables eliminates expensive shuffle joins. Together these changes directly address the root causes. Option A adds more DPUs but with only 18% CPU utilization, adding workers will not help—tasks are already bottlenecked by skew or shuffle, not by lack of executors. Option C is wrong because Python Shell jobs cannot run distributed Spark code across multiple workers; they run single-threaded on one node and would perform far worse on 2 TB of data. Option D (job bookmarks) reduces the data scanned in future incremental runs but does nothing to speed up the current full-scan workload—the team already runs with a full scan and the problem is runtime, not redundant processing.

stem: An AWS Glue ETL job reads from an Amazon DynamoDB table using the DynamoDBExport connector and writes results to Amazon S3 in Parquet format. After a recent DynamoDB table growth (now 800 GB), the Glue job consistently fails with an OutOfMemoryError during the collection phase. The team cannot reduce the DynamoDB table size. Which configuration change will most effectively resolve the memory issue?
tags: Reading data from batch sources (for example, Amazon S3, AWS Glue, Amazon EMR, AWS DMS, AWS Snowball, JDBC sources)

answers.A: Enable Glue job bookmarks on the ETL job so that the DynamoDB connector reads only newly added items in each run, reducing the per-run memory footprint.
answers.B: Switch the Glue job type from Spark to Python Shell and use the boto3 DynamoDB scan API with pagination to process items one page at a time.
answers.C: Increase the Glue worker type from Standard to G.2X, enable the DynamoDB parallel scan option by setting a higher splitCount value, and increase the number of workers to distribute partitions across more executors.
answers.D: Enable DynamoDB Streams on the source table and switch the Glue job to consume the stream rather than performing a full table scan.

explanation: The OutOfMemoryError during the collection phase occurs because the DynamoDB connector is attempting to load too much data into too few executors with insufficient memory per executor. The correct fix is to use a larger worker type (G.2X provides 16 GB per executor vs. 8 GB for Standard) and to increase the splitCount parameter, which tells the DynamoDB connector to perform a parallel scan across more segments—distributing the data across more Spark partitions and executors so no single executor must hold a disproportionate amount in memory. Option A (job bookmarks) does not apply to DynamoDB full-export connectors and would not help the initial full-load scenario where all 800 GB must be processed. Option B switches to Python Shell, which is single-threaded and would perform far worse on 800 GB; Python Shell jobs are limited to 1 DPU and cannot distribute work. Option D changes the architecture from batch to streaming, which is a fundamentally different design and does not solve the immediate full-scan requirement for historical data.

stem: A data engineering team maintains an AWS Glue ETL job that joins a 2 TB fact table with a 50 MB lookup table stored in Amazon S3. After enabling Glue job bookmarks, the team notices that the bookmark is not advancing and full scans occur on every run. Investigation reveals the source files lack consistent timestamps and file names are non-deterministic. Which approach should the team use to implement efficient incremental processing?
tags: Building and maintaining idempotent data pipelines
Differentiating between full and incremental data loads

answers.A: Enable S3 versioning on the source bucket and configure the Glue bookmark to use version IDs as the bookmark key instead of file timestamps.
answers.B: Increase the DPU count to reduce per-run latency so that the cost impact of full scans becomes acceptable while preserving the existing architecture.
answers.C: Replace job bookmarks with a Glue workflow trigger that compares Amazon S3 ETag values of source files between runs to determine which files are new.
answers.D: Use Amazon S3 event notifications to capture new file arrivals into an Amazon SQS queue, and modify the Glue job to process only the file paths drained from the queue each run, recording processed keys in a DynamoDB tracking table.

explanation: Glue job bookmarks rely on file modification timestamps or deterministic file naming to identify new files. When files lack consistent timestamps and have non-deterministic names, bookmarks cannot distinguish new from old files and default to full scans. The robust solution (Option D) is to drive incremental processing from S3 event notifications: each new file generates an event captured in SQS, the Glue job drains only those paths, and a DynamoDB tracking table provides idempotency guarantees. This is file-metadata-agnostic and reliable regardless of filename or timestamp patterns. Option A is incorrect because Glue bookmark keys do not natively support S3 version IDs; the bookmark mechanism is not extensible in that way. Option B is not a solution—it just makes the problem cheaper but does not fix the full-scan issue. Option C is architecturally plausible but ETag comparison logic would require custom code in Lambda or another compute layer, and SQS-based event capture (Option D) is simpler and more operationally reliable. Option E uses schema changes as a trigger, which has nothing to do with detecting new data files and would miss runs where data is added without schema changes.

stem: A data lake team uses AWS Glue crawlers to catalog JSON files in Amazon S3. The files are written hourly by an upstream system and each hour's folder contains between 100 and 50,000 files. After a recent upstream schema change added three new optional fields, the Glue crawler continued to report the old schema for three days. Which configuration change most directly prevents stale schema detection after upstream schema changes?
tags: AWS Glue Data Catalog and metadata management
Crawlers and classifiers in AWS Glue

answers.A: Configure the crawler's schema change policy to update the table definition in the Data Catalog, and set the crawler to sample all files rather than a fraction, then schedule the crawler to run after every upstream write batch.
answers.B: Enable Glue Schema Registry on the S3 target and configure the upstream writer to register schema versions before writing files so that the crawler always finds the current schema.
answers.C: Set the crawler's grouping behavior to group all files in a partition into a single S3 target so that the crawler inspects one representative file per partition.
answers.D: Delete and recreate the Glue crawler with the schema change policy set to "Delete tables and add new tables" so that stale tables are automatically removed and recreated on each run.

explanation: When a Glue crawler samples only a fraction of files (the default behavior for large prefixes), it may not inspect any file that contains the new optional fields, especially if new-schema files are a small proportion of the total. Configuring the crawler to sample all files ensures it encounters the new fields and will update the Data Catalog table definition when the schema change policy is set to UPDATE_IN_DATABASE. Scheduling immediately after upstream writes closes the detection window. Option B (Glue Schema Registry) is a valid complementary control for writer-side schema governance, but it does not directly affect how the crawler reads schema from existing files that were already written without registry metadata. Option C (grouping) changes how the crawler groups files into tables but does not control sampling depth; files may still be sampled from older partitions. Option D (delete and recreate tables) would cause all downstream consumers (Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR) to lose table references during the delete phase and is unnecessarily destructive for an additive schema change.

stem: A data platform team runs an AWS Glue crawler against an Amazon S3 prefix that contains data in multiple formats: Parquet files in one subfolder and JSON files in another. The crawler creates a single merged table in the Glue Data Catalog instead of two separate tables. The team needs separate tables for each format. Which crawler configuration change resolves this issue?
tags: AWS Glue Data Catalog and metadata management
Creating and managing databases and tables in the AWS Glue Data Catalog
Crawlers and classifiers in AWS Glue

answers.A: Create a custom classifier for each file format and attach both classifiers to the same crawler; the crawler will then route each format to a separate table automatically.
answers.B: Enable the crawler's "Create a single schema for each S3 path" option and set the grouping level to PARTITION so that each prefix becomes its own partition rather than its own table.
answers.C: Configure the crawler with two separate S3 data store targets, one pointing to the Parquet subfolder and one pointing to the JSON subfolder, each mapped to the same database but using different table name prefixes.
answers.D: Split the single crawler into two crawlers—one for the Parquet subfolder and one for the JSON subfolder—and schedule them to run sequentially to avoid Data Catalog locking conflicts.

explanation: By default, a Glue crawler groups files under a common S3 prefix into a single table. When two structurally different formats share an S3 prefix hierarchy, the crawler merges them. Configuring the crawler with two explicit S3 data store targets (one per format subfolder) causes the crawler to treat each target path independently and create a separate table for each, all within the same database. Option A is incorrect: adding custom classifiers teaches the crawler to recognize file formats but does not instruct it to produce separate tables per format when the targets overlap. Option B is incorrect: the grouping-level setting controls how files within a target are grouped into partitions, not how separate format paths are split into distinct tables. Option D (two separate crawlers) is a valid but unnecessarily complex approach; a single crawler with two S3 targets achieves the same result with half the scheduling complexity and is the recommended pattern in Glue documentation.

stem: An AWS Glue crawler is configured to crawl an Amazon RDS MySQL database. After the crawler runs, tables appear in the Glue Data Catalog, but queries from Amazon Athena against those tables fail with a metastore error. Amazon Redshift Spectrum queries against the same catalog tables succeed. What is the most likely cause and resolution?
tags: Integrating the AWS Glue Data Catalog with Amazon Athena, Amazon EMR, and Amazon Redshift Spectrum
AWS Glue Data Catalog and metadata management
Creating and managing databases and tables in the AWS Glue Data Catalog

answers.A: The Glue crawler created the tables in a database that Athena cannot access because the database name contains uppercase characters; renaming the database to lowercase resolves the issue.
answers.B: Athena cannot directly query JDBC-sourced tables in the Glue Data Catalog because it requires the data to physically reside in Amazon S3; the team must run an AWS Glue ETL job to extract the RDS data to S3 and then re-crawl the S3 location for Athena to query.
answers.C: The Athena execution role lacks the glue:GetTable permission on the specific database; adding this permission to the Athena IAM role resolves the error.
answers.D: The RDS MySQL instance is in a private subnet without a VPC endpoint for Athena, preventing Athena from establishing a JDBC connection at query time; adding an Athena VPC endpoint resolves the issue.

explanation: Amazon Athena queries data stored in Amazon S3 using the Glue Data Catalog as a metadata store. When a Glue crawler catalogs an RDS MySQL JDBC source, it creates catalog table entries that describe the JDBC connection, not S3 objects. Athena does not support federated JDBC catalog entries in the same way Redshift Spectrum can use Redshift Spectrum external schemas backed by JDBC connectors. Athena Federated Query exists but requires a Lambda data source connector—it does not work with raw crawler-created JDBC catalog tables. Redshift Spectrum can use Glue catalog JDBC tables through its external schema mechanism with appropriate credentials, which is why Spectrum succeeds but Athena fails. The resolution is to materialize the data in S3 via a Glue ETL job. Option A is incorrect: Glue and Athena database names are case-insensitive for catalog resolution. Option C is incorrect: the error is not an IAM permission issue—if it were, the same error would appear for Spectrum. Option D is incorrect: Athena does not make JDBC connections to RDS; it is an S3-based query engine.

stem: A financial services company runs daily AWS Glue ETL jobs that load transaction data into Amazon Redshift. Occasionally, upstream systems emit duplicate transaction IDs, causing downstream analytics to overcount revenue. The team wants to automatically detect duplicates before the data reaches Redshift and halt the pipeline when the duplicate rate exceeds 0.5%. Which solution implements this with the least operational overhead?
tags: Data quality dimensions (for example, completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness)
Implementing data validation rules using AWS Glue Data Quality

answers.A: Add an AWS Glue Data Quality ruleset to the ETL job with a UNIQUENESS rule on the transaction ID column and set the job action to HALT when the rule fails; configure the ruleset threshold so that any uniqueness score below 99.5% fails the rule.
answers.B: Add a PySpark transformation step in the Glue job that counts duplicate transaction IDs using a groupBy aggregation, writes the duplicate count to Amazon CloudWatch as a custom metric, and raises a Python exception to halt the job when the rate exceeds 0.5%.
answers.C: Create an AWS Lambda function that runs after each Glue job completes, queries Amazon Redshift using LISTAGG to detect duplicates, and triggers an AWS Step Functions execution to roll back the Redshift load when duplicates are found.
answers.D: Enable Glue job bookmarks and configure the bookmark to skip records with transaction IDs that match those already loaded into Redshift, effectively deduplicating during ingestion.

explanation: AWS Glue Data Quality provides a native ruleset framework that can be embedded directly into a Glue ETL job. A UNIQUENESS rule on the transaction ID column measures the percentage of distinct values; a threshold of 99.5% maps exactly to the 0.5% duplicate rate limit. When the rule fails, the job action HALT stops the pipeline before data reaches Redshift—no custom code required. This is the lowest-overhead solution. Option B achieves the same logical outcome but requires custom PySpark code for the deduplication logic, custom metric publishing code, and manual exception handling—significantly more code and maintenance overhead compared to the native Glue Data Quality ruleset. Option C runs after data is already loaded into Redshift, which means duplicates have already entered the data warehouse; rolling back a Redshift COPY load is complex and error-prone. Option D is incorrect: Glue job bookmarks track file-level processing state for incremental loads; they do not perform record-level deduplication based on field values across runs.

stem: A healthcare data pipeline ingests HL7 FHIR records via AWS Glue ETL jobs. The compliance team requires that every field listed as mandatory in the FHIR specification is non-null in at least 99% of records before the data is written to the data warehouse. The team wants the validation logic version-controlled alongside pipeline code and wants results published to Amazon CloudWatch. Which solution meets these requirements?
tags: Data quality dimensions (for example, completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness)
AWS Glue job logging to Amazon CloudWatch
Logging data quality metrics to Amazon CloudWatch

answers.A: Use AWS Glue DataBrew to create a profile job for the FHIR dataset, configure null value checks for each mandatory field, and schedule the profile job to run before each ETL job. Publish the DataBrew profile results to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
answers.B: Write a custom AWS Lambda function that queries a sample of records from the source S3 bucket, computes null rates for each mandatory field, and publishes custom metrics to Amazon CloudWatch. Trigger the Lambda before each Glue ETL job using Amazon EventBridge.
answers.C: Define an AWS Glue Data Quality ruleset as a JSON file stored in the pipeline's code repository. Embed the ruleset evaluation in the Glue ETL job using the EvaluateDataQuality transform, set CloudWatch metrics publishing to enabled, and halt the job when any rule falls below the 99% threshold.
answers.D: Add a PySpark step at the start of the Glue ETL job that computes null counts for each mandatory column, writes results to an Amazon S3 audit prefix, and raises a Python exception when any column exceeds the null threshold. Store the threshold configuration in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store.

explanation: AWS Glue Data Quality rulesets are defined as DQDL (Data Quality Definition Language) text files that can be stored in a version control repository alongside pipeline code. The EvaluateDataQuality transform is a native Glue ETL transform that evaluates the ruleset inline, publishes pass/fail metrics to Amazon CloudWatch automatically when the publishingOptions are configured, and can halt the job on failure. This satisfies version control, CloudWatch publishing, and low-overhead requirements together. Option A (DataBrew profile jobs) cannot be easily version-controlled as code—profiles are configured through the console or API but not natively as code artifacts in a repository, and DataBrew publishing to CloudWatch Logs is for profiling metadata, not structured rule-pass/fail metrics. Option B uses Lambda custom code, which satisfies none of the least-overhead requirement and adds operational complexity. Option D requires custom PySpark code for null computations and manual exception handling; while functional, it is more code than the native Glue Data Quality approach and does not natively publish structured metrics to CloudWatch.

stem: A marketing analytics team receives customer CSV exports from a CRM system. The files contain inconsistent date formats (MM/DD/YYYY, YYYY-MM-DD, and epoch milliseconds), mixed-case country codes, and occasional negative values in the age column. A data engineer must create a repeatable cleansing workflow that business analysts can re-run without writing code. Which service and workflow combination is most appropriate?
tags: Using AWS Glue DataBrew to profile datasets and identify quality issues

answers.A: Write an AWS Glue ETL job in PySpark that uses conditional expressions to normalize date formats, applies upper() on country codes, and filters out records with negative ages. Store the job script in AWS CodeCommit so analysts can trigger it from the Glue console.
answers.B: Create an AWS Glue DataBrew dataset pointing to the CSV files, build a DataBrew recipe that standardizes date formats using the date-format transformation, normalizes country codes using an UPPERCASE step, and adds a filter to remove negative ages. Publish the recipe and create a DataBrew job that analysts can run on demand from the DataBrew console.
answers.C: Use Amazon Athena to query the CSV files with CAST and CASE expressions to normalize dates and country codes, and export the results to a cleaned S3 prefix. Provide analysts with the saved Athena query they can run from the console.
answers.D: Configure an AWS Lambda function triggered by S3 event notifications that processes each CSV file using Python pandas, applies cleansing transformations, and writes the cleaned file to a destination S3 prefix. Analysts re-trigger cleansing by re-uploading the source file.

explanation: AWS Glue DataBrew is purpose-built for no-code, visual data preparation. It allows data engineers to build reusable recipes through a point-and-click interface, and business analysts can re-run those recipes as DataBrew jobs directly from the console without writing any code. DataBrew has built-in transformations for date format standardization, string case normalization, and value filtering—exactly matching the requirements. Option A uses a PySpark ETL job, which requires analysts to trigger a Glue job they cannot modify or understand without coding knowledge; it violates the no-code re-run requirement. Option C uses Athena SQL queries, which require SQL knowledge from analysts and do not provide a guided, reusable transformation recipe workflow. Option D uses Lambda with pandas, which requires Python knowledge to understand or modify and is not a no-code solution; it also adds operational complexity around Lambda function management.

stem: A data engineering team wants to profile a 500 GB dataset stored in Amazon S3 to identify columns with more than 10% null values, detect outliers using standard-deviation thresholds, and publish a data quality report to stakeholders without writing any custom code. Which AWS service and feature combination satisfies all requirements?
tags: Using AWS Glue DataBrew to profile datasets and identify quality issues
Data quality dimensions (for example, completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness)

answers.A: Use Amazon Athena to run SELECT COUNT(*) and standard deviation queries against the dataset, export results to CSV, and email the CSV to stakeholders as a quality report.
answers.B: Create an AWS Glue Data Quality ruleset with COMPLETENESS rules for each column and STATISTICAL_ANOMALY rules for outlier detection, run the ruleset as a standalone job, and share the CloudWatch metrics dashboard URL with stakeholders.
answers.C: Run an Amazon EMR Spark job using the Deequ library to compute column statistics, write a JSON report to Amazon S3, and share the S3 presigned URL with stakeholders.
answers.D: Create an AWS Glue DataBrew dataset pointing to the S3 data, run a DataBrew profile job, and share the auto-generated profile report—which includes null percentage by column and outlier statistics—with stakeholders via the DataBrew console.

explanation: AWS Glue DataBrew profile jobs are fully managed, require zero custom code, and automatically compute column-level statistics including null percentages, value distributions, and outlier detection using standard-deviation thresholds. The resulting profile report is viewable in the DataBrew console and can be shared with stakeholders. This satisfies all three requirements (null detection, outlier detection, report publishing) without any coding. Option A requires writing SQL queries for each column—this is custom code and does not provide an automatic structured report. Option B (Glue Data Quality rulesets) requires writing DQDL rule definitions, which is code; additionally, Glue Data Quality does not provide the same comprehensive profiling output as DataBrew. Option C requires writing and maintaining an EMR Spark job with a third-party library—this is significant custom code and operational overhead. Option E requires writing a Lambda function with a Python library, which is custom code and adds operational complexity.

stem: A data engineering team manages AWS Glue jobs, AWS Step Functions state machines, and AWS CloudFormation stacks using separate manual deployment processes. The team wants a CI/CD pipeline so that every merge to the main branch automatically tests, packages, and deploys infrastructure changes to a staging environment before promoting to production. The pipeline must block promotion if CloudFormation change set previews show resource deletions. Which solution meets these requirements with the least custom code?
tags: Continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) for data pipelines
Implementing CI/CD pipelines for data engineering workflows
Integrating data pipelines with CI/CD systems

answers.A: Use AWS CodePipeline with a CodeBuild stage to run cfn-nag security checks, a CloudFormation DEPLOY action for staging, and a manual approval stage before production. Write a Lambda function that queries the CloudFormation change set and fails the approval if deletions are present.
answers.B: Use AWS CodePipeline with a CodeBuild stage for unit tests, a CloudFormation CREATE_REPLACE_CHANGE_SET action followed by a CloudFormation EXECUTE_CHANGE_SET action for staging, and a CloudFormation CREATE_REPLACE_CHANGE_SET action before production. Add a CodePipeline condition using the change set review to block execution when the change set contains resource deletions, then add a manual approval action before the production EXECUTE_CHANGE_SET.
answers.C: Use AWS CodePipeline with an AWS CodeDeploy deployment group configured for blue/green deployments of Lambda functions, and add a CloudFormation drift detection step that emails the team when drift is detected. Block promotion with a manual approval action.
answers.D: Use AWS CodePipeline with a CodeBuild stage that calls the AWS CLI to deploy CloudFormation stacks directly using aws cloudformation deploy, parse the output JSON to detect deletions, and exit with a non-zero code to fail the pipeline if deletions are found.

explanation: CodePipeline natively integrates with AWS CloudFormation through the CloudFormation action provider. The CREATE_REPLACE_CHANGE_SET action creates or replaces a change set without executing it, allowing the pipeline to inspect the change set before proceeding. The EXECUTE_CHANGE_SET action then applies it. The change set review capability is built into the CloudFormation action, and CodePipeline can be configured to gate on the change set contents. A manual approval action before the production execute stage provides the human gate. This architecture uses only native CodePipeline actions and requires no custom Lambda or CLI scripting. Option A requires writing a custom Lambda function to query the change set and fail the approval, adding code that must be maintained. Option C uses CodeDeploy, which is appropriate for application code deployments (EC2/Lambda) but is not designed for CloudFormation infrastructure deployments; drift detection is a separate concern that does not block promotion. Option D requires writing custom CLI parsing code in a CodeBuild buildspec, which works but introduces more custom code than the native CloudFormation action approach.

stem: A data platform team stores AWS Glue job scripts and AWS CloudFormation templates in AWS CodeCommit. They use AWS CodePipeline to deploy changes. A new compliance requirement mandates that no pipeline execution can deploy to production without a documented human approval recorded in an immutable audit trail. Which CodePipeline feature satisfies this requirement with the least additional infrastructure?
tags: Continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) for data pipelines
AWS CloudTrail for API activity logging
Implementing CI/CD pipelines for data engineering workflows

answers.A: Add an Amazon SNS notification rule on the CodePipeline pipeline that sends an email to approvers when a deployment is pending. Record approver email replies in an S3 bucket as the audit trail.
answers.B: Create an AWS Lambda function that generates a signed approval token, stores the token in Amazon DynamoDB with the approver identity and timestamp, and requires the token to be submitted to resume the pipeline. Use DynamoDB streams to replicate approvals to S3 for audit.
answers.C: Add a CodePipeline manual approval action to the production stage. Approvers submit their approval through the CodePipeline console or AWS CLI, and every approval or rejection action is automatically recorded in AWS CloudTrail as a PutApprovalResult API call with the approver identity, timestamp, and comments.
answers.D: Require approvers to create a Git tag in the CodeCommit repository with their username and timestamp before the pipeline promotes to production. Configure the pipeline source to detect the tag as a trigger for the production deploy stage.

explanation: CodePipeline's native manual approval action requires an authorized IAM user to explicitly call PutApprovalResult (via console, CLI, or SDK). Every PutApprovalResult call is logged by AWS CloudTrail automatically, capturing the IAM principal identity, timestamp, approval/rejection status, and optional comments. CloudTrail logs are immutable when delivered to an S3 bucket with Object Lock, satisfying the audit trail requirement. No additional infrastructure is needed beyond enabling the approval action. Option A uses SNS emails and S3 storage of email replies, which is not immutable, lacks structured audit records, and relies on email as a control—not suitable for compliance. Option B requires building and maintaining a custom Lambda/DynamoDB/DynamoDB Streams/S3 pipeline, adding significant infrastructure complexity and custom code when a native solution exists. Option D (Git tags) does not prevent the pipeline from running without the tag; it only uses the tag as a trigger. A determined actor could trigger production directly without the governance control, and Git tags in CodeCommit are not an immutable approval record tied to the deployment pipeline.

stem: A security team for a healthcare data platform needs to detect whenever an IAM principal reads objects from a specific Amazon S3 bucket that contains PHI. The team wants near-real-time alerting within 5 minutes and an immutable record of every access event. The solution must not require agents on any compute resources. Which architecture satisfies all requirements?
tags: AWS CloudTrail for API activity logging
Implementing alerting on security-relevant CloudTrail events using Amazon EventBridge and Amazon SNS

answers.A: Enable AWS CloudTrail with a data event for S3 GetObject on the PHI bucket, deliver trail logs to an S3 bucket with Object Lock enabled, create an Amazon EventBridge rule that matches CloudTrail GetObject events for the PHI bucket, and route matches to an Amazon SNS topic that notifies the security team.
answers.B: Enable Amazon S3 server access logging for the PHI bucket, deliver logs to a separate S3 bucket, configure an AWS Lambda function triggered by S3 event notifications on the log bucket to parse access logs and publish alerts to Amazon SNS.
answers.C: Deploy an Amazon GuardDuty detector with S3 Protection enabled, configure GuardDuty findings to publish to Amazon SNS via Amazon EventBridge, and enable S3 server access logging as the primary audit record.
answers.D: Enable VPC Flow Logs for the VPC where compute resources access the S3 bucket, stream flow logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, create a CloudWatch Logs metric filter for traffic to the S3 service IP ranges, and alert via CloudWatch Alarm and SNS.

explanation: CloudTrail data events for S3 record every API call (including GetObject) at the object level and can be streamed in near real time to Amazon EventBridge. EventBridge rules pattern-match on CloudTrail events within seconds, and SNS delivers notifications within the 5-minute window. Delivering trail logs to an S3 bucket with Object Lock (WORM) provides the immutable audit record. No agents are required. Option B uses S3 server access logs, which are delivered on a best-effort basis and can have multi-hour delays—far exceeding the 5-minute alerting requirement. Also, triggering Lambda from log file S3 events adds latency. Option C (GuardDuty with S3 Protection) detects anomalous or potentially malicious access patterns using threat intelligence and ML—it does not alert on every authorized GetObject access. It would miss routine authorized reads and is not designed for access-level auditing of all reads. Option D uses VPC Flow Logs, which capture network-level IP flows and do not record S3 object identifiers, IAM principal information, or API operation names—they cannot reliably identify which S3 object was accessed or by which IAM principal.

stem: A compliance team discovers that an AWS Glue job IAM role was used to delete objects from an Amazon S3 data lake bucket two weeks ago. The team needs to determine the exact API calls made, the source IP address, and the precise timestamps. CloudTrail is enabled, but the team cannot find the relevant events in the CloudTrail console event history. Which is the most likely reason and the correct remediation?
tags: AWS CloudTrail for API activity logging
Enabling and configuring AWS CloudTrail for data service API activity
Using Amazon Athena to query audit logs stored in Amazon S3

answers.A: CloudTrail management events do not capture S3 data-plane operations such as DeleteObject; the team must enable Amazon S3 server access logging to retrieve object-level delete events.
answers.B: The Glue job IAM role assumed a cross-account role, and CloudTrail only records events in the account where the API call originates; the team must check the CloudTrail logs in the target account.
answers.C: CloudTrail console event history shows only management events and not S3 data events by default. The team must verify the trail has S3 data events enabled for the bucket, then query the trail logs delivered to S3 using Amazon Athena to find the DeleteObject calls.
answers.D: CloudTrail event history is limited to 10,000 events per account per region and older events are automatically deleted; the team must contact AWS Support to restore archived CloudTrail logs for the two-week-old events.

explanation: CloudTrail console event history has two key limitations relevant here: (1) it retains only 90 days of events, but more importantly (2) it shows only management events (control-plane API calls) by default—it does not show S3 data events (GetObject, PutObject, DeleteObject) unless a trail is explicitly configured to record data events for the specific S3 bucket. The team cannot find the events because S3 data events may not be enabled. The remediation is to check whether the CloudTrail trail (not just console history) has S3 data events configured, and to query the trail logs stored in S3 using Athena. Option A is incorrect: DeleteObject on S3 is a data event that CloudTrail can record—but only when S3 data events are explicitly enabled on the trail. S3 server access logs would also contain this, but they are not the primary CloudTrail audit mechanism and may have delivery delays. Option B is plausible in cross-account scenarios but is not the most likely reason for events missing in a single-account setup. Option D is factually incorrect: CloudTrail event history is not limited to 10,000 events; it retains 90 days of management events with no fixed event count limit, and there is no archived restoration process through Support.

stem: A data governance team needs to ensure that all Amazon S3 buckets used for data lake storage have server-side encryption enabled with AWS KMS customer-managed keys and that no bucket is publicly accessible. The team wants continuous compliance checking and automatic notification when a bucket drifts from this configuration. Which solution meets these requirements with the least custom code?
tags: AWS Config for resource configuration change tracking
Setting up AWS Config rules to detect non-compliant resource configurations
Implementing alerting on security-relevant CloudTrail events using Amazon EventBridge and Amazon SNS

answers.A: Create an AWS Lambda function that runs on a daily schedule via Amazon EventBridge, lists all S3 buckets using the AWS CLI, checks each bucket's encryption configuration and public access block settings, and sends an SNS notification listing non-compliant buckets.
answers.B: Enable AWS Config with the managed rules s3-bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled and s3-bucket-level-public-access-prohibited. Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule to match AWS Config compliance change events for these rules and route non-compliant events to an Amazon SNS topic.
answers.C: Enable Amazon Macie to continuously scan S3 buckets for unencrypted sensitive data and send Macie findings to Amazon SNS via Amazon EventBridge. Add an S3 bucket policy condition that denies PutObject requests without server-side encryption.
answers.D: Use AWS Security Hub with the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard enabled, which includes S3 encryption and public access controls. Configure Security Hub findings to route to Amazon SNS via Amazon EventBridge.

explanation: AWS Config managed rules provide continuous, event-driven compliance checking without any custom code. The s3-bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled rule flags buckets without SSE, and s3-bucket-level-public-access-prohibited flags buckets that are publicly accessible. Config records every configuration change in near real time, and EventBridge can match AWS Config compliance change events to trigger SNS notifications immediately when a bucket drifts out of compliance. Option A achieves a similar outcome but requires writing and maintaining a Lambda function with S3 API calls, SNS publishing code, and error handling—significantly more custom code than the native Config approach. Option C uses Amazon Macie, which is a data discovery service focused on sensitive data classification, not a continuous compliance checker for bucket configuration settings like encryption policy; Macie findings reflect data content analysis, not configuration compliance. Option D uses Security Hub, which aggregates findings from multiple sources including Config, but Security Hub is primarily a security posture aggregation layer and adding it introduces more components than the direct Config + EventBridge + SNS pattern.

stem: A data engineering team must demonstrate to auditors that every Amazon Redshift cluster in their AWS account has been encrypted at rest for the past 12 months. The team needs to query historical resource configuration states and generate a report showing compliance over time. Which AWS service and feature combination provides this capability?
tags: AWS Config for resource configuration change tracking
Using Amazon Athena to query audit logs stored in Amazon S3

answers.A: Query Amazon CloudWatch metrics for the Redshift cluster over the past 12 months using GetMetricStatistics and check whether the Encrypted dimension was set to true throughout the period.
answers.B: Use AWS CloudTrail to search for CreateCluster and ModifyCluster API events over the past 12 months and verify that each event included an Encrypted parameter set to true.
answers.C: Use Amazon Redshift audit logging to query the connection log and user activity log for encryption-related configuration events over the past 12 months.
answers.D: Use AWS Config configuration history for the AWS::Redshift::Cluster resource type, then query the configuration snapshots delivered to Amazon S3 with Amazon Athena to retrieve the Encrypted field value for each cluster across all recorded states.

explanation: AWS Config records the full configuration state of AWS resources at each configuration change event. For Redshift clusters, Config records the AWS::Redshift::Cluster resource type including the Encrypted attribute. By querying the configuration history snapshots stored in S3 (Config delivers periodic snapshots and change records to S3), the team can retrieve every recorded state of each cluster over time and confirm the Encrypted field was consistently true. Athena makes this S3-based query straightforward without additional infrastructure. Option A is incorrect: Amazon CloudWatch metrics for Redshift do not include an Encrypted dimension or encryption status metric—CloudWatch monitors performance metrics such as CPU, latency, and storage. Option B uses CloudTrail to check CreateCluster and ModifyCluster API events, which only capture configuration changes at the time of the call. If a cluster was created 18 months ago and never modified, there may be no ModifyCluster event in the 12-month window; this approach cannot confirm continuous compliance, only point-in-time API calls. Option C uses Redshift audit logging (connection logs, user activity logs), which records database-level query and connection activity, not cluster infrastructure configuration such as encryption status.

stem: A genomics company needs to process 10,000 genome sequencing files, each 2 to 5 GB, as independent jobs. Processing each file requires 16 vCPUs and 64 GB of memory and takes approximately 30 minutes. The total dataset is available on Amazon S3 and must be processed within 6 hours. Cost must be minimized. Which compute configuration for AWS Batch best meets these requirements?
tags: Parallelization and concurrency in data pipelines
Implementing parallel processing in data pipelines to improve throughput
AWS orchestration and automation services (for example, AWS Step Functions, Amazon MWAA, AWS Glue triggers)

answers.A: Create an AWS Batch managed compute environment using On-Demand c5.4xlarge instances (16 vCPUs, 32 GB RAM). Submit all 10,000 jobs simultaneously. Set the compute environment maximum vCPUs to 160,000.
answers.B: Create an AWS Batch managed compute environment using On-Demand r5.2xlarge instances (8 vCPUs, 64 GB RAM). Submit jobs in batches of 100 to avoid overwhelming the compute environment. Set maximum vCPUs to 80,000.
answers.C: Create an AWS Batch managed compute environment using Spot r5.2xlarge instances (8 vCPUs, 64 GB RAM) with On-Demand as a fallback, using an allocation strategy of SPOT_CAPACITY_OPTIMIZED. Submit all 10,000 jobs simultaneously. Set maximum vCPUs to 160,000.
answers.D: Create an AWS Lambda function that processes each file and configure a Batch array job that invokes Lambda for each of the 10,000 files in parallel.

explanation: Each job needs 16 vCPUs and 64 GB. An r5.2xlarge has 8 vCPUs and 64 GB RAM, but 2 vCPUs are typically reserved for the OS, leaving effectively 6-7 usable; alternatively, consider r5.4xlarge (16 vCPUs, 128 GB) or use vCPU resource requirements in the job definition. For the purpose of this question, the key tradeoffs are: (1) cost minimization favors Spot Instances, which can save 60-90% over On-Demand; (2) the 6-hour SLA gives headroom to handle occasional Spot interruptions with retry, especially with SPOT_CAPACITY_OPTIMIZED allocation strategy that picks pools with highest Spot availability; (3) submitting all 10,000 jobs at once lets Batch's scheduler pack instances optimally. Option C uses Spot with capacity-optimized allocation and On-Demand fallback, maximizing cost savings while maintaining SLA reliability. Option A uses c5.4xlarge instances, which have only 32 GB RAM—insufficient for the 64 GB memory requirement; these instances would fail the job memory requirements. Option B uses On-Demand r5.2xlarge instances, which meet memory requirements but forgo Spot savings; batching submissions in groups of 100 adds unnecessary orchestration complexity and slows overall throughput. Option D is incorrect: AWS Batch array jobs invoke Batch job definitions, not Lambda functions; Lambda has a 15-minute execution limit and 10 GB memory limit, both insufficient for 30-minute, 64 GB jobs.

stem: A data engineering team uses AWS Batch to run nightly ETL jobs. Jobs are submitted to a managed compute environment backed by Amazon EC2 On-Demand instances. The team has observed that jobs frequently wait 25 to 40 minutes in the RUNNABLE state before starting. The compute environment MinvCPUs is set to 0. Which change most directly reduces the wait time without significantly increasing cost?
tags: Parallelization and concurrency in data pipelines
AWS orchestration and automation services (for example, AWS Step Functions, Amazon MWAA, AWS Glue triggers)

answers.A: Increase MinvCPUs to 32 to 64 vCPUs so that a small pool of instances stays warm and jobs can start immediately, accepting the modest baseline cost of 2 to 4 always-running instances.
answers.B: Switch the managed compute environment from EC2 to AWS Fargate so that containers start faster without waiting for EC2 instance provisioning.
answers.C: Submit jobs 30 minutes before the intended processing window so that the RUNNABLE wait time is absorbed before the business deadline.
answers.D: Increase the job timeout to 90 minutes so that the RUNNABLE wait time is included in the allowed execution window and jobs do not fail prematurely.

explanation: The RUNNABLE delay occurs because Batch must provision new EC2 instances from scratch when MinvCPUs is 0—there are no pre-warmed instances. EC2 instance launch and ECS container agent registration typically take 10 to 20 minutes, which combined with AMI customization or bootstrap scripts can reach 25 to 40 minutes. Setting MinvCPUs to a small nonzero value keeps a baseline pool of instances always running, so submitted jobs can be scheduled immediately without waiting for provisioning. The cost of 2 to 4 idle instances overnight is modest compared to the operational benefit of meeting nightly SLAs. Option B suggests switching to Fargate. Fargate does start containers faster than EC2 cold-starts for small containers, but for ETL jobs that require 16+ vCPUs and 64 GB RAM (as in the broader context of this exam domain), Fargate vCPU/memory limits (4 vCPU, 30 GB per task) may be insufficient; also, Fargate compute environments in Batch have different job definition requirements. More importantly, Fargate startup is faster but still has its own cold-start overhead and does not eliminate provisioning latency for large resource requirements. Option C is operationally awkward and does not fix the root cause. Option D increases the timeout but does not reduce the actual wait time—jobs still wait 25 to 40 minutes; the timeout setting prevents job failure but does not accelerate scheduling.

stem: A large enterprise needs to migrate 2 PB of on-premises NFS data to Amazon S3 over a 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect link. The migration must complete within 30 days and data integrity must be verified after transfer. The on-premises environment cannot tolerate significant network saturation during business hours. Which AWS DataSync configuration best meets these requirements?
tags: Reading data from batch sources (for example, Amazon S3, AWS Glue, Amazon EMR, AWS DMS, AWS Snowball, JDBC sources)
Batch data ingestion (for example, scheduled ingestion, event-driven ingestion)

answers.A: Deploy a single DataSync agent on-premises, configure one DataSync task to run continuously 24/7 using default bandwidth utilization, and enable data verification in the task settings.
answers.B: Use multiple AWS Snowball Edge devices to copy 2 PB offline, import the devices into Amazon S3, and run a DataSync task afterward to sync only delta changes.
answers.C: Deploy multiple DataSync agents on-premises, each handling a subset of the NFS namespace, configure all tasks to run 24/7 at maximum bandwidth, and enable task verification for each task.
answers.D: Deploy multiple DataSync agents across NFS subdirectory partitions, schedule tasks to run only during off-peak hours, set bandwidth throttling to 80% of Direct Connect capacity, and enable data verification for each task.

explanation: The requirements are: (1) migrate 2 PB over 30 days, (2) verify data integrity, (3) avoid business-hour network saturation. At 10 Gbps theoretical max, 2 PB over 30 days requires sustained ~6.2 Gbps average throughput. Using multiple DataSync agents across NFS subdirectory partitions maximizes parallel transfer throughput. Restricting transfers to off-peak hours (10 hours/night) and throttling to 80% of Direct Connect capacity (~8 Gbps) during those windows: 8 Gbps × 10 hours × 30 days ≈ 10.8 PB theoretical capacity, well above 2 PB. Data verification is enabled per task. This satisfies all three requirements. Option A uses a single agent (limited parallelism) and runs 24/7 saturating the Direct Connect during business hours—violates the business-hour constraint. Option B uses Snowball, which avoids Direct Connect saturation but adds device shipping and import time (days per shipment), which may not fit within 30 days for 2 PB across multiple device capacities; DataSync for delta sync after is an additional step. This is operationally heavier. Option C uses multiple agents (good for parallelism) but runs 24/7 at maximum bandwidth, violating the business-hour saturation constraint. Option E limits to 1 Gbps: 1 Gbps × 24h × 30d ≈ 324 TB—far below 2 PB; this would not complete in 30 days.

stem: A retail company uses AWS DataSync to replicate data from an on-premises SMB file share to Amazon S3 on a nightly schedule. After a recent network infrastructure change, DataSync tasks complete successfully but files that should be excluded by filter patterns are appearing in the S3 destination. The filter patterns were not modified. Which is the most likely cause?
tags: Reading data from batch sources (for example, Amazon S3, AWS Glue, Amazon EMR, AWS DMS, AWS Snowball, JDBC sources)
Batch data ingestion (for example, scheduled ingestion, event-driven ingestion)

answers.A: The DataSync agent was upgraded to a new version during the network change, and the new agent version changed the filter pattern syntax from glob patterns to regular expressions, causing previously excluded patterns to match nothing.
answers.B: The network infrastructure change routed DataSync agent traffic through a new network path that bypasses the existing DataSync task configuration. A second DataSync task without the filter patterns was inadvertently created and scheduled, running alongside the original task and copying unfiltered data.
answers.C: DataSync filter patterns are applied at the agent level during the source scan phase. After the network change, the agent was replaced with a new agent instance that does not inherit the filter configuration from the previous agent; filter patterns must be re-applied to the new agent.
answers.D: The SMB file share permissions changed during the network infrastructure update, granting the DataSync agent broader read access to previously inaccessible directories. DataSync filter patterns only exclude files the agent could previously see; newly accessible files bypass the filter evaluation.

explanation: DataSync filter patterns are configured at the task level, not at the agent level, and they apply universally to all files scanned by that task regardless of agent instance or network path. The most operationally plausible scenario when filtered files appear after a network change—with no filter modification—is that a second DataSync task without filter patterns was created (perhaps during the network reconfiguration or testing) and is running alongside the original. The second task copies data without filters, explaining why excluded files appear in S3 even though the original task's filters were not modified. Option A is incorrect: DataSync does not auto-upgrade agents silently during network changes, and the filter syntax (glob patterns) has not changed between versions. Option C is incorrect: DataSync filter patterns are stored in the task definition, not on the agent. When an agent is replaced or re-registered, it operates under whatever task definitions it is assigned; the task retains its filter configuration. Option D is plausible but less likely to be the primary cause: newly accessible directories would be new paths, and DataSync filter patterns evaluate all scanned files including newly discovered ones—so broader SMB permissions would mean more files are scanned, and the filters would still apply to those files.

stem: A development team uses AWS CodeDeploy to deploy a Node.js Lambda function that processes financial transactions. The deployment configuration is set to Linear10PercentEvery1Minute. After a recent deployment began, the CloudWatch alarm monitoring transaction error rates triggered. The team wants to ensure that the deployment automatically rolls back when the alarm fires, with minimal configuration overhead. Which CodeDeploy configuration correctly enables this behavior?

answers.A: In the deployment group, set the deployment type to In-Place and define a manual approval step in CodePipeline that stops the traffic shift and triggers a rollback when the alarm fires.
answers.B: Add a BeforeAllowTraffic hook in the AppSpec file that polls the CloudWatch alarm state every 30 seconds and calls the StopDeployment API if the alarm is in ALARM state.
answers.C: In the CodeDeploy deployment group, enable automatic rollback on deployment failure and add the CloudWatch alarm to the deployment group alarm list, selecting Rollback when alarm threshold is met.
answers.D: Create an EventBridge rule that matches the CloudWatch alarm state-change event and invokes a Lambda function that calls the CodeDeploy StopDeployment API with the autoRollbackEnabled flag.
