explanation: CodeDeploy deployment groups natively support CloudWatch alarm-based automatic rollback. When the specified alarm transitions to ALARM during a deployment, CodeDeploy automatically stops traffic shifting and rolls back to the previous version — no custom Lambda or polling logic is needed. Option A is incorrect because in-place deployments do not apply to Lambda functions deployed via CodeDeploy, and manual approval steps do not perform automatic rollback. Option B is incorrect because BeforeAllowTraffic hooks run before traffic is shifted, not during the linear shift, and polling from a hook is not a supported pattern. Option D is incorrect because the StopDeployment API does not accept an autoRollbackEnabled flag at call time; rollback behavior is configured at the deployment group level, and this approach adds unnecessary complexity.

stem: A company manages a microservices application deployed with AWS CodeDeploy using a blue/green deployment strategy on Amazon ECS. After a new version is deployed, validation tests fail and the engineering team needs to roll back immediately. The current deployment is in the traffic-shifting phase, with 30% of production traffic already routed to the replacement task set. What is the fastest way to return all traffic to the original task set and terminate the replacement task set?

answers.A: In the CodeDeploy console or via the AWS CLI, call StopDeployment with the autoRollbackEnabled flag set to true, which redirects all traffic to the original task set and terminates the replacement task set.
answers.B: Update the ECS service desired count of the replacement task set to zero in the ECS console; the load balancer will automatically detect the missing targets and route all traffic back to the original task set.
answers.C: Delete the replacement task set directly through the ECS console; CodeDeploy will detect the missing task set, mark the deployment failed, and reroute traffic to the original task set automatically.
answers.D: Modify the Application Load Balancer listener rule weights manually in the EC2 console to set the original target group weight to 100 and the replacement target group weight to zero.

explanation: The StopDeployment API with autoRollbackEnabled=true is the official CodeDeploy mechanism for immediately halting an in-progress blue/green deployment, rerouting all traffic to the original (blue) task set, and terminating the replacement (green) task set. This is atomic and managed by CodeDeploy. Option B would leave the CodeDeploy deployment in an indeterminate state and does not trigger a managed rollback. Option C would cause an error because CodeDeploy still owns the task set lifecycle during a deployment; manually deleting it bypasses the deployment controller and can leave the load balancer in an inconsistent state. Option D manually adjusts the load balancer but does not notify CodeDeploy to clean up the replacement task set, leaving orphaned resources.

stem: An e-commerce company uses AWS CodePipeline to deploy a serverless application. The pipeline has Source (CodeCommit), Build (CodeBuild), and Deploy (AWS SAM) stages. The security team requires that every deployment to production be approved by a named principal from the release-managers group before proceeding. The approval notification should be sent via email with a link to review the build artifacts. Which solution meets these requirements with the least operational overhead?

answers.A: Add a Lambda invoke action before the Deploy stage that sends an email via Amazon SES, waits for a reply, and calls the PutApprovalResult API only if the reply contains an approval token.
answers.B: Add a Manual Approval action before the Deploy stage. Configure the action with an Amazon SNS topic that notifies the release-managers group. Pipeline execution pauses until an authorized approver approves or rejects the action in the CodePipeline console.
answers.C: Configure an EventBridge rule to detect the pipeline execution state change to STARTED and invoke a Lambda function that checks group membership via IAM and conditionally calls PutApprovalResult.
answers.D: Create an AWS Step Functions state machine with a task token that emails the release-managers group, waits for a callback, and resumes the pipeline by calling the CodePipeline PutApprovalResult API with the approval token.

explanation: CodePipeline has a built-in Manual Approval action type that pauses the pipeline until an authorized user approves or rejects it via the console, CLI, or API. An SNS topic can be attached so approvers receive an email notification with a direct review link. This requires no custom code beyond SNS configuration. Option A is unnecessary complexity — SES reply parsing for approval is fragile and requires custom Lambda logic. Option C is also overly complex and does not truly pause the pipeline for human review. Option D uses Step Functions correctly for human-approval workflows but adds significant setup overhead when CodePipeline already provides the feature natively.

stem: A DevOps engineer maintains a CodePipeline pipeline that builds and deploys a container image to Amazon ECS. A broken commit merged to the main branch caused the pipeline to fail in the Build stage, blocking all downstream deployments for several hours. The team wants to validate commits before they reach the main branch to prevent a broken build from blocking the pipeline. Which approach best addresses this using native AWS developer tooling?

answers.A: Add a pre-build phase in the CodeBuild buildspec.yml that runs a git clone of the main branch and executes unit tests against the merged code before building the container image.
answers.B: Create a second CodePipeline pipeline triggered by pull-request events from the CodeCommit repository that runs build and test stages, blocking merging until the pipeline succeeds.
answers.C: Enable pipeline notifications through Amazon SNS so that developers are alerted immediately when a build fails, allowing them to push a fix commit within the same hour.
answers.D: Configure a separate CodeBuild project to trigger on each CodeCommit pull request via EventBridge. The project runs unit tests and posts build status to the pull request. Configure a CodeCommit approval rule requiring green CodeBuild status before a PR can be merged to main.

explanation: CodeCommit supports approval rule templates and can surface build status from CodeBuild on pull requests. Configuring EventBridge to trigger a CodeBuild project on pull request events and blocking merges until the build is green prevents broken commits from reaching the main branch. Option A tests after the commit is already on main and does not prevent the broken commit from entering the branch. Option B describes a valid concept but CodePipeline does not natively trigger on pull-request events; that requires an EventBridge rule and CodeBuild — Option D is the precise description. Option C only improves reaction time; it does not prevent the broken build from entering the pipeline.

stem: A retail company is designing an order fulfillment workflow involving sequential steps: payment authorization, inventory reservation, shipping label generation, and customer notification. Some steps can take up to 10 minutes. On failure at any step, all previously completed steps must be compensated (reversed). The team wants a managed workflow with clear execution state visibility. Which AWS service and pattern best satisfies these requirements?

answers.A: Implement an AWS Step Functions Standard Workflow using a saga pattern, where each state invokes a Lambda function for the step and Catch blocks invoke compensation Lambda functions on failure.
answers.B: Implement an AWS Step Functions Express Workflow using parallel states for each step and configure a CloudWatch Logs destination to capture execution history for visibility.
answers.C: Implement the workflow using an Amazon SQS FIFO queue per step, where each Lambda consumer enqueues a message to the next queue on success or sends a message to a dead-letter queue for compensation.
answers.D: Implement the workflow using Amazon EventBridge with a custom event bus, where each step publishes a domain event and a set of Lambda rules implement compensation logic by matching failure events.

explanation: AWS Step Functions Standard Workflows support long-running executions (up to 1 year), exactly-once execution semantics, and full execution history with visual state map. The saga pattern implemented via Catch blocks on each state cleanly handles compensation logic when a step fails. Option B is incorrect because Express Workflows are designed for high-volume, short-duration workflows with at-least-once execution; execution history is not stored in Step Functions and full visibility requires CloudWatch Logs queries. Option C using SQS FIFO queues requires significant custom orchestration logic and lacks built-in state visualization and compensation management. Option D using EventBridge is a choreography pattern that is difficult to reason about for compensation logic and does not provide workflow state visibility.

stem: A developer is implementing an AWS Step Functions state machine that calls an external payment gateway API using an HTTP task. The API occasionally returns HTTP 429 errors. The state machine must retry automatically with exponential backoff and stop retrying after 5 attempts. If all retries are exhausted, the workflow must route to a failure-notification state rather than failing the entire execution. Which state machine configuration achieves this?
tags: Fault-tolerant design patterns (for example, retries with exponential backoff and jitter, dead-letter queues)

answers.A: On the Task state, add a Catch field matching States.TaskFailed with Next set to FailureNotification. Add a Retry field with MaxAttempts of 5 and BackoffRate of 2. The Catch will trigger only after all retries are exhausted.
answers.B: Wrap the payment API call in a Lambda function that implements retry logic with exponential backoff internally. On final failure, the Lambda throws a custom exception that the state machine catches and routes to FailureNotification.
answers.C: On the Task state, define a Retry field with ErrorEquals set to States.ALL, MaxAttempts set to 5, and BackoffRate set to 2. Define a Catch field with ErrorEquals set to States.ALL and Next set to FailureNotification.
answers.D: Configure a Wait state after the Task state that delays execution, then loops back to the Task state for a retry. Use a DynamoDB counter to track the attempt number, and after 5 iterations route to FailureNotification.

explanation: Step Functions natively supports Retry and Catch on Task states. Retry with MaxAttempts=5 and BackoffRate=2 handles exponential backoff automatically. After all retries are exhausted and the state still fails, the Catch field routes execution to FailureNotification rather than failing the execution. States.ALL is the correct error matcher for any error type. Option A uses States.TaskFailed in the Catch, which does not catch all error types that can arise from HTTP task integrations; States.ALL is more appropriate here. Option B moves retry logic into Lambda, bypassing Step Functions built-in retry capabilities and adding unnecessary code. Option D using a Wait state and DynamoDB counter manually reimplements what Step Functions provides natively, adding latency and complexity.

stem: A gaming company streams real-time player event data through Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with 10 shards. A Lambda function processes events via an event source mapping. During peak hours, some shards have a processing lag exceeding 60 seconds while others are idle. The application must process events from each player in strict order, but events from different players can be processed concurrently. Which configuration change reduces per-shard lag while preserving per-player ordering?

answers.A: Increase the number of shards to 20 using the Kinesis UpdateShardCount API. More shards distribute events more evenly and automatically increase Lambda concurrency across the stream.
answers.B: Enable enhanced fan-out for the Kinesis stream. Enhanced fan-out provides each Lambda event source mapping with a dedicated 2 MB/s throughput per shard, reducing read latency.
answers.C: Configure the event source mapping with BisectBatchOnFunctionError enabled. This setting splits a failed batch in half and retries each half separately, reducing the effective batch size and improving throughput.
answers.D: Configure the event source mapping with ParallelizationFactor set to 10. Lambda partitions each shard into sub-shards by partition key, allowing up to 10 concurrent invocations per shard while preserving order within each partition key.

explanation: ParallelizationFactor (1-10) allows Lambda to process multiple sub-batches from a single Kinesis shard concurrently. Lambda splits the shard by partition key, guaranteeing that records with the same partition key (player ID) are processed in order while records with different partition keys can be processed in parallel. This directly addresses per-shard lag without re-sharding. Option A (re-sharding) increases overall capacity but requires data redistribution and does not address the imbalance within existing shards at the Lambda concurrency level. Option B (enhanced fan-out) reduces read throttling by giving the consumer dedicated throughput but does not increase the number of concurrent Lambda invocations per shard. Option C (BisectBatchOnFunctionError) is a failure-handling feature for error recovery, not a throughput scaling mechanism.

stem: An analytics company ingests log data from IoT sensors via Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with 20 shards. A consumer application using the Kinesis Client Library (KCL) falls behind during peak ingestion windows. CloudWatch metrics show high GetRecords latency and throttling at the shard level due to multiple consumer applications sharing the same read throughput. The team wants to reduce throttling and increase consumer read throughput without increasing the shard count. Which approach resolves the problem?

answers.A: Switch the Kinesis stream from on-demand capacity mode to provisioned mode and manually set the shard count to a higher value to increase throughput capacity.
answers.B: Register the consumer application as an enhanced fan-out consumer using RegisterStreamConsumer. Enhanced fan-out provides each registered consumer with a dedicated 2 MB/s read throughput per shard via HTTP/2 server push, eliminating contention from the shared GetRecords limits.
answers.C: Increase the GetRecords call frequency in the KCL consumer from the default one call per second to one call every 200 milliseconds per shard to retrieve records more quickly.
answers.D: Enable server-side encryption on the Kinesis stream using AWS KMS to reduce the processing overhead per record, freeing throughput capacity for higher record ingestion rates.

explanation: Enhanced fan-out provides each registered consumer its own dedicated 2 MB/s per shard throughput delivered via HTTP/2 server push (SubscribeToShard), completely independent of other consumers. This eliminates read-side throttling caused by multiple consumers sharing the standard 2 MB/s GetRecords limit without changing the shard count. Option A switches capacity mode and increases shards, which changes the shard count — explicitly ruled out by the question. Option C is incorrect because the standard GetRecords API limit is one call per second per shard per consumer; polling more frequently causes additional throttling errors. Option D is incorrect because KMS encryption has no effect on Kinesis read throughput limits.

stem: A team manages a multi-tier AWS application using AWS CloudFormation. A developer accidentally changed the DeletionPolicy on an Amazon RDS database from Retain to Delete in a template update. The operations team caught the change before it was deployed. The team uses a CI/CD pipeline where templates are committed to CodeCommit and deployed via CodePipeline. Which preventive control most effectively catches this type of policy-sensitive change before it reaches production?

answers.A: Enable CloudFormation drift detection on all stacks. Drift detection identifies differences between the running stack and the template and alerts the team to unauthorized changes before deployment.
answers.B: Configure a CloudFormation stack policy on the RDS stack that denies all updates to the database resource, preventing any template change from modifying the resource.
answers.C: Add a CodeBuild action in the pipeline before the Deploy stage that runs cfn-lint for syntax validation and a custom script that compares DeletionPolicy values in the submitted template against a known-safe policy list. Fail the build if a violation is found.
answers.D: Enable CloudTrail data events for CloudFormation and create a CloudWatch Alarm that triggers an SNS notification when an UpdateStack API call is detected, alerting the team to review the change.

explanation: Adding a static analysis stage in the CI/CD pipeline using cfn-lint and a custom validation script catches the DeletionPolicy violation before the template is deployed — a true preventive control. Option A (drift detection) identifies differences between the running stack and the last deployed template but cannot compare a new template before it is applied; it is a detective control, not preventive. Option B (stack policy) is preventive but blocks all updates to the resource, not just DeletionPolicy changes — this would prevent legitimate schema updates as well. Option D is a detective control that alerts after the UpdateStack call is made, after the deployment has started, not before.

stem: A development team defines AWS infrastructure using a single CloudFormation template stored in CodeCommit. The same template must be deployed to development, staging, and production environments with different parameter values (for example, instance types and database sizes). The team wants to avoid maintaining three separate template copies. How should deployments be structured to use environment-specific values from a single template?

answers.A: Define a Parameters section in the CloudFormation template for environment-specific values. Create a separate JSON parameter file for each environment. In the CodePipeline CloudFormation deploy actions, reference the environment-specific parameter file for each stage using parameter overrides.
answers.B: Create three separate CloudFormation templates using CloudFormation macros to share common resource definitions. Store all three templates in CodeCommit and deploy them independently per environment.
answers.C: Use AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store to store all environment-specific values and reference them directly in the template using the resolve:ssm dynamic reference syntax, eliminating the need for per-environment parameter files.
answers.D: Create a CloudFormation StackSet with one stack instance per environment account and pass environment-specific values through StackSet operation-level parameter overrides per stack instance.

explanation: CloudFormation Parameters combined with per-environment JSON parameter override files is the standard pattern for environment-specific deployments from a single template. CodePipeline CloudFormation deploy actions accept parameter override files natively, making per-environment deployment straightforward. Option B uses three separate templates, violating the single-template requirement and creating maintenance overhead. Option C (SSM dynamic references) can work but couples the template to SSM path naming conventions and makes parameter values less visible at deploy time; parameter files (Option A) are more explicit and portable across accounts. Option D (StackSets) is designed for deploying the same stack to multiple AWS accounts or regions from a management account, not for environment-specific parameter variation within a single-account CI/CD pipeline.

stem: A company runs a production web application on AWS Elastic Beanstalk using a load-balanced environment with 8 instances. A new application version must be deployed with zero downtime. The deployment must limit the blast radius of a bad release — only a subset of instances should be running the new version at any point — and the environment must maintain full production capacity throughout the rollout. Which Elastic Beanstalk deployment policy satisfies all requirements?

answers.A: Use the All at once deployment policy. All instances are updated simultaneously, providing the fastest deployment; a subsequent redeployment of the previous version rolls back if errors occur.
answers.B: Use the Rolling deployment policy with a batch size of 2 instances. Two instances are updated at a time; the remaining 6 continue serving traffic, and no additional capacity is launched.
answers.C: Use the Rolling with additional batch deployment policy with a batch size of 2 instances. Elastic Beanstalk launches 2 additional instances before updating the existing fleet, ensuring all 8 original instances serve traffic throughout the rollout.
answers.D: Use the Immutable deployment policy. Elastic Beanstalk launches a full parallel set of 8 new instances in a separate Auto Scaling group and routes all traffic to them after health checks pass.

explanation: Rolling with additional batch launches a new batch of instances (equal to the batch size) before updating the existing fleet, ensuring total capacity never drops below the original 8 instances. This achieves zero downtime, limited blast radius (only 2 instances at a time run the new version), and full capacity throughout. Option A (All at once) causes a brief period where all instances run the new version simultaneously and there is downtime during the update. Option B (Rolling without additional batch) reduces capacity by the batch size during updates — 6 of 8 instances serve traffic while 2 are being updated — violating the full-capacity requirement. Option D (Immutable) achieves zero downtime and blast-radius isolation but doubles the instance count temporarily; it does not maintain exactly the original 8 instances serving traffic while limiting the new version to a subset.

stem: A startup runs a Python Flask application on AWS Elastic Beanstalk. The production database connection string is currently stored as a hardcoded Elastic Beanstalk environment property visible in plaintext through the Elastic Beanstalk console. The security team flagged this as a critical finding and requires the secret to be injected securely at runtime without modifying the application code. Which approach best resolves the finding?

answers.A: Store the connection string in an Elastic Beanstalk environment variable using the Elastic Beanstalk console. Environment variables are not committed to source control and are separate from the application code.
answers.B: Encrypt the connection string using AWS KMS and embed the ciphertext in the Elastic Beanstalk environment configuration file in the CodeCommit repository. The application decrypts the value at startup using the KMS Decrypt API.
answers.C: Store the connection string as a SecureString in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Reference the Parameter Store key as a dynamic reference in the Elastic Beanstalk environment configuration using resolve:ssm-secure.
answers.D: Store the connection string in AWS Secrets Manager. Use an Elastic Beanstalk .ebextensions configuration file with a container_commands entry to retrieve the secret at instance startup using the AWS CLI and inject it into the application environment without storing it in plaintext anywhere.

explanation: AWS Secrets Manager is the purpose-built service for storing and rotating application secrets. Using .ebextensions to retrieve the secret at instance startup via the AWS CLI keeps the secret out of source control, out of plaintext environment configurations, and out of the Beanstalk console. Secrets Manager also supports automatic rotation. Option A removes the secret from source control but leaves it exposed as a plaintext value in the Elastic Beanstalk console and API responses. Option B stores ciphertext in source control, which is an improvement but still a risk for ciphertext exposure and does not support automatic rotation. Option C (Parameter Store SecureString with resolve:ssm-secure) is a valid pattern but Elastic Beanstalk does not natively support the resolve:ssm-secure dynamic reference syntax in environment property values — this syntax works in CloudFormation templates, not Beanstalk configuration.

stem: A mobile application allows users to sign in with their Google account. After sign-in, the app must access the user's private photos stored in Amazon S3 under a prefix uniquely scoped to each user's identity. The team uses Amazon Cognito for identity management. Which implementation correctly scopes each authenticated Google user's S3 access to only their own prefix?

answers.A: Configure an Amazon Cognito identity pool with Google as a federated identity provider. Attach an IAM role to the identity pool with an S3 bucket resource ARN that includes the Cognito identity ID policy variable (${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}) as the object prefix, limiting each user to their own folder.
answers.B: Configure an Amazon Cognito user pool with Google as a social sign-in provider. After the user authenticates, use the user pool JWT ID token to call the S3 API directly. S3 validates the JWT and enforces the access scope based on the email claim.
answers.C: Configure an Amazon Cognito identity pool with Google as a federated identity provider. After authentication, use the identity pool OpenID Connect token to call the S3 GetObject API directly. The OIDC token acts as a bearer token accepted by the S3 service endpoint.
answers.D: Configure an Amazon Cognito user pool with Google social sign-in. After the user authenticates, use the ID token to call AWS STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity and manually construct an IAM session policy that restricts the user to their S3 prefix.

explanation: Cognito identity pools are designed for exactly this pattern: federate external identity providers such as Google and vend temporary AWS credentials via STS. The IAM role policy attached to the authenticated role can use the ${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub} policy variable to scope each user's S3 access to a unique prefix matching their Cognito identity ID. Option B is incorrect because S3 does not accept Cognito user pool JWTs as authorization tokens; S3 requires AWS SigV4-signed requests with IAM credentials. Option C is incorrect because Cognito identity pool OpenID tokens must be exchanged for AWS credentials via GetCredentialsForIdentity before making AWS API calls; they cannot be used directly as S3 bearer tokens. Option D describes a valid flow in concept but is unnecessarily manual — Cognito identity pools internally perform the STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity exchange so developers do not need to call STS directly.

stem: A developer is building a single-page application (SPA) that authenticates users through Amazon Cognito user pools using the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow with PKCE. After authentication, the app calls a backend REST API protected by Amazon API Gateway. Which sequence correctly implements the PKCE flow for a public client?

answers.A: The SPA sends the client secret alongside the authorization code to the Cognito token endpoint. Cognito validates the client secret, confirms the authorization code, and returns ID, access, and refresh tokens. The SPA sends the access token as a session cookie in API Gateway requests.
answers.B: The SPA generates a random code verifier, derives a code challenge as BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier)), and includes the code challenge in the authorization request. After receiving the authorization code, the SPA exchanges it at the token endpoint by sending the code verifier. Cognito verifies the code verifier against the stored challenge and returns tokens. The SPA sends the access token in the Authorization: Bearer header of API Gateway requests.
answers.C: The SPA includes the plaintext code verifier directly in the authorization request URL to the Cognito hosted UI. Cognito stores the verifier and returns an authorization code. The SPA exchanges the code for tokens by sending the authorization code alone, with no additional verification parameter.
answers.D: The SPA uses the implicit grant flow where Cognito returns ID and access tokens directly in the URL fragment after the authorization redirect. The SPA extracts the access token from the fragment and attaches it to API Gateway requests as a query string parameter.

explanation: PKCE for public clients works as follows: the client generates a cryptographically random code verifier, computes the code challenge as BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier)), includes code_challenge and code_challenge_method=S256 in the authorization request, then after receiving the authorization code, sends the code verifier (not the challenge) to the token endpoint. Cognito verifies the verifier against the stored challenge before issuing tokens. Access tokens are sent in the Authorization: Bearer header for API Gateway. Option A describes the confidential client flow using a client secret — PKCE is designed to replace the client secret for public clients like SPAs where secrets cannot be safely stored. Option C incorrectly sends the plaintext verifier in the authorization request, which defeats the purpose of PKCE. Option D describes the implicit flow, which is deprecated and not recommended for SPAs because tokens in URL fragments are exposed in browser history.

stem: A distributed microservices application processes customer orders through five Lambda functions connected via Amazon SQS queues. The team experiences intermittent order failures and cannot determine which function is responsible. They need end-to-end tracing that links the initial API call through all downstream Lambda invocations and SQS message passes into a unified view. Which instrumentation approach provides this with the fewest code changes?

answers.A: Enable CloudWatch Logs for all Lambda functions and write a CloudWatch Logs Insights query that correlates log entries across all functions using a shared order ID field extracted from the SQS message payload.
answers.B: Implement custom tracing where each Lambda function generates a unique trace ID, appends it to outbound SQS message attributes, and logs it to CloudWatch Logs. Downstream functions read and log the trace ID, creating a correlatable log chain.
answers.C: Enable AWS X-Ray active tracing on all Lambda functions and enable X-Ray tracing on the SQS queues. X-Ray automatically propagates the trace context through SQS message attributes, linking all segments into a single trace and service map without code changes.
answers.D: Deploy the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) Lambda layer on all functions. Configure an OpenTelemetry Collector to aggregate traces and forward them to X-Ray. Manually inject and extract the W3C TraceContext header from SQS message attributes in each function.

explanation: X-Ray active tracing on Lambda combined with X-Ray tracing enabled on SQS automatically propagates the X-Ray trace header through SQS message system attributes. When a downstream Lambda function receives the SQS message, X-Ray continues the existing trace, creating a unified service map showing the full end-to-end request path with timing. This requires only configuration changes — no code modifications. Option A uses CloudWatch Logs Insights for correlation by a shared order ID, which works for log-based analysis but requires structured logging with order IDs already present, and does not provide visual service maps or timing breakdowns. Option B is a valid DIY approach requiring custom code changes in every function. Option D using ADOT also propagates trace context effectively but requires deploying a Lambda layer and configuring a collector, more operational overhead than enabling X-Ray natively.

stem: A developer is debugging a production issue where a Lambda function that processes SQS messages intermittently logs an Access Denied error when calling DynamoDB PutItem. The error occurs on a subset of invocations and appears to correlate with specific DynamoDB partition keys. The team needs to determine whether the root cause is an IAM policy misconfiguration, DynamoDB throttling, or a code-level error, using AWS-native observability tools. Which combination of tools and steps most efficiently identifies the root cause?

answers.A: Check the Lambda function CloudWatch Errors metric and review VPC Flow Logs for rejected network connections to the DynamoDB VPC endpoint to determine if the issue is network-level or IAM.
answers.B: Enable CloudTrail data events for DynamoDB and run a CloudTrail Insights query to detect anomalous PutItem call volumes on the affected partition keys, then cross-reference with IAM policy simulator output.
answers.C: Redeploy the Lambda function with additional print statements to log the full IAM context and DynamoDB request parameters, then use CloudWatch Logs Insights to filter for invocations with errors.
answers.D: Enable X-Ray active tracing on the Lambda function. For failing invocations, the DynamoDB subsegment in the X-Ray trace shows the exact error type (AccessDeniedException versus ProvisionedThroughputExceededException) and the affected table. Cross-reference CloudWatch DynamoDB ThrottledRequests metrics to confirm the root cause.

explanation: X-Ray traces capture subsegment-level details for AWS SDK calls, including the error type, HTTP status code, and the specific DynamoDB operation and table. This allows the developer to immediately distinguish an AccessDeniedException (IAM) from a ProvisionedThroughputExceededException (throttling) from a ConditionalCheckFailedException (code logic) without any code changes or redeployment. CloudWatch DynamoDB metrics confirm whether throttling correlates with the failure window. Option A is incorrect because VPC Flow Logs track network-layer connections and cannot identify IAM or application-layer errors. Option B using CloudTrail can identify API call patterns but CloudTrail delivery can take several minutes, and it does not provide per-invocation correlation that X-Ray offers. Option C requires a redeployment and adds log volume without the structured, per-invocation SDK subsegment context that X-Ray captures automatically.

stem: A gaming leaderboard application uses Amazon ElastiCache for Redis to cache player rankings with a lazy loading strategy. Load tests show a high cache miss rate during the first 30 minutes after a new tournament starts, causing thousands of concurrent database requests simultaneously (thundering herd). The team wants to reduce this thundering herd effect without significantly increasing cache memory usage. Which strategy best addresses this?
tags: Caching strategies (for example, write-through, read-through, lazy loading, TTL)

answers.A: Switch from lazy loading to a write-through caching strategy. Every database write also populates or updates the Redis cache immediately, ensuring the cache is always warm when reads occur.
answers.B: Implement probabilistic early expiration in the application: before a cache entry's TTL expires, a small random percentage of requests proactively regenerate the cache entry from the database, spreading the refresh load across multiple requests rather than concentrating it at TTL expiry.
answers.C: Implement a Redis SETNX-based mutex lock so that only the first request for a missing cache key fetches the database and populates the cache; all other concurrent requests spin-wait until the key is populated.
answers.D: Increase the cache TTL from the current setting to 24 hours. A longer TTL keeps leaderboard data warm for the entire tournament duration, avoiding cache misses after the initial population.

explanation: Probabilistic early expiration (also called cache stampede prevention) proactively refreshes cache entries slightly before their TTL expires by selecting a small random subset of requests to trigger early regeneration. This spreads the database refresh load across multiple requests in a controlled way rather than allowing a synchronized miss when the TTL expires. Option A (write-through) populates the cache on writes but does not solve the cold-start thundering herd at tournament start when leaderboard data has not yet been read into the cache. Option C (mutex lock with SETNX) prevents multiple simultaneous database fetches for the same key but serializes requests behind the lock, causing queuing latency without reducing the total database load during the cold period. Option D (long TTL) reduces miss frequency after the initial population but does not solve the thundering herd at the moment the new tournament starts when the cache is still cold.

stem: A social networking application stores user session data in Amazon ElastiCache for Redis (single-node). Amazon ECS tasks connect to the single Redis endpoint. During routine ElastiCache node replacement events, the application experiences approximately 20 seconds of connection failures, causing HTTP 5xx errors. The team wants to minimize session unavailability during node replacements with minimal application code changes. Which solution best achieves this?

answers.A: Migrate from a single-node cluster to an ElastiCache Redis replication group with Multi-AZ enabled and automatic failover. Configure the application to connect using the replication group primary endpoint and add connection retry logic with exponential backoff to handle the brief failover window.
answers.B: Enable ElastiCache Global Datastore with a secondary cluster in a second AWS Region. The application connects to the primary region endpoint; during a failure, Global Datastore promotes the secondary cluster to primary within seconds.
answers.C: Add five read replicas to the ElastiCache Redis cluster in separate Availability Zones. During a primary node failure, the application switches its connection to a read replica endpoint until the primary is restored.
answers.D: Enable ElastiCache cluster mode (Redis Cluster) with 3 shards and one replica per shard. Configure the application with the cluster configuration endpoint and update session writes to use Redis Cluster hash slots.

explanation: Multi-AZ with automatic failover for an ElastiCache Redis replication group means that when the primary node is replaced or fails, ElastiCache automatically promotes a replica to primary and updates the replication group primary endpoint's DNS record. Because the application connects via the DNS-based primary endpoint (not a hardcoded IP), the endpoint automatically resolves to the new primary after failover, requiring only connection retry logic to handle the brief DNS propagation and promotion window. Option B (Global Datastore) is designed for cross-region disaster recovery, not single-region node maintenance events, and adds cost and complexity beyond what is needed. Option C is incorrect because read replicas cannot accept write operations; routing session writes to a read replica would fail. Option D (Cluster mode) is a valid high-availability architecture but requires application-side updates to use the cluster configuration endpoint and correctly route writes to hash slots — more code changes than the question allows.

stem: A DevOps team uses AWS AppConfig to manage feature flags for a high-traffic Lambda-based API. A new feature flag must be deployed to 10% of invocations first, monitored for 15 minutes, then expanded to 100% if no CloudWatch alarm threshold is exceeded. The team requires that AppConfig automatically roll back the configuration if the alarm triggers during the monitoring window. Which AppConfig deployment strategy configuration achieves this?

answers.A: Create a deployment strategy with Growth type set to Exponential and Deployment duration set to 15 minutes. AppConfig automatically rolls back when the Lambda function error rate exceeds the threshold defined in the deployment strategy alarm settings.
answers.B: Create a deployment strategy with Growth type set to Linear and Final bake time set to 15 minutes. AppConfig rolls back automatically when the deployment timer expires if Lambda functions report errors via the AppConfig ReportDeploymentStatus API.
answers.C: Create a deployment strategy with Growth type set to Linear, Growth factor set to 10%, Deployment duration set to 1 minute, and Final bake time set to 15 minutes. Attach a CloudWatch alarm to the AppConfig environment. AppConfig monitors the alarm during the bake window and initiates an automatic rollback if the alarm enters ALARM state.
answers.D: Create a deployment strategy with Growth type set to Exponential and deploy the AWS AppConfig Lambda extension on all functions. The extension polls AppConfig every 45 seconds; if it detects configuration errors, it calls the AppConfig StopDeployment API to halt the rollout.

explanation: AppConfig supports deployment strategies with a configurable growth factor and final bake time. A Linear strategy with a 10% growth factor applied over a 1-minute deployment duration followed by a 15-minute bake time matches the requirements. Attaching a CloudWatch alarm to the AppConfig environment enables AppConfig to automatically roll back the configuration if the alarm triggers during the bake window. Option A (Exponential growth) would expand beyond 10% progressively during the deployment duration rather than holding at 10% for the monitoring phase. Option B is incorrect because AppConfig does not roll back based on a ReportDeploymentStatus API called by Lambda; automatic rollback is triggered by attached CloudWatch alarms. Option D is incorrect because Lambda extensions fetch configuration but do not have authority to call StopDeployment; rollback is managed by AppConfig based on alarm state, not extension logic.

stem: A developer uses AWS SAM to build a serverless application with a Lambda function triggered by Amazon API Gateway. The developer wants to run integration tests locally against the full request-response cycle — including API Gateway request mapping, Lambda execution, and response transformation — before pushing any code. The developer's workstation has Docker installed. Which SAM CLI command sequence achieves local integration testing of the complete API-to-Lambda flow?

answers.A: Run sam build followed by sam deploy --guided targeting a development AWS account. Send integration test requests to the deployed API Gateway endpoint URL in the cloud.
answers.B: Run sam build to compile the application, then run sam local start-api to start a local HTTP server that emulates API Gateway request mapping and invokes the Lambda function inside a local Docker container. Send HTTP requests to the local endpoint to execute the full integration test suite.
answers.C: Run sam build followed by sam local invoke with a JSON test event file. Review the Lambda function output and exit code to validate the response payload and handler logic.
answers.D: Run sam local generate-event apigateway aws-proxy to generate a sample API Gateway event payload, then pipe the output to sam local invoke to test the Lambda function with the generated event locally.

explanation: sam local start-api starts a local HTTP server that fully emulates the API Gateway request/response cycle and invokes the Lambda function inside a local Docker container. This allows full integration testing of the API Gateway-to-Lambda path including request mapping templates, authorization, and response transformation without deploying to AWS. Option A deploys to a live AWS account, which is valid for integration testing but is not local, requires AWS credentials, and incurs cost. Option C (sam local invoke) invokes the Lambda function in isolation with a static JSON event file but does not emulate the API Gateway layer — it bypasses request mapping and response transformation, so it tests only the Lambda handler in isolation. Option D also uses sam local invoke with a generated event, which still tests only the Lambda handler without the full API Gateway emulation provided by sam local start-api.

stem: A company runs a multi-tenant SaaS platform on AWS Lambda. Each Lambda function reads a JSON configuration document from AWS AppConfig at startup. During a recent incident, a misconfigured document caused Lambda cold starts to fail for 8 minutes before the team manually rolled back. The team wants AppConfig to validate every new configuration version against a JSON Schema before deployment, and automatically roll back within 2 minutes if the error rate on Lambda invocations rises above 5% after deployment. Which combination of AppConfig features meets these requirements?
tags: AWS AppConfig deployment strategies for safe configuration changes
AWS AppConfig for application configuration management
Managing application configurations using AWS AppConfig with deployment strategies

answers.A: Add a JSON Schema validator as a Lambda extension. Use the Linear20PercentEvery6Minutes deployment strategy and set a CloudWatch alarm on LambdaErrors to trigger a manual rollback.
answers.B: Add a JSON Schema validator as an AppConfig validator of type JSON_SCHEMA. Use a Linear deployment strategy with a 2-minute interval. Configure a CloudWatch alarm on Lambda error rate and link it to the AppConfig deployment to trigger automatic rollback.
answers.C: Add a JSON Schema validator as an AppConfig validator of type LAMBDA. Use the AllAtOnce deployment strategy and configure an EventBridge rule on AppConfig deployment events to invoke a rollback Lambda function when error rate exceeds 5%.
answers.D: Store the JSON Schema in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Before each AppConfig deployment, invoke a CodeBuild project that validates the document. If validation passes, deploy with AllAtOnce strategy and configure CloudWatch alarm-based rollback.

explanation: AppConfig natively supports JSON_SCHEMA validators that check a configuration version against a schema before deployment begins — preventing invalid documents from ever reaching production. For automatic rollback, AppConfig integrates directly with CloudWatch alarms: when a linked alarm fires during the deployment window, AppConfig rolls back automatically without manual intervention. The Linear deployment strategy allows specifying the bake time interval, making 2-minute granularity achievable. Option A incorrectly relies on a Lambda extension for schema validation rather than AppConfig's built-in validator, and manual rollback is too slow. Option C uses a LAMBDA validator (valid, but more complex) and the AllAtOnce strategy eliminates baking time, defeating canary-style rollback. Option D places validation outside AppConfig entirely and does not use AppConfig's native alarm-based rollback.

stem: A mobile gaming company uses AWS AppConfig to manage feature flags for a real-time multiplayer game running on Amazon ECS tasks. A new game-mode feature flag must be rolled out to 10% of ECS tasks for 15 minutes, then to 100% only if no application errors are detected. The rollout must be fully automated and must not require redeployment of ECS tasks. Which AppConfig deployment strategy and validation approach satisfies these requirements?
tags: AWS AppConfig deployment strategies for safe configuration changes
Implementing feature toggles using AWS AppConfig
Using AWS AppConfig to dynamically change application behavior without redeployment

answers.A: Use the Canary10Percent20Minutes managed deployment strategy. Deploy to ECS tasks by triggering a rolling ECS service update. Link a CloudWatch alarm to the deployment for automatic rollback.
answers.B: Create a custom deployment strategy with GrowthType LINEAR, GrowthFactor 10, and DeploymentDurationInMinutes 15. Attach an ALLOW_REVERT CloudWatch alarm. Update AppConfig configuration; ECS tasks poll for changes via the AppConfig SDK without redeployment.
answers.C: Create a custom AppConfig deployment strategy with GrowthType EXPONENTIAL, initial 10% bake, and FinalBakeTimeInMinutes 15. Attach a CloudWatch alarm for automatic rollback. ECS tasks poll the AppConfig SDK to retrieve updated flags dynamically without redeployment.
answers.D: Use the AllAtOnce managed deployment strategy to update the feature flag. Configure an EventBridge rule to monitor ECS error metrics and invoke a Lambda function that calls the AppConfig StopDeployment API if errors exceed threshold.

explanation: AppConfig deployment strategies support an initial growth percentage (10%) with a final bake time. When ECS tasks use the AppConfig SDK (AWS AppConfig Agent or SDK GetConfiguration call) with polling, they receive updated configuration values dynamically without any ECS service redeployment. Linking a CloudWatch alarm to the deployment enables automatic rollback if errors appear during the 15-minute bake window. Option A incorrectly requires an ECS rolling redeployment, which violates the no-redeployment requirement. Option B uses LINEAR growth starting at 10%, which would roll to 20% after 15 minutes rather than waiting at 10% for validation. Option D uses AllAtOnce, which bypasses the 10% canary stage entirely and relies on a manual Lambda-based rollback mechanism rather than AppConfig's native alarm integration.

stem: A DevOps team at a financial institution manages application configurations for 12 microservices using AWS AppConfig. A compliance audit requires that every configuration change be validated by a custom business-logic check (for example, verifying that rate-limit thresholds do not exceed regulatory limits) before deployment. The validation logic is complex and cannot be expressed as a JSON Schema. The team wants the fewest operational components to maintain. Which approach meets the compliance requirement with least maintenance overhead?
tags: AWS AppConfig for application configuration management
Managing application configurations using AWS AppConfig with deployment strategies

answers.A: Configure an AppConfig LAMBDA validator that invokes an AWS Lambda function containing the business-logic validation. AppConfig calls this Lambda synchronously before every deployment; if the Lambda returns an error, AppConfig rejects the configuration version.
answers.B: Create an AWS CodePipeline with a build stage that runs the validation logic as a CodeBuild project. On success, the pipeline calls the AppConfig StartDeployment API. On failure, the pipeline fails and no deployment occurs.
answers.C: Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule that triggers on AppConfig CreateHostedConfigurationVersion events. The rule invokes a Lambda function for validation and, if it fails, calls the AppConfig DeleteHostedConfigurationVersion API to remove the invalid version.
answers.D: Store validation logic in AWS Systems Manager Automation. Create an AppConfig deployment strategy with FinalBakeTimeInMinutes long enough for the Automation runbook to complete. If runbook fails, trigger manual rollback via the AppConfig RollbackDeployment API.

explanation: AppConfig natively supports two validator types: JSON_SCHEMA and LAMBDA. A LAMBDA validator synchronously invokes a specified Lambda function with the proposed configuration content before the deployment starts. If the Lambda returns an HTTP error or times out, AppConfig rejects the version and no deployment proceeds. This is the fewest-component solution: one Lambda function, no additional pipeline or EventBridge rules needed. Option B requires maintaining a full CodePipeline and CodeBuild project, increasing operational overhead. Option C uses an EventBridge-driven post-creation deletion approach, which is asynchronous and creates a race condition — the invalid version exists briefly before deletion. Option D has no native AppConfig integration for SSM Automation pre-validation, and manual rollback defeats the automation goal.

stem: A DevOps team uses AWS CodeBuild to compile and test a Node.js application. The team wants CodeBuild to run Jest unit tests and publish the test results as a test report that appears in the CodeBuild console, with individual test-case pass/fail details. The project must also cache node_modules between builds to reduce build time. Which buildspec.yml configuration achieves both requirements?
tags: Implementing test reports using AWS CodeBuild test reporting

answers.A: In the build phase, run 'jest --json --outputFile=results.json'. In the reports section, specify type: JUNITXML with files: results.json. In the cache section, set type: LOCAL with modes: [CUSTOM_CACHE] and paths: [node_modules].
answers.B: In the post_build phase, run 'jest --coverage'. In the artifacts section, include coverage/lcov.info. In the reports section, specify type: CLOVERXML with files: coverage/lcov.info. In the cache section, set type: S3 with location pointing to an S3 bucket.
answers.C: In the build phase, run 'jest --reporters=jest-junit'. In the reports section, specify type: JUNITXML with files: junit.xml. Set cache type to LOCAL with modes: [DOCKER_LAYER_CACHE] and paths: [node_modules].
answers.D: In the build phase, run 'jest --reporters=jest-junit' to produce junit.xml. In the reports section, specify type: JUNITXML with files pointing to junit.xml. In the cache section, set type: LOCAL with modes: [CUSTOM_CACHE] and paths: [node_modules].

explanation: CodeBuild test reporting requires that tests output a supported format (JUnit XML, NUnit XML, Cucumber JSON, Visual Studio TRX, or TestNG XML). The jest-junit reporter produces JUnit XML output. The buildspec reports section with type JUNITXML and the path to junit.xml instructs CodeBuild to parse results and display individual test details in the console. For caching node_modules (a local directory), LOCAL cache with CUSTOM_CACHE mode and the node_modules path is the correct approach. Option A uses --json which produces a JSON file, not JUnit XML; CodeBuild does not support a JSON test report type. Option B uses CLOVERXML which is a code-coverage format, not a test result format, and lcov.info is not Clover XML. Option C correctly uses jest-junit but sets cache mode to DOCKER_LAYER_CACHE, which caches Docker image layers, not local directories like node_modules.

stem: A company's CodePipeline pipeline builds a Docker image in AWS CodeBuild, pushes it to Amazon ECR, and deploys to Amazon ECS. The build team notices that every CodeBuild run rebuilds all Docker layers from scratch, significantly increasing build time. The team wants to use Docker layer caching in CodeBuild. They also need the ECR image URI output by the build phase available in the deploy stage as a CodePipeline variable. Which buildspec.yml configuration satisfies both requirements?
tags: Configuring AWS CodeBuild projects including build environments, build specifications, and artifacts
AWS CodePipeline pipeline stages and actions

answers.A: Enable PRIVILEGED mode on the CodeBuild project. In the buildspec cache section, set type LOCAL with modes [DOCKER_LAYER_CACHE]. After the push, write the image URI to a file listed under exported-variables in the env section; reference the variable in the deploy stage using the CodePipeline namespace syntax.
answers.B: Enable PRIVILEGED mode on the CodeBuild project. In the buildspec cache section, set type S3 with location pointing to an S3 bucket. After the push, write the image URI to a file listed under artifacts. Retrieve the image URI in the deploy stage by downloading the artifact.
answers.C: Enable PRIVILEGED mode on the CodeBuild project. In the buildspec cache section, set type LOCAL with modes [CUSTOM_CACHE] and paths set to /var/lib/docker. After the push, write the image URI to a Parameter Store key using the AWS CLI; retrieve it in the deploy stage with a Lambda action.
answers.D: Run CodeBuild with a custom AMI that pre-populates Docker layer cache. In the buildspec, set cache type to LOCAL with modes [SOURCE_CACHE]. After the push, export the image URI using the printf command in the post_build phase env section.

explanation: Docker layer caching in CodeBuild requires PRIVILEGED mode (necessary to run Docker-in-Docker) and LOCAL cache with the DOCKER_LAYER_CACHE mode. To pass the image URI between CodeBuild and a downstream CodePipeline stage, CodeBuild supports exported-variables in the buildspec env section — these become CodePipeline output variables accessible via the namespace of the action. Option B uses S3 cache, which does not support Docker layer caching — S3 cache stores arbitrary files. Option C uses CUSTOM_CACHE and manually caches /var/lib/docker — this is not reliable and bypasses CodeBuild's Docker layer cache management. The SSM approach adds unnecessary Lambda overhead. Option D's SOURCE_CACHE caches the source code, not Docker layers, and env section printf does not produce exported variables.

stem: A security-conscious company uses AWS CodeBuild to build a Python application. The buildspec.yml runs pip install, executes unit tests with pytest, and performs a static security scan with Bandit. The team wants the build to fail immediately when Bandit finds any HIGH severity vulnerability, but the build should continue and collect all pytest results even if some tests fail — producing a full test report in CodeBuild. Which buildspec.yml structure implements this behavior correctly?
tags: Integrating test frameworks with AWS CodeBuild

answers.A: In the build phase, run Bandit first with 'bandit -r . -l'; if it exits non-zero, halt. Run pytest with 'pytest --junitxml=results.xml || true' to prevent test failures from stopping the build. In the reports section, specify JUNITXML pointing to results.xml. In post_build, fail the build by checking the Bandit exit code stored in an environment variable.
answers.B: In the build phase, run Bandit with 'bandit -r . --severity-level high'; if it exits non-zero, the phase fails and the build stops. Run pytest with 'pytest --junitxml=results.xml || true' so test failures do not stop artifact collection. In the reports section, specify JUNITXML pointing to results.xml.
answers.C: In the build phase, run 'bandit -r . --severity-level high || true' so Bandit never fails the build. In post_build, check Bandit's exit code; if non-zero, exit 1. Run pytest with 'pytest --junitxml=results.xml'. In the reports section, specify JUNITXML.
answers.D: In the install phase, run Bandit. In the build phase, run pytest. In the post_build phase, fail the build if Bandit found HIGH issues by checking a flag file. In the reports section, specify JUNITXML pointing to results.xml.

explanation: To fail the build immediately on HIGH Bandit findings, the 'bandit --severity-level high' command must run without '|| true' — a non-zero exit code in a buildspec phase stops the build at that point. To allow pytest to run to completion and collect all results even when tests fail, use '|| true' to suppress the non-zero exit. CodeBuild's reports section then parses the JUnit XML file regardless of test outcome. Option A stores Bandit exit code and checks it in post_build — this is unnecessarily complex and won't fail the build immediately. Option C suppresses Bandit failures with '|| true' during the build phase, delaying the failure to post_build — this does not fail the build immediately. Option D places Bandit in the install phase and checks a flag file in post_build — install phase failures do stop the build immediately, but pytest would never run, preventing test report collection.

stem: A DevOps team uses AWS CloudFormation to provision infrastructure. They need a custom resource backed by an AWS Lambda function to register an application with a third-party SaaS monitoring service during stack creation. If the registration fails, the stack should roll back. During stack deletion, the same Lambda function must deregister the application. The team notices that when the Lambda function times out (no response sent to the pre-signed URL), CloudFormation waits 60 minutes before marking the resource as failed. How should the team ensure CloudFormation receives a failure signal promptly if the Lambda function throws an unhandled exception?
tags: AWS CloudFormation custom resources for extending IaC capabilities
Creating AWS CloudFormation custom resources backed by Lambda

answers.A: Set the Lambda function timeout to 55 seconds so it always completes before CloudFormation's 60-minute wait. Add a try/catch block that sends a SUCCESS response to the pre-signed URL on success and a FAILURE response on any exception.
answers.B: Wrap the Lambda handler in a try/catch. On exception, write the failure to an SNS topic. Configure an EventBridge rule to detect the SNS publication and send the FAILURE response to the CloudFormation pre-signed URL.
answers.C: Wrap the Lambda handler in a try/catch. On exception, send a FAILURE response directly to the CloudFormation pre-signed URL within the catch block and re-raise or return. Always send either SUCCESS or FAILURE in all code paths before the Lambda exits.
answers.D: Configure a CloudFormation stack policy that reduces the custom resource timeout to 5 minutes. On exception, log the error to CloudWatch Logs; CloudFormation will detect the absence of a response and fail the resource after 5 minutes.

explanation: CloudFormation custom resources backed by Lambda require the Lambda function to explicitly send a response (SUCCESS or FAILURE) to the pre-signed URL provided in the event. If no response is sent, CloudFormation waits up to the resource's ServiceTimeout (default 60 minutes). The correct approach is to wrap all logic in try/catch and send a FAILURE response to the pre-signed URL in the exception handler — this signals CloudFormation immediately and triggers rollback. Option A correctly adds try/catch but does not address unhandled exceptions thrown before the catch — however A is structurally similar to C; the difference is C emphasizes always sending a response in all code paths, which is the architectural best practice. Option B adds unnecessary complexity via SNS and EventBridge. Option D is incorrect — CloudFormation stack policies control update restrictions, not custom resource timeouts, and logging alone does not signal CloudFormation.

stem: A company provisions Route 53 private hosted zones and VPC associations using AWS CloudFormation. They have a requirement to automatically associate a new VPC with an existing private hosted zone that resides in a different AWS account. CloudFormation does not natively support cross-account Route 53 VPC associations. The team implements a CloudFormation custom resource. During a stack update where only unrelated resources change, the custom resource unnecessarily re-triggers the cross-account association. Which approach prevents the custom resource from re-invoking when its inputs have not changed?
tags: AWS CloudFormation custom resources for extending IaC capabilities
AWS CloudFormation stack updates and change sets
Creating AWS CloudFormation custom resources backed by Lambda

answers.A: Set the DeletionPolicy of the custom resource to Retain. This prevents CloudFormation from re-evaluating or invoking the backing Lambda during any subsequent stack update that does not explicitly modify the resource.
answers.B: Use a CloudFormation condition that compares the current VPC ID or hosted zone ID to its previous value. Attach the condition to the custom resource so CloudFormation skips invoking the Lambda when the condition evaluates to false during stack updates.
answers.C: Add a Metadata block to the custom resource containing a static value. CloudFormation evaluates the Metadata section and skips the Lambda invocation entirely when the Metadata content has not changed between two consecutive stack deployments.
answers.D: Ensure the custom resource properties passed to the Lambda function (VPC ID, hosted zone ID, account ID) are stable — do not include timestamps or random values. CloudFormation only invokes the Lambda with RequestType Update when a property value actually changes; if no property changes, the resource is not re-evaluated.

explanation: CloudFormation triggers a custom resource Lambda invocation on stack updates only when at least one of the resource's Properties changes. If the properties (VpcId, HostedZoneId, AccountId, etc.) remain the same between updates, CloudFormation does not invoke the Lambda for that resource. The key discipline is ensuring no dynamic or volatile values (timestamps, random seeds) are embedded in Properties. Option A's DeletionPolicy Retain prevents deletion of the resource but does not affect update invocation logic. Option B is incorrect — CloudFormation Conditions control whether a resource is created or deleted, not whether an existing resource is updated; a resource with a false condition would be deleted, which is not desired. Option C is incorrect — Metadata changes do not affect CloudFormation resource update logic; only Properties changes trigger updates.

stem: A company's security team mandates that all CloudFormation stacks deployed via AWS CodePipeline must be validated against organization policies before any ChangeSet is created. Specifically, every S3 bucket resource must have ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration with aws:kms, and every EC2 security group must not allow ingress from 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22. The team wants to enforce these rules without modifying individual team templates. Which solution implements policy-as-code enforcement in the pipeline with the least custom code?
tags: AWS CloudFormation Guard for policy-as-code validation
Using AWS CloudFormation Guard to validate templates against policies
AWS CodePipeline pipeline stages and actions

answers.A: Add a CodeBuild stage to the pipeline before the CloudFormation deploy stage. In the buildspec, install cfn-guard and run 'cfn-guard validate --data template.json --rules policies/' against a rules directory in the source repository. If cfn-guard exits non-zero, the stage fails and the pipeline stops.
answers.B: Add an AWS Config rule that evaluates CloudFormation stacks after deployment. If a stack violates policy, trigger an SSM Automation runbook to delete the non-compliant stack and notify the team.
answers.C: Add a Lambda invoke action to the pipeline before the deploy stage. The Lambda function parses the CloudFormation template JSON and raises an exception if required fields are missing. Lambda action failure stops the pipeline.
answers.D: Use a CloudFormation stack policy that denies updates to S3 and EC2 security group resources unless they include required encryption and ingress restrictions. This prevents non-compliant stacks from creating resources.

explanation: AWS CloudFormation Guard (cfn-guard) is a purpose-built policy-as-code tool for validating CloudFormation templates against declarative rules. Running cfn-guard in a CodeBuild stage before deployment provides pre-deployment enforcement with no custom parsing code — the rules are expressed in cfn-guard's rule language and live alongside the templates. If validation fails, the CodeBuild action exits non-zero, failing the pipeline stage before any ChangeSet is created. Option B is post-deployment (reactive, not preventive) and requires deleting deployed stacks, which is disruptive. Option C requires writing custom JSON parsing logic in Lambda — higher maintenance than cfn-guard rules. Option D — CloudFormation stack policies restrict who can update resources during stack updates, not what configuration resources are created with; they are not equivalent to content-level policy validation.

stem: A platform engineering team writes AWS CloudFormation Guard rules to enforce that all AWS::RDS::DBInstance resources use MultiAZ: true and StorageEncrypted: true. During testing, the team runs cfn-guard against a template where the MultiAZ property is set via a CloudFormation Parameter with a default of true, but the template does not hardcode the value. The cfn-guard rule fails even though the deployed stack would use MultiAZ. What is the correct explanation and resolution?
tags: AWS CloudFormation Guard for policy-as-code validation
Using AWS CloudFormation Guard to validate templates against policies
AWS CloudFormation intrinsic functions and pseudo-parameters

answers.A: cfn-guard resolves CloudFormation intrinsic functions like Ref before evaluating rules. The rule fails because the Parameter default is in a different template section than the resource; relocating the default directly into the resource property block causes cfn-guard to see the literal value and the rule passes.
answers.B: cfn-guard supports Ref resolution for Parameters but requires an explicit --parameters flag at runtime to inject parameter values into the evaluation context. Adding --parameters MultiAZ=true to the cfn-guard validate command causes the tool to resolve the Ref and evaluate the rule against the injected value.
answers.C: cfn-guard evaluates templates statically and does not resolve CloudFormation intrinsic functions like Ref or Fn::If. When a property is set via Ref to a Parameter, cfn-guard sees the raw Ref object and cannot confirm the resolved value satisfies the constraint. Teams should hardcode critical compliance values or use cfn-guard rules that explicitly check AllowedValues on the referenced Parameter.
answers.D: cfn-guard requires templates to be in YAML format to perform intrinsic function resolution. JSON templates cause cfn-guard to skip Ref evaluation entirely. Converting the template to YAML and rerunning cfn-guard resolves the Ref evaluation issue for Parameters with default values.

explanation: cfn-guard performs static template analysis and does not execute CloudFormation's intrinsic function evaluation (Ref, Fn::If, Fn::Select, etc.) at validation time. When a property is set via Ref to a Parameter, cfn-guard sees the raw {'Ref': 'ParameterName'} object, not the resolved value. This means cfn-guard cannot verify that the resolved parameter value satisfies the constraint. Teams must be aware of this limitation: for critical compliance controls, either hardcode the values or use cfn-guard's ability to check that Ref objects reference Parameters with specific AllowedValues constraints. Option A is incorrect — cfn-guard does not resolve Refs regardless of where the default is placed. Option B is incorrect — cfn-guard does not have a --parameters flag for runtime resolution. Option D is incorrect — cfn-guard supports both JSON and YAML templates equally.

stem: A large enterprise is setting up a new AWS environment using AWS Control Tower. The security team needs to enforce that no IAM user with console access can be created in any account except the management account. They also need any new AWS account enrolled in Control Tower to automatically inherit this guardrail. A junior administrator suggests adding a Service Control Policy (SCP) to each OU manually. Which Control Tower mechanism should the team use instead, and why?
tags: AWS Control Tower for multi-account governance
Using AWS Control Tower to establish a well-architected multi-account environment
AWS Organizations and service control policies (SCPs)
Setting up AWS Organizations with SCPs to enforce governance guardrails

answers.A: Enable the Control Tower strongly recommended guardrail 'Disallow creation of IAM users without MFA' on all registered OUs. This guardrail prevents console access for users without MFA and automatically applies to new accounts enrolled in the OU.
answers.B: Enable a preventive Control Tower guardrail implemented as an SCP that denies CreateUser and CreateLoginProfile API calls. Apply the guardrail at the OU level in Control Tower; when new accounts are enrolled into the OU, Control Tower automatically applies the guardrail's SCP to the account.
answers.C: Create a custom SCP via AWS Organizations that denies CreateUser calls and attach it to the Root. Because Control Tower accounts inherit the Root SCP, the policy automatically applies to all accounts including new enrollments.
answers.D: Use AWS IAM Identity Center to federate all access and disable IAM user creation by removing the IAMFullAccess permission set from all accounts. New accounts enrolled in Control Tower will not have IAMFullAccess permission sets attached.

explanation: Control Tower guardrails are governance rules applied at the OU level. Preventive guardrails are implemented as SCPs. When a guardrail is enabled on an OU in Control Tower, it is automatically applied to all accounts currently in that OU and to any new accounts enrolled into that OU — satisfying the automatic inheritance requirement. This is the purpose-built mechanism and avoids manual SCP management. Option A's MFA guardrail does not prevent IAM user creation; it restricts existing users without MFA, which is a different control. Option C attaches an SCP to the Root via Organizations directly, bypassing Control Tower's guardrail tracking and drift detection — this causes Control Tower to report configuration drift. Option D removes permission sets but does not prevent IAM API calls by accounts that have other admin-level IAM policies.

stem: A company uses AWS Control Tower to govern 60 AWS accounts across three OUs: Development, Staging, and Production. The security team detects that an account in the Production OU has a non-compliant resource — a public S3 bucket — that violates a detective Control Tower guardrail. The team wants to understand the complete automated remediation path that Control Tower uses for detective guardrails. Which statement correctly describes how Control Tower detective guardrails report and remediate violations?
tags: AWS Control Tower for multi-account governance
AWS Config rules for configuration compliance monitoring
Implementing AWS Config rules to enforce configuration compliance

answers.A: Detective guardrails in Control Tower are implemented as AWS Config rules deployed in each enrolled account. When a resource violates the rule, Config marks it as NON_COMPLIANT and the finding appears in Control Tower's Account Factory dashboard. Control Tower does not automatically remediate violations — the team must configure a separate AWS Config remediation action or SSM Automation runbook to auto-remediate.
answers.B: Detective guardrails in Control Tower are implemented as AWS CloudTrail-based EventBridge rules. When a non-compliant API call is made, EventBridge triggers a Lambda function that both reports the violation to Control Tower and automatically reverts the resource to the compliant state.
answers.C: Detective guardrails in Control Tower are implemented as AWS Security Hub findings. Control Tower aggregates findings across all accounts in the Security Hub management account and automatically creates SSM OpsCenter OpsItems for each violation, which teams then remediate manually.
answers.D: Detective guardrails in Control Tower are implemented as SCPs that allow only compliant API calls. When a non-compliant resource is detected, the SCP prevents further modifications to the resource until compliance is restored, effectively auto-remediating the violation.

explanation: Control Tower detective guardrails are implemented as AWS Config rules deployed and managed by Control Tower across all enrolled accounts. Config evaluates resources against these rules and reports NON_COMPLIANT status, which is surfaced in the Control Tower console. Control Tower detective guardrails are purely detective — they do not automatically remediate violations. Teams that want auto-remediation must separately configure AWS Config remediation actions (which can invoke SSM Automation runbooks). This is an important distinction from preventive guardrails (SCPs), which block non-compliant actions. Option B incorrectly describes the mechanism as EventBridge/CloudTrail-based and claims auto-remediation. Option C confuses the mechanism — detective guardrails are Config-based, not Security Hub-based. Option D describes preventive guardrails (SCP-based), not detective ones.

stem: A company runs a customer-facing web application on AWS Elastic Beanstalk using a single-instance environment (not load-balanced). The team needs to deploy a new version with zero downtime. They are evaluating Elastic Beanstalk deployment policies. Which deployment policy maintains application availability during a deployment in a single-instance environment?
tags: AWS Elastic Beanstalk platform and environment management
Deploying and managing applications using AWS Elastic Beanstalk

answers.A: Use the Rolling deployment policy with a batch size of 1. Beanstalk deploys to the single instance while keeping the load balancer routing traffic. The instance is briefly unavailable during deployment but traffic resumes immediately.
answers.B: Use the Rolling with additional batch policy. Beanstalk launches an extra instance, deploys to it, then terminates the original. This maintains capacity and availability throughout the deployment.
answers.C: Use the Immutable deployment policy. Beanstalk creates a temporary Auto Scaling group with a new instance, validates the deployment, then swaps traffic — maintaining availability throughout the deployment on a single-instance environment.
answers.D: Use the Blue/Green deployment by cloning the environment, deploying to the clone, and using Beanstalk's Swap Environment URLs feature. This maintains full availability because the original environment continues serving traffic until the URL swap.

explanation: For single-instance Elastic Beanstalk environments (no load balancer), Rolling and Rolling with additional batch policies are designed for load-balanced environments and do not apply to single-instance environments. Immutable deployments for single-instance environments do create a new instance in a temporary Auto Scaling group, but during single-instance deployments there can still be a brief DNS/EIP reassignment period. The safest approach for zero downtime in any Beanstalk environment is Blue/Green via environment cloning and Swap Environment URLs — the original environment continues serving all traffic until the DNS swap, and traffic can be reverted instantly if issues arise. Option A is incorrect for a single-instance environment because Rolling requires a load balancer to shift traffic. Option B is also load-balancer-dependent. Option C (Immutable) is the next best option but can have brief interruption during EIP reassignment in single-instance mode.

stem: A company deploys a web application on AWS Elastic Beanstalk with a load-balanced, auto-scaling environment. The team uses the Rolling with additional batch deployment policy. During a deployment, the team observes that health checks fail on the new batch and the deployment gets stuck in an InProgress state. The team wants deployments that fail health checks to automatically roll back without manual intervention. Which Elastic Beanstalk configuration change achieves this?
tags: Configuring Elastic Beanstalk rolling deployments with batch size policies
AWS Elastic Beanstalk platform and environment management

answers.A: Switch to the Immutable deployment policy and enable enhanced health reporting. Beanstalk automatically rolls back Immutable deployments when health checks fail.
