answers.B: Enable the 'Ignore health check' option and configure a CloudWatch alarm on Beanstalk environment health. When the alarm fires, trigger a Lambda function to call the Beanstalk UpdateEnvironment API with the previous version label.
answers.C: Configure Beanstalk's deployment preferences to set HealthCheckSuccessThreshold and enable 'Automatically roll back after failed deployments' in the environment configuration. For Rolling with additional batch, Beanstalk will cancel and roll back when a batch fails health checks.
answers.D: Switch to the Blue/Green deployment using Swap Environment URLs. Configure a CloudWatch alarm on the green environment and, if health checks fail, swap URLs back to the blue environment.

explanation: Elastic Beanstalk supports automatic rollback configuration via the deployment preferences setting 'Automatically roll back after failed deployments' (available through the console or the aws:elasticbeanstalk:command namespace option RollbackLaunchOnFailure). When enabled, if a deployment batch fails health checks, Beanstalk automatically rolls back the deployment without manual intervention. This works with Rolling with additional batch. Option A (Immutable with enhanced health) does support automatic rollback for Immutable deployments, but the question specifically asks about fixing the existing Rolling with additional batch setup without switching policies. Option B adds unnecessary complexity with Lambda and ignores health checks. Option D switches to a different deployment methodology entirely and does not address rolling back a stuck rolling deployment.

stem: A company's development teams use Python packages from PyPI. The security team requires that all packages consumed by CodeBuild builds must be sourced through AWS CodeArtifact to enable package scanning and to prevent developers from pulling untrusted packages directly from the internet. The company wants upstream packages from PyPI to be automatically cached in CodeArtifact when first requested. How should the team configure CodeArtifact and CodeBuild to enforce this requirement?
tags: Publishing and consuming packages using AWS CodeArtifact
Implementing artifact management using AWS CodeArtifact and Amazon S3

answers.A: Create a CodeArtifact repository with PyPI as a direct package source in the repository policy. In CodeBuild, configure the pip.conf to point to the CodeArtifact repository endpoint and use an IAM role with GetAuthorizationToken permission. CodeArtifact proxies and caches PyPI packages automatically.
answers.B: Create a CodeArtifact repository. Add a strict repository policy that blocks all GetPackageVersionAsset calls unless the package is already cached. In CodeBuild, configure pip to use the CodeArtifact endpoint. Pre-populate the repository by running pip download for all approved packages.
answers.C: Create a CodeArtifact domain and a CodeArtifact repository. Add PyPI as an upstream repository for the CodeArtifact repository. In CodeBuild, configure the pip.conf to point to the CodeArtifact endpoint with a login token. When pip requests a package not yet in CodeArtifact, CodeArtifact fetches it from PyPI upstream and caches it.
answers.D: Create a CodeArtifact repository and a separate upstream-only repository connected to PyPI. Configure a CodeArtifact resource policy that allows CodeBuild's IAM role to read from the main repository. Use a CodePipeline stage to periodically sync packages from PyPI to CodeArtifact before builds consume them.

explanation: CodeArtifact supports upstream repositories — you connect a CodeArtifact repository to external package sources like PyPI, npm, Maven Central, etc. When a client requests a package not yet cached, CodeArtifact fetches it from the upstream source and caches it automatically. In CodeBuild, configuring pip to use the CodeArtifact endpoint (obtained via aws codeartifact get-repository-endpoint and login) routes all pip install calls through CodeArtifact. Option A incorrectly describes PyPI as a 'direct package source in the repository policy' — PyPI is configured as an upstream repository, not a policy statement. Option B's approach of blocking uncached packages defeats the purpose of dynamic caching and pre-populating packages is operationally burdensome. Option D adds an unnecessary second repository and a synchronization pipeline; CodeArtifact's upstream feature handles this natively.

stem: A company uses AWS CodeArtifact to host internal Maven packages consumed by multiple teams. A team publishes a new version of a shared library but accidentally includes a breaking API change. Other teams' builds begin to fail. The package publishing team wants to prevent the broken version from being consumed while they prepare a fix, without deleting the package version (for audit purposes). Which CodeArtifact action achieves this with least disruption?
tags: Publishing and consuming packages using AWS CodeArtifact

answers.A: Use the CodeArtifact UpdatePackageVersionsStatus API to set the package version status to Archived. Archived versions remain in the repository for audit purposes but are not returned in package version list operations and clients will not resolve the archived version during dependency resolution.
answers.B: Use the CodeArtifact DeletePackageVersions API to delete the specific version. Set the expectedStatus parameter to Published to confirm deletion of only the published version, preserving other audit metadata in CodeArtifact logs.
answers.C: Update the CodeArtifact repository resource policy to add a Deny statement for GetPackageVersionAsset on the specific package version ARN. This prevents clients from downloading the broken version while keeping the version visible in the repository.
answers.D: Use the CodeArtifact PutPackageOriginConfiguration API to set the restriction to BLOCK for the package. This prevents any version of the package from being published or consumed until the restriction is lifted.

explanation: CodeArtifact package versions have statuses: Published, Unfinished, Unlisted, Archived, Disposed, and Deleted. Setting a version to Archived via UpdatePackageVersionsStatus prevents dependency resolution tools from selecting that version (it is not returned in list operations by default) while preserving the version's assets for audit access. Option B deletes the version, which violates the requirement to keep it for audit purposes. Option C requires crafting a resource policy with ARN-level Deny on package version assets — this is technically possible but complex and not the purpose-built mechanism for this use case. Option D's PutPackageOriginConfiguration controls whether packages can be published to the repository from external sources or directly, not whether specific versions can be consumed.

stem: A company has multiple AWS accounts: a shared-services account hosting an AWS CodeArtifact domain, and 10 developer accounts where CodeBuild projects run. Developers in the developer accounts need to publish and consume packages from the CodeArtifact domain in the shared-services account. The solution must follow least-privilege principles. Which configuration correctly enables cross-account CodeArtifact access?
tags: Publishing and consuming packages using AWS CodeArtifact
AWS IAM roles, policies (identity-based, resource-based, permissions boundaries, SCPs)

answers.A: In the shared-services account, attach an IAM policy to the CodeArtifact domain that grants codeartifact:* to all principals in the developer accounts. In developer accounts, attach an IAM policy to CodeBuild service roles granting codeartifact:GetAuthorizationToken.
answers.B: Create IAM roles in the shared-services account with CodeArtifact permissions. In developer accounts, configure CodeBuild service roles to assume these cross-account roles. Use the assumed role credentials to call GetAuthorizationToken and obtain a scoped token for package operations.
answers.C: Enable VPC peering between developer account VPCs and the shared-services VPC. Configure a CodeArtifact VPC endpoint in the shared-services account. Developer accounts access CodeArtifact directly over the peered VPC without IAM cross-account configuration.
answers.D: In the shared-services account, add a CodeArtifact domain policy (resource-based policy) that grants codeartifact:GetAuthorizationToken and repository-specific actions to the IAM roles used by CodeBuild in the developer accounts. CodeBuild in developer accounts calls GetAuthorizationToken using the cross-account permission, then uses the token for package operations.

explanation: Cross-account CodeArtifact access requires a resource-based policy on the CodeArtifact domain and/or repository that grants the external account's principals the necessary permissions. GetAuthorizationToken is a domain-level action that must be permitted in the domain policy for cross-account callers. Once a caller has GetAuthorizationToken permission granted by the resource policy, they can call it using their own credentials and receive a scoped authorization token for package operations. Option A is close but uses codeartifact:* (overly permissive) and IAM identity policies alone cannot grant cross-account CodeArtifact access — resource-based policies on the domain/repository are required. Option B (cross-account role assumption) works but adds complexity; the resource-based policy approach in D is simpler and purpose-built. Option C is incorrect — VPC peering is a network-level control and does not bypass IAM authorization for CodeArtifact.

stem: A financial services company requires that all AWS API activity across 25 member accounts be logged to a centralized, tamper-evident S3 bucket in a dedicated security account. The logs must be delivered within 15 minutes of the API call and must detect if any log file has been modified or deleted. The security team also needs to search API call history across all accounts by a specific IAM user within a 1-hour window. Which architecture satisfies all requirements with the least operational overhead?
tags: AWS CloudTrail for audit logging and security event detection
Setting up CloudTrail trails for multi-Region and multi-account logging
AWS CloudTrail for API activity logging

answers.A: Create individual CloudTrail trails in each member account with S3 delivery to the security account bucket. Enable CloudTrail log file validation in each trail. Query logs using Amazon Athena with a partition-based table across all account prefixes.
answers.B: Enable CloudTrail as an AWS Organizations trail from the management account targeting all member accounts. Configure delivery to a centralized S3 bucket in the security account. Enable log file integrity validation on the trail. Use CloudTrail Lake to run event queries filtered by userIdentity and time window.
answers.C: Enable AWS Config in all member accounts with CloudTrail as a configuration recorder. Forward Config findings to the security account using an aggregator. Use CloudWatch Logs Insights in the security account to query CloudTrail events across accounts.
answers.D: Create a CloudTrail trail in each member account. Enable CloudWatch Logs integration on each trail and deliver logs to a CloudWatch log group in the security account via cross-account subscription filters. Use CloudWatch Logs Insights for querying.

explanation: An AWS Organizations trail created from the management account automatically applies to all current and future member accounts — no per-account configuration needed. Logs are centralized to a single S3 bucket in the security account. Log file integrity validation uses SHA-256 hash chaining that detects modification or deletion of log files. CloudTrail Lake provides a managed query engine for searching CloudTrail events across accounts without requiring Athena setup, S3 partitioning, or schema management. Option A requires creating and maintaining 25 individual trails — high operational overhead. Option C is incorrect — AWS Config records resource configuration changes, not API activity; it does not replace CloudTrail. Option D requires cross-account CloudWatch log subscription filters (complex setup) and delivers logs 5-15 minutes later than direct S3 delivery.

stem: A company's security operations team wants to automatically detect when any IAM role in any member account is modified to allow the AdministratorAccess policy and immediately revoke the attachment. The detection and remediation must occur within 5 minutes of the API call. The solution must work across all accounts in AWS Organizations. Which architecture achieves this?
tags: AWS CloudTrail for audit logging and security event detection
Processing CloudTrail events to detect and respond to security incidents
Amazon EventBridge event buses (default, custom, partner)

answers.A: Enable AWS Config rule 'iam-policy-no-statements-with-admin-access' in all member accounts with auto-remediation. The Config rule evaluates IAM roles and triggers an SSM Automation runbook to detach AdministratorAccess if found.
answers.B: Create a CloudTrail trail for all member accounts. Configure CloudWatch Logs metric filters to detect AttachRolePolicy events where the policyArn matches AdministratorAccess. Trigger a CloudWatch alarm that invokes a Lambda function to detach the policy.
answers.C: Enable an EventBridge rule in each member account (or via Organizations) to match CloudTrail AttachRolePolicy events where policyArn contains AdministratorAccess. Route matching events to a central EventBridge custom bus in the security account. A Lambda function subscribed to the central bus calls IAM DetachRolePolicy in the member account via a cross-account role.
answers.D: Use AWS Security Hub with the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard enabled in all member accounts. Configure Security Hub to aggregate findings to the security account. Create an EventBridge rule on Security Hub findings to trigger Lambda remediation.

explanation: CloudTrail logs the AttachRolePolicy API call in near real-time (within 15 seconds typically). EventBridge can pattern-match on CloudTrail events using event patterns targeting the specific API and policy ARN. Using an EventBridge Organizations rule or per-account rules forwarding to a central custom event bus enables cross-account event routing. A Lambda function in the security account then assumes a cross-account role in the source account and detaches the policy — achieving sub-5-minute detection and remediation. Option A (Config rule) evaluates on a scheduled or change-triggered basis, but Config rule evaluation latency can exceed 5 minutes for IAM policy changes and auto-remediation adds additional delay. Option B (CloudWatch metric filters) adds latency because CloudTrail must first deliver to CloudWatch Logs (5-15 min). Option D (Security Hub) is for aggregating security findings, not for real-time CloudTrail event matching; Security Hub finding delivery is not sub-5-minute.

stem: A company undergoes an internal audit. The auditor asks for evidence of all S3 bucket policy changes made in the past 90 days across 30 AWS accounts, including who made the changes, from which IP address, and what the exact API call was. The company has a multi-Region CloudTrail trail but logs are stored unpartitioned in S3. The auditor needs results within 2 hours. Which approach produces the required evidence most efficiently?
tags: AWS CloudTrail for audit logging and security event detection
AWS CloudTrail for API activity logging
Setting up CloudTrail trails for multi-Region and multi-account logging

answers.A: Create an Athena table over the S3 CloudTrail logs using a Glue crawler to discover account and region partitions. Query Athena filtering on eventName IN ('PutBucketPolicy','DeleteBucketPolicy') and the 90-day eventTime range. Results include userIdentity, sourceIPAddress, and requestParameters.
answers.B: Use the CloudTrail console Event History feature, filtering by resource type S3 and the required date range. Export filtered events to CSV; the CSV file includes userIdentity and sourceIPAddress for each API call across all 30 accounts.
answers.C: Write a Python script using Boto3 to call cloudtrail.lookup_events for each of the 30 accounts, filtering by AttributeKey=ResourceType and AttributeValue=AWS::S3::Bucket. Aggregate and deduplicate results across all accounts and regions.
answers.D: Enable AWS Config in all 30 accounts and use the Config resource configuration history for S3 buckets. Export the configuration history timeline to show the identity and timestamp of each policy change, including sourceIPAddress and full API call details.

explanation: Athena over S3 CloudTrail logs is the standard approach for ad-hoc historical queries across large log volumes. A Glue crawler or manual DDL creates a partitioned table, and Athena queries can filter on eventName, eventTime, and return all fields including userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress, and requestParameters. This scales to 30 accounts and 90 days within the 2-hour window. Option B (Event History in console) only shows the last 90 days of events for a single account and region, and does not aggregate across 30 accounts. Option C (lookup_events API) has a maximum look-back of 90 days but is limited to 50 results per page and is rate-limited — querying 30 accounts programmatically for 90 days of S3 events would exceed the 2-hour window. Option D (Config) records resource configuration snapshots, not the API call details like sourceIPAddress; Config does not replace CloudTrail for this use case.

stem: A large enterprise manages 80 AWS accounts across four organizational units (OUs) using AWS Organizations. The infrastructure team needs to deploy a standardized VPC configuration—including subnets, route tables, NAT gateways, and VPC Flow Logs enabled to a central S3 bucket—to all existing and future accounts in two specific OUs. New accounts joined to those OUs must receive the configuration automatically without manual intervention. Which approach meets these requirements with the least operational overhead?
tags: AWS Organizations and AWS Control Tower
Infrastructure as code (IaC) (for example, AWS CloudFormation)

answers.A: Create an AWS CloudFormation template and deploy it using a CodePipeline pipeline that is triggered by an Amazon EventBridge rule when a new account joins the OU. Grant the pipeline cross-account IAM role permissions to each member account.
answers.B: Create an AWS CloudFormation StackSet with service-managed permissions targeting the two specific OUs. Enable automatic deployment with account filtering set to the target OUs and enable the option to deploy to new accounts as they are added to the OU.
answers.C: Use AWS Service Catalog to create a portfolio containing the VPC CloudFormation template. Share the portfolio to the target OUs and require account administrators to provision the product upon account creation using a lifecycle hook.
answers.D: Create an AWS Lambda function triggered by AWS Organizations account creation events that assumes a role in each new account and deploys the CloudFormation stack using the boto3 CloudFormation client with the VPC template stored in Amazon S3.

explanation: B is correct. CloudFormation StackSets with service-managed permissions integrate natively with AWS Organizations. When targeting OUs directly and enabling automatic deployment, StackSets automatically provision the stack in new accounts added to those OUs without any additional automation. This is the lowest-overhead approach. Option A uses CodePipeline and EventBridge, which adds considerable complexity and requires managing cross-account roles manually. Option C uses Service Catalog but still requires manual provisioning by account administrators, not automatic deployment. Option D uses Lambda to deploy stacks, which requires managing the Lambda, its IAM role, event integration, and error handling—significantly more overhead than native StackSet automation.

stem: A company uses a large AWS CloudFormation nested stack hierarchy with a root stack and eight nested stacks that together deploy a three-tier web application. A recent security audit discovered that several Security Group rules and IAM policies in deployed stacks no longer match the templates stored in the repository—a result of ad-hoc manual changes. The team needs a strategy to detect and remediate configuration drift continuously, alert on future drift, and require minimum changes to existing tooling. Which solution best meets these requirements?
tags: Infrastructure as code (IaC) (for example, AWS CloudFormation)
Automated monitoring and remediation strategies (for example, AWS Config rules)
Determining the most appropriate logging and monitoring strategy

answers.A: Create an AWS Lambda function that calls cloudformation:DetectStackDrift on each stack every hour. Store results in Amazon DynamoDB. Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on a custom metric the Lambda publishes when drift is detected and send notifications via Amazon SNS.
answers.B: Enable AWS Config continuous recording and create a custom AWS Config rule that compares live resource configurations against the desired CloudFormation template values stored in an S3 bucket. Trigger an AWS Systems Manager Automation document to remediate out-of-compliance resources.
answers.C: Enable drift detection on the root stack using CloudFormation drift detection, which recursively checks all nested stacks. Create an Amazon EventBridge scheduled rule to invoke drift detection daily and another rule on the CloudFormation drift detection completion event to publish results to an SNS topic. Use AWS Config rules to alert on non-compliant resource changes in real time.
answers.D: Use AWS Systems Manager Configuration Compliance to scan CloudFormation stacks against baseline documents defined in Systems Manager. Create a Maintenance Window to run the scan nightly and send non-compliance reports to an S3 bucket.

explanation: C is correct. CloudFormation drift detection natively supports nested stacks—detecting drift on the root stack initiates detection across all nested stacks. Scheduling it with EventBridge and routing completion events to SNS provides alerting. Combining this with AWS Config rules enables real-time detection of individual resource changes between drift scans. Option A can work but requires significant custom code for scheduling, metric publishing, and result storage. Option B requires building a custom Config rule that can compare live configurations to CloudFormation template values—a complex and fragile approach since templates are parameterized. Option D uses Systems Manager Compliance, which is not designed for CloudFormation template drift detection and cannot compare live resources against CloudFormation stack definitions.

stem: A financial services company has workloads across 40 AWS accounts organized into OUs in AWS Organizations. Compliance requirements mandate that all Amazon RDS databases and Amazon EFS file systems must be backed up daily with a 90-day retention period, that backups must be stored in a dedicated backup account, and that member accounts must not be able to delete or modify backup vault lock settings. The security team must receive an alert if any resource goes 25 hours without a successful backup. Which solution meets all requirements with the least operational overhead?
tags: Designing an effective backup and restoration strategy
AWS Organizations and AWS Control Tower
Recommending a strategy for central logging and audit

answers.A: Enable AWS Backup in the Organizations management account. Create an org-level backup policy targeting all RDS and EFS resources with 90-day retention and cross-account copy to the backup account vault. Enable Vault Lock in compliance mode. Create an EventBridge rule for backup job failures routed to SNS. Use Backup Audit Manager for compliance reports.
answers.B: Deploy an AWS Lambda function in each member account that creates daily backups of RDS and EFS resources and copies them to the backup account. Use Amazon CloudWatch Events to schedule the Lambda. Enable S3 Object Lock on the backup account S3 bucket to prevent deletion.
answers.C: Create an AWS Config rule that checks whether RDS and EFS resources have backup plans. Set up AWS Systems Manager Automation to create backups when the rule detects non-compliance. Enable S3 Versioning on the backup storage bucket and set lifecycle rules for 90-day retention.
answers.D: Create a CloudFormation StackSet that deploys an AWS Backup plan with a 90-day retention policy to each member account, configured to copy backups to a centralized vault in the backup account. Apply an SCP that denies backup:DeleteBackupVault actions for all member accounts. Monitor backup jobs with a CloudWatch dashboard per account.

explanation: A is correct. AWS Backup integrates with AWS Organizations to centrally manage backup policies across all accounts using backup policies applied at the OU or root level. Vault Lock in compliance mode prevents even the root user from deleting backups or changing lock settings, satisfying the immutability requirement. EventBridge + SNS handles alerting on backup failures within the 25-hour window. AWS Backup Audit Manager provides compliance reporting. Option B requires deploying and maintaining Lambda functions in every account, which is high operational overhead. Option C uses AWS Config and Systems Manager, which are reactive, not proactive backup mechanisms, and S3 Object Lock is separate from native backup vaulting. Option D uses StackSets plus SCPs—functional but considerably more operational effort than centralized AWS Backup policies, and StackSets do not automatically apply to new accounts without additional automation.

stem: A healthcare company runs a patient records application on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL in us-east-1. Regulatory requirements mandate an RPO of 4 hours and an RTO of 2 hours for the database. Backups must be stored in a geographically separate AWS Region (us-west-2) and must be encrypted with a customer-managed key that the company controls. The company does not want to run a standby database continuously in us-west-2. Which solution meets all requirements at the lowest ongoing cost?
tags: Designing disaster recovery solutions based on RTO and RPO requirements
Disaster recovery strategies (for example, backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, multi-site active-active)

answers.A: Enable automated RDS backups in us-east-1 with a 4-hour backup window. Manually copy snapshots to us-west-2 using a Lambda function triggered every 4 hours. Encrypt the copied snapshots with a KMS customer-managed key in us-west-2. Restore the database from the latest snapshot in us-west-2 when a disaster occurs.
answers.B: Create an RDS read replica in us-west-2 encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key. Promote the replica when a disaster occurs. Configure automated backups on the primary with a 1-day retention. Estimated RPO is near-zero and RTO is under 30 minutes.
answers.C: Use AWS Backup to create a backup plan that backs up the RDS cluster every 4 hours and copies each recovery point to a vault in us-west-2 encrypted with a customer-managed AWS KMS key. Enable cross-Region copy in the backup plan. Restore from the us-west-2 vault to a new RDS instance when a disaster event occurs.
answers.D: Configure RDS automated backups and enable cross-Region automated backup replication to us-west-2. Use the AWS-managed KMS key in us-west-2 for encryption. Create an AWS CloudFormation template to re-create the RDS instance configuration for rapid restoration.

explanation: C is correct. AWS Backup supports cross-Region copy of RDS recovery points, and the backup plan can specify a customer-managed KMS key for encrypting the copied vault in us-west-2. A 4-hour backup frequency satisfies the 4-hour RPO. Restoring from an existing recovery point can be completed within the 2-hour RTO. There is no continuously running standby instance, minimizing cost. Option A achieves similar outcomes but requires custom Lambda automation that adds operational overhead. Option B uses a read replica, which is a warm standby strategy—more expensive since it runs continuously—and was not requested. Option D uses built-in RDS cross-Region replication, which is valid, but requires using a customer-managed KMS key; Option D specifies an AWS-managed key, which does not meet the customer-control requirement.

stem: A company runs a public-facing web application behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in us-east-1. The security team requires that all TLS certificates used on the ALB be automatically renewed before expiry, that private keys never leave AWS infrastructure, and that the company be notified 60 days before any certificate expires. A separate internal microservices API runs on an Amazon EKS cluster behind an internal Network Load Balancer (NLB) and requires mTLS with certificates issued from the company's internal private CA. Which solution meets both sets of requirements?
tags: Deploying encryption strategies for data at rest and data in transit
Encryption keys and certificate management (for example, AWS KMS, AWS Certificate Manager)
Specifying inbound and outbound network flows based on business and technical requirements

answers.A: Request a public ACM certificate for the ALB domain. Configure ACM to send expiration notifications via Amazon SNS at 60 days. Import the company's private CA root certificate into ACM to issue certificates for the NLB. Configure the EKS pods to present client certificates signed by the imported CA.
answers.B: Use Let's Encrypt with certbot running on an EC2 instance to issue and renew certificates for the ALB. Store the renewed certificate in AWS Secrets Manager and automate rotation with a Lambda function that updates the ALB listener. Use AWS Private CA to issue server and client certificates for the NLB and configure cert-manager in EKS to manage certificate lifecycle.
answers.C: Request a public ACM certificate for the ALB. Enable ACM managed renewal and set up a CloudWatch alarm on the ACM CertificateExpiryInDays metric to alert at 60 days. Use a self-signed CA certificate stored in AWS Secrets Manager to issue certificates for NLB mTLS. Rotate secrets manually on a schedule.
answers.D: Request a public ACM certificate for the ALB domain; ACM manages renewal automatically and private keys never leave AWS. Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the days-to-expiry metric published by ACM to SNS at the 60-day threshold. Create an AWS Private CA and use ACM to issue server and client certificates from it for the NLB. Deploy cert-manager with the AWS Private CA plugin in the EKS cluster to automate certificate issuance and renewal for mTLS.

explanation: D is correct. ACM-issued public certificates are automatically renewed and private keys are managed entirely within AWS—they are never exported. ACM publishes a DaysToExpiry metric to CloudWatch, enabling an alarm at 60 days to notify via SNS. AWS Private CA (formerly ACM PCA) is the correct service for issuing certificates from a company-controlled private CA. cert-manager with the AWS Private CA plugin automates certificate lifecycle within EKS for mTLS. Option A incorrectly suggests importing a private CA root into ACM; ACM does not act as an issuing CA for imported roots—AWS Private CA is the correct service. Option B uses Let's Encrypt with external tooling and Secrets Manager rotation, which does not guarantee private keys never leave AWS. Option C uses a self-signed CA stored in Secrets Manager with manual rotation, which violates the private key protection requirement and does not scale.

stem: A multinational company hosts its e-commerce platform using Amazon CloudFront in front of an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in us-east-1. The company uses a custom domain with a wildcard certificate. During a security review, the team identifies that the connection between CloudFront and the ALB origin is using HTTP, not HTTPS. The team must enforce end-to-end TLS encryption with certificates signed by a trusted CA, must not use self-signed certificates on the ALB, and must maintain zero downtime during the transition. Which steps accomplish this? (Select TWO)
tags: Deploying encryption strategies for data at rest and data in transit
Encryption options for data at rest and data in transit

answers.A: Request an ACM certificate in us-west-2 for the ALB domain and attach it to the ALB HTTPS listener. Update the CloudFront origin protocol policy to HTTPS only.
answers.B: Request an ACM certificate in us-east-1 for the ALB's domain name and attach it to a new HTTPS listener on the ALB. Update the CloudFront origin protocol policy to HTTPS only and set the origin SSL/TLS protocols to match.
answers.C: Generate a self-signed certificate using OpenSSL, upload it to IAM as a server certificate, and associate it with the ALB HTTPS listener. Update CloudFront to use HTTPS for origin connections.
answers.D: Keep the existing CloudFront viewer-facing certificate in us-east-1 in place. Update the CloudFront distribution origin settings to use HTTPS only after the ALB HTTPS listener is active, ensuring no traffic interruption.
answers.E: Move the CloudFront distribution to us-east-1 to co-locate it with the ALB, then enable HTTPS on the ALB using an ACM certificate issued in eu-west-1.

explanation: B and D are correct. ACM certificates for ALB use must be provisioned in the same Region as the ALB (us-east-1). Attaching the ACM certificate to the ALB's HTTPS listener and then updating the CloudFront origin to use HTTPS only completes the end-to-end TLS chain. Performing the ALB listener update first and then switching CloudFront ensures zero downtime. Option A is incorrect because ACM certificates for ALB must be in the same Region as the ALB (us-east-1, not us-west-2). Option C uses a self-signed certificate, which the requirement explicitly forbids. Option E incorrectly suggests moving CloudFront or using an eu-west-1 certificate—CloudFront distributions are global and the ALB certificate must be in the ALB's Region.

stem: A gaming company operates an online multiplayer game that requires low-latency UDP connections from players worldwide to game servers running on Amazon EC2 instances in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. The company wants to route each player to the nearest healthy Region automatically, support static anycast IP addresses for client SDK configuration, and protect against UDP flood DDoS attacks. Application Load Balancers cannot handle UDP traffic. Which solution meets all requirements?
tags: Evaluating connectivity options for on-premises, co-location, and cloud integration
AWS networking concepts (for example, Amazon VPC, AWS Direct Connect, AWS VPN, transitive routing, AWS container networking)

answers.A: Create an AWS Global Accelerator with two endpoint groups (us-east-1 and eu-west-1), each pointing to a Network Load Balancer fronting the EC2 game servers. Enable endpoint health checks. Global Accelerator provides static anycast IPs, routes over the AWS backbone to the nearest healthy endpoint, and AWS Shield Standard protects against DDoS.
answers.B: Configure Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing with health checks pointing to an Elastic IP in each Region. Players resolve the domain to the lowest-latency Region. Associate the EC2 instances directly with the Elastic IPs. Enable Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall to block malicious UDP packets.
answers.C: Deploy an Amazon CloudFront distribution with two origins in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Configure origin failover. Use CloudFront's IP anycast network to route players to the nearest Regional fleet. Enable AWS WAF on the CloudFront distribution to mitigate DDoS attacks on UDP traffic.
answers.D: Create an AWS Transit Gateway with peering between us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Assign Elastic IPs to game server instances and publish them to a custom DNS resolver. Use AWS Shield Advanced to protect the Elastic IPs from DDoS.

explanation: A is correct. AWS Global Accelerator is designed for non-HTTP protocols including UDP. It provides two static anycast IP addresses that route traffic over the AWS global backbone to the nearest healthy endpoint group. Network Load Balancers support UDP and can front the EC2 game server fleet. AWS Shield Standard protects Global Accelerator endpoints from DDoS automatically. Option B uses Route 53 latency routing, which routes based on DNS latency (not network path) and involves DNS TTL delays for failover—not ideal for real-time gaming. Route 53 DNS Firewall does not block UDP game traffic. Option C uses CloudFront, which is an HTTP/HTTPS CDN and does not support arbitrary UDP protocols. Option D uses Transit Gateway peering, which is for inter-VPC and hybrid connectivity, not global traffic routing from end users to game servers.

stem: A company deploys a customer-facing API globally. The current architecture uses Amazon Route 53 with latency-based routing and health checks pointing to Application Load Balancers in us-east-1 and ap-southeast-1. The team wants to migrate to AWS Global Accelerator for consistent latency improvement. During the migration, they need to perform a controlled traffic shift where only 10% of requests go to the new Global Accelerator endpoints initially, with the ability to increase gradually based on error rate metrics, and roll back within 60 seconds if errors spike. Which approach meets these requirements?
tags: Selecting services to develop deployment strategies and implement appropriate rollback mechanisms
Determining an application or upgrade path for new services and features

answers.A: Create the Global Accelerator with both Regional ALBs as endpoints. Remove the Route 53 latency routing records and replace the DNS entry with the Global Accelerator DNS name. Monitor error rates in CloudWatch and manually roll back by removing Global Accelerator endpoints if errors spike.
answers.B: Create the Global Accelerator and configure endpoint traffic dials to set each endpoint group at 10% of total capacity. Gradually increase endpoint group traffic dials to 100%. Revert by setting dials back to 0% if errors are detected.
answers.C: Keep the existing Route 53 latency-based records pointing to the ALBs. Create the Global Accelerator with the same ALBs as endpoints. Add a second Route 53 weighted record for the Global Accelerator DNS name with weight 10, and the existing ALB records with weight 90. Gradually shift weight to the Global Accelerator record. Roll back by setting the Global Accelerator record weight to 0.
answers.D: Use AWS CodeDeploy to perform a linear traffic shifting deployment from the Route 53 ALB records to the Global Accelerator DNS name, with CloudWatch alarms configured to auto-rollback. Set the deployment configuration to shift 10% per step.

explanation: C is correct. Keeping Route 53 weighted routing records for both the existing ALBs (weight 90) and the new Global Accelerator DNS name (weight 10) allows a controlled, gradual traffic shift. Adjusting weights is instantaneous in Route 53 and setting the Global Accelerator weight to 0 provides fast rollback well within 60 seconds. Option A removes existing records upfront, losing the ability to gradually shift or roll back without re-creating records. Option B misunderstands Global Accelerator traffic dials—traffic dials control the proportion of traffic routed to a specific endpoint group but do not shift traffic between Global Accelerator and an alternative path. Option D uses CodeDeploy, which is designed for application deployments (EC2, Lambda, ECS), not for DNS-level traffic shifting between Global Accelerator and Route 53 records.

stem: A financial services company has a 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection at a colocation facility providing connectivity to its primary AWS Region (us-east-1). The company runs latency-sensitive trading workloads and cannot tolerate interruptions if the Direct Connect connection fails. The company also has a secondary data center in a different metropolitan area. The network team must design a fully redundant hybrid connection that maintains traffic on the Direct Connect path under normal conditions, automatically fails over to a backup path, and uses the BGP routing protocol for path selection. Which architecture provides the required redundancy?
tags: Evaluating connectivity options for on-premises, co-location, and cloud integration
AWS networking concepts (for example, Amazon VPC, AWS Direct Connect, AWS VPN, transitive routing, AWS container networking)
Designing disaster recovery solutions based on RTO and RPO requirements

answers.A: Create a second 10 Gbps Direct Connect connection from the same colocation facility to a different Direct Connect location in us-east-1. Configure both connections with the same BGP prefix lengths so that AWS ECMP load-balances across both. Configure VPN as a tertiary backup.
answers.B: Provision a second Direct Connect connection from the secondary data center to a different AWS Direct Connect location. Attach both connections to a Direct Connect Gateway linked to a Transit Gateway. Configure the secondary with longer AS_PATH prepends so normal traffic flows over the primary. BGP automatically fails over to the secondary when the primary drops.
answers.C: Establish an AWS Site-to-Site VPN from the primary data center as the primary connection. Configure Direct Connect as the backup, using BGP local preference to prefer VPN. Set up AWS Transit Gateway as the hub for VPC connectivity.
answers.D: Use the existing Direct Connect connection and create an AWS VPN CloudHub configuration with two VPN tunnels from the primary data center to two different virtual private gateways in us-east-1. Route Direct Connect traffic normally and use VPN CloudHub as failover.

explanation: B is correct. AWS recommends using two Direct Connect connections from separate locations and/or separate data centers for maximum resilience. Connecting the secondary data center to a different Direct Connect location provides geographic diversity. Using AS_PATH prepending on the secondary connection signals BGP to prefer the primary. Both connections attached to the same Direct Connect Gateway and Transit Gateway ensures seamless failover when the primary drops. Option A uses two connections from the same colocation facility, which does not protect against a facility-level failure. Option C reverses the preference—placing VPN as primary violates the requirement to use Direct Connect as the primary path. Option D uses VPN CloudHub, which is designed to interconnect on-premises sites through VPN, not to complement a Direct Connect connection as a failover path.

stem: A company is migrating its on-premises data warehouse (50 TB) to Amazon Redshift in us-west-2. The current on-premises network has a 1 Gbps internet connection. The migration must be completed within 10 days and must not saturate the internet connection, which is needed for production traffic. The company has a colocation facility near an AWS Direct Connect partner location. After the migration, the on-premises ELT tools must continue to send daily incremental data (approximately 100 GB/day) to Redshift with consistent low latency. Which combination of services and steps best meets these requirements? (Select TWO)
tags: Data migration options and tools (for example, AWS DataSync, AWS Snow Family, AWS Database Migration Service)
Selecting the appropriate database migration mechanism
Selecting tools to use for migration

answers.A: Order an AWS Direct Connect hosted connection (1 Gbps or higher) through a Direct Connect partner at the colocation facility for the ongoing incremental data transfer after migration. This provides dedicated bandwidth that does not share the internet circuit.
answers.B: Use AWS DataSync to transfer the 50 TB initial data set over the existing 1 Gbps internet connection with throttling set to 80% of link capacity, completing the transfer in roughly 12–14 days.
answers.C: Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) with full-load mode to migrate the 50 TB data warehouse from on-premises to Redshift over the internet connection within the 10-day window.
answers.D: Request an AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device, load the 50 TB data warehouse export files onto it, ship it to AWS, and have AWS import the data to an S3 bucket. Use Amazon S3 COPY commands or AWS Glue to load the data into Redshift.
answers.E: Provision an AWS Storage Gateway Volume Gateway at the colocation facility and mount it on the on-premises server. Copy the data warehouse files through the Volume Gateway to Amazon S3 and then COPY into Redshift over the 10-day window.

explanation: A and D are correct. 50 TB at 1 Gbps (realistically 70-80% utilization to avoid saturating production traffic) would take approximately 14-18 days over the internet—too slow for the 10-day window. AWS Snow Family (Snowball Edge) provides physical data transport that bypasses the network entirely: ship the device, AWS imports to S3, then load to Redshift. This comfortably meets the 10-day requirement. After migration, an AWS Direct Connect hosted connection provides dedicated bandwidth for the daily 100 GB incremental loads with consistent latency without competing with internet traffic. Option B uses DataSync over the internet, which would take too long and would saturate the connection. Option C uses DMS, which transfers data over the network—same bandwidth problem—and DMS is designed for database replication, not bulk data warehouse export. Option E uses Storage Gateway, which also requires network bandwidth and would saturate the internet connection.

stem: A company has recently consolidated 30 AWS accounts under AWS Organizations. Employees currently log into each account using individual IAM users with passwords stored in a shared password manager. The security team requires: (1) single sign-on using the company's existing Okta identity provider, (2) multi-factor authentication enforced at the IdP level, (3) least-privilege access with permission sets defined centrally, and (4) audit logs of all console and API access per user. The team wants minimum ongoing credential management. Which solution meets all requirements?
tags: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and AWS IAM Identity Center
Developing a strategy for centralized security event notifications and auditing

answers.A: Create a SAML 2.0 identity provider in each AWS account and configure trust relationships with Okta. Create IAM roles in each account with appropriate permissions and assign them to Okta groups. Configure Okta MFA policies. Enable AWS CloudTrail in each account.
answers.B: Use Amazon Cognito as an intermediary identity broker between Okta and AWS. Create a Cognito User Pool federated with Okta. Map Cognito groups to IAM roles in each account using Cognito Identity Pools. Enforce MFA in the Cognito User Pool. Enable CloudTrail for all accounts.
answers.C: Configure AWS Directory Service (Managed Microsoft AD) in the management account and synchronize it with Okta using Azure AD Connect. Enable AWS IAM Identity Center with Managed AD as the identity source. Create permission sets and assign them to directory groups. Enable CloudTrail in all accounts.
answers.D: Enable AWS IAM Identity Center in the management account. Configure Okta as an external SAML 2.0 identity source with SCIM provisioning to synchronize users and groups automatically. Create permission sets with least-privilege IAM policies and assign them to account groups. MFA is enforced in Okta. AWS CloudTrail records all API activity per account.

explanation: D is correct. AWS IAM Identity Center natively supports external SAML 2.0 identity providers like Okta and SCIM-based automatic user provisioning. This eliminates manual IAM user management. Permission sets are defined centrally in IAM Identity Center and pushed to member accounts. MFA is enforced at the Okta level (the IdP), satisfying the requirement without additional AWS configuration. CloudTrail records all console and API access. Option A requires configuring SAML IdPs and IAM roles in each account individually—high operational overhead and no centralized permission management. Option B uses Cognito, which is designed for application-level authentication (customer-facing), not workforce AWS console access across multiple accounts. Option C uses Managed AD with Okta synchronization, which adds complexity—Okta already supports SAML federation directly with IAM Identity Center without requiring a managed directory.

stem: A company uses AWS IAM Identity Center with an external SAML identity provider. The company has 15 AWS accounts across three business units (BU-A, BU-B, BU-C), and each BU has developers, read-only analysts, and administrators. Currently, permission sets are assigned account-by-account for each role, resulting in 45 assignment records. New accounts are added frequently. The security team wants to ensure that when a new account is created in a BU's OU, the correct permission sets are automatically applied to the right groups without manual steps. Which solution minimizes ongoing manual assignment work?
tags: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and AWS IAM Identity Center

answers.A: Create an AWS Lambda function triggered by CloudTrail events for Organizations account creation. The function calls the IAM Identity Center API to create account assignments for the new account based on a mapping table stored in DynamoDB.
answers.B: Use AWS CloudFormation StackSets with service-managed permissions to deploy a custom resource backed by a Lambda function that calls the IAM Identity Center API to create permission set assignments. Target StackSets at the OU level so new accounts automatically receive the assignments.
answers.C: Enable attribute-based access control (ABAC) in IAM Identity Center. Configure the IdP to pass a custom attribute (for example, BusinessUnit) in SAML assertions. Create permission sets with IAM condition keys that match the BusinessUnit attribute to the account's tag. Tag each account with its BU.
answers.D: Create a Service Control Policy (SCP) at each OU level that grants the appropriate permissions to IAM Identity Center groups. Use IAM Identity Center account assignments only for administrator roles; delegate developer and analyst access through SCPs.

explanation: C is correct. ABAC in IAM Identity Center allows permission set policies to reference identity attributes (like BusinessUnit) passed via SAML assertions from the IdP. Tagging AWS accounts with their BU and using IAM conditions like aws:ResourceTag or PrincipalTag allows the same permission sets to work across all accounts in all BUs without per-account assignments. When a new account is tagged appropriately, the existing ABAC policies automatically scope access correctly. Option A uses Lambda + CloudTrail events, which can work but introduces custom automation that must be maintained. Option B uses StackSets with Lambda-backed custom resources, which is more complex and requires maintaining custom code. Option D misunderstands SCPs—SCPs set maximum permissions (guardrails) but cannot grant access; they cannot replace IAM Identity Center account assignments.

stem: A company operates 25 AWS accounts managed by AWS Organizations. The security team must enforce the following across all accounts: (1) AWS WAF rules blocking OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities must be attached to all public-facing Application Load Balancers and CloudFront distributions; (2) Security Groups must not allow inbound traffic on port 22 (SSH) from 0.0.0.0/0; (3) the security team must receive alerts when non-compliant resources are detected. New accounts must inherit these policies automatically. Which service and approach meets all requirements with minimum ongoing configuration?
tags: AWS security, identity, and compliance tools (for example, AWS CloudTrail, AWS IAM Access Analyzer, AWS Security Hub, Amazon Inspector)
Developing a strategy for centralized security event notifications and auditing
Recommending services to reduce risks from common threats (for example, DDoS, SQL injection)

answers.A: Enable AWS Firewall Manager in the Organizations management account with AWS Config enabled in all member accounts. Create a Firewall Manager WAF policy targeting all ALBs and CloudFront distributions with an AWS Managed Rules rule group for OWASP Top 10. Create a Firewall Manager Security Group policy to audit and remediate Security Groups allowing SSH from 0.0.0.0/0. Configure Firewall Manager SNS notifications for non-compliant resources. New accounts inherit policies automatically.
answers.B: Create AWS Config rules in every account using a StackSet: one rule checking WAF association on ALBs and CloudFront, one rule checking Security Group ingress rules. Use AWS Systems Manager Automation to remediate non-compliant resources. Subscribe CloudWatch Events to Config compliance notifications per account.
answers.C: Use AWS Security Hub with the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard enabled across all accounts. Create custom Security Hub findings filters for WAF association and SSH Security Group checks. Configure Security Hub to send alerts to an SNS topic using EventBridge rules. Remediate using GuardDuty automated response playbooks.
answers.D: Create a Service Control Policy (SCP) that denies the creation of Security Groups with inbound rules allowing port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0. Use AWS Lambda functions deployed by a StackSet to attach WAF ACLs to any new ALB or CloudFront distribution. Trigger Lambda with EventBridge rules for resource creation events.

explanation: A is correct. AWS Firewall Manager is purpose-built for centralizing WAF, Security Group, and Shield Advanced policies across AWS Organizations accounts. WAF policies can target ALBs and CloudFront distributions organization-wide with managed rule groups. Security Group policies can audit and auto-remediate overly permissive rules. Firewall Manager automatically applies policies to new accounts joined to the organization. SNS notifications can be configured for compliance violations. Option B uses Config rules and StackSets, which requires more setup per account and does not provide automatic policy application to new accounts. Option C uses Security Hub, which is an aggregation and findings management tool—it does not enforce WAF attachments or remediate Security Groups automatically. Option D uses SCPs for denying bad Security Groups (valid guardrail) but SCPs cannot attach WAF ACLs, and Lambda-based WAF attachment is custom code requiring maintenance.

stem: A global e-commerce company has experienced multiple volumetric DDoS attacks targeting its Amazon CloudFront distributions and Application Load Balancers across 10 AWS accounts. The security team wants to enable AWS Shield Advanced across all accounts, ensure that AWS WAF rate-based rules are applied to all ALBs, receive cost protection for DDoS-related scaling charges, and have access to the AWS DDoS Response Team (DRT). Currently the company has no centralized security management. Which solution addresses all requirements with the least configuration effort?
tags: AWS managed security services (for example, AWS Shield, AWS WAF, Amazon GuardDuty, AWS Security Hub)
Recommending services to reduce risks from common threats (for example, DDoS, SQL injection)
Evaluating the cost and benefit of adopting managed security services

answers.A: Enable AWS Shield Advanced individually in each of the 10 accounts. Create WAF rate-based rules in each account and attach them to all ALBs. Request DRT support via the Shield Advanced console in each account. Apply for DDoS cost protection in each account separately.
answers.B: Create an AWS Organizations management account SCP that requires all accounts to enable Shield Advanced. Deploy WAF rate-based rules using a CloudFormation StackSet. Contact AWS Support to enable DRT access from each account individually.
answers.C: Enroll all 10 accounts in AWS Shield Advanced through the AWS Firewall Manager console using a Shield Advanced policy scoped to the Organizations management. Create a Firewall Manager WAF policy with a rate-based rule and apply it to all ALBs organization-wide. Designate the management account for DRT access. Shield Advanced provides consolidated DDoS cost protection across enrolled accounts.
answers.D: Enable AWS Security Hub in the management account and use the DDoS resilience standard. Create EventBridge rules that trigger Lambda to enable Shield Advanced in each member account. Deploy WAF rules using AWS Config remediation actions. Open a support ticket for DRT access.

explanation: C is correct. AWS Firewall Manager can manage Shield Advanced enrollment across all Organization accounts through a Shield policy, replacing the need to enable Shield Advanced account by account. Firewall Manager WAF policies apply rate-based rules to all ALBs org-wide. Shield Advanced provides DDoS cost protection and DRT access for enrolled accounts, and DRT access can be configured centrally. Option A requires individually enabling Shield Advanced, WAF, and DRT in each of the 10 accounts—high operational effort. Option B uses an SCP to require Shield Advanced, but SCPs cannot enable services—they only allow or deny API actions. StackSets for WAF are functional but less automated than Firewall Manager policies. Option D uses Security Hub (a findings aggregator) and Lambda automation, which does not natively manage Shield Advanced enrollment across accounts.

stem: A retail company stores raw clickstream data in Amazon S3 as compressed JSON files, partitioned by date and hour. A data engineering team runs daily ETL jobs using AWS Glue to transform the data and load it into Amazon Redshift for BI reporting. Recently, ETL job run times have increased from 20 minutes to over 3 hours because the S3 dataset has grown to 50 billion small files (averaging 10 KB each). The Glue DPU count has been increased to 100 with no improvement. Queries in Redshift also run slowly. Which combination of changes most effectively resolves the performance issues? (Select TWO)
tags: AWS analytics services for modernization (for example, Amazon Kinesis, Amazon Athena, AWS Glue)
Selecting and implementing the appropriate services to improve performance
AWS storage services and their characteristics

answers.A: Use AWS Glue job bookmarks and enable the Glue native S3 grouping feature (groupFiles: inPartition) to group many small files into larger logical splits during reads, reducing the number of tasks and JVM overhead.
answers.B: Increase the Glue worker type from G.1X to G.2X and add more DPUs to provide more memory per executor, helping each task handle the large number of individual file reads more efficiently.
answers.C: Run a one-time compaction Glue job that reads the small S3 files and rewrites them as larger Parquet files (128 MB–1 GB), repartitioned by date. Going forward, use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose with dynamic partitioning and buffering to write larger files to S3 at ingestion time.
answers.D: Enable AWS Glue auto-scaling with minimum DPUs of 10 and maximum of 200, allowing Glue to dynamically allocate executors based on the actual workload volume without manual tuning.
answers.E: Move the raw clickstream data from S3 to Amazon EFS and mount it to the Glue job via the EFS network connection option, providing faster POSIX file system access than the S3 API.

explanation: A and C are correct. The root cause is the small-file problem in S3. Each tiny file requires a separate S3 API call and creates a Spark task with scheduling overhead—this dominates job time regardless of DPU count. Option A uses Glue's groupFiles feature to combine many small files into larger logical partitions during job execution, significantly reducing the number of tasks. Option C addresses the root cause permanently by compacting existing data into larger Parquet files and improving future ingestion by using Kinesis Data Firehose buffering to write larger files. Parquet also improves Redshift query performance through columnar storage. Option B adds more memory per executor but does not address the fundamental scheduling overhead of millions of tiny tasks. Option D enables auto-scaling, which adjusts DPU count dynamically but does not fix the small-file problem. Option E uses EFS, which is not designed for Glue data lake workloads and would actually perform worse than S3 at scale.

stem: A company is building a central data lake on Amazon S3 using AWS Lake Formation. Multiple producer teams write data to S3 in different formats (CSV, JSON, Parquet). Consumer teams use Amazon Athena and Amazon Redshift Spectrum to query the data. The data governance team requires: (1) column-level access control so that analysts can query only approved columns (for example, no PII columns); (2) automated schema discovery as new data lands; (3) data quality validation before data is made queryable. Which architecture satisfies all three requirements?
tags: Data retention, data sensitivity classification, and data regulatory requirements
Designing large-scale application architectures for a variety of access patterns

answers.A: Use S3 bucket policies to restrict access to specific prefixes for each consumer team. Run an AWS Lambda function on S3 PutObject events to validate schema using a custom validator. Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering to optimize storage. Manage column restrictions by creating Athena views that exclude PII columns.
answers.B: Configure AWS Glue crawlers to run on a schedule and update the Glue Data Catalog with discovered schemas. Use AWS IAM resource-based policies on Glue catalog tables to restrict column access. Run AWS Glue DataBrew quality rules before each Glue ETL job.
answers.C: Use Amazon Macie to detect PII in S3 objects and move flagged files to a restricted prefix. Run Glue crawlers for schema discovery. Use S3 bucket policies to block access to restricted prefixes. Consumer teams query only non-restricted prefixes via Athena.
answers.D: Configure AWS Glue crawlers to automatically discover schemas and register tables in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Use AWS Lake Formation column-level permissions to restrict access to approved columns for each IAM principal or role. Configure AWS Glue Data Quality rules (DQDL) to validate incoming data quality and quarantine records failing checks before tables are updated in the Data Catalog.

explanation: D is correct. AWS Lake Formation provides native column-level permissions that integrate with the Glue Data Catalog and are enforced for both Athena and Redshift Spectrum queries—no views needed. Glue crawlers handle automated schema discovery as new data arrives. AWS Glue Data Quality (DQDL rules) can validate data at ingestion time and route failing records to a quarantine location before the table is updated. Option A uses Athena views for column restriction, which can be bypassed if users access the underlying tables directly; Athena views also require manual maintenance. Option B uses Glue IAM policies for column restriction, but IAM policies on Glue catalog tables do not enforce column-level access for Athena queries—Lake Formation permissions are required. Option C uses Macie for PII detection (useful) but the approach of moving files to restricted prefixes does not enforce column-level access and is inflexible.

stem: A company runs a batch image processing application on a fleet of on-premises servers. The application pulls jobs from a queue, processes images (CPU-intensive, typically 5–30 minutes per job), and stores results in a shared NFS volume. The company wants to migrate to AWS with minimal application code changes. The new architecture must scale the number of processing workers automatically based on queue depth, must not require management of EC2 instances, and must support reading and writing to a shared file system accessible by all concurrent worker containers. Which architecture best meets these requirements?
tags: Containers (for example, Amazon ECR, Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS)
Identifying and evaluating the appropriate compute architecture
Fault isolation features of AWS services (for example, Availability Zones, Amazon S3 replication, AWS Auto Scaling)

answers.A: Use AWS Lambda with an Amazon SQS trigger. Each Lambda function invocation processes one image job. Store results in Amazon S3. Mount an Amazon EFS file system to Lambda using the EFS integration. Scale Lambda concurrency based on SQS queue depth automatically.
answers.B: Containerize the processing application and push the image to Amazon ECR. Create an Amazon ECS cluster using AWS Fargate launch type. Define an ECS task definition that mounts an Amazon EFS file system. Use an Amazon SQS queue for job distribution. Configure an Application Auto Scaling policy on the ECS service that scales based on the SQS ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible metric. Fargate manages underlying compute.
answers.C: Containerize the application and push to ECR. Deploy the ECS service with the EC2 launch type using Spot Instances. Configure EC2 Auto Scaling to scale based on SQS queue depth. Mount an instance store volume on each EC2 instance as the shared file system.
answers.D: Use AWS Batch with a managed compute environment backed by Fargate. Define a job definition that reads from SQS. Store results in Amazon S3. Configure an AWS Batch job queue with priority-based scheduling and auto-scaling. Use Amazon FSx for Lustre as the shared file system mounted to Batch compute environments.

explanation: B is correct. Amazon ECS with Fargate launch type eliminates EC2 instance management. The application can be containerized with minimal code changes. Amazon EFS provides a POSIX-compliant shared file system mountable by multiple concurrent Fargate tasks, replacing the on-premises NFS volume. Application Auto Scaling based on SQS queue depth scales the ECS service in and out automatically. Option A uses Lambda, which has a 15-minute maximum execution timeout—insufficient for jobs lasting up to 30 minutes. Also, Lambda ephemeral storage is limited and cannot serve as a shared NFS mount. Option C uses EC2 launch type (requires instance management) and instance store (not shared across multiple instances). Option D uses AWS Batch with Fargate, which is a valid batch processing approach; however, FSx for Lustre requires more complex setup and is optimized for HPC workloads rather than a simple NFS replacement. EFS in option B more closely replaces the on-premises NFS semantics with less configuration.

stem: A company runs a microservices application on Amazon ECS with EC2 launch type. The EC2 instances in the cluster are running at approximately 30% average CPU and memory utilization. The operations team spends significant time patching and maintaining the EC2 instances. The team wants to eliminate EC2 instance management, improve resource utilization efficiency, and reduce costs while keeping the same ECS task definitions and service configuration. Individual tasks are stateless and have no dependency on instance-level storage. Which approach best meets these requirements?
tags: Adopting managed services as required to reduce infrastructure provisioning and patching overhead
Identifying opportunities to use serverless and managed services to reduce operational overhead
Selecting purchasing options to minimize costs for a given workload

answers.A: Keep the ECS cluster on EC2 launch type. Enable EC2 Auto Scaling to scale down instances during low-utilization periods. Use AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager to automate OS patching. Purchase Savings Plans for the EC2 instances to reduce costs.
answers.B: Migrate the ECS cluster to Amazon EKS on EC2. Kubernetes' bin-packing scheduler will improve resource utilization. Use managed node groups for automated node patching. Purchase EC2 Reserved Instances for the EKS nodes.
answers.C: Migrate the ECS services to use the Fargate launch type. Update the ECS service definitions to specify FARGATE as the launch type. Right-size the CPU and memory in the task definitions to match actual workload requirements. Purchase Fargate Savings Plans to reduce per-task costs. AWS manages all underlying compute.
answers.D: Enable ECS Fargate Spot for all services. Configure ECS capacity providers with a base of 0 Fargate On-Demand tasks and a weight of 1 for Fargate Spot. This eliminates EC2 management while reducing costs by up to 70% versus On-Demand Fargate.

explanation: C is correct. Migrating from EC2 launch type to Fargate eliminates all EC2 instance management—no patching, no capacity planning. Existing ECS task definitions require only a launch-type update (and possibly network mode adjustment to awsvpc). Fargate Savings Plans reduce per-task costs. Right-sizing task definitions improves cost efficiency. Option A keeps EC2 instances, which requires continued patching—does not meet the requirement to eliminate instance management. Option B moves to EKS, which requires learning Kubernetes and uses EC2 managed node groups—still requires node management (though less than unmanaged). Option D uses only Fargate Spot, which can be interrupted at any time—for microservices requiring consistent availability, using 100% Spot without an On-Demand base is risky. A combination (base On-Demand + Spot) is more appropriate, which is what C implies with Fargate Savings Plans.

stem: A company uses AWS Control Tower to manage its AWS Organization. The company wants to enforce the following customizations on every new account enrolled in Control Tower: (1) deploy a specific VPC configuration with private subnets in three AZs and no default VPC; (2) enable AWS Config with a specific delivery channel pointing to a central S3 bucket; (3) apply a custom IAM password policy. These customizations must be applied automatically when a new account is vended through Account Factory and must not require manual steps after account creation. Which solution implements this?
tags: AWS Organizations and AWS Control Tower
Infrastructure as code (IaC) (for example, AWS CloudFormation)

answers.A: Use the Customizations for AWS Control Tower (CfCT) solution. Define a CloudFormation template for the VPC, Config delivery channel, and IAM password policy in the CfCT manifest. CfCT automatically deploys these resources to new accounts when Account Factory provisions them, triggered by Control Tower lifecycle events.
answers.B: Create an AWS CloudFormation StackSet targeted at the root OU. The StackSet deploys the VPC, Config delivery channel, and IAM password policy templates. New accounts added to the organization automatically receive the StackSet stacks through service-managed deployments.
answers.C: Write an AWS Lambda function triggered by the CreateManagedAccount Control Tower lifecycle event. The Lambda assumes an OrganizationAccountAccessRole in the new account and deploys three separate CloudFormation stacks: one for the VPC, one for Config, and one for the IAM policy.
answers.D: Use AWS Service Catalog to create a product containing the VPC, Config, and IAM password policy configurations. Share the product to all OUs in Organizations. Configure Account Factory to launch the Service Catalog product as part of the account vending workflow.

explanation: A is correct. AWS provides an official solution called Customizations for AWS Control Tower (CfCT) that integrates with Control Tower lifecycle events to deploy CloudFormation templates or SCPs automatically to new accounts. It is triggered by Account Factory events without any additional Lambda or custom code. This is the AWS-recommended approach for this exact use case. Option B uses StackSets with service-managed permissions targeted at the root OU, which does work for new accounts joining the OU but is less integrated with Control Tower's Account Factory and does not handle Control Tower-specific lifecycle nuances (like the account not yet being fully configured when first added). Option C uses Lambda with lifecycle events—functionally possible but requires custom code, error handling, and maintenance. Option D uses Service Catalog, which requires configuration in Account Factory and relies on administrators launching the product—not fully automatic without additional customization.

stem: A company's cloud finance team needs to implement cost governance across 50 AWS accounts. Requirements include: (1) each business unit must receive an alert when its monthly spend reaches 80% and 100% of its allocated budget; (2) the DevTest OU must automatically stop all EC2 instances if spending exceeds 110% of budget to prevent runaway costs; (3) cost visibility reports must be generated showing spend by service and by cost allocation tag (Environment, Team); (4) forecasted overage alerts must trigger at least 2 weeks before month end. Which combination of AWS services and features meets all requirements? (Select TWO)
tags: AWS cost and usage monitoring tools (for example, AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, AWS Cost and Usage Report)
Monitoring cost and usage with AWS tools
Developing an effective tagging strategy that maps costs to business units

answers.A: Create one AWS Organizations-level Cost and Usage Report (CUR) with hourly granularity and resource-level data. Use Amazon Athena and Amazon QuickSight to build cost dashboards. Enable AWS Cost Explorer for each business unit account and set up individual Cost Explorer budget alerts per account.
answers.B: Create AWS Budgets for each business unit in the management account with actual cost alert thresholds at 80% and 100%, plus a forecasted cost alert threshold configured to trigger when AWS projects month-end spend will exceed budget. Configure budget actions to run an SSM Automation document that stops EC2 instances in the DevTest OU accounts when the 110% actual threshold is breached.
answers.C: Use AWS Cost Anomaly Detection to identify unusual spending patterns and trigger alerts. Create cost allocation tags for Environment and Team. Enable AWS Cost Explorer to generate monthly cost reports by service and tag. Configure SNS notifications for anomaly alerts.
answers.D: Enable the Cost and Usage Report (CUR) at the management account level with daily granularity and resource IDs enabled. Activate the Environment and Team cost allocation tags in the Billing console. Use Amazon Athena and QuickSight to build reports showing spend by service and tag across all linked accounts.
answers.E: Create AWS Config rules that check for untagged resources and trigger remediation to stop EC2 instances that lack required tags. Use CloudWatch billing alarms per account for 80% and 100% thresholds. Use Trusted Advisor cost optimization recommendations as the forecasting mechanism.

explanation: B and D are correct. AWS Budgets supports actual cost alerts at multiple thresholds (80%, 100%, 110%) and forecasted cost alerts that project month-end spend—these can be set to trigger weeks in advance. Budget Actions can automatically execute SSM Automation documents, allowing automated EC2 instance stopping when the DevTest OU exceeds 110% of budget. AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) at the management account level captures spend across all linked accounts with resource-level detail. Enabling cost allocation tags for Environment and Team makes those dimensions filterable in CUR-based reports in Athena/QuickSight. Option A combines CUR with Cost Explorer for alerting—Cost Explorer alerts are limited in flexibility and cannot trigger automated remediation actions. Option C uses Cost Anomaly Detection, which detects unexpected changes rather than tracking against a fixed budget, and does not provide automated remediation. Option E uses CloudWatch billing alarms, which have limited granularity and cannot trigger SSM automation for EC2 stopping; Config rule remediation is not designed for spend-based triggers.

stem: A global financial company has two AWS Direct Connect dedicated connections (10 Gbps each) at the same Direct Connect location for redundancy. A network architect reviews the design and notes that if the Direct Connect location itself experiences an outage, both connections will be lost simultaneously. The architect must redesign the hybrid connectivity to meet the highest level of SLA resiliency. What should the architect implement?
tags: Redundancy patterns for Direct Connect (dual connections, LAG)
Designing resilient Direct Connect architectures with redundant connections across Direct Connect locations

answers.A: Create a Link Aggregation Group (LAG) combining both existing connections at the same Direct Connect location to increase aggregate bandwidth and enable automatic failover at the port level.
answers.B: Add a third 10 Gbps dedicated connection at the same Direct Connect location to provide three independent physical paths through a single facility.
answers.C: Provision a second dedicated Direct Connect connection at a geographically separate Direct Connect location, and configure BGP with AS path prepending to establish Active/Active or Active/Passive routing across both locations.
answers.D: Enable BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection) on both existing connections at the same location to decrease failure detection time and achieve sub-second failover between the two links.

explanation: AWS Direct Connect resiliency best practice (Maximum Resiliency) requires connections at separate Direct Connect locations. If both connections terminate at the same facility, a location-level failure eliminates all connectivity. The solution is to provision at least one connection at a second, geographically separate Direct Connect location, configuring BGP so traffic can fail over between locations. Option A (LAG) increases bandwidth and provides port-level redundancy but does not protect against a location-level failure. Option B adds a third connection at the same location, which still does not protect against a site outage. Option D (BFD) reduces failure detection time but has no bearing on physical location redundancy.

stem: A manufacturing company connects its on-premises ERP systems to AWS using a private VIF over AWS Direct Connect. The company needs to also access AWS public service endpoints (such as Amazon S3 and Amazon SQS) from its on-premises network through the same Direct Connect connection without traversing the public internet. The current architecture uses only one virtual interface. What is the most operationally efficient solution?
tags: Private VIF, public VIF, and transit VIF
AWS Direct Connect configuration including physical connections and virtual interfaces
Configuring Direct Connect virtual interfaces (private, public, transit) and BGP peering

answers.A: Modify the existing private VIF to add the public S3 and SQS service CIDR ranges as BGP prefixes so on-premises traffic destined for those services routes through the private VIF to a NAT gateway in the VPC.
answers.B: Create a separate public VIF on the same Direct Connect connection, peer with AWS public BGP ASN, and configure on-premises routing to send S3 and SQS traffic through the public VIF using the AWS-advertised public prefixes.
answers.C: Create an AWS Site-to-Site VPN over the existing private VIF to encrypt traffic, then configure split tunneling to route public AWS service traffic through the VPN tunnel.
