After the retention period, documents must be automatically deleted. The company also needs to automatically identify any PII in newly uploaded documents. Which design satisfies all requirements?

answers.A: Enable S3 Versioning and configure a lifecycle expiration policy to delete objects after 7 years. Enable S3 Object Lock in governance mode with a 7-year retention period. Use Amazon Macie to classify objects and identify PII.
answers.B: Enable S3 Versioning and S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a 7-year default retention period. Configure an S3 lifecycle expiration rule for objects after 7 years. Enable Amazon Macie with scheduled discovery jobs on the bucket to identify PII automatically.
answers.C: Store documents with SSE-KMS encryption and schedule automatic KMS key deletion after 7 years to effectively expire access. Use Amazon Comprehend triggered by S3 event notifications to classify documents for PII.
answers.D: Enable S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with indefinite retention and rely on an SCP to prevent deletion. Configure Macie for PII identification and trigger automatic expiration via a Lambda function after 7 years.

explanation: B is correct because S3 Object Lock in compliance mode is the only mechanism that prevents deletion by any user including root during the retention period (governance mode can be bypassed by privileged users). A lifecycle expiration rule handles automatic deletion after the retention period. Amazon Macie is the AWS-native service for PII discovery in S3 and supports scheduled classification jobs. A is wrong because governance mode can be overridden by users with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permissions; only compliance mode prevents root from overriding retention. C is wrong because scheduling KMS key deletion is not a supported immutability pattern; it renders all encrypted objects permanently unreadable rather than securely deleting them. Amazon Comprehend is out of scope for this exam. D is wrong because Object Lock in compliance mode with indefinite retention cannot be overcome by a Lambda function, so automatic expiration would fail.

stem: A financial institution must retain customer transaction records in Amazon S3 for exactly 10 years and prevent any modification or deletion during the retention period by any principal including root. Amazon Macie must scan the bucket and route PII findings to the security team automatically and in near real time. Which design fully satisfies all requirements?

answers.A: Configure S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a 10-year default retention period and enable S3 Versioning. Use IAM policies to deny s3:PutObjectTagging after upload. Configure Amazon Macie discovery jobs on the bucket and use EventBridge to route PII findings to SNS for the security team.
answers.B: Use S3 Object Lock in governance mode with a 10-year retention period. Configure S3 Batch Operations to tag objects at upload. Set up a Macie custom data identifier and use a Lambda function invoked by S3 event notifications to email the security team on findings.
answers.C: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering with a 10-year minimum storage duration and configure bucket policies to deny DeleteObject. Run Macie analysis on a monthly schedule and export findings to an S3 report bucket.
answers.D: Configure S3 Object Lock in compliance mode. Run Macie on-demand analysis every 24 hours via a CloudWatch Events schedule. Use Amazon SQS to queue findings for batch processing by the security team the following business day.

explanation: A is correct because Object Lock in compliance mode prevents deletion or modification by any user including root for the 10-year period. IAM policy Deny statements on s3:PutObjectTagging and s3:DeleteObjectTagging prevent post-upload metadata changes. Amazon Macie scheduled jobs continuously scan the bucket, and EventBridge natively receives Macie finding events and routes them to SNS for near-real-time security team notification. B is wrong because governance mode allows users with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention to delete objects before retention expires, violating the root-prevention requirement. C is wrong because S3 Intelligent-Tiering is a storage class optimization feature, not an immutability mechanism; bucket policy denying DeleteObject is insufficient because delete markers can still be created. D is wrong because 24-hour scheduled scans and next-business-day batch processing do not constitute near-real-time alerting.

stem: A company uses AWS Organizations with the following OU structure: Root OU with an SCP that allows all actions, Workloads OU inheriting from Root, and Production OU (under Workloads) with an SCP that explicitly denies s3:DeleteBucket. An IAM policy attached to a developer role in a Production account explicitly allows s3:DeleteBucket. The developer attempts to delete an S3 bucket. What is the result and why?

answers.A: The deletion succeeds because the IAM policy explicitly allows s3:DeleteBucket and IAM identity-based policies take precedence over SCPs at the account level.
answers.B: The deletion is denied because the Production OU SCP explicitly denies s3:DeleteBucket, and an explicit SCP Deny cannot be overridden by any IAM policy in the account, regardless of privilege level.
answers.C: The deletion is denied because the Root OU SCP allowing all actions creates a default-deny posture; only actions explicitly allowed in both the SCP and the IAM policy succeed.
answers.D: The deletion succeeds because SCPs only restrict IAM roles assumed via cross-account federation and do not affect roles used directly within the same account.

explanation: B is correct because in AWS Organizations, an explicit Deny in an SCP cannot be overridden by any IAM policy at any level — identity-based, resource-based, or permission boundary. SCP Deny statements are enforced as guardrails before IAM policy evaluation; even an administrator policy cannot override an SCP Deny. A is wrong because IAM policies never take precedence over SCP Deny statements; SCPs are organization-level guardrails that bound all principals in the account. C is wrong because the Root OU SCP allowing all actions is effectively a whitelist that imposes no additional restrictions; it is the Production OU explicit Deny that controls the outcome. D is wrong because SCPs apply to all IAM principals in the account including users, roles, and federated identities, regardless of how they are accessed.

stem: A security team enables Amazon Macie on a company AWS account. Macie quickly identifies sensitive data findings in an existing S3 bucket containing legacy customer records. However, after 72 hours, Macie has generated zero findings for a new S3 bucket that was recently populated with records migrated from an on-premises database. What is the most likely explanation, and what corrective action should the team take?

answers.A: Macie has a mandatory 72-hour initialization period for new S3 buckets; the team should wait at least one additional day before determining that no findings exist for the bucket.
answers.B: Macie only analyzes S3 buckets that carry a macie-scan-enabled tag with value true; the new bucket is missing this required tag so Macie skips it automatically.
answers.C: Macie generates findings only for buckets that already existed when Macie was first enabled in the account; newly created buckets require a separate manual scan request through the AWS CLI or console.
answers.D: Macie sensitive data discovery jobs target a defined scope of S3 buckets. The new bucket was not included in the existing job scope. The team should update the discovery job to include all buckets or create a new job targeting the new bucket.

explanation: D is correct because Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery jobs are configured with a specific bucket scope. When a new bucket is created after a job has been set up, it is not automatically included unless the job was configured to target all current and future buckets. The team must update the existing job scope or create a new discovery job targeting the new bucket. A is wrong because Macie does not have a 72-hour warm-up period for new buckets; this is not a documented Macie feature. B is wrong because Macie does not use S3 bucket tags to determine scan scope; scope is configured within the Macie job definition itself. C is wrong because Macie can discover data in buckets created at any time; it is not limited to buckets that existed before Macie was enabled.

stem: A company wants to expose a single internal microservice running in a private VPC subnet to a partner organization. The partner must connect using private RFC 1918 IP addresses, must not be able to initiate connections to any other resource in the company VPC, and must not learn the company internal VPC CIDR range from routing information. Which network architecture satisfies all constraints?

answers.A: Establish a VPC peering connection between the company VPC and the partner VPC. Restrict route tables to advertise only the microservice subnet CIDR. Use security groups to limit inbound access from the partner to the microservice port.
answers.B: Create an AWS Transit Gateway shared with the partner account via AWS RAM. Configure Transit Gateway route tables with blackhole routes for all company subnets except the microservice subnet.
answers.C: Deploy a Network Load Balancer in front of the microservice. Create an AWS PrivateLink endpoint service referencing the NLB. Share the endpoint service name with the partner. The partner creates an interface VPC endpoint pointing to the service. Traffic flows privately without exposing the company VPC CIDR.
answers.D: Deploy an AWS Site-to-Site VPN between the company VPC and the partner on-premises network. Configure static routes to advertise only the microservice host route to the partner.

explanation: C is correct because AWS PrivateLink is architecturally designed for this use case: exposing a specific service to another network without revealing the broader VPC CIDR or allowing lateral movement. The partner connects to a named endpoint service and can only reach the NLB, not any other resource in the VPC. VPC CIDR information is not propagated in PrivateLink connections. A is wrong because VPC peering exposes both VPC CIDR ranges in the route tables of each side, violating the CIDR-hiding requirement. Additionally, peering does not inherently prevent lateral movement to other subnets if route tables are misconfigured. B is wrong because Transit Gateway also involves route propagation between peered networks, and complex blackhole configurations are error-prone; CIDR exposure still occurs. D is wrong because Site-to-Site VPN requires advertising the VPC CIDR (or subnet CIDR) to the partner, exposing network topology.

stem: A security operations center receives hundreds of daily security findings from Amazon GuardDuty, AWS Security Hub, and Amazon Inspector. The team suffers from alert fatigue and is missing high-priority events. They need to: (1) normalize findings from all three services into a single format, (2) suppress known-false-positive findings from a trusted vulnerability scanner IP range, and (3) route CRITICAL findings to a third-party incident platform within 5 minutes of finding creation. Which architecture achieves all three goals with the least custom code?
tags: AWS Security Hub security posture management

answers.A: Create three Lambda functions, one per service, to normalize findings into a common JSON format stored in DynamoDB. A fourth Lambda polls DynamoDB every 5 minutes and calls the third-party API for CRITICAL records not matching trusted IPs.
answers.B: Configure AWS Security Hub to aggregate findings from GuardDuty and Inspector (Security Hub normalizes all findings to ASFF automatically). Create Security Hub automation rules to suppress findings from the trusted scanner IP range. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule matching CRITICAL Security Hub findings and invoke a Lambda function that calls the third-party incident platform API.
answers.C: Enable Amazon OpenSearch Service with an ingestion pipeline from Security Hub, GuardDuty, and Inspector. Build dashboards to filter findings and configure OpenSearch alerting to call the third-party API webhook for critical events.
answers.D: Deploy Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to ingest events from all three services. Write a Kinesis consumer Lambda to normalize findings, filter scanner IPs, and call the third-party API. Buffer events in a 5-minute Kinesis window before processing.

explanation: B is correct because AWS Security Hub is purpose-built for finding aggregation and normalization. It converts findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, and other services into the AWS Security Finding Format (ASFF), eliminating custom normalization code. Security Hub automation rules suppress findings matching specific criteria such as trusted scanner IPs. EventBridge receives Security Hub CRITICAL finding events in near real time and invokes a Lambda function to call the third-party platform within seconds of finding creation, well within 5 minutes. A is wrong because three separate normalization Lambda functions with DynamoDB and 5-minute polling is complex and introduces up to 5-minute latency per poll cycle, potentially missing the SLA. C is wrong because an OpenSearch ingestion pipeline from multiple services requires significant configuration and more custom code than option B. D is wrong because a 5-minute Kinesis buffering window deliberately introduces up to 5 minutes of latency, which means findings may arrive at the platform after the 5-minute requirement.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: A financial services firm is building a generative AI system that routes customer inquiries through a supervisor agent. The supervisor must delegate credit-risk queries to a credit-analysis sub-agent and account-history queries to a transaction-history sub-agent. Occasionally a query spans both domains, requiring both sub-agents to contribute partial answers before the supervisor synthesizes a final response. The team wants to implement this using Amazon Bedrock. Which architectural pattern best supports this multi-agent collaboration requirement?
tags: Agentic AI workflows and multi-agent orchestration
Multi-agent collaboration patterns and orchestration with Amazon Bedrock
Agentic AI design patterns (for example, ReAct, plan-and-execute, multi-agent orchestration)
Amazon Bedrock Agents configuration (for example, action groups, knowledge bases, orchestration strategy, memory)

answers.A: Configure a single Amazon Bedrock Agent with two action groups—one for credit-risk tools and one for account-history tools—using a chain-of-thought orchestration strategy to invoke both groups sequentially when a query spans domains.
answers.B: Configure a supervisor Amazon Bedrock Agent that invokes a credit-analysis sub-agent and a transaction-history sub-agent as named collaborators using multi-agent collaboration, allowing the supervisor to call both sub-agents and synthesize their partial responses.
answers.C: Deploy both sub-agents as separate Amazon Bedrock Flows and wire them together with an AWS Step Functions state machine that the supervisor Lambda function invokes sequentially, aggregating results before passing them back to the foundation model.
answers.D: Use a single Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base that indexes both credit-risk and transaction-history documents, configure the supervisor agent to retrieve from both indexes simultaneously, and rely on the LLM's in-context reasoning to synthesize a response.

explanation: Option B is correct. Amazon Bedrock supports multi-agent collaboration where a supervisor agent can invoke registered sub-agents as collaborators and synthesize their outputs. This natively addresses the requirement for the supervisor to delegate to domain-specific sub-agents and combine partial answers, including cross-domain queries requiring both sub-agents. Option A a single agent with multiple action groups cannot independently reason and coordinate as separate specialist agents; all tool calls share one orchestration context, limiting specialization. Option C using Step Functions externalizes orchestration to custom infrastructure rather than using native multi-agent collaboration, adding complexity and maintenance burden. Option D a knowledge base retrieves documents but does not execute agent-to-agent delegation or specialized reasoning that sub-agents provide.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: A logistics company builds a multi-agent system on Amazon Bedrock where a planner agent decomposes shipment optimization requests and dispatches subtasks to a route-calculation sub-agent and an inventory sub-agent. During load testing, the team observes that the supervisor agent intermittently re-invokes a sub-agent that already completed its task, causing duplicate side effects in the inventory system. Which root cause and remediation best explains and resolves this behavior?
tags: Agentic AI workflows and multi-agent orchestration
Multi-agent collaboration patterns and orchestration with Amazon Bedrock
Implementing appropriate error handling, retry logic, and fallback behaviors for agentic workflows
Amazon Bedrock Agents configuration (for example, action groups, knowledge bases, orchestration strategy, memory)

answers.A: The supervisor agent's foundation model lacks sufficient context window to retain sub-agent completion status. The remediation is to switch to a larger-context foundation model so prior sub-agent responses fit within a single inference call.
answers.B: The inventory sub-agent action group Lambda function times out intermittently, causing the Bedrock runtime to retry the invocation transparently. The remediation is to increase the Lambda timeout and add exponential backoff within the function.
answers.C: The inventory sub-agent action groups are not returning structured confirmation payloads that the supervisor can reliably parse as task completion signals. The supervisor's LLM re-invokes due to ambiguity. The remediation is to define explicit structured response schemas for each action group and update the supervisor agent's prompt instructions to treat the completion field as final.
answers.D: The Amazon Bedrock multi-agent collaboration feature does not deduplicate sub-agent invocations. The remediation is to add an idempotency check in the inventory sub-agent Lambda function using an Amazon DynamoDB table keyed on the session ID and task ID.

explanation: Option C is correct. When sub-agent action groups return unstructured or ambiguous completion signals, the supervisor LLM cannot deterministically recognize that the subtask is done. Its reasoning loop may interpret the response as incomplete and retry the invocation, causing duplicate side effects. Defining explicit structured response schemas (for example, a JSON object with a 'status': 'completed' field) and updating the supervisor's orchestration prompt to treat that field as a terminal signal eliminates the ambiguity. Option A context window size affects how much history the model retains, but the re-invocation pattern on an already-completed task is a signal-parsing issue, not a context length issue. Option B Lambda timeouts cause failures, not silent duplicate invocations from the supervisor; retries from the Bedrock runtime are bounded and would surface as errors. Option D idempotency in the Lambda is a necessary defense-in-depth measure but does not address the root cause—the supervisor should not be re-invoking in the first place.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: An e-commerce company wants to build an AI shopping assistant that can autonomously search a product catalog, check real-time stock levels, apply discount rules, and finalize an order, taking multiple steps and adjusting its plan based on intermediate results. The team is evaluating agentic AI patterns. Which pattern is most appropriate for this scenario, and why?
tags: Agentic AI patterns (for example, tool use, chain-of-thought reasoning, ReAct, multi-agent orchestration)
Agentic AI workflows and multi-agent orchestration
Differentiating between foundation model types and selecting the appropriate model for a given use case

answers.A: ReAct (Reasoning + Acting), because it interleaves thought steps with tool invocations, allowing the agent to observe intermediate results—such as stock-level API responses—and adjust subsequent actions dynamically before finalizing the order.
answers.B: Zero-shot chain-of-thought prompting, because it generates a full multi-step reasoning chain in a single LLM call, covering catalog search, stock checks, discount logic, and order finalization without external tool calls.
answers.C: Plan-and-execute with a static plan, because the agent first enumerates all required API calls in a fixed sequence and then executes them in order, ensuring deterministic behavior for the transactional order workflow.
answers.D: Self-consistency prompting, because it samples multiple independent reasoning paths, selects the majority answer for each decision, and thereby reduces errors in discount rule application before submitting the order.

explanation: Option A is correct. The ReAct pattern interleaves reasoning traces with tool-use actions. After each tool invocation—such as a stock check or catalog search—the agent observes the result and decides the next action dynamically. This adaptive loop is essential for a shopping workflow where intermediate API results (for example, out-of-stock status) must change subsequent steps. Option B zero-shot chain-of-thought is a single-call prompting technique with no tool-use loop; it cannot query live APIs for stock or submit real orders. Option C a static plan-and-execute approach commits to a fixed action sequence before observing results, which cannot adapt to dynamic conditions like stockouts discovered mid-execution. Option D self-consistency samples multiple response paths and takes a majority vote—it is an evaluation technique for reducing reasoning errors in a single call, not an architecture for multi-step tool use against real systems.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: A legal firm is designing an AI assistant that must reason through a multi-step contract review process: identifying clauses, cross-referencing statutory definitions, flagging ambiguities, and producing a structured risk report. A junior engineer proposes using a chain-of-thought prompting technique in a single LLM call. A senior engineer argues for a ReAct-based agentic approach. Which statement best justifies adopting the ReAct pattern over a single chain-of-thought prompt for this use case?
tags: Agentic AI patterns (for example, tool use, chain-of-thought reasoning, ReAct, multi-agent orchestration)
Hallucination, grounding, and factual accuracy in LLM outputs
Identifying scenarios where RAG is preferable to fine-tuning or in-context learning

answers.A: ReAct requires less prompt engineering than chain-of-thought because the model automatically decomposes the contract review task into sub-steps without any explicit instructions about the reasoning structure.
answers.B: ReAct grounds each reasoning step against external tool calls—such as statutory definition lookups—so the model's conclusions are verified against authoritative sources rather than relying solely on parametric knowledge, which reduces hallucination risk for specialized legal content.
answers.C: Chain-of-thought prompting has a strict token limit that makes it incapable of processing contracts longer than a few pages, whereas ReAct circumvents this limit by distributing reasoning across multiple LLM calls.
answers.D: ReAct is preferable because it can be implemented without an LLM, using a rule-based engine for the 'Act' step, which removes model non-determinism from the contract review pipeline entirely.

explanation: Option B is correct. The fundamental advantage of ReAct over single-pass chain-of-thought in a legal context is grounding: ReAct interleaves reasoning with actual tool invocations (such as querying a statutory database or a case-law retriever), so each reasoning step is informed by retrieved factual content rather than the model's potentially stale or inaccurate parametric knowledge. This materially reduces hallucination risk in high-stakes legal analysis. Option A is inaccurate—ReAct typically requires more careful prompt engineering to define the thought/action/observation loop correctly, not less. Option C mischaracterizes chain-of-thought; context window length is a property of the underlying model and applies equally to both patterns. Option D is incorrect because the 'Act' step in ReAct specifically uses the LLM to decide which tool to call and how to interpret the observation; removing the LLM from the Act step would not be ReAct.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: A healthcare company needs to fine-tune a 70-billion-parameter open-source LLM for clinical note generation using Amazon SageMaker AI. The fine-tuning job processes 800 GB of tokenized training data. The team must minimize training time and cost while keeping the job within AWS. Which infrastructure configuration is most appropriate for this workload?
tags: AWS infrastructure for AI/ML workloads (for example, AWS Trainium, AWS Inferentia, GPU-backed EC2 instances)
Amazon SageMaker AI training jobs for model fine-tuning
Choosing the appropriate customization approach based on data availability, budget, and performance requirements

answers.A: Use a single ml.p4d.24xlarge instance (8x A100 GPUs, 320 GB GPU memory) with DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 sharding to fit the 70B model across GPUs, storing checkpoints to Amazon EFS for fast recovery.
answers.B: Use an Amazon SageMaker AI Automatic Model Tuning job across a fleet of ml.g5.xlarge instances, distributing each hyperparameter configuration to a separate instance to parallelize the training search.
answers.C: Use an Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster with AWS Trainium2 (trn2) nodes and SageMaker model parallelism, which is optimized for large-scale LLM training at lower per-hour cost than equivalent GPU instances.
answers.D: Use Amazon EC2 Spot Instances of type p3.16xlarge with Amazon SageMaker managed warm pools, and implement checkpoint-and-resume logic every 500 steps to tolerate spot interruptions across the 800 GB dataset.

explanation: Option C is correct. Amazon SageMaker HyperPod provides a purpose-built, resilient cluster environment for large-scale foundation model training. AWS Trainium2 (trn2) accelerators are purpose-designed for LLM training workloads and offer significantly lower per-FLOP cost than GPU-backed instances for sustained training jobs. SageMaker model parallelism handles the sharding required for a 70B parameter model across multiple accelerators. This combination minimizes both training time and cost for an 800 GB tokenized dataset. Option A a single p4d.24xlarge has sufficient GPU memory for 70B with ZeRO-3 but using a single node is a throughput bottleneck for 800 GB of data and does not minimize training time; EFS is also slower than S3 for checkpoint storage. Option B Automatic Model Tuning runs hyperparameter search across configurations—it is not a distributed training framework for a single fine-tuning job. Option D Spot p3.16xlarge instances have older V100 GPUs with lower memory bandwidth than modern accelerators; checkpoint-and-resume logic adds engineering complexity and Spot interruptions on a 70B training job would cause significant delays.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: A startup deploys a real-time image captioning service powered by a large vision-language model hosted on Amazon SageMaker AI. The service must serve 500 concurrent inference requests with P99 latency under 300 ms per request. The current ml.g5.xlarge instance saturates at 50 concurrent requests. Which infrastructure change best addresses the throughput and latency requirements?
tags: AWS infrastructure for AI/ML workloads (for example, AWS Trainium, AWS Inferentia, GPU-backed EC2 instances)
Amazon SageMaker AI inference optimization features (for example, multi-model endpoints, inference recommender, model compilation)
Latency vs. throughput trade-offs for different application patterns

answers.A: Migrate the SageMaker endpoint to ml.inf2.48xlarge instances backed by AWS Inferentia2 chips, compile the vision-language model using AWS Neuron SDK for Inferentia2, and configure SageMaker endpoint auto scaling to maintain one instance per 50 concurrent requests.
answers.B: Switch to ml.g5.12xlarge instances (4x A10G GPUs) and enable SageMaker multi-model endpoints to pack multiple model replicas onto the same instance, routing concurrent requests across replicas to increase throughput.
answers.C: Deploy multiple ml.g5.xlarge instances behind an Application Load Balancer and use SageMaker asynchronous inference to queue overflow requests, processing them as capacity becomes available.
answers.D: Apply INT4 quantization to the vision-language model and redeploy it on the same ml.g5.xlarge instance. Quantization will increase throughput by 10x, enabling the single instance to handle 500 concurrent requests.

explanation: Option A is correct. AWS Inferentia2 (inf2) is purpose-built for high-throughput, low-latency inference, offering significantly higher requests-per-second per dollar than GPU instances for compiled models. The AWS Neuron SDK compiles the model for the Inferentia2 architecture, unlocking the hardware's optimized matrix multiply units. Pairing with SageMaker auto scaling to maintain one instance per 50 concurrent requests linearly scales throughput to 500 concurrent requests while maintaining sub-300 ms P99 latency. Option B multi-model endpoints share GPU memory across multiple models on one instance; for a single large vision-language model this does not increase per-request throughput and the g5.12xlarge's 4 GPUs still impose a ceiling below 500 concurrent requests. Option C asynchronous inference queues requests—it explicitly does not meet a synchronous P99 latency SLA because queued requests can wait indefinitely. Option D INT4 quantization reduces model size and increases token throughput but a 10x throughput improvement from quantization alone is not reliably achievable for vision-language models, and the claim that a single instance handles 500 concurrencies is not justified by quantization alone.

stem: A media company wants to build a searchable archive of broadcast interviews. The archive must transcribe audio from MP4 files, extract named entities (such as person names and organizations) from the transcript, and index results for keyword and semantic search. The company requires fully managed AWS services to minimize operational overhead. Which combination of AWS services best meets these requirements?
tags: AWS purpose-built AI services and their generative AI extensions (for example, Amazon Lex, Amazon Transcribe, Amazon Polly, Amazon Rekognition, Amazon Textract, Amazon Comprehend, Amazon Kendra)
AWS data services relevant to generative AI pipelines (for example, Amazon S3, AWS Glue, Amazon Kinesis, Amazon OpenSearch Service)
Matching purpose-built AWS AI services to appropriate generative AI application components

answers.A: Use Amazon Textract to extract text from MP4 files, Amazon Rekognition to identify named entities in the transcripts, and Amazon Kendra to build the searchable index with both keyword and semantic search.
answers.B: Use Amazon Transcribe to transcribe audio from the MP4 files, Amazon Comprehend to extract named entities from the transcripts, and Amazon OpenSearch Service to index transcripts and entities for hybrid keyword and semantic search.
answers.C: Use Amazon Polly to convert the MP4 audio to text transcripts, Amazon Comprehend to extract entities, and Amazon Kendra to power keyword and semantic search over the indexed transcripts.
answers.D: Use Amazon Transcribe to generate transcripts, Amazon Rekognition to detect persons and organizations in the transcript text, and Amazon OpenSearch Service to index and search the results.

explanation: Option B is correct. Amazon Transcribe is the purpose-built managed service for converting audio files (including MP4) to text transcripts. Amazon Comprehend is the purpose-built NLP service for named entity recognition (NER), identifying person names, organizations, and other entity types in text. Amazon OpenSearch Service supports both keyword (BM25) and semantic (k-NN vector) search, making it ideal for a hybrid searchable archive. Option A Amazon Textract is designed for document image and PDF extraction, not audio files; Amazon Rekognition performs image and video visual analysis, not NER on text. Option C Amazon Polly is a text-to-speech service that converts text to audio—it is the opposite of what is needed (audio-to-text). Option D Amazon Rekognition performs visual analysis on images and video frames, not named entity extraction from text transcripts.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: A retail company wants to enhance its e-commerce search with visual similarity: when a customer uploads a photo, the system must identify the clothing category, generate an embedding of the image, and return the five most visually similar products from a catalog. The company already uses Amazon OpenSearch Service for product search. Which combination of AWS services implements this pipeline with the least custom model development?
tags: AWS purpose-built AI services and their generative AI extensions (for example, Amazon Lex, Amazon Transcribe, Amazon Polly, Amazon Rekognition, Amazon Textract, Amazon Comprehend, Amazon Kendra)
Matching purpose-built AWS AI services to appropriate generative AI application components
Identifying the appropriate vector store for a given RAG architecture based on scale, latency, and existing infrastructure

answers.A: Use Amazon Textract to extract product descriptions from the uploaded image, embed the description using an Amazon Bedrock embedding model, and query Amazon OpenSearch Service with a k-NN vector query to return similar products.
answers.B: Use Amazon Rekognition DetectLabels to get clothing category labels, pass the labels as a text query to Amazon Kendra, and return the top-5 Kendra search results as similar products.
answers.C: Train a custom Amazon SageMaker AI computer vision model to generate image embeddings, deploy it as a real-time endpoint, embed the uploaded image and all catalog images, and store embeddings in Amazon OpenSearch Service for k-NN search.
answers.D: Use Amazon Rekognition to classify the clothing category from the uploaded image, generate an image embedding using an Amazon Bedrock multimodal embedding model, store catalog embeddings in Amazon OpenSearch Service, and perform a k-NN vector search to return the five most similar products.

explanation: Option D is correct. Amazon Rekognition provides managed image classification and label detection without custom model training. Amazon Bedrock provides multimodal embedding models (such as Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings) that generate image embeddings without any custom model development. Storing catalog product embeddings in Amazon OpenSearch Service's existing k-NN index and querying with the uploaded image embedding returns visually similar products—all using fully managed services. Option A Amazon Textract is a document extraction service that processes text in PDFs and scanned documents, not visual feature extraction from product photos; it cannot generate image embeddings. Option B Amazon Kendra is a document search service optimized for natural language text queries, not image-to-image visual similarity search via vector embeddings. Option C training a custom SageMaker computer vision model requires significant ML development effort and labeled data, which contradicts the 'least custom model development' requirement.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: A news summarization platform wants to roll out an updated fine-tuned Amazon Bedrock model that generates shorter, punchier summaries. The team wants to compare user engagement between the current model and the new model under real traffic conditions, routing 10% of requests to the new model while monitoring key quality metrics before committing to a full cutover. Which deployment strategy and AWS services implement this requirement?
tags: A/B testing and canary deployment patterns for generative AI model updates
Model monitoring concepts for generative AI (for example, output quality drift, latency degradation, cost anomalies)
Amazon CloudWatch metrics and alarms for Amazon Bedrock and Amazon SageMaker AI
Designing A/B testing strategies to compare model versions or prompt variations

answers.A: Implement a canary deployment by routing 10% of inference requests to the new model via a weighted routing rule in the application layer (such as AWS Lambda with a random number check). Tag each request with the model version, log outputs and user engagement metrics to Amazon CloudWatch using custom metrics, and define a CloudWatch alarm to halt the canary if engagement or quality metrics degrade.
answers.B: Deploy both the current and new model as separate Amazon Bedrock on-demand model IDs, configure Amazon API Gateway to route 10% of traffic to the new model endpoint using a stage variable, and use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to stream logs to Amazon S3 for offline analysis.
answers.C: Use Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor to set up an A/B test between the current and new model by configuring two production variants on a SageMaker endpoint with a 90/10 traffic split, and monitor data quality reports in SageMaker Studio.
answers.D: Purchase provisioned throughput for both models, configure Amazon CloudFront with two origin groups pointing to each model's inference endpoint, and use CloudFront's origin failover to route 10% of cache misses to the new model.

explanation: Option A is correct. For Amazon Bedrock on-demand models, there are no native traffic-split endpoints equivalent to SageMaker multi-variant endpoints. The standard canary pattern is to implement weighted routing in the application layer (Lambda or API Gateway stage variable with a randomized routing check), tag each request with the model version, emit custom metrics to Amazon CloudWatch, and define alarms that trigger rollback if monitored quality or engagement metrics fall outside acceptable bounds. This gives full observability and a clear rollback trigger. Option B Amazon API Gateway stage variables do not implement statistical traffic splitting by percentage—stage variables are per-stage configuration values, not request-level routing weights; this approach would need a Lambda authorizer or custom integration to implement splitting. Option C SageMaker multi-variant endpoints support A/B traffic splitting natively, but only for models deployed on SageMaker AI endpoints, not for Amazon Bedrock managed model APIs. Option D CloudFront origin failover is a high-availability mechanism, not a traffic-splitting tool; it routes to the secondary origin only on failure, not on a percentage basis.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: A company running a customer support chatbot on Amazon Bedrock observes that a new prompt template variant produces higher LLM-as-judge helpfulness scores in offline evaluation. Before promoting the new template to 100% of traffic, the team wants to run a statistically rigorous live experiment comparing user satisfaction between the current and new template. Which approach correctly implements this A/B test in a production Amazon Bedrock environment?
tags: A/B testing and canary deployment patterns for generative AI model updates
Designing A/B testing strategies to compare model versions or prompt variations
Amazon Bedrock Model Invocation Logging for capturing inputs and outputs
Human evaluation frameworks (for example, preference ranking, Likert scale scoring)

answers.A: Enable Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management version control and configure the Bedrock runtime to automatically split traffic 50/50 between the two prompt template versions, then analyze the resulting CloudWatch metrics to determine the winning variant.
answers.B: Deploy both prompt templates to separate Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, route half of user sessions to each knowledge base, and compare retrieval quality scores from each knowledge base as a proxy for prompt template effectiveness.
answers.C: Implement session-level assignment in the application layer: hash the session ID modulo 2 to assign each user to control or treatment, apply the corresponding prompt template, enable Amazon Bedrock Model Invocation Logging to capture inputs and outputs, and instrument the application to collect post-interaction satisfaction ratings keyed to the session group.
answers.D: Use Amazon SageMaker Clarify to run an automated bias and fairness comparison between the two prompt templates on a held-out evaluation dataset, then promote the template with higher Clarify scores to production traffic.

explanation: Option C is correct. Statistically rigorous A/B testing of prompt templates in Amazon Bedrock requires session-level group assignment to prevent the same user from seeing both variants (which would contaminate the experiment). Hashing the session ID provides a deterministic, balanced 50/50 split. Enabling Model Invocation Logging captures the full input/output record for each request, allowing reproducible post-hoc analysis. Collecting user satisfaction ratings (the true success metric) keyed to the session group provides the outcome variable needed for statistical comparison. Option A Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management handles versioning and deployment of prompt templates but does not provide native traffic-splitting between template versions at the runtime level—traffic assignment must be implemented in the application layer. Option B knowledge base routing is irrelevant to prompt template testing; the two templates operate at the inference layer, not the retrieval layer. Option D SageMaker Clarify is designed for bias detection and model explainability on structured ML datasets, not for live A/B comparison of conversational prompt templates.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: A financial regulator requires a healthcare company to provide a complete audit trail of all Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel API calls, including the identity of the caller, the model ARN, and the timestamp of each call, for a period of seven years. The audit trail must be tamper-evident and stored immutably. Which combination of AWS services and configurations satisfies this requirement?
tags: AWS CloudTrail logging for generative AI API calls and audit purposes
AWS CloudTrail and Amazon Bedrock Model Invocation Logging for audit trails
Data security controls for generative AI (for example, encryption at rest and in transit, AWS KMS, VPC endpoints)
Compliance frameworks relevant to AI workloads (for example, GDPR, HIPAA, SOC 2)

answers.A: Enable Amazon Bedrock Model Invocation Logging and configure it to write logs to an Amazon S3 bucket with Object Lock in COMPLIANCE mode with a seven-year retention period. Model Invocation Logging captures caller identity, model ARN, and timestamps alongside request and response payloads.
answers.B: Enable AWS CloudTrail in all regions with a trail that captures management and data events for Amazon Bedrock. Configure the trail to deliver logs to an Amazon S3 bucket with S3 Object Lock in COMPLIANCE mode and a seven-year retention period. Enable CloudTrail log file validation to ensure tamper-evidence.
answers.C: Configure Amazon CloudWatch Logs to receive Amazon Bedrock API call logs, set a CloudWatch Log Group retention period of seven years, and enable CloudWatch Logs Insights queries to retrieve caller identity and model ARN from stored log events.
answers.D: Deploy an AWS Lambda function that intercepts every Bedrock InvokeModel call, extracts caller identity and model ARN from the event context, and writes records to an Amazon DynamoDB table with point-in-time recovery enabled for seven years.

explanation: Option B is correct. AWS CloudTrail is the authoritative service for recording AWS API calls, including Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel events. CloudTrail records include the caller identity (IAM principal ARN), the API action, the resource ARN (model ARN), the timestamp, and the source IP. Delivering trail logs to S3 with Object Lock in COMPLIANCE mode prevents any user, including the root account, from deleting or modifying log files before the retention period expires, satisfying the tamper-evident immutability requirement. Enabling log file validation (SHA-256 hash chain) provides cryptographic tamper evidence. Option A Amazon Bedrock Model Invocation Logging captures request and response payloads for ML observability purposes, but it does not record the IAM caller identity in the same authoritative, tamper-evident format that CloudTrail does, and it is not designed as a compliance audit log. Option C CloudWatch Logs can retain log data but does not natively implement immutable COMPLIANCE-mode retention; log groups can be deleted by authorized principals. Option D a custom Lambda interceptor is not tamper-evident, is not an authoritative source of record for API calls, and relies on the Lambda being correctly invoked for every call—any invocation bypass would create gaps in the audit trail.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: A security team investigating a potential data exfiltration incident suspects that an IAM role was used to invoke Amazon Bedrock models with unusually large prompt payloads. The team must identify the specific API calls, the caller identity, and the request parameters within the last 30 days. Which AWS service and configuration provides this information?
tags: AWS CloudTrail logging for generative AI API calls and audit purposes
AWS CloudTrail and Amazon Bedrock Model Invocation Logging for audit trails
Identity and access management for generative AI services (for example, IAM roles, resource-based policies, service control policies)

answers.A: Query AWS CloudTrail event history or a configured trail for InvokeModel events within the last 30 days, filtering by the suspected IAM role ARN in the userIdentity field. CloudTrail records the caller identity, API action, model ARN, request timestamp, and source IP for each Bedrock API call.
answers.B: Query Amazon Bedrock Model Invocation Logs in the designated Amazon S3 bucket, filtering records by the IAM role ARN in the log metadata field. Model Invocation Logs capture the full request and response payloads alongside the caller identity.
answers.C: Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights to search the /aws/bedrock/ log group for InvokeModel events in the last 30 days, correlating entries by the session token included in each log event to identify the specific IAM role.
answers.D: Run an Amazon Athena query against the AWS Config configuration history table to identify all Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel calls made by the suspected IAM role within the 30-day investigation window.

explanation: Option A is correct. AWS CloudTrail is the definitive source for AWS API call records, including Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel. Each CloudTrail event includes the userIdentity block (containing the caller's IAM role ARN, account, and assumed-role session name), the event time, the API action, and the request parameters including the model ARN. Querying CloudTrail event history (for 90-day lookback) or a persistent trail delivers exactly what the security investigation requires. Option B Amazon Bedrock Model Invocation Logging captures request/response payloads and is valuable for ML observability and content auditing, but its primary purpose is not security incident investigation; critically, it may not be enabled in all accounts by default, and its log schema focuses on model I/O content, not IAM identity tracing. The question asks specifically about caller identity and request parameters in a security context, which CloudTrail covers authoritatively. Option C there is no native /aws/bedrock/ CloudWatch Logs log group for API call events; CloudWatch Logs receives application logs or service-specific operational logs, not API control-plane events, which are CloudTrail's domain. Option D AWS Config records configuration changes to AWS resources but does not capture API call events or their parameters; it tracks resource state changes, not invocation-level API call history.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: A compliance officer at a healthcare company is reviewing the responsible AI documentation for an Amazon Bedrock foundation model before approving its use in a clinical decision-support application. The officer needs to understand the model's intended use cases, evaluation results, known limitations, and potential harms. Which AWS resource provides this structured transparency documentation for Amazon Bedrock foundation models?
tags: AWS AI Service Cards and model transparency documentation
Responsible AI principles (for example, fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy, safety, robustness)
Documenting AI model capabilities, limitations, and intended use cases using model cards

answers.A: The Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation report, which is generated automatically for each foundation model and includes benchmark scores, bias measurements, and recommended use case documentation that the compliance officer can download from the AWS console.
answers.B: The AWS Well-Architected Framework Machine Learning Lens, which provides best practices for responsible AI and documents the evaluation standards AWS applies to services including Amazon Bedrock foundation models.
answers.C: AWS AI Service Cards, which AWS publishes for its AI services and foundation models available through Amazon Bedrock, providing structured documentation of intended use cases, design considerations, limitations, responsible AI design choices, and performance evaluations.
answers.D: The Amazon SageMaker Model Registry model card associated with the foundation model, which providers must populate with evaluation metrics and limitations before the model can be listed in Amazon Bedrock.

explanation: Option C is correct. AWS AI Service Cards are the formal transparency documentation published by AWS for its AI services and foundation models available through Amazon Bedrock. They follow a structured format covering intended uses, design and safety considerations, performance evaluations, known limitations, and responsible AI practices—exactly the information a compliance officer needs before approving a high-stakes clinical application. Option A Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation is a service that customers use to run their own evaluations against models; it does not automatically generate and publish vendor-level transparency documentation for the foundation models themselves. Option B the AWS Well-Architected Machine Learning Lens provides architectural guidance and best practices but does not supply model-specific transparency documentation (intended uses, limitations, evaluation results) for individual foundation models. Option D Amazon SageMaker Model Registry model cards are customer-managed artifacts that customers create for models they own and deploy; third-party foundation model providers listed in Amazon Bedrock do not populate SageMaker model cards, and AWS AI Service Cards are the official AWS-published transparency vehicle.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: An AI governance team at a bank is assembling documentation to satisfy a regulatory audit of its Amazon Bedrock-powered loan underwriting tool. The audit requires evidence of how the foundation model was evaluated for bias, what performance benchmarks were run, and what potential failure modes were identified before deployment. Which AWS-provided resource should the team consult, and what supplementary internal artifact must the team produce?
tags: AWS AI Service Cards and model transparency documentation
Responsible AI principles (for example, fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy, safety, robustness)
Amazon SageMaker Clarify for detecting bias in AI/ML models
Documenting AI model capabilities, limitations, and intended use cases using model cards

answers.A: Consult the AWS AI Service Card for the foundation model to obtain AWS's vendor-level transparency documentation, including bias evaluations and known limitations. Supplement this with an internally produced model card documenting the bank's fine-tuning datasets, custom bias evaluations using Amazon SageMaker Clarify, deployment context, and observed failure modes specific to loan underwriting.
answers.B: Consult the Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation automated evaluation report for the foundation model to retrieve benchmark scores. Supplement this with an Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor data quality report run against the production inference endpoint to document bias drift over time.
answers.C: Consult the AWS Audit Manager report for the Amazon Bedrock service, which consolidates all compliance evidence including model bias reports. Supplement this with an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard exported as a PDF showing inference latency and error rate trends.
answers.D: Consult the AWS Artifact compliance report for Amazon Bedrock, which includes third-party attestation of bias evaluations and benchmark results. Supplement this with an internally run ROUGE-L benchmark on a held-out loan decision dataset.

explanation: Option A is correct. AWS AI Service Cards are the official vendor-level transparency documentation for Amazon Bedrock foundation models, providing the bias evaluation methodology, performance benchmarks, and identified limitations that the audit requires for the model as supplied by AWS. However, an AI Service Card covers the model in its general context; the bank must also produce its own model card documenting fine-tuning decisions, the specific datasets used, domain-specific bias evaluations (appropriately run with Amazon SageMaker Clarify on loan decision outcomes), the deployment context, and failure modes observed in the bank's specific use case. Option B Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation is a customer-run evaluation service; it produces results for the customer's test cases, not vendor-level documentation of general model bias evaluation—the audit requires provenance from AWS, not just customer test results. Option C AWS Audit Manager collects evidence for compliance frameworks (SOC 2, PCI DSS, etc.) but does not publish model bias evaluations or benchmark results; it is an evidence collection tool, not a model transparency source. Option D AWS Artifact provides third-party compliance reports (SOC, PCI) and regulatory agreements for AWS services, not model-specific bias evaluation documentation; ROUGE-L is a text-generation metric not appropriate for loan underwriting decision quality evaluation.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: A content marketing team wants to automate a multi-step blog post creation pipeline. The pipeline must: (1) classify the topic of a user request, (2) retrieve relevant brand guidelines from a knowledge base, (3) generate a draft using a large language model, and (4) run a content moderation check before returning the draft. The team requires deterministic step sequencing and the ability to visually inspect and modify the pipeline without code changes. Which Amazon Bedrock feature best meets these requirements?
tags: Amazon Bedrock Flows for building deterministic generative AI workflows
Amazon Bedrock Agents configuration (for example, action groups, knowledge bases, orchestration strategy, memory)
Guardrails integration with agents for safety and compliance

answers.A: Amazon Bedrock Agents with an orchestration strategy configured to process the four steps sequentially using action groups, because agents support multi-step task decomposition and can be updated by modifying action group Lambda functions without rebuilding the agent.
answers.B: An AWS Step Functions state machine with four states (classify, retrieve, generate, moderate), each state invoking an AWS Lambda function or Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel API call, because Step Functions provides deterministic sequencing and visual workflow editing.
answers.C: An AWS Glue ETL workflow with four jobs connected in a dependency graph, because Glue provides a visual pipeline canvas and supports calling Amazon Bedrock for the generation and classification steps.
answers.D: Amazon Bedrock Flows, which allows the team to build a deterministic generative AI workflow with visual nodes for prompt processing, knowledge base retrieval, and guardrails integration, and to modify the pipeline visually in the AWS console without code changes.

explanation: Option D is correct. Amazon Bedrock Flows is purpose-built for creating deterministic, multi-step generative AI workflows using a visual node-based editor in the AWS console. It natively supports prompt nodes, knowledge base retrieval nodes, condition nodes, and guardrails integration nodes—covering all four pipeline steps (classify, retrieve, generate, moderate) without code. The visual canvas allows non-engineers to inspect and modify the pipeline. Option A Amazon Bedrock Agents use LLM-driven orchestration that is non-deterministic by design; the agent decides at runtime which action groups to invoke and in what order, which does not guarantee the strict step sequencing required. Option B AWS Step Functions satisfies determinism and has a visual editor (Workflow Studio), but it is a general-purpose orchestration service that requires Lambda functions for each Bedrock integration step—it is not a purpose-built generative AI workflow tool and requires more code than Bedrock Flows. Option C AWS Glue is an analytics and ETL service; it does not provide native Amazon Bedrock integration nodes and is not designed for generative AI pipeline orchestration.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: A company uses Amazon Bedrock Flows to orchestrate a three-step product description pipeline: (1) a prompt node that extracts product attributes, (2) a knowledge base retrieval node that fetches competitor comparisons, and (3) a generation node that produces the final description. During testing, the team notices that when the knowledge base returns zero results the generation node produces generic, ungrounded descriptions. Which modification to the Flow design best handles this conditional branch?
tags: Amazon Bedrock Flows for building deterministic generative AI workflows
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases configuration and capabilities
Implementing appropriate error handling, retry logic, and fallback behaviors for agentic workflows

answers.A: Add a retry loop in the knowledge base retrieval node configuration to re-query the knowledge base up to three times before passing results to the generation node, reducing the frequency of zero-result responses.
answers.B: Insert a condition node after the knowledge base retrieval node that checks whether the result count is zero. If zero, route to an alternative prompt node that instructs the model to produce a description from product attributes only, clearly labeled as unverified. If results exist, route to the standard generation node.
answers.C: Configure the generation node with a fallback system prompt that is automatically activated when the knowledge base retrieval node returns an empty result set, overriding the standard prompt without adding a condition node.
answers.D: Replace the knowledge base retrieval node with an Amazon Bedrock Agent action group that queries the knowledge base and implements its own fallback logic in a Lambda function, returning synthesized competitor data even when the knowledge base has no entries.

explanation: Option B is correct. Amazon Bedrock Flows supports condition nodes that evaluate expressions over the outputs of upstream nodes. Adding a condition node that checks whether the knowledge base retrieval result count equals zero allows the flow to branch: zero results go to an alternative prompt node that generates a product-attributes-only description with an appropriate disclaimer, while non-zero results continue to the standard generation node. This deterministically prevents ungrounded generic descriptions and is a native Flows capability. Option A retrying the knowledge base query when results are absent will not produce results if no relevant documents exist; the retry loop wastes latency without fixing the root cause. Option C Bedrock Flows generation nodes do not natively support per-condition fallback system prompts triggered by upstream node outputs without a condition node; this is not a supported Flows configuration. Option D replacing the knowledge base retrieval node with an agent action group introduces non-deterministic LLM orchestration (agent reasoning) into a flow that is supposed to be deterministic, and fabricating competitor data in the Lambda contradicts product integrity.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: A startup wants to build a serverless document Q&A API. Users submit a PDF document and a question via HTTPS. The API must extract text from the PDF, embed the text, retrieve relevant passages, and return an LLM-generated answer—all within a single synchronous request with a maximum end-to-end response time of 25 seconds. The team requires zero server management. Which AWS architecture best meets these requirements?
tags: Serverless architectures for generative AI applications (for example, AWS Lambda, Amazon API Gateway, Amazon Bedrock)
RAG pipeline components (for example, document ingestion, chunking, embedding, vector storage, retrieval, augmentation, generation)
Designing scalable, serverless generative AI backends using AWS Lambda, Amazon API Gateway, and Amazon Bedrock

answers.A: Use Amazon API Gateway (REST API) to accept the request, invoke an AWS Lambda function with a 25-second timeout. The Lambda function calls Amazon Textract to extract text from the PDF, calls Amazon Bedrock to embed the extracted text, performs an in-memory nearest-neighbor search over the embedded chunks, and calls Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel to generate the answer, returning it synchronously.
answers.B: Use Amazon API Gateway to accept the request, write the PDF to Amazon S3, publish an event to Amazon SQS, and return a job ID to the caller. A separate Lambda function polls SQS, performs the extraction, retrieval, and generation pipeline, and writes the answer to Amazon DynamoDB. The client polls a status endpoint until the answer is available.
answers.C: Deploy the extraction, embedding, retrieval, and generation logic as an AWS Fargate container behind an Application Load Balancer. Use Amazon ECR to store the container image and configure Fargate auto scaling to handle concurrent requests, eliminating Lambda timeout constraints.
answers.D: Use Amazon API Gateway with a Lambda integration where Lambda calls AWS Step Functions Express Workflow synchronously. The workflow orchestrates Textract, Amazon Bedrock embedding, vector search in Amazon OpenSearch Service Serverless, and Amazon Bedrock generation, completing within the 25-second synchronous execution window.

explanation: Option A is correct. A fully serverless architecture using Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda with a 25-second timeout satisfies all constraints: zero server management, synchronous response, and the 25-second SLA. Lambda can call Amazon Textract synchronously for text extraction, use Amazon Bedrock's embedding API to embed chunks, perform in-memory cosine similarity search over the small per-request chunk set, and call Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel for generation—all within a single Lambda invocation. This requires no persistent vector store because the document is user-submitted per request and the chunk count is small enough for in-memory search. Option B uses an asynchronous polling pattern that does not return a synchronous response, violating the requirement for a single synchronous request/response flow. Option C AWS Fargate is not serverless from a management perspective; it requires container image management, ALB configuration, and auto-scaling policies—it contradicts the zero server management requirement. Option D while Step Functions Express Workflows do support synchronous execution and the workflow would work functionally, adding a Step Functions layer introduces additional latency (state machine initialization overhead) and cost for what can be accomplished in a single Lambda invocation; it also requires managing the OpenSearch Serverless collection, which adds operational complexity beyond zero server management.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: A media company builds a serverless real-time subtitling assistant backed by Amazon Bedrock. An Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API receives audio chunks from broadcast clients, invokes an AWS Lambda function for each chunk, and the Lambda function calls Amazon Transcribe for speech-to-text, then passes the transcript to Amazon Bedrock for caption enhancement. During peak broadcasts, Lambda concurrency reaches its account limit and callers receive throttling errors. Which architecture change reduces throttling with the least operational overhead?
tags: Serverless architectures for generative AI applications (for example, AWS Lambda, Amazon API Gateway, Amazon Bedrock)
Asynchronous invocation patterns for long-running generative AI tasks
Designing scalable, serverless generative AI backends using AWS Lambda, Amazon API Gateway, and Amazon Bedrock

answers.A: Replace the WebSocket API with an Amazon API Gateway REST API and implement HTTP long polling from broadcast clients so that each client maintains only one open connection, reducing the number of concurrent Lambda invocations during peak broadcasts.
answers.B: Deploy an Amazon ECS cluster running the Transcribe and Bedrock integration logic as a container service, remove Lambda from the path, and route WebSocket messages directly to the ECS tasks via an Application Load Balancer, eliminating Lambda concurrency limits.
answers.C: Place an Amazon SQS queue between the API Gateway WebSocket Lambda (which enqueues audio chunk events) and a separate processing Lambda (which polls SQS, calls Transcribe, and calls Bedrock). Configure the processing Lambda's reserved concurrency to stay below the account limit and set SQS batch size to buffer bursts, smoothing the processing rate.
answers.D: Request a Lambda concurrency limit increase from AWS Support to match the maximum expected peak concurrency, and configure Lambda Provisioned Concurrency for the function to eliminate cold starts during broadcast spikes.

explanation: Option C is correct. Inserting an Amazon SQS queue decouples the high-frequency inbound WebSocket events from the processing Lambda that calls Amazon Transcribe and Amazon Bedrock. The WebSocket Lambda only enqueues a small message (the audio chunk reference), which is very fast and requires minimal concurrency. The processing Lambda polls SQS with event source mapping, and its reserved concurrency cap smooths the throughput to stay within account limits while SQS buffers the burst. This is a standard serverless backpressure pattern that requires no infrastructure management. Option A switching from WebSocket to REST with long polling changes the client architecture substantially (breaking real-time requirements) and does not fundamentally reduce the number of concurrent Lambda invocations processing the same volume of audio chunks. Option B deploying an ECS cluster requires container management, load balancer configuration, and auto-scaling setup—significantly more operational overhead than adding an SQS queue, contradicting the 'least operational overhead' requirement. Option D requesting a concurrency limit increase addresses the immediate ceiling but does not provide backpressure or burst smoothing; during sustained peak beyond the new limit, throttling recurs, and provisioned concurrency reduces cold starts but does not increase the concurrency ceiling.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: A software company wants to automate code review using a multi-agent Amazon Bedrock system. A supervisor agent receives a GitHub pull request diff and must dispatch subtasks to: a style-check sub-agent (verifying code style), a security-review sub-agent (identifying vulnerabilities), and a test-coverage sub-agent (checking coverage). All three sub-agents must complete before the supervisor synthesizes a final review. The company requires that all inter-agent communication remain within AWS without custom orchestration code. Which Amazon Bedrock capability supports this pattern natively?
tags: Multi-agent collaboration patterns and orchestration with Amazon Bedrock
Agentic AI workflows and multi-agent orchestration
Amazon Bedrock Agents configuration (for example, action groups, knowledge bases, orchestration strategy, memory)
Designing multi-agent systems with supervisor and sub-agent patterns

answers.A: Amazon Bedrock multi-agent collaboration, where the supervisor agent is configured with the three sub-agents registered as named collaborators. The supervisor's foundation model routes subtasks to each collaborator, collects their responses, and synthesizes the final review—all managed by the Bedrock runtime without custom orchestration code.
answers.B: Amazon Bedrock Flows with three parallel prompt nodes for style, security, and coverage checks, a join node that aggregates the three outputs, and a final generation node for the supervisor's synthesis—enabling parallel execution within a deterministic flow without custom code.
answers.C: Three separate Amazon Bedrock Agents invoked sequentially by an AWS Lambda function using the Bedrock Agents runtime API. Lambda collects each agent's response and passes it as context to the next agent, culminating in a final synthesis call to the supervisor agent.
answers.D: An Amazon Bedrock Agent with three action groups, one for each review domain, where each action group invokes a separate AWS Lambda function that runs the style, security, and coverage checks and returns results to the supervisor agent's orchestration loop.

explanation: Option A is correct. Amazon Bedrock's native multi-agent collaboration feature allows a supervisor agent to register sub-agents as collaborators and delegate subtasks to them. The Bedrock runtime manages the inter-agent communication, waits for all collaborator responses, and passes them back to the supervisor for synthesis—no custom orchestration code required. This is the native AWS solution for supervisor/sub-agent patterns within Amazon Bedrock. Option B Amazon Bedrock Flows parallel nodes execute prompt nodes or knowledge base nodes in parallel; however, Flows do not natively host other Amazon Bedrock Agents as sub-nodes—the parallel nodes process LLM prompts or retrieve from knowledge bases, not orchestrate independent agents with their own reasoning loops. Option C sequential Lambda-based invocations add custom orchestration code, which the requirement explicitly prohibits, and sequential execution wastes time when all three reviews could proceed concurrently. Option D a single agent with three action groups keeps all reasoning in one agent context—it does not instantiate three independent specialist agents with separate reasoning contexts; the style, security, and coverage checks are performed by Lambda functions, not by reasoning agents, reducing the depth of analysis available.

exam: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
stem: A customer experience team builds a real-time chat interface powered by Amazon Bedrock. Users expect to see tokens streaming to the browser as they are generated, without waiting for the full response. The backend uses AWS Lambda and Amazon API Gateway. The current implementation buffers the complete Bedrock response in Lambda before returning it, causing a perceived delay of 8 to 12 seconds. Which architectural change enables true token-level streaming to the browser with the least operational overhead?
tags: Streaming inference and real-time response patterns
Serverless architectures for generative AI applications (for example, AWS Lambda, Amazon API Gateway, Amazon Bedrock)
Implementing streaming response patterns using Amazon Bedrock's streaming API and Amazon API Gateway WebSocket APIs

answers.A: Replace Amazon API Gateway with an Application Load Balancer fronting a containerized Node.js server on AWS Fargate. The Node.js server uses the Amazon Bedrock InvokeModelWithResponseStream API and pipes the token stream directly to the browser over a persistent HTTP/2 connection.
answers.B: Keep the existing REST API. Modify the Lambda function to call Amazon Bedrock InvokeModelWithResponseStream, store each token chunk in Amazon ElastiCache for Redis as it arrives, and have the browser poll a separate REST endpoint every 200 ms to fetch accumulated tokens from the cache.
answers.C: Replace the REST API with an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API. The Lambda function calls Amazon Bedrock InvokeModelWithResponseStream, iterates over the streaming response chunks, and sends each chunk back to the browser connection using the API Gateway Management API's PostToConnection method.
answers.D: Keep the REST API. Enable Amazon API Gateway response streaming for the Lambda integration and update the Lambda function to return a chunked transfer encoding response, forwarding Bedrock token chunks as they arrive through the API Gateway streaming buffer.

explanation: Option C is correct. Amazon API Gateway WebSocket APIs maintain a persistent bidirectional connection between the browser and the backend. The Lambda function invokes Amazon Bedrock's InvokeModelWithResponseStream API, which returns an async stream of token chunks. For each chunk, Lambda calls the API Gateway Management API PostToConnection to push the chunk directly to the browser over the open WebSocket—achieving true token-level streaming with no polling, no additional infrastructure, and no container management. Option A using Fargate and an ALB achieves the streaming goal but requires container management, ECR image maintenance, and ALB configuration, adding significant operational overhead compared to the serverless WebSocket approach. Option B polling every 200 ms is not true streaming—it introduces visible latency between tokens and generates high API call volume; ElastiCache also adds infrastructure management overhead. Option D Amazon API Gateway REST API does not support true server-sent streaming where the server pushes chunks as they are generated; standard Lambda proxy integrations buffer the response until Lambda returns, which is the exact problem being solved. While Lambda response streaming exists as a feature, it requires specific function URL configuration or streaming-enabled integrations, not the standard API Gateway REST proxy integration described.

stem: A research institute publishes a 90 TB genomics dataset in Amazon S3 for approved university teams. The institute must keep paying for storage, but each university must pay for its own downloads and requests. The teams access the objects directly from their own AWS accounts. Which solution meets these requirements with the least operational overhead?
tags: Access options (for example, an S3 bucket with Requester Pays object storage)

answers.A: Create a CloudFront distribution for the bucket and require each university to use signed URLs issued from its own AWS account.
answers.B: Enable Requester Pays on the S3 bucket and grant the approved AWS accounts permission to read the required objects.
answers.C: Copy the dataset into one S3 bucket per university account and use S3 Batch Operations to refresh changed objects weekly.
answers.D: Use AWS Data Exchange to create a private product and require each university to subscribe before downloading objects.

explanation: Option B is correct because S3 Requester Pays keeps storage charges with the bucket owner while charging authenticated requesters for requests and data transfer. Option A centralizes delivery through the institute account, so requester billing is not achieved. Option C duplicates storage and creates synchronization overhead. Option D can distribute datasets commercially, but it adds marketplace workflow and is not the least operational approach for direct S3 account-based access.

stem: A media company stores large reference video files in Amazon S3. External production vendors in separate AWS accounts download different subsets several times a month. The company wants vendors to pay download-related S3 costs while the company retains ownership and lifecycle control of the source objects. What should a solutions architect recommend?
tags: Access options (for example, an S3 bucket with Requester Pays object storage)

answers.A: Enable Requester Pays on the source bucket and use bucket policies to allow only the approved vendor account principals.
answers.B: Create one CloudFront key group per vendor and configure signed cookies for downloads from the source bucket.
answers.C: Replicate approved objects to vendor-owned S3 buckets and expire the replicas with lifecycle rules after 30 days.
answers.D: Create presigned URLs from an IAM role in the company account and send the URLs to each vendor for download.

explanation: Option A is correct because Requester Pays is designed for authenticated requesters to pay S3 request and transfer charges while the bucket owner keeps control of the objects. Option B controls access through CloudFront but does not shift S3 requester charges to vendor accounts. Option C can move costs but duplicates data and requires per-vendor replication management. Option D grants temporary access from the owner account and keeps billing tied to the company account.

stem: A retail application uses Amazon RDS for MySQL. Storage grows unpredictably during seasonal promotions, but the team wants to avoid emergency storage changes and does not want to overprovision for the annual peak. Downtime for storage expansion is not acceptable. Which configuration best meets these requirements?
tags: Determining when storage auto scaling is required
Database capacity planning (for example, capacity units, instance types, Provisioned IOPS)

answers.A: Create a larger RDS read replica before each promotion and promote the replica if free storage drops below the threshold.
answers.B: Schedule an AWS Lambda function to increase allocated RDS storage by a fixed amount every Friday during promotions.
answers.C: Enable RDS storage autoscaling and set a maximum storage threshold that supports the expected seasonal peak.
answers.D: Migrate the database to Amazon EC2 with LVM volumes and extend the filesystem when CloudWatch alarms trigger.
